Forgive Us Our Trespasses

by thetalee

Summary

Buck can only hope, after how awful the year previous was, that the new year will be better. He has a clean bill of health, and he gets to do the job he loves, even if he isn't doing it at the 118 any more. But the world is about to go to hell around him, and it's another Buckley sibling's turn to have an uninvited ghost intrude back in their lives.

Notes

Hello again, all. I just want it to be known that I was not originally going to do a full rewrite of anything past the season 3 Christmas episode, but here we are!

Here's the requisite playlist. Enjoy.

See the end of the work for more notes

Chapter 1

The exam room was chilly, and the hospital gown was breezy. Buck sat on the bed, the paper covering wrinkling beneath him as he swung his legs. He was excited and anxious: a few days ago, he’d gone in so they could remove the rod and screws that were put in to help his leg bones heal correctly. He’d stopped taking the blood thinners in preparation for it, and hadn’t started them back since.

He would either be leaving the hospital with really good news today, or absolutely crushed.

The doctor who had been overseeing everything with Buck’s recovery, Dr. Wright, was examining the most recent x-rays of his leg. The man’s face wasn’t giving away any of his thoughts, and Buck’s anxiety was starting getting incrementally worse as he craned his neck to see the images for himself. It was a bunch of pictures of his leg bones, looking significantly less like a jigsaw puzzle than they were nearly a year ago.

“The bone has fused nicely where the screws were,” the doctor finally said with a nod. He tapped on one of the images. “And there’s minimal scar tissue.”

“I- I feel good, Doc,” Buck said. “I abseiled down an elevator shaft the other day, and there wasn’t a twinge. Not even when I had to kick the emergency hatch open.”

“That’s good, just be sure you’re not doing anything too over the top with it. I don’t want to be operating on you again.”

“I make no promises,” he joked, and then asked, “What about the clots?”

That was the most important part, what all his nerves were caught on. If they were still there, if he had to be on the blood thinners forever, if they never found out the cause…

“Scans are clear,” Dr. Wright told him. Buck felt like he deflated with the relief of it. “There’s been no sign of clots since we took you off the blood thinners. I think we can confidently say that those screws were the source of your problem.”

“So they’re gone?” Buck asked, hand moving to clutch his thigh. “No screws, no more clots?”

“They’re gone,” the doctor confirmed. “No more clots.”

It felt like a giant weight being lifted off of Buck’s shoulders, one he hadn’t realized had gotten so heavy. He’d grown up knowing, being repeatedly told by his mother, that he was born with a very specific purpose: to make his brother better, if he ever got sick again. And he knew, no matter what he did or how badly he screwed up, that he was always good for that. At least until the embolism. People who’d had a deep vein thrombosis couldn’t donate blood marrow, not as long as they didn’t know the cause.

But they knew the cause, they’d removed the cause. If Danny had another cancer scare, there’d be no reason for worry. Buck could fix it again, just like he was supposed to.

“Mr. Buckley,” Dr. Wright said, “it is my pleasure to give you a clean bill of health. So go get dressed and get out of here.”

“Thank you, for everything,” Buck said, hopping off the bed. “Um, no offense, but I hope I never see you again.”

“Hey, you never know.”

“Really?” Buck gave the laughing man a flat stare.

When he was once again dressed in actual clothes, he stepped out into the waiting room. Danny got to his feet and met him halfway, looking as anxious now as Buck had felt earlier. His brother’s eyes ran over him, checking him over for any sign that things might’ve gone wrong.

“Well?” Danny asked. “What did the doctor say?”

“Clean bill of health,” Buck answered with a broad smile. “No clots.”

“But what about your leg? Everything good?”

“That’s what the doctor said.”

“Good.” He flung an arm around Buck’s shoulders. “I’d take you out somewhere to celebrate, but…”

“Yeah, I get it. You’re gonna be cutting it close as is.”

Danny just shrugged, as if it didn’t matter to him whether or not he made it to his therapy appointment on time. Buck wasn’t sure how he felt about his brother seeing a therapist, he couldn’t tell if it was helping or not. Oftentimes his brother would come back to the apartment, quiet and a little moody, but there’d been more than one day that he didn’t come back at all. Buck figured he was going to Austin’s on those days.

What he did know was that the thought of going to see a therapist himself made his skin crawl.

“We’ll go somewhere on our next day off,” Danny said as he led them both to the stairs. “Wait, no, all of you are going out for Chimney’s birthday.”

In actuality, today was Chimney’s birthday, but the man’s day was all booked up. Something about visiting the Lees, and then dinner with Maddie. Buck wasn’t entirely certain, he just knew the man was too busy to spend his actual birthday with friends. But that was fine, because he had plans of his own.

“You could come too, y’know,” Buck pointed out.

“Can’t,” Danny said. “It’s scheduled for the same day as me and Michael’s support group.”

Buck couldn’t help the snort of laughter. Their “support group” consisted entirely of just the two of them, and he knew for a fact their time together was spent drinking. Probably more than was strictly advisable for a man going through radiation in the hopes of killing a brain tumor, but Buck didn’t have a medical degree and so his opinions were invalid. Or so he’d been told by his drunk brother the one time he brought it up, except with more colorful phrasing.

Once he was back at the apartment, his brother taking off again almost as soon as he was inside the building, Buck started getting ready for that evening. Not that there was much he needed to do to get ready, but he still wanted to look his best. A run through the shower, followed by the requisite primping in front of the mirror and then tugging on clothes that weren’t fancy, but also weren't obviously the first things he dragged out of his closet.

The problem with living in Los Angeles is that, at certain times of day, a person had to add at least an hour to travel times. Plus, Buck had to make a stop on the way, so that was more time added. Traffic simply sucked if you weren’t driving ten tons of engine with sirens. It meant that, when he finally pulled the jeep to a stop in front of Eddie’s house, it felt like he’d been on the road for forever.

Buck grabbed the flowers he bought from the passenger seat and hopped out, jogging up the sidewalk to the front door. He had a key to let himself in, just like Eddie did for the apartment, but there was something about picking the other up for a date that always had them knocking at the door. Not that they’d had much opportunities for dates in the last couple of months: Eddie had picked up extra shifts to help pay for a new truck.

It was Carla who answered the door when he knocked.

“Well don’t you just look handsome,” she teased with a smile, stepping aside to let him in. “Eddie! Your boy is here!”

There were heavy footsteps coming down the hall, along with giggling. Eddie rounded the corner, Chris thrown over his shoulder like a bag of flour, legs kicking in the air. Buck watched his boyfriend light up at the sight of him.

“Hey!” Eddie bent over a little, carefully dropping Chris onto the couch. Buck took the moment to appreciate the jeans that Eddie was wearing, and the way they fit on him. He wasn’t very subtle about it, either: Carla let out a snort and smacked him on the arm. “I hope I’m dressed okay, you haven’t exactly told me where we’re going.”

“It’s just dinner and a movie.” Buck thrust the flowers at him. “Here.”

Eddie’s smile went soft as he took the flowers from him. It had been awkward the first time Buck gave him flowers, because Shannon had obviously never done it and Eddie grew up with all of Helena and Ramon’s particular views on masculinity being dripped into his ears. Even now, he still didn’t look like he knew quite how to handle it.

“Thank you,” Eddie whispered, leaning in to kiss him. “Carla, where’s…?”

“In the cabinet, I’ll go get it,” the home aid said, flapping her hand at him and shuffling off to the kitchen. 

“You had your doctor’s appointment today, right? How did that go?”

“Clean bill of health,” Buck told him, thumping at his thigh with his fist. “No screws, no clots. No more coughing up blood in people’s backyard.”

“And we’re very thankful for that,” Eddie said. “Right, Chris?”

“Right!” Chris bobbed his head where he sat.

“Here we go.” Carla bustled back in with a vase half-full of water and a pair of scissors. She sat the vase down on the table behind the couch, and took the flowers from Eddie to first cut off the ends and then put them into the case. “Well go on, you two. No point waiting around here. Go get your romance on.”

Eddie tossed his head back with a laugh.

“Alright, Carla,” he said. “Chris, you be good.”

“Okay, Dad.”

“Don’t you worry about a thing,” Carla told them both. “Stay out as long as you like.”

Buck wondered how much of that was because she remembered all of his and Abby’s failed dates, interrupted or simply canceled because of Abby’s mom. He knew that she felt bad for it, but as much as she wanted Abby to have a life outside of her sick mother, Patricia’s well-being had been Carla’s priority. Just like Chris’ well-being was her priority now. If Chris needed his father this evening, then she wouldn’t hesitate to interrupt this date, either. But thankfully, it wasn’t as likely to happen.

The place they were eating at before the movie was chosen for a couple reasons. One of them was that it was close to the theater, so they wouldn’t be pressed for time. But the biggest, most important reason, was that Buck was a little shit and knew how his boyfriend would react to it.

Eddie was talking when they pulled into the parking lot, not really paying attention. Not until the jeep was parked and he looked out the windshield to see the Denny’s sign looming above them. He sat in the passenger seat in silence for a moment, simply staring, and then he turned and punched Buck in the bicep. Hard.

“You asshole,” he said, though the laughter took quite a bit of the heat from the words. “This is where we’re eating?”

“I was feeling nostalgic,” Buck told him. “‘Sides, we got interrupted last time.”

His boyfriend rolled his eyes and hopped out, heading for the entrance. Buck hurried to join him, grabbing his hand when he caught up and obnoxiously swinging both their arms in exaggerated motions until Eddie tugged him hard enough to almost pull him off his feet. They got inside and got seated, their legs intertwining beneath the table.

“Should I even ask what we’re going to see?” Eddie asked as he looked through the laminated menu.

“There’s that horror movie out that I was wanting to see,” Buck said, and then threw him a grin. “Unless that’s too scary for you.”

“I will call an Uber right now.”

Buck threw his head back and laughed.

“I’ll stop teasing,” he promised. His boyfriend shot him a look of utter disbelief. “Okay, so, tell me about that call yesterday. Y’know, the one with the skydiver.”

“I had to stand on top of the engine as we sped down the runway…”

After two months, Daniel still wasn’t certain if therapy was entirely worth it. He’d purposefully gone out of his way to find someone that didn’t work with the department, because while he knew that doctor/patient confidentiality was a thing, he didn’t actually trust that one of the department therapists - like Frank - wouldn’t decide to go squealing to someone. Hell, he didn’t know if he trusted this one not to do something like that.

One thing this Dr. White had going for her was that she wasn’t easily flustered. Early on, Daniel got annoyed with her and her questions about him and about growing up. He just blurted out the fact that used to sell his body for money, part of him hoping for some sort of reaction. Except she just raised an eyebrow, and then asked how that got started.

She’d also, within a couple sessions, start bandying about acronyms and labels. Apparently, being antisocial was considered a personality disorder. Who knew? And when he talked about Buck, about the fact that his baby brother was made for him and that meant Daniel had a duty of care, when he told her that Buck was why he packed up and moved states twice, that had her getting out questionnaires for him to take the next time he saw her.

Mostly, though, the few sessions they’d had together were spent talking about either the last year or his time in El Paso. The former was fine, he could talk about watching Buck beneath the truck and watching him cough up blood and how Daniel lost basically a whole day when he thought his brother was gone forever. And sure, okay, she was yet another person casting judgment on him for tearing Nash a new one, not that he particularly needed that, nor was ever going to apologize for it.

Talking about El Paso, though, was a crapshoot. If they stuck to the topics of Buck and Eddie and Alma, or getting into firefighting, or most of the johns and janes he saw, it was fine. But sometimes they’d get onto a subject that he would very much not like to talk about, thanks, but Dr. White would just keep picking and picking until he did.

That eventually had the good doctor throwing out yet another acronym, one that Daniel loudly scoffed at. He did not have PTSD, complex or otherwise, thanks very much.

He never went back to the apartment after those particular sessions, whether Buck was there or not. Especially if he knew Buck was home. On those days, he would leave Dr. White’s office with the incessant urge to snap at everyone around him, and the need to go hide somewhere. He almost always ended up at Austin’s, instead.

When Daniel let himself in, Austin was wiping down the counter in the kitchen while on the phone with… Someone, Daniel didn’t know and didn’t particularly care at the moment. He stumbled across to the couch, toeing off his shoes and tossing his jacket in the corner before letting himself flop down onto it. There was one of Austin’s sweaters hanging over the arm, threadbare with a hole near the bottom hem. Daniel didn’t really think about it as he grabbed the thing and pulled it on, tugging the collar of it to his face as he did his best to bury himself between the couch cushion and the black-gray-white-purple striped throw pillow.

He listened - his eyes were closed, and his face was pressed into the couch - as Austin moved about in the kitchen, talking to… Daniel was fairly certain it was his brother, Ethan. There was a different flavor of teasing that Austin used when talking to him, compared to when he talked to his sister. For a while, Daniel just laid there and breathed and listened, drifting off a little, until Austin finished up the phone call. Then there was the sound of a cabinet being opened and closed, before soft footsteps that padded to the couch and came to a stop beside.

“Here.” Austin’s voice had him lifting his head, enough to see the man was kneeling beside the couch. He was holding up a resealable bag of Skittles; Daniel didn’t hesitate to snag it from him. “Difficult day?”

Daniel didn’t answer right away. He, instead, tore open the bag and dug out one of the colorful pieces of candy, held it between his fingers as he looked at it.

“We talked about Officer Drake,” he finally said, popping the piece into his mouth,

“Oh.”

Officer Drake was one of the things he did not like talking about when it came to El Paso. Austin knew a little, Alma knew more. Buck knew nothing about him, hopefully didn’t even know the man existed; Daniel had put up with a lot to make sure it stayed that way. He didn’t see the point in talking about him now, ‘cause the guy was all the way in Texas. He was yesterday’s problem.

Not that Dr. White had seemed to agree with that statement.

“She keeps trying to give me labels.” Daniel spat the word out. “Now she thinks I have PTSD.”

“Well,” Austin said. “You did freak out the one time Attica brought out the handcuffs to play with.”

“Why did I even tell you about that?” he whined.

“You were drunk and I am a good listener,” the other man said, before standing up. “I’m gonna cook dinner. You good here?”

“Yeah.” Daniel nodded, setting the bag of skittles on the end table before flopping face first into the couch cushion again.

He heard Austin walk away, and then a door open somewhere deeper in the apartment. A few moments later, Austin was back and laying a blanket over him. Daniel was almost positive it was the comforter from Austin’s own bed. Neither of them said anything as Daniel pulled the blanket up to cover his face, so he could better hide from the world for a bit longer.

Not for the first time, he ended up falling asleep on Austin’s couch.

Chimney, in Eddie’s opinion, was not acting quite like someone excited to celebrate his birthday. Sure, okay, technically it was past his birthday, but the guy got cake today. Very good cake, actually. He’d sent pictures of it to Buck, just to be a little shit, and got a series of crying emojis in response.

“Hey, Chim.” Bobby was at the kitchen island, reboxing the leftover cake. “You mind if I take some of this home for Harry and May?”

“Sure,” Chimney said. He’d been moodily poking at his slice with his fork rather than eating it. Even Hen, who’d been utterly absorbed with whatever the hell she was doing on her laptop, managed to devour her portion. “Knock yourself out.”

“Thank you.”

“How’re they doing, anyway?” Eddie asked, half-turned in his seat to face Bobby.

“Well, Michael’s upbeat and fighting,” the captain answered.

“Oh, I know how upbeat he is. I accidentally went over one night when he and Danny were having their support group.” Read: getting very drunk together. “But what about the kids?”

“I think Harry’s okay, but I’m more worried about May. She’s got a better understanding of what’s going on.”

“That’s ‘cause older siblings don’t have the luxury of blissful ignorance,” Chimney said. Eddie furrowed his brow and turned around to look at the man. “They understand the truth, even if they don’t want to.”

Oh, yeah, Eddie was fairly certain he knew the problem here, now.

“Buck likes to joke that the younger siblings get all the brains,” he said. Behind him, Bobby let out a laugh, and Eddie realized he didn’t know where the captain fell when it came to older or younger siblings. “I take it you’re not gonna agree with that any more than me.”

Chimney lifted his head to frown at him in confusion.

“How did you…?”

“Maddie told Buck who told me, obviously,” Eddie told him, and then turned to Bobby to say, “His brother Albert is in town.”

“Albert is my younger half- brother from Korea,” Chimney clarified. “He just showed up on my doorstep. Not quite the birthday surprise I was expecting.”

“You could’ve had a worse surprise,” Eddie said, thinking back to his and Buck’s 18th birthdays.

“When do we get to meet him?” Bobby asked.

“Well, that doesn’t really seem necessary,” Chimney hedged. “He’s gonna be leaving soon, anyways. My dad insisted on it.”

“Oh, c’mon, man. He’s your brother," Eddie said, smacking him lightly on the arm. “You can get to know him.”

“It just feels weird to me. Sure, we share some of the same DNA, but he’s still practically a stranger to me.”

“I keep telling you.” Hen, done with whatever she was doing, came to join them. She had a folder, from which she pulled out sheets of paper to hand out. “Family comes to us in different ways, lean into it. And don’t think you’re sending him away without meeting all of us. I know you.”

“Uh.” Eddie held up the paper he was given. Paper s actually, because Hen had given him three as opposed to Chimney and Bobby’s one. “What is this?”

“Talking points regarding Henrietta and Karen Wilson,” Bobby read off.

“Social services is vetting Karen and me to become foster parents,” Hen explained. “We listed each and every one of you as references, as well as Buck and Dan-”

“You listed Danny as a reference?” Eddie flipped through the sheets, skimming through the bullet points.

“Yes, so make sure he and Buck get a copy of that, because I need you all to sing our praises when they call.”

“These specific twenty-six praises?”

“Karen made the list. She is very thorough.”

She looked, and sounded, so damn fond of her wife at that moment.

“Hen, we know you,” Bobby told her. “We don’t need some piece of paper to remind us of your many wonderful qualities.”

“I appreciate that, Cap, but I’d rather you didn’t improvise,” Hen said. “The stakes are very high.”

She did a look around, clearly making sure they all had a copy, before going off with a final,

“Memorize, people!”

“I guess we have homework,” Eddie said, keeping his voice low. “Joy.”

Chimney let out a grunt that he chose to assume was in agreement.

Chapter 2

Chapter Notes

I just want to use this space here to brag how, way back in May, in Yesterday's Ghosts, I came up with Buck playing tight end in football.
(the writers most definitely came up with it for the same obvious reason i did.)

Chimney mightn’t have appreciated his younger half-brother showing up in his life, but Albert was alright in Eddie’s opinion. They were having some downtime after a call involving someone being partially eviscerated with a bulldozer, Chimney and Hen not yet returned from transporting the patient to the hospital, when Albert showed up. He was endearingly awkward at first and despite there being only a handful of years between them, Eddie couldn’t help but feel that it might as well have been an eternity. He was pretty much just a kid, in a way that Eddie didn’t remember being allowed to be at that age.

That awkwardness melted away as they got to know him better, until Albert was fitting right in, talking and joking. He was very interested in hearing about his big brother, happily soaking up the stories that the others offered up. Even Austin, the usually silent and reserved man, threw in one or two. And at one point, while Bobby was cooking, Albert cheerfully gave him a tutorial on how to make Korean dumplings.

The paramedics returned just as they’d finished setting the dining table and were sitting down, the timing not at all a coincidence - one of them had texted Bobby to say they were almost back. The pair were in high spirits, Chimney calling out to them as they crested the top of the stairs.

“Okay, guys! Grossest cases to talk about while we eat, we’ll go first…”

Chimney trailed off as they came to a stop, eyes caught on the sight of his brother sitting with them.

“Hey, bro!” Albert gave him a wave.

“What are you doing here?”

“I wanted to see you, see where you work,” the younger man said with a shrug. “Your captain said you were on the way back from the hospital. I, uh. I heard you saved a man’s life.”

“Yeah, we don’t really talk about that stuff here,” Chimney told him, and then shot Austin a glare when the man didn’t even bother smothering his laughter. “You can’t really show up without calling.”

“Man, Buck and I would go over and bother Danny at his old station all the time,” Eddie said, with a careless flap of the wrist. “And Albert here gave Cap a recipe for Korean dumplings.”

“Who are Buck and Danny?” Albert asked, tilting his head a little.

“Maddie’s brothers.”

“Oh.” The kid nodded. “Well, I grew up watching my mother make mandu every other day. The best thing is she can freeze ‘em in bulk, pop ‘em in a pan, and boom. Lunch.”

“I will keep that in mind,” Bobby said from where he sat at the other end of the table.

“Even better, I snack on them at ball games.”

Eddie perked up at that.

“You like baseball?” he asked.

“Very much,” Albert confirmed with a nod.

“I used to play back in high school. We should go to a game together, we can drag Buck along.”

“He’s probably not gonna be here that long,” Chimney cut in. He did not, once Eddie actually took stock of him, seem like he was pleased with either his brother being here, or his brother being here and getting along with all of them.

Hen scoffed and smacked him in the stomach, going over to properly greet Albert.

“Hi, I’m Hen.” She sat down in the empty chair beside him. “Your brother’s long-time bestie.”

“It is a pleasure to meet you,” Albert said with a smile.

Hen glanced up, to where Chimney was still standing, When Eddie followed her gaze, he saw the man roll his eyes before stomping past to grab a seat by Bobby.

“I’m sure you have a lot of questions about your brother,” Hen said.

“Yeah, I do. Do you know why they call him Chimney?”

Hen grimaced.

“A question that isn’t that one,” she said. “You’re too young.”

Buck wasn’t exactly the biggest fan of karaoke. Sure, he had a whole routine down when it came to singing Eye of the Tiger, but that was less about impressing people with his (poor) singing skills and more about showing off with one-armed push-ups. Chimney, though, did enjoy karaoke, hence why they were at a karaoke bar for his birthday.

Not that Chimney seemed to be enjoying himself or anything. Ever since he showed up with Maddie, in the middle of Hen and Albert’s actually kinda good duet, he’d been a bit of a Debbie Downer. Even now, while they were entertaining themselves with a game of pool and getting to know Albert a bit more - or at all, in Buck’s case - Chimney was sitting off to the side with Maddie. Honestly, he seemed to be sulking a bit while he drank, not that Buck could figure out why.

Younger brothers were gifts, non-refundable ones at that, and Chimney should be considering himself blessed. Obviously, not all younger brothers could be as awesome as Buck, but he wasn’t gonna hold that against Albert. Especially since they did have a bit in common, sorta kinda. Like fleeing from home, and parents, to get some breathing room.

“I get it,” Buck said. He watched as Eddie leaned over the pool table to line up and take his shot, eyes trailing over him. His boyfriend caught him, smirked, and stretched a bit further than was probably necessary before straightening up. “Sometimes you gotta put a little mileage between yourself and home so you can figure out what you want and who you are. Or, sometimes, a relationship goes so sour you flee the state. And the country.”

Eddie, having rounded the table to take his next shot, glowered at him. Buck grinned in response.

“I don’t know what I’d have done if I hadn’t enlisted,” Eddie said. “Probably be working with my pops.”

“Nah, you’d have gotten into firefighting sooner,” Buck said.

Eddie tilted his head in thought, and then shrugged. He also didn’t argue the point.

“Please don’t encourage him to go off to war,” Maddie scolded.

“There is as much virtue to the noble warrior as there is to the most enlightened of scholars,” Albert said.

“That.” Eddie was grinning like an idiot and pointing at the younger man. “What he said.”

Buck’s boyfriend was adorable. To make his feelings about that clear, he went over and kissed him. Because he could. And because Eddie was successfully getting over his reticence to public displays of affection with Buck, melting into it now rather than stiffening up with nerves like he would just months prior.

“Okay, you’ve had your ten seconds!” Maddie crowed, popping their bubble. “Break it up.”

Buck blew a raspberry at her.

“Listen, everyone has their path,” Hen said, even as she chuckled at their antics. “You just do you, Albert.”

“I will,” Albert declared with a firm nod. “I will do me.”

Buck and Eddie burst out in laughter.

“You, uh, you might want to watch your phrasing there, buddy,” Buck said.

“Says the guy who, on our birthday, tried to show off his Spanish and told Tia Pepa that he had sixteen anuses,” Eddie teased.

Buck squawked and punched him in the arm, making him screw up his shot, while everyone else laughed. It even got Chimney to break out of his funk enough to snicker.

“I just need a little of my brother’s courage,” Albert said. It was his turn so he rounded the table, going to the side that Chimney and Maddie were sitting at, for his shot. “You know, he did not let Father dictate his life. He took a stand, got out. Came to America to follow his dreams.”

That wasn’t actually the way Buck heard it happened, but he opted not to say anything as Albert took his shot. Chimney was staring at his brother’s back, a strange expression on his face. It made something in Buck’s stomach twist with unease.

“There was no stand,” Chimney said, finally breaking his prolonged silence. He set his drink on the railing behind him. “I didn’t get out, I was left behind.”

“Chim,” Maddie tried, placing her hand on his shoulder.

Chimney pulled away from her.

“See,” he said, “most of my life, all I wanted was for him to see me, to be proud of me, be proud to call me his son. But no matter what I did, I was always invisible. Because you are the only son that he cares about. You have all his attention, all his love, and you just walked away from it all. Which I guess is easy for you, because you’ve never had to work for it.”

Buck looked to Maddie, to see if she was going to do anything to reel her boyfriend back in. Her expression was one of misery, embarrassment, and resignation. Also, maybe, a bit of sympathy. Buck had sympathy for Chimney, too, because both he and Maddie knew what it was like to have their parents show clear favoritism to another. While he did everything he could to at least be able to pretend like his mother cared about him, Maddie ran straight into Doug’s arms. But just because he understood where Chimney was coming from, that didn’t mean he didn’t think the man was being an asshole.

He kinda wished Danny was here, because he knew Danny would step in and put a stop to this. But Danny wasn’t here, it was just Buck and Maddie and their friends, all of them watching while Chimney verbally tore into a kid half his age who absolutely did not deserve it. Danny wasn’t here, but Buck was.

“Hey,” he snapped, putting himself in between the brothers. “Just because your father’s a piece of shit, doesn’t mean you need to take it out on him, man.”

“See!?” Chimney exclaimed, throwing out his hands. He knocked over his empty bottle, not that he paid it much mind. “Look at that! Everybody loves Albert.”

“No, I just think you’re being a jerk.”

The other man let out a scoff, face twisted, and Buck realized that he didn’t actually know how much Chimney had to drink. 

“You do not know what my life was like at home,” Albert said, stepping out slightly from behind Buck.

“I know that you have always had a family! That I’ve always been trying to piece one together!” Chimney shot back. Buck almost asked about the Lees, but managed to bite his tongue at the last minute. “These people are all that I have, you don’t get to take them, too.”

“No one’s taking us away, Chim.” Eddie had finally found his voice again.

“I do not wish to take anything from you.” Albert sounded like he was about to cry. “I’m your brother.”

“You are not my brother,” Chimney spat. “I had a brother. His name was Kevin. He died.”

He got to his feet. Buck moved to keep himself between the two of them.

“See, you didn’t come to me because you wanted to be my brother,” Chimney told Albert, tone scathing. “You came to me because you needed something from me.”

That was apparently the breaking point for Albert, Buck heard more than saw the way he tossed his pool stick onto the table. When he turned, he managed to catch the sight of Albert’s retreating back as he ran. Buck chased after him, not bothering to waste any more time with Chimney.

Albert ended up running right outside of the bar, coming to a stop on the curb of the sidewalk. He stood there, arms wrapped around himself and head bowed, and Buck opened and closed his mouth several times as he tried to come up with something to say. What he finally came up with was,

“So Chimney was an asshole.”

The statement didn’t get the laugh that Buck might have expected. Albert scuffed the ground with the heel of his shoe, sending bits of loose gravel falling into the road.

“He wasn’t wrong,” he said. “It was presumptuous of me to show up on his doorstep.”

Buck let out a sigh and rubbed at the back of his neck.

“Maybe? I dunno, I do that kinda shit with Danny all the time. And Maddie, she showed up a couple years ago out of the blue after years of barely talking to either of us. It’s just… Siblings, man.”

“Howard does not want me here.”

It would be very nice if Buck was able to argue the point, except Chimney’s own words made it very difficult. Which was just completely unfathomable to him. He couldn’t imagine a world where he wouldn’t be ecstatic to have Danny and Maddie randomly crashing into his life.

“You can stay at mine and Danny’s tonight, if you want,” Buck offered, and then started patting his pockets for his phone. “I should probably…”

“Hey.” Eddie stepped out to join them, coming to a stop at Buck’s side. “Albert, are you…?”

Albert shrugged.

“He’s gonna spend the night at the apartment,” Buck told his boyfriend, ignoring the fact that Albert hadn’t actually agreed to that. “I’ll see you later, okay?”

“Okay.” Eddie leaned in to kiss him goodbye. “I’ll go tell Maddie where you went.”

“C’mon.” Buck watched his boyfriend go back inside before turning to Albert, smacking him on the shoulder. “I’m parked over there, let’s go.”

Albert followed along like a lost little duckling, staying silent the entire time.

Daniel and Michael called their irregular get-togethers their “support group,” but Daniel was under no delusion that it mostly served as an excuse to get drunk together and bitch. About the cancer itself; about the nurses, especially the ones who were just a bit too cloyingly sweet with their cheerfulness; about the nausea that came from poisoning their bodies in the hopes of fixing it.  Daniel hadn’t really talked much with other cancer patients and survivors since he rang that bell and got out. And what Michael was going through wasn’t quite the same, he wasn’t sealed inside a clean room like Rapunzel in her tower, but he still got it.

“So- So - So all of that,” Michael was saying, words slightly slurred as he gestured widely. Daniel tracked the glass in his hand, certain there was about to be whiskey all over the place again. “All of that was for nothin’! All that time, pukin’ my guts out, and it was for nothin’!”

“The radiation didn’t do anything?” Daniel asked, refilling his own glass. He’d known what kind of night it was going to be when Michael came in and drained two glasses of whiskey - the good stuff, too - in a row.

“The damn thing didn’t get bigger,” Michael said. “But it didn’t shrink, either.”

“My parents ended up making a whole ass person to fix me. What are you gonna do? The surgery?”

“Yeah. Cut open my head, let ‘em dig it out.”

“Maybe they’ll use an ice cream scoop.”

Michael guffawed, the way that obnoxiously drunk people did. Loud and with his entire body, his drink sloshing out of his glass and onto the dining table they were sitting at. Daniel grabbed the nearby towel and mopped it up, not that the other man even noticed.

“I told Harry and May,” Michael said with a sigh, mood plummeting as fast as it rose. “Sat ‘em down with ‘Thena and Bobby.”

“How did they take it?” Daniel asked, pulling Michael’s glass to himself so he could refill it, too. He upended the bottle afterwards, frowning when he realized he’d just emptied it.

“Harry took it fine, I distracted him with Gamestop if he did well enough on his math test.” Michael took back his glass, though he didn’t drink from it yet.

“Ugh, God, math. Maddie and me were excited if Buck just didn’t fail. The kid’s hopeless with numbers.”

“But May,” the man said, like Daniel hadn’t spoken. “She’s too smart, like her mother. She’s worried.”

“And you don’t want her to be worried, especially since there’s nothing she can do,” Daniel said. “So you don’t tell her what’s going on, you lie and say everything’s fine.”

“Yup.” Michael threw back his drink, managing to down it all in one go, and set the glass down hard on the table.

“Dumbass.” Was it still hypocrisy if Daniel was speaking from experience? “She’ll find out, and then she’ll be worried and pissed. And then you’ll be stuck with dinners that set your mouth on fire for the next month.”

Michael scrunched his face up in confusion, because Daniel’s experience was not universal, as he reached for the whiskey bottle. His expression morphed into a scowl when it lifted it up to peer down the inside of the neck.

“This was full, earlier,” he stated, a bit accusatively.

“That was before you started drinking.”

He turned the scowl onto Daniel, only for it to disappear with a sigh as he set the bottle down again.

“That’s probably a sign I should be done,” Michael said, pushing himself out of his chair. He wobbled on his feet for a moment, and then sat back down heavily. “No, that was the sign.”

“Probably,” Daniel agreed. He got up and headed for the kitchen cabinets, pulling out a glass that he filled up with tap water from the sink. Michael looked grateful when he took it from him. “I’ll order you an Uber.”

“Thanks.”

The door opened before Daniel could actually pull out his phone and follow through. Buck came bursting through, as he always did, but it was the person who hesitantly followed him inside that caught Daniel’s attention.

“Really, squirt? I thought we were past the period of your life where you brought strangers home after a night out,” Daniel teased. He figured he could probably guess who the kid was, though. It was just a question of why.

“Funny,” Buck drawled. “This is Albert, Chimney’s brother. Albert, Danny. And that’s Michael over there.”

The kid, Albert, raised his hand to give them both a shy wave.

“And he’s here because?”

“He and Chimney had- Okay, it wasn’t really a fight, but…” Buck trailed off with a shrug, lips drawn. “Chim was being an asshole.”

Daniel let out a sigh.

“Right, okay. You goin’ to Eddie’s?” he asked. His brother nodded. “Then the kid can take your bed tonight. Mind taking Michael home?”

“Sure.”

Between the two of them, they managed to get Michael down to Buck’s jeep without the man falling over. Daniel took note of the fact that his brother didn’t bother packing an overnight bag before leaving again, but he chose not to dwell too much on it. He wasn’t surprised, because Buck was spending just as many nights at Eddie’s as he was at the apartment.

When Daniel got back upstairs, he found that Albert hadn’t moved far, the kid looking like a lost little puppy that someone abandoned on the side of the road. Daniel heaved out a sigh and started cleaning up from him and Michael, tossing the empty bottle into the recycling and the glasses into the sink. With that done, he pulled out a thing of popcorn and tossed it into the microwave.

“Bathroom’s there,” he told Albert, pointing at the door. “That’s my room, that’s Buck’s. Pretty sure his sheets are clean, but I can pull out new ones if you’d like.”

“Thank you.”

“Take a seat, relax. The couch is old but it isn’t gonna bite you.”

Daniel watched Albert gingerly sit himself down, perching on the edge of the cushions and stiff as a board. When the popcorn was done popping, he poured it into a bowl and went over to join him. He skimmed through Netflix for something to watch - not Supernatural, because Austin’s sister kept nagging at him to watch it and now it was a point of pride - and set the bowl between himself and Albert. 

Maddie texted him to check in, because Buck had called her and given her an update. From her, Daniel got more details about what had happened and had to agree with his brother’s assessment. He managed to resist poking the bear, opting to keep his opinions regarding Chimney in that moment to himself.

It took a bit, but the kid gradually relaxed and started talking. Tentatively at first, and then with the same kind of openness as Buck. He was very elated to hear where his brother got his nickname from, something that Austin had shared with Daniel some time ago. And he was happy, too, to hear about the various emergencies Daniel had responded to, both in Los Angeles and in El Paso.

Eventually, in the middle of another episode of some show about lawyers, Albert fell silent. When Daniel looked over, the kid was awkwardly splayed against the arm of the couch. He paused the show, debated waking him up and getting him moved to Buck’s bed, before deciding to cover him up with a blanket and slipping a pillow under his head.

Albert was awake before him the next morning, wide-eyed and bushy tailed and helping himself to a bowl of cereal. They didn’t talk much while Daniel got himself his own breakfast of knock-off fruit loops, the pair of them eating in companionable silence. Afterwards, they booted up a game and Daniel entertained himself by destroying the kid.

A knock at the door paused the game. When Daniel answered it, he found an awkward looking Chimney on the other side.

“Yes?” Daniel didn’t bother getting out of the way, blocking the doorway by leaning against the frame. He saw the other man’s eyes flicker down to where the baseball bat was leaning against the wall, just inside the door.

“I came to talk to Albert?” The words left Chimney’s mouth like a question. “To apologize. For being an asshole.”

“Good.” Daniel pushed himself off and let him in. “I’ll be in the shower. Yell if you need anything, Albert.”

“Thank you, Danny,” the kid said. 

Chimney made a face, but Daniel ignored him.

He took his time in the shower, even while he kept an ear out to make sure Chimney wasn’t making an ass of himself again. When he came out, clean and in fresh clothes, the two of them were sitting at the dining table and happily chatting away. Daniel assumed it was a productive talk, then.

Still, though, he took the time before the pair left to make sure Chimney knew to not be an asshole to the kid again.

Chapter 3

Chapter Notes

Brief life update, just because - In the past week, my mother had knee replacement surgery (she's doing fine, and is probably gonna have a gnarly scar); I had someone try to blackmail me, only to be thwarted by the fact that I have neither the money to spare nor the shame required to fall for it; and the cat distribution system saw fit to send me a new kitten. His name is Mittens, and he has thumbs!

Also, if I was giving these chapters titles, this one would be, "In Which Eddie Channels His Inner Danny"

Also, also: If you've read Darling, So It Goes, and Hold Steady, you already know my opinions regarding Ana Flores. It hasn't changed with time.

Daniel was not good at poker. This was a fact that he was well aware of, which was why he’d yet to take up Mehta’s invitation to that poker game he mentioned forever ago. But he also loved his sister, which was why he’d accepted her invite. When he’d shown up, he wasn’t entirely certain who all he would see. Albert, maybe, since he was staying on their couch; one or both of the Wilsons, definitely. He hadn’t expected for the only other person there to be Josh, from dispatch.

He immediately suspected that something was up, but he went along with it regardless because it wasn’t like he was about to pass up an opportunity to see Maddie. Even if it meant he ended up embarrassing himself with a game of poker, losing hand after hand. Being the arm candy was so much better.

“How are you so bad at this?” Maddie asked, after yet another lost round. This one had been worse, because Daniel saw the pair of aces in his hand and had the briefest of hopes that maybe he’d managed one single victory that night.

“Because he sucks at poker,” Josh said, and then turned immediately apologetic when Daniel turned to him. “Spoken by someone who also sucks at poker. No judgment, but uh… Maybe you should quit while you’re behind?”

“I don’t think anyone ever actually explained the rules to me,” Daniel confessed, placing his finger on the lip of his half-empty beer bottle and tilting it side-to-side. 

“That explains so much,” Chimney said.

“Who needs more wine?” Maddie asked, getting out of her seat. 

It was a stupid question. The only one of them besides her that was drinking wine was Josh, who raised his empty glass at her as she went by.

“Do you have anything stronger?” Daniel asked.

“Nope.” Maddie pulled the bottle of wine out of the fridge and headed back to the table.

“Thanks again for having me,” Josh said. “This was fun.”

“I guess,” Daniel grumbled as he took a long draw of his drink. Maddie laughed at him as she sat back down, refilling first Josh’s glass and then her own.

“Well, all of our couple friends were busy,” Chimney said, gathering the cards back up. “So we figured we’d target solos.”

“If I didn’t know better,” Josh started, and Daniel saw his eyes flicker his way, “I’d say you were setting us up.”

“Oh, no.” Maddie exaggeratedly shook her head. “No, no. I like you way too much to set you up with my brother.”

Daniel gave his sister a squinty-eyed glare. She, in turn, took a drink of her wine and avoided his gaze. Maddie was a lying liar that lied, because this was absolutely an attempt to pair them up. Chimney, when he looked at the man, didn’t look too shifty, so he was either an unknowing part of this plot or his acting skills were better than Maddie’s.

“You targeted the solos, huh,” Daniel said. “Where’s Albert?”

“He is on a date,” Chimney answered.

“Good for him.”

“What about Buck?” Josh asked, glancing between Maddie and Daniel. “I figured he’d show up to hang out, solo or not.”

“Oh, no, he’s doing something far more important than hanging out with us,” Daniel drawled. “Parent-teacher conferences are tonight.”

“He went with Eddie?” Maddie guessed.

“Yup.” Daniel popped the p. “More power to him, ‘cause I do not miss going to those things. Not at all.”

“I bet you were called in all the time, huh?” Chimney joked. His laughter caught in his throat and he froze in his seat when Daniel turned to glare at him. He relaxed when Daniel let out a sigh and drained the rest of his drink.

“All the damn time,” he admitted, setting down the empty bottle with a clink. “Usually because he kept getting distracted or couldn’t sit still. Or because of his math grades. It got better in El Paso. Not the math part.”

Daniel sometimes wondered how much of that improvement had to do with the different teachers and how much of that had to do with Buck sharing so many classes with Eddie. Or if it was getting him away from their parents, or if it was having football to focus on, or being older, or some other thing. Or maybe even a combination of everything.

Josh opened his mouth, like he was about to say or ask something, and then closed it. He looked across the table to Chimney, the pair of them wearing similarly puzzled expressions, before they both turned to Maddie. She shook her head and waved them off, obviously knowing what they weren’t saying. Daniel debated whether or not he cared enough to ask what that was about, and decided that he didn’t.

The conversation moved on from Buck, but it kept somehow coming back around to Daniel. Specifically, his sister kept making sideways comments about his (lack of) dating life at the moment. He wasn’t sure if Josh noticed it, though he did get into a minor rant about modern dating in LA. Daniel just rolled his eyes and kept moving forward, until they were finishing up their last round of poker and Josh’s uber was arriving to get him home.

“Seriously, Maddie?” Daniel hissed at his sister the moment they were alone, with Josh gone and Chimney in the bathroom. “You’re trying to set me up with your coworkers now?”

His sister looked for the briefest moment as if she was about to deny it, only to throw up her hands.

“I think he’d be good for you,” she said. “Or at least better than whatever you have going on now.”

“I am perfectly fine with how things are now,” he told her. “Trust me, if I wanted to, I can go out and find someone to fu-”

“Too much information,” Maddie interrupted, holding out a hand to shut him up. “I just- I just want you to be happy, okay?”

“I am happy, Mads.”

His sister rolled her eyes and crossed her arms over her chest, the tilt of her head telling him he was in for an argument.

“You sat there on Christmas and told me you were in love with someone who didn’t love you back.”

“I didn’t say that exactly,” Daniel said. Not that he was denying it at all. “Look, Maddie, it’s- it’s okay-”

His sister scoffed. Loudly.

“It is!” he protested. “Austin isn’t- He just doesn’t- I know that he cares about me, okay? He just doesn’t feel for me the same way I feel for him. And that’s okay! I knew going into this that he never would, and I don’t need him to.”

“I’m just worried that you’re letting yourself be used.”

“Maybe I don’t mind being used.” Daniel watched his sister’s face twist into some mixture of horror, disgust, and righteous anger. “But he isn’t using me. I’m fine, I’m happy, with what Austin and I have now.”

“Dan-”

“And I really don’t need you trying to set me up with your friends, Maddie,” he told her, heading for the door. “Seriously. Don’t need it, don’t want it.”

She opened her mouth, no doubt to continue arguing the point, but he managed to slip out and close the door behind him before she could.

“Which room are we looking for?” Buck asked, craning his neck to look around the hallway of Christopher’s school.

“Room two-oh-three,” Eddie answered, glancing between the paper in his hands and the room numbers on the walls. His face morphed into a confused scowl. “It just went from two-oh-one to two-oh-five.”

“Okay, I know I’m bad at numbers, but I’m pretty sure that’s not how it works.”

“It’s the next one on the left,” Carla told them, leading the way. “Lab classrooms have a different layout.”

“Of course they do,” Eddie grumbled.

Buck decided to trust her on that, because out of the three of them, she was the one who walked these halls the most often. And these were much fancier halls than the underfunded public school he and Eddie went to in El Paso. No chipping paint, all the light fixtures worked, there weren’t any suspicious stains on the ceiling. Actually…

He glanced up. The ceiling looked like an actual ceiling, none of those mineral-fiber tiles that almost always had holes from pencils and chunks torn out from them. Buck wasn’t sure if that was an aesthetic choice or a functional one.

“Thank you again for coming.” Eddie’s voice had Buck tuning back in from his temporary distraction. “Don’t know if we’d-” He gestured between Buck and himself. “-be able to navigate the confusing waters of parent-teacher night without you.”

“Yeah, my experience was mostly spent sitting there while the teachers complained that I didn’t pay enough attention in class,” Buck admitted.

“Because you didn’t. Probably why you kept having to copy my notes.”

Eddie smiled oh-so-prettily in the face of Buck’s glare.

“Knowing these things is sorta my job,” Carla pointed out, smirking at their antics. “Now, you’re gonna follow me lead. Try to ignore these teachers’ corny jokes.”

“Don’t worry, I have years of experience with that,” Eddie assured her. Buck smacked his arm, because he could recognize when his boyfriend was teasing him.

The first teacher was Chris’ math teacher, who opened up with a joke about numbers that won’t sit still. Buck found it funny, which the guy seemed to appreciate. The long and the short of that meeting was that Chris, thankfully, seemed to have inherited his math skills from Shannon. Something they were all thankful for.

After the math teacher was the music teacher, with a joke about bandstands and taking away their chairs. None of them laughed at that one, not even Buck. And after her was the science teacher.

“Christopher shows a great interest in science,” she told them. There’d only been two chairs, so Buck was gingerly perched on a table in the front row while he prayed it didn’t break beneath him. “Though he does keep telling other students that tsunamis aren’t a big deal. Which is unhelpful.”

Eddie and Carla turned in their seats to give Buck a pointed stare. He, at the same time, let out a laugh that he tried to muffle with his hand. The teacher, meanwhile, tilted her head as she looked between them.

“That’s-” Buck cleared his throat, raised his hand. “My fault…? Uh, he and I were on the pier when…”

“Oh,” the teacher said. And then, with her eyebrows skyrocketing, “Oh.”

“I’ll make sure to talk to him about it,” Eddie assured her.

“Thank you.”

They started to get up from their seats to head for the next one, the teacher obviously done with them with the way she was focusing on her notes on her desk. Except Eddie froze partway out of his chair and asked, a bit confused,

“No jokes?”

The teacher looked up, frowned in thought, and said,

“I try to tell chemistry jokes, but there’s no reaction.”

Buck let out a snort of laughter; the teacher beamed at him.

“You were not kidding about the jokes,” Eddie told Carla later, while they sat waiting on Chris’ English teacher. The white board said her name was Ms. Flores, and once again, there’d only been the two chairs set in front of her desk. The tables did not look nearly as stable as the ones in the science classroom, so Buck was leaning against the back of Eddie’s chair.

“Hopefully this one has a better shtick,” Carla said.

The door opened then, with Ms. Flores finally joining them. She was already talking before she was fully inside the room.

“So sorry to keep you waiting,” she said as she made her way to her desk. “My last student’s father asked a surprising amount of questions.”

“I’m sure he did,” Carla said, she and Eddie standing up.

“Good to see you again, Mrs. Price,” Ms. Flores said, shaking first Carla’s and then Eddie’s hand. “And you must be Mr. Diaz.”

“Please, call me Eddie. It’s short for-”

“Edmundo?”

“Most people guess Eduardo,” he said, surprise lacing his voice.

“Growing up, I had a grandfather named Edmundo,” Ms. Flores said, leaning in a little. “He was my favorite.”

Ms. Flores was young and pretty, latina. Everything that Ramon and Helena would probably love to have in a daughter-in-law.  Also, more importantly, Buck was pretty sure she was trying to flirt with Eddie. He immediately decided that he did not like this woman, with an intensity that caught him off guard.

“Hi!” Buck broke in, plastering himself to Eddie’s side, one hand snaking around his boyfriend’s waist. He did not offer his other hand for her to shake. “I’m Buck.”

She looked vaguely flustered, quickly saying,

“Let’s talk about Christopher."

Buck glowered at her as they sat. Everybody but him at least, and he once again leaned against Eddie. Or maybe draped was a better word for it. 

“He’s been doing really well in my class,” Ms. Flores said. Buck preened on the kid’s behalf. “His verbal skills have definitely improved. He’s still a little shy about reading out loud, but he definitely understands the material. I attribute that to him being read to from an early age, so bravo there.”

She smiled at Eddie. Buck resisted the urge to reach across the desk and claw it off her face.

“Nah.” Eddie shook his head, seemingly oblivious to the way Buck was glaring at the woman. Carla hadn’t, though. Carla was half-turned in her seat, looking like she was fighting to contain laughter. “We have his mother to thank for that.”

“Christopher tells me you’ve kept it up since she’s been gone.”

“I try to do the voices, but she was better at it,” Eddie said. “Buck’s been picking up the slack.”

Buck beamed at the teacher, even though she’d barely looked his way once.

“Christopher is also,” Ms. Flores said, moving on as she shuffled through her notes, “one of our most popular students. He loves making the other kids laugh.”

“Is that a problem?” Eddie asked, sounding concerned, and he tilted his head back to give Buck a flat glare. Like it was somehow his fault that Chris was more extroverted than his father.

“Not at all,” Ms. Flores told him. “He’s a very sweet and kind boy. You’re doing a great job.”

“Damn right, he is,” Buck said, clapping his hands onto Eddie’s shoulders.

Carla finally let her laughter out as soon as they were out of the classroom, before the door was even fully shut behind them. She kept it up as they headed for the exit, Eddie shooting concerned looks her way.

“So- So-” Carla paused, gasped for breath. “We gonna talk about that?”

“That Chris is a funny, popular genius?” Buck asked, even though he knew that wasn’t what she meant.

“How you were five seconds away from peeing on Eddie to mark your territory.”

Eddie’s nose scrunched up. It was cute.

“I wasn’t that bad,” Buck protested, though only half-heartedly.

“Yeah, you were,” Carla threw back with another laugh. “I’m gonna go. Drive safe, boys.”

“You got it.” Eddie waved at her as she went, and then turned on Buck. “Seriously?”

“She was flirting with you!”

“No she wasn’t.”

“Yeah, she was,” Buck said, and then pitched his voice up higher as he mocked, “Edmundo was my favorite grandfather.”

“Are you done?” his boyfriend asked, looking very unimpressed.

Buck thought for a minute, and then he put his hands on the side of Eddie’s face to pull him in. The kiss didn’t start that deep, but it was quickly approaching it by the time Buck finally broke it off and pulled away. Eddie’s face was flushed, lips still parted.

“Now I’m done,” Buck said, dropping his hand to grab Eddie’s. “C’mon, let’s head back to the house.”

“Y- Yeah,” Eddie stammered, stumbling a little as he followed Buck to the jeep. “Okay.”

It was one of the - awful, boring, lonely - days when Eddie and Buck’s shifts didn’t line up. Technically speaking, Buck hadn’t even been scheduled to work today, but he was covering for someone on another shift. Something about a kid’s recital. He’d tripped over himself to do it, citing all the times someone had covered for Danny when there was a football game.

The point was, that meant Eddie was home alone, trying to remember how he used to fill his time, when he got the phone call Carla. And now here he was, rushing through the front hall of his son’s school and beelining for the doors that led to the center courtyard. He spotted Carla and Ms. Flores standing together, talking.

“What the hell happened?” he demanded the moment he burst through the second set of doors and into the open air.

“I told you Christopher is fine,” Carla said. “You didn’t have to come down here. It’s just some scrapes and bruises.”

That sounded like a damn good reason for Eddie to be here. 

“He hurt himself?” He glared at Ms. Flores, and watched her shaky smile fall completely. “How?”

“Well. It turns out that Christopher and skateboards don’t get along very well,” was Carla’s cheerful sounding explanation.

He turned on Ms. Flores.

“You let him skateboard?”

“I am so sorry, Mr. Diaz,” she said. “We didn’t know one of the kids had brought a skateboard.”

“You didn’t know? He could’ve broken his neck.”

“I know, and I feel terrible. The other kids were showing him how to ride it and they didn’t know that-”

“Didn’t they?” he interrupted. “No, let’s push the kid with CP around on a skateboard for fun.” Suddenly, Eddie had a new understanding of those stories and jokes about Danny putting the fear of God into Buck’s bullies as a kid. The moment he knew which little shits- “You let them make a fool of my son.”

“Eddie,” Carla tried to cut in, but he ignored her, all of his attention on the teacher that was entrusted with his son’s safety.

“I- I promise you, that isn’t what happened here,” Ms. Flores said, trying to defend herself. Another door opened and Chris came out, escorted by another aide; Eddie caught a glimpse of relief on the woman’s face in the brief moment before he was turning and kneeling in front of Chris.

The first thing he really saw was the blood on his kid’s uniform shirt, standing out against the pale blue. Then the darker stains on the knees of his slacks, which were slightly ripped. There were more scrapes on his elbows and arms, too.

“Are you okay?” he asked him, after he was done checking him over.

“I’m sorry about my clothes,” Chris said.

“No, don’t worry about that, we can get new ones,” Eddie assured him.

“I could run to the house,” Carla offered. “Get some clean clothes for him to change into.”

“No, we’re done for the day,” Eddie declared. He picked up his kid, hefting him onto his hip like he was still the tot he’d rarely seen in person. “Come on, we’re leaving.”

“But school isn’t over,” Chris complained, even as he wrapped his arms around Eddie’s neck, careful of his crutches.

“It is now.”

Eddie shot Ms. Flores one final venomous glare before turning and stomping off, heading for the front office so he could sign Chris out and take him off.

Once home, the blaze of anger was kept fed as he tended to Chris’ cuts and scrapes, as he listened to the sharp hisses of pain as he cleaned each one. It was soothed, somewhat, when Principal Summers called him with an update. The fact that the kids responsible were going to have consequences of some sort, and not just be allowed to get off scot-free, made him feel better. He was still pretty damned pissed, though.

“So should I expect some kid’s head on a spike at tomorrow’s drop-off?” Carla asked, the moment he got off the phone. She was chopping up veggies at the kitchen counter for an afternoon snack for Chris.

“They sent skateboard kid home early,” he told her. “Principal’s gonna meet with the parents in the morning, figure out what the punishment should be.”

“And what about the kid who fell off the skateboard?”

Eddie froze, his blood going ice cold and then burning hot in an instant.

“You think I should punish Chris for getting hurt?”

“No,” Carla was quick to deny. “But I think you should talk to him about how he got hurt. I know Christopher wants to be like all the other kids, but…”

“You want me to tell him he’s different?” Eddie asked, a little dumbly.

“He already knows that,” she said. “You need to teach him what it means. That he has limitations.”

“I am not going to tell my kid that,” he told her, resisting the urge to bite her head off like he had Ms. Flores’. He stomped out of the kitchen and into the dining room, where Chris was sitting at the table in fresh, unbloodied clothes. It didn’t take much effort to soften his voice when he spoke to him. “Hey, buddy. How’re you feeling?”

“Dumb,” was Chris’ answer.

“What?” Eddie moved Chris’ crutches and sat down in the chair they’d been leaning on. “What are you talking about?”

“Everybody saw me fall.”

“People fall, it happens,” Carla said, coming in with a glass of milk and a plate with Chris’ snack. She set it on the table in front of him. “It’s nothing to be embarrassed about.”

“Do you know how many times I’ve seen Buck eat dirt? A lot. It’s been a lot of times,” Eddie said. “That boy should’ve never pressured you into getting on that skateboard.”

“It was my idea.”

Chris’ words took Eddie aback. And he did not appreciate the way Carla was suddenly so smug.

“It was your idea to get on the skateboard?” he asked, needing to make sure.

“It looked fun. It wasn’t.”

“Chris.” Eddie sighed. “Why would you do that? You had to know it’d be dangerous.”

“You always said I can do anything,” Chris told him, making the effort to look him in the eye. “You- You lied.”

And Eddie did not know what to say to that.

Chapter 4

Chapter Summary

General heads up for canon-typical violence, or at least the aftermath of it. Also a heads up for Ana Flores and the author's heavily telegraphed opinions of her.

While Eddie didn’t look the most despondent that Daniel had ever seen him, it might’ve been close. He’d come over to the apartment while Buck was still on shift, making his immediate way to the fridge and pulling out a beer. No words were exchanged until he’d popped it open and took a long draw of it. Then, he told Daniel what was wrong.

Apparently, Chris had an accident involving a skateboard at that fancy school of his. Eddie, understandably, was a mite upset about it. Daniel sympathized with him there, because he’d always hated watching Buck take a tumble. The reason for Eddie’s morose mood was not, however, his kid’s scraped knees and palms. No, instead it was because his kid called him a liar. That, and why he called Eddie a liar.

“Boohoo,” Daniel told him, taking a seat at the dining table with his own drink. Eddie, sitting across from him, sent him a look of betrayal. “Kids call their parents liars, it happens. Pretty sure you did it.”

“Well it feels a little different when you hear it coming out of your own kid,” Eddie shot back.

“Just wait until he gets to the oh-so-fun ‘you can’t tell me what to do’ phase. Pretty sure Buck’s still in that phase.”

Eddie snorted at that, and then sighed as he set down his bottle.

“He’s right, though. Chris, I mean. I lied to him,” he said. “Or maybe I lied to myself. Either way, I feel like a fool. I spent years trying to convince my kid to believe in the Easter Bunny, and now I’ve gotta tell him none of it’s real.”

“The hell are you talking about?” Daniel asked, taking a swig of his drink.

“I’m talking about the fact that he is different from other kids,” Eddie said. “He has CP, there’s a lot he can’t do because of it.”

Daniel stared at him, bottle held loosely in his fingers. He was too stunned to be properly angry, at least at first. He set his bottle down and sat up straighter in his chair, giving the younger man a flat glare.

“Fuck that,” Daniel bit out. Eddie cringed from his harsh tone. “Your kid falls off a skateboard one time, and you’re throwing in the towel? You decide Chris can’t do anything?”

“That’s not-” Eddie tried to say, but Daniel talked over him.

“Do you know how many times I watched Buck eat shit when Maddie and I were teaching him how to ride a bike? Or when he was learning how to skateboard?” he asked. “A lot. It was a lot, Eddie. And sure, yeah, it sucked to watch him get hurt like that. But we didn’t once tell him to give it up, that he just couldn’t do it.”

“This is different.”

“How?”

“Chris has CP,” Eddie said. “He just can’t do what the other kids do.”

“Bull-fucking-shit,” Daniel spat, leaning forward across the table. “The world sucks enough as it is without you giving up on him after a single fall. Chris wants to learn how to ride a skateboard? Your job is to do your best to make that happen. He wants to play football-”

“Chris doesn’t-”

“You do your best to make that happen. He wants you there at his games? You find a way to fucking be there for his games. Simple as that.”

“It’s not that simple, Danny.” Eddie sounded like he was on the verge of losing his temper. “Chris uses crutches for a reason. He can’t stay on a skateboard.”

“So be his dad,” Daniel told him. “And find a way that he can.”

Maddie had been, initially, excited for Josh when he told her he was dipping his toe into the dating pool again. Sure, she was disappointed that he was meeting someone online instead of things working out with Dan as she’d meant for them to. But that didn’t matter, not really. Not when he’d been excited as he told her about the guy he was talking to.

It still would’ve been nice if it had been Dan, though, because Maddie was not looking forward to watching her brother get his heart broken. The weird thing between Dan and Austin had been okay, back when she was under the impression that they were both secretly something more and simply weren’t admitting to it. Now that Dan had told her, to her face, that he was in love with the other man and knew that Austin did not, would not feel that way…

Well, now it just made her both sad and a little bit angry for her brother.

Sad and a little bit angry for Josh, too, as she rushed through the hospital halls. Josh was supposed to have been on a date, a date with a guy that he was so excited to start something with. But on what should have been a wonderful and happy night, he’d called her from the hospital. Maddie wasn’t sure what she was expecting to see, when she burst into the room he was in. But it wasn’t for the sight that greeted her.

Josh’s face was a mess, one side of his face swollen, including his eye on that side.  There was blood staining his sweater, and bruises blooming across his skin.

“Oh my God. Are you okay?” she blurted out. It was a stupid question, not when she could see the answer with her own eyes. "What happened?”

“I got jumped,” he answered, a bit stiffly. It probably, it definitely, hurt to talk. “They took my keys, my phone, my wallet. Beat the crap out of me. For a minute there, I… I thought they were gonna kill me.”

His voice broke on the last few words, and so did Maddie’s heart.

“Was this after your date? The movie thing?”

“It was my date. He set me up, him and his friend. I never even saw it coming.”

“I am so sorry,” she told him, reaching out to hug him and stopping before she really raised her arms. She wasn’t certain where else he was hurt, or if he’d even want to be touched right now.

“I’m an idiot,” Josh said, laughing a little. That sad kind of laugh that carried no humor. “I thought he was sweet. That he liked me.”

“No, no, you just…” Maddie shook her head. “You just trusted the wrong person, that’s all.”

“Mr. Russo?” The man’s voice had Maddie turning to see the detective that walked in, dressed in business casual with a jacket and with a notepad in his hand. He was chewing gum and he smelled strongly enough of cigarette smoke that it made her wrinkle her nose. “Officers canvassed the cemetery. They didn’t find your phone, but they did recover your keys and your wallet. All the cash was gone, though.”

There was a drawl to his words that reminded her of Eddie, especially after a couple drinks.

“At least they saved me the hassle of replacing all my credit cards and IDs,” Josh sighed.

“It’s all waitin’ for you down at the station,” the detective said. “But I can go ahead and take your statement now.”

“Does it have to be tonight?” Josh asked. “I’m just… I’m just really worn out.”

Something like annoyance crossed over the detective’s face, but Maddie didn’t focus on that.

“You know what?” She looked between the two of them, before settling on Josh. “You can just stay with me tonight and I’ll drive you to that station in the morning.”

“Sure.” The detective sighed, though he didn’t put away the notepad just yet. “Did you recognize either man that attacked you? Spot any identifiable features?”

“No,” Josh lied. “Sorry.”

Maddie stared at him; Josh refused to look at her.

“Well, you ain’t givin’ us much to work with,” the detective told him. “You should set your expectations.”

“No, I know the drill,” Josh said. “I just want to get out of here and put this whole night behind me.”

“I’m not keepin’ you here,” the detective said, and then turned to Maddie. “You said he’ll be stayin’ with you, Ms…?”

“Maddie Buckley,” she answered.

The detective’s eyebrows went up and then his lips slowly curved into a smile. There was something weird about it. Something unsettling.

“Well then,” he said, tucking away his notepad into his pocket and handing her a card. “Call if you think of anythin’ else, Mr. Russo.”

“I will,” Josh said, though that was almost certainly another lie.

The detective, still smiling, tipped an imaginary hat to the pair of them before leaving the room. His footsteps were heavy, she noticed, and he swaggered a little. Maddie ignored it though, to shoot Josh an accusing glare.

“Don’t,” he begged. “I already feel like a fool. I don’t need the rest of the world in on the joke.”

Maddie didn’t like it. She understood it, but she didn’t like it.

“Fine,” she said, and glanced at the card that the detective had given her. On it was the contact information for someone named Lucas Drake.

Buck smiled as he felt arms wrap around him and a chest press into his back. Eddie perched his chin onto his shoulder, taking exaggerated sniffs of the air.

“That’s smelling good,” he said, nuzzling into Buck’s neck. It made him shiver.

“I used the last of your bacon,” Buck said, using a spatula to nudge the strips around on the skillet. “And the eggs.”

“We’ll do a grocery run, I’ll make a- Oh.”

Eddie stopped mid sentence, face turned slightly. He no doubt spotted the list that Buck made that morning and stuck to the fridge door. There was silence, and then Eddie was burying his face into Buck’s shoulder.

“One joke,” Buck warned. “One single word about me being a housewife…”

“No jokes here.” Eddie stepped away, hands raised. “Lo prometo.”

Buck squinted at him over his shoulder, because he did not trust that promise. Especially with the way that Eddie was smiling. 

“Make yourself useful,” he said. “Get me plates.”

“Tan mandón,” Eddie tutted, going for the cabinets and pulling out plates for them. He stacked them, and then grabbed forks and cups, too. “Hey, you’re still going with me to talk to Chris’ teacher, right?”

“‘Course.” Buck turned off the burners and started plating the food. “Someone’s gotta make sure you don’t bite her head off again. We wouldn’t want her to flunk Chris for it.”

He threw his boyfriend the prettiest smile he could manage. Eddie, in turn, shot him a dour glare.

Buck had gone through a myriad of emotions when he heard about the incident with the skateboard. The first, and most important, was the need to make sure Chris was okay, which didn’t go away until he got off shift and could go over to Eddie’s to see for himself. But there were also the slivers of absolute glee when Carla, throwing looks of disapproval Eddie’s way, retold how the man reacted to Ms. Flores when he arrived.

He wasn’t especially proud of that particular emotion, not in that context. But he also wasn’t about to deny its existence, either.

Between the two of them, they managed to get the plates and cups and cutlery to the dining table. Eddie made a stop to get the orange juice out of the fridge, balancing it precariously between everything. When he called for Chris to come eat, the kid trundled out hesitantly.

“I don’t feel well,” he quietly complained, still dressed in his pajamas.

“You sick?” Eddie asked, and Chris nodded. He set down the last of everything and then went over, placing the back of his hand on Chris’ forehead, letting out a disbelieving hum. “You sure?”

“I don’t wanna go.”

Buck and Eddie shared a look, and then Eddie let out a sigh. He bent down and picked Chris up, carrying him into the living room and sitting him down on the couch. Buck followed after them.

“You’re still upset about the other day?” Eddie asked, perching himself on the edge of the coffee table.

“I just wanna be like everyone else.”

“I know, but…”

Eddie trailed off with a sigh and glance towards Buck.

“But I’m not,” Chris finished for him. “I have CP.”

“No, that’s- I mean, yes-” Eddie shook his head. “There are things that you’re not gonna be able to do as easily as other kids can.”

“But that doesn’t mean that you can’t do it at all, okay?” Buck knelt down between the couch and the coffee table, next to their legs. “You fell down, and that’s okay. That doesn’t mean you failed, or that you’ll never succeed. It just means you get back up and try again.”

“Yeah.” Eddie nodded, even as there was a note of uncertainty in his voice. “You tried something and it didn’t work out. Maybe the next time it does.”

“But you can skateboard,” Chris pointed out.

“Do you know how many times I fell when I was learning?” Buck asked him, and then pointed at Eddie. “Or how many times your dad fell when I was teaching him?”

“A lot,” Eddie said. “But do you know what I can’t do?”

“Cook,” was Chris’ immediate suggestion. Buck couldn’t help but laugh.

“That isn’t nice.” Eddie was pouting a little.

“But it’s true,” Buck said, and then ducked to avoid being smacked for it.

“I have a black thumb, I’ve killed every plant that’s ever been given to me,” Eddie said, and then poked Chris in the knee. “Your science teacher told us that you did the best job out of your whole class growing plants from seeds, so there’s something you’re better at than me.”

“Really?”

“Really,” he confirmed to his son with a nod. “And I don’t want you to ever stop trying, but maybe… Maybe, until you get a little older, we try new things together. Okay?”

“Okay,” Chris whispered.

“You’re not like any other kid. You’re my kid,” Eddie said, leaning forward to wrap his arms around Chris. “And I love you more than anything in the world.”

They ate breakfast, got Chris to school, and did the grocery run. Buck sent a list of supplies for Danny to get from the hardware store, and received only minor complaints in response. It was almost entirely for show.

It was at the end of the school day, when the student were being let out, that they went to talk to Ms. Flores. She was packing up, ready to head home, when Eddie first poked his head through the door and then slid the rest of the in. Buck entered behind him, and saw the teacher looked a bit hesitant at their appearance. He stuck by the door, not wanting to crowd the poor woman, while Eddie went to where she stood behind her desk.

“Mr. Diaz,” she said. “And… Buck.”

Right, he hadn’t actually given her his last name. Oh well, she’d just have to deal.

“Eddie, please. I just wanted to apologize for the other day. I was out of line, and you didn’t deserve that.”

“You had every right to be upset,” Ms. Flores said. She relaxed, shoulders losing their line of tension, now that she knew she wasn’t about to have her head bitten off again. “It’s my job to look after your son and I failed to do that. I’m just relieved that Christopher is okay.”

“I fight so hard to try and protect him, I forget that falling down is a part of life,” Eddie said. “It’s supposed to teach us how to get back up, right?”

“Yes. There’s a lot to be said for getting back on the horse,” she said. “But there’s also some value in learning that you don’t like horses.”

Eddie, face scrunched up in confusion, glanced Buck’s way. Buck just shrugged, equally as clueless.

“I’m sorry?” Eddie asked, chuckling a little.

“Sometimes, our limitations tell us when to stop,” the teacher said. “But sometimes, they can-”

“Pardon my accent,” Buck interrupted, pushing himself off the wall he was leaning against. His fists were clenched at his side, fingernails biting into his palms. “But. ¿Qué carajo?”

“Buck!” Eddie’s eyes were wide and dancing with mirth. Ms. Flores, meanwhile, was entirely taken aback.

“Excuse me?”

“You’re his teacher,” Buck said. “You don’t just- So, what, he fell off a skateboard, and that means he should just pack it in?”

“That’s not what I’m saying, Mr…?”

“Buck. You just said it.”

Ms. Flores let out a huff.

“What I’m saying is that he fell off a skateboard the other day. But maybe tomorrow, he’ll write the next great American novel.”

“But he doesn’t want to write the next great American novel,” Buck pointed out to her. “He wants to ride a skateboard.”

“Sometimes our limitations get in the way of what we want,” Ms. Flores shot back. Eddie’s brow was furrowed as he stared at her. “Which is as valuable of a lesson as learning to get back up.”

“Have you ever heard of Jim Abbott?” Buck asked her. “The baseball player?”

“I don’t really follow the sport.”

“He was on the US team for the Eighty-Eight Olympics. Pitched the final game, helped win them an unofficial gold medal - it was just a demonstration sport that year. And in the Nineties, when he was playing for the Yankees, he pitched a no-hitter. Which means- Eddie, what does that mean?”
