“It means he played the whole game and didn’t allow a batter to reach first base,” his boyfriend dutifully answered. “Not by the batter hitting the ball, anyway.”

“I read his book when I was in the hospital, recovering from my leg being crushed. Good thing I didn’t let my limitations stop me there. I probably wouldn’t be a firefighter.” Buck told Ms. Flores. She scowled at the remark. “Y’know what makes all of that really impressive, though? It’s the fact that Abbott did all that and he was born with only one hand. He practiced switching his glove to his throwing hand so that he could field after he pitched.”

“That’s… Impressive,” Ms. Flores said.

“It is! I bet he fumbled a lot of balls at first,” he said. “Wanna guess how many times a teacher told him to give it up and do something else?”

The room fell silent, Buck and Ms. Flores glaring at each other. Eddie looked between them and then cleared his throat.

“I think we should probably grab Chris and head home,” he said. “Uh. Sorry, again, for… Yeah.”

He crossed the room, grabbing Buck as he went by and practically dragging him out. Buck didn’t stop glaring at the teacher until the door was swinging shut between them, blocking her from view. Only then did he finally turn around.

“If Chris fails her class, we’re blaming you,” Eddie said. “Right?”

“She better not fail him,” Buck said, digging out his phone and calling his brother. “That fu- Danny! Please tell me you got everything, because I need this teacher to choke on her words.”

Eddie knew that his boyfriend sometimes had the tendency of getting hyperfixated on things that caught his attention. Sometimes to the point that he’d lose track of time. Between their shifts and the project that Buck was working on with his brother, his current focus, Buck hadn’t been over to the house for a few days. Chris complained a little, especially since he couldn’t go to the apartment. Not without possibly ruining the surprise.

On the day that the project was finished, they decided to do the reveal at the park. Eddie wasn’t entirely certain how the brothers were transporting the contraption, because there was no way that it would fit in Danny’s car. It might, might, fit in the back of Buck’s jeep. But figuring out the logistics of it was not Eddie’s job. His job was getting Chris to where he needed to be.

“I don’t want to be here,” his son complained as they made their way across the park, other kids on skateboards parting around them.

“Trust me,” Eddie told him. “It’ll be fun.”

He pointed down the way, where Buck and Danny were waiting with the surprise covered by a blue tarp. Chris looked up, smiling at the sight of them. When they tore the tarp off, revealing the contraption that they managed to put together, Chris’ face turned to confusion and wonder.

“What’s that?” he asked.

“You wanted to ride a skateboard,” Eddie told him, kneeling down so they were eyelevel. “We found a way that you can. So let’s try it together, okay?”

Chris nodded frantically, curls bouncing, with a smile stretched across his face that was as bright as the sun. He hurried down the sidewalk, as fast as he could, excitement palpable. Buck stepped forward and scooped him up in a hug as soon as he got close.

Eddie wasn’t entirely certain where Buck got the design from. It was, in essence, a cage on wheels that was made out of PVC pipe stuck together. In the middle, a harness dangled from bungee cords. At the bottom, a skateboard was attached the same way.

They got Chris in a helmet - because while Eddie was positive that his kid wasn’t going to fall in this thing, there was no point in risking it - and into the harness. And that bright smile stayed on his face the entire time that Eddie and Buck pushed him along, with Danny filming on his phone.

Chapter 5

Eddie had not stepped foot in a bowling alley since he was in high school. During a period when his father was away on one of his many, many out-of-state trips for work, his mother practically shoved his sisters at him, telling him to find something to do with them for the day. It was Buck who came up with bowling and so the two of them took Eddie’s sisters. It was stupid and it was fun.

They were called to this one initially because, and this was apparently an actual quote, the bowling balls were bleeding. When they arrived, there was a bored looking employee just inside. He barely looked up from his phone when Bobby, in full turnouts, approached him to ask,

“Are you in charge here?”

The guy, in a display of natural leadership, just shrugged.

“I guess.”

“Thank God you’re here!” Another employee, much younger - a teenager - came to a skidding stop. He was slightly out of breath, having clearly sprinted from wherever he came from. “She’s this way.”

The new kid, obviously more aware of the situation than his coworker, started leading them farther inside the building.

“Her name’s Arlene Branson, she’s the owner,” he briefed them. The words came out of his mouth at a clipped pace, subdued anxiety lacing every syllable. “She was working on lane five when the pin setter came down on her. I wasn’t sure what to do, so I shut off the power to stop it from cycling again. I didn’t think I should move it until you guys got here.”

“You did the right thing,” Bobby assured the kid. “What’s your name?”

“Garrett, sir.”

They followed Garrett behind the lanes. The area was almost entirely taken up by the machinery, with just enough space by the wall for them to walk in a single file. There was a woman calling for help, and the teenager sprinted ahead to reach her.

“Arlene, I’m here,” he assured the woman from a spot out of their way while they clambered for space around her, climbing on top of the unmoving machines. Eddie did his best to avoid stepping in the blood splatter. “These people are gonna help you, okay?”

“I’ve got a compound fracture, more outside than in,” Chimney announced. Eddie could see Arlene’s arm, and the bits of bone sticking out of it near where the pinsetter came down. “Pulse is very weak.”

“She’s lost a lot of blood,” Hen said, unwrapping the IV cord from around a bag of saline. “Starting fluids.”

“Do you know how to move this thing?” Bobby asked Garrett.

“How to release it? Not really,” the kid answered. “I’ve only watched Arlene do it.”

Arlene looked up, hair sticking with sweat to her pale face.

“Manual,” she managed to grit out. The kid’s head shot up.

“Right! Manual release! Which is… Somewhere around here.”

He got up from where he was crouched and started looking around the back wall. When he located what he was looking for, he shot past Bobby and grabbed it from where it hung from the wall. It looked like the lever for a hand crank.

“Here.” Garret held it out; Eddie carefully crawled closer to take it from him. “Put this in the back, then turn it.”

Eddie did so, after taking a moment to locate where to insert it, while Hen and Chimney gave updates about her deteriorating condition. He didn’t turn it just yet, because there was still the matter of stabilizing her.

“I’ll get the tourniquet,” he told them. “Tie the arm, get her out.”

“I don’t know if that’d work,” Hen warned. “Right now, this cross brace is the only thing keeping her arm in place. The minute you move it, she’ll bleed more.”

Eddie almost, almost, pointed out that that was what the tourniquet was for. Chimney spoke up before he lost that particular battle, pointing out that,

“Given how broken her bones are, it’ll be like tying off a wet bag of rocks.”

He was right, Eddie had to admit. For the tourniquet to be effective, he’d have to tie it so tight that the circulation would be cut off entirely. They might as well just free her by cutting it off right here if they did that.

“Any suggestions?” Bobby asked, looking at them all in turn. When none were forthcoming, he even looked to Garrett. The poor kid threw his hands up and stepped back, clearly at just as much of a loss as them.

The obvious way to go about it wasn’t going to work. They needed something outside of the box…

Eddie dug into his pocket, pulling out his phone and pulling up his contacts. He ignored Bobby’s incredulous sounding “Seriously?” as he waited for the call to be picked up. When it did, Buck’s smiling face filled the screen.

“Hey, Eds! What-” He cut himself off and rolled his eyes when someone in the background said something that Eddie couldn’t quite make out. “Ignore Nola, she’s a sore winner. Anyway, what’s… Are you on a call? Why are you calling me?”

“Yeah, um. We need a second opinion for….” 

Eddie tried to figure out how to explain this, and then just opted to turn his phone around and show Buck what they were working with. His boyfriend let out a drawn out “Oh.” It apparently drew an audience, because there was the sound of people jostling for space that was followed by even more “Oh” s. 

“I didn’t realize we could use lifelines.” A guy’s voice, and one Eddie definitely did not recognize. “Can I do that next time? Tell the cap I want to phone a friend? Oh! Oh! Ask an audience member.”

“Shut up, Jon. Go bother Danny,” Buck said. The guy, Jon, let out a loud laugh. “Uh… Okay. Tourniquet? Wait, no, you wouldn’t need me for that.”

“A tourniquet won’t work,” Eddie said. “Because-”

“A wet bag of rocks!” Chimney raised his voice so Buck could hear him.

“Right, that.”

“Then why don’t you…” Buck trailed off. Eddie kept the phone positioned so the other man could see what they were working with, even as he moved his head to glance at the screen. His boyfriend’s face was a mask of concentration. “Embrace the cross brace.”

“Don’t take her arm out, use what she’s stuck in?” Eddie was pretty sure he was following along with the man’s thought process.

“Yeah! Cut the- What is her arm caught in?”

“Pinsetter,” Garrett offered.

“Thank you, uh. Person. Did you guys get a new probie?” Buck asked, and then immediately moved on without Eddie even needing to get him back on track. “Cut the pinsetter here- Shi- Shoot.”

“You just tried to point it out to us through the screen,” Eddie teased. “Didn’t you?”

 “No, shut up.” That would be a yes. “Uh. The, um, the… Box? That her arm is in. Cut it from the rest of the machine, and then weld the loose parts so that it all stays together. It’ll act like-”

“Like a splint,” Bobby finished for him. He was peering at the pinsetter, tapping lightly at the spots that Buck was talking about. He grabbed his radio and thumbed it on. “Jones, bring the stick welder and the gear for it.”

“Got it, Cap.”

“My job here is done,” Buck announced. “I’ll take my thanks in the form of food.”

“I’ll bring over some of Abuela’s tamales,” Eddie offered. His boyfriend let out a cheer and said his goodbyes before ending the call.

When Austin arrived, carrying everything they needed to turn the cross brace into an impromptu splint, they got to work. It actually worked quite well, even if the end result was a bit awkward, especially with how they’d had to leave the gurney at the end of the walkway. Eddie was tasked with holding up the arm trapped in the cross brace until they could get her properly situated, so that the weight didn’t cause any more damage.

Arlene was a trooper, though. Even as they were wheeling her out to the ambulance, she was making sure Garrett knew what to do in her absence. He was being left in charge, and had apparently earned himself a promotion. The last Eddie saw of him, he was using his newfound power to fire the indifferent employee from earlier.

It wasn’t often that Daniel went to Michael’s apartment. They normally had their “support group” meetings at Daniel’s place. But Daniel was already going to be out and about in this part of town and Michael was currently on a course of chemo, after deciding against the riskier (but more likely to work) brain surgery.

“What are you drinking?” Daniel asked as he took a seat, eying the cup that Michael was holding. It smelled a bit like grass.

“Green tea. Hen said that it’s supposed to help the chemo work better.” He took a sip and grimaced lightly. “I hate it.”

“Probably better than whiskey, all things considered.” Honestly, the nature of their get-togethers would have to change. Daniel was pretty sure that it was ill-advised to get drunk while on chemo, not that he would actually know; he’d been well below the drinking age while he was fighting that particular battle. “And the tents?”

There were two of them, packed away in their bags, one sitting on top of the long table and the other propped up to lean against the end of it.

“Loaners from Hen,” Michael said. “She brought them, the tea, and that new little girl of hers, Nia. Have you met her yet?”

“I haven’t. Buck has, when he inflicted himself upon her the other day,” Daniel said. “Why did she bring over tents?”

“I’m taking Harry camping. Bobby’s coming with us.”

“Are you sure you’re up for that?”

“Man, not you, too,” Michael groaned. “This is a tradition. Harry and I go camping every year, and I am not going to miss out on this one. And my doctor has cleared me for this. If my doctor doesn’t see a problem with me going camping-”

“Woah, woah, hey.” Daniel waved his hands, trying to cut the other man off from the rant. “Look, I fully understand wanting to cram in as much time as you can with your kid, I fully support you on that-”

“Good.”

“I just meant… I remember being on chemo,” he said. “It kicks your ass, man. The nausea, the fatigue. Are you going to feel up to doing this?”

“Doesn’t matter,” Michael said with a shake of his head. “All I have for sure is today. This might be the last time I can ever do this with him again, and I am not going to miss it.”

“Take plenty of water.” Daniel wasn’t going to argue with the man over this, not when it was something he wholeheartedly agreed with. “Nash is going with you, right? Have him drive, so you can nap on the way and back. And talk to Harry before you go. He’s nowhere near as bad as Buck was at that age, because that kid sprinted after everything that caught his attention, but he’s still a kid. He’s gonna want to go off on an adventure the moment you get there, and you will not be up for it.”

Michael stared at him for a moment, blinking, before nodding.

“Yeah. Yeah, okay,” he said. “I feel like I should be taking notes.”

“Just take it easy,” Daniel told him. “You will feel like shit. You will be dragging yourself along. Just expect for everything to take longer than you’re used to.”

“We always plant a tree, whenever we go,” Michael said. “The first thing we do, after getting everything set up, is go find the perfect spot for it. It takes a while.”

“Maybe you’ll feel like going on a hike.” Daniel shrugged. “Or maybe you’ll have to crash for an hour or two.”

“Well, I am aiming for the former,” Michael said. He took another sip of his tea. “Nope, still hating this.”

Daniel hung out with Michael for a bit longer, before he had to leave to keep his appointment. Dr. White’s office was not actually all that far from the man’s apartment. The inside of it was sparsely furnished, with a grouping of armchairs that faced each other in the middle of the room. A desk was in the corner, by the window, with certificates and photographs hanging on the wall in frames. A large fern was spreading its leaves in one of the corners.

“So, Doc.” Daniel was slouched in one of the chairs, foot already tapping at the floor. “What lovely thing are you going to make me talk about today?”

“Up to you.” Dr. White was sitting primly in the chair across from him, legs crossed and her little notepad in her lap. “We could talk about Hershey, if you’d like. Or El Paso. We could talk about Buck, or your parents. Or we could pick back up with Officer-”

“Or we could not,” Daniel snapped. “We talked about him last time.”

“And talking about him upset you,” was her needless observation. Daniel hated it. “Where did you go afterwards?”

He furrowed his brows and frowned at her.

“Where did I go?”

“After our time ended,” she clarified. “When you left here, where did you go? What did you do?”

“I went to Austin’s,” he answered after a moment.

“Why?” she asked. “You could’ve gone home. Or you could’ve gone to your sister.”

He shrugged, refusing to give the answer. Dr. White just sat there patiently, however, and the room fell into a silence broken only by the extra loud ticking of the clock on the wall.. Finally, he sighed and, not looking at her, said,

“He’s safe. I guess.”

“Safe, how?”

“I don’t know, he just is,” Daniel snapped. “He doesn’t keep asking questions like that, for one.”

“You’ve called him an asshole before,” Dr. White reminded him.

“Because he is an asshole. It’s his fault I’m doing this.”

“Is that the only reason he’s an asshole?”

“No.” He couldn’t help but scoff. “The guy will sit there and eavesdrop on the people around him, and then he’ll turn around and talk shit about them. Funny shit, but still. And half of what comes out of his mouth is sarcasm.”

“So if he is such an asshole,” Dr. White said, “why was it him that you went to after we spent a session talking about Officer Drake?”

“It just- It just was, okay?” Daniel gritted out. “I don’t know, it’s Austin.”

She let out a low hum.

“You know, you’ve talked a little about him before, but I’m not sure you’ve told me how the two of you met. I’m not even sure you’ve clearly said what you are to each other.”

Daniel eyed her, not quite trusting the sudden change in topic.

“I’m his fake boyfriend,” he told her with a shrug.

“Fake boyfriend,” she repeated.

“Yeah. His mom kept trying to set him up with people,” Daniel explained. “And one day, he was complaining to me about it - again - and I offered to pretend to be his boyfriend. I mean, it wasn’t that different to what I did before.”

“And why did he need a fake partner, instead of a real one?”

“Because he’s not interested in any of that,” he said. “I’ve seen women and men both try to flirt with him, he just doesn’t notice. Doesn’t care. I know he’s explained to his parents that he’s ace, but they just never really got it, I guess.”

Dr. White nodded, pen moving across her notepad. Daniel scowled at it.

“And how long have you two been… Pretending?” she asked.

“Four years.” He saw her eyebrow raise up high and his scowl deepened. “Shut up.”

“I didn’t say anything.”

Daniel’s scoff was not kind.

“How did this… Arrangement? I think I’ll call it an arrangement,” Dr. White said. “How did this come about?”

“Are we just going to talk about Austin for the entire hour?” he asked in turn.

“Unless there’s something else you’d like to talk about.”

There wasn’t, actually, and Daniel didn’t much mind talking about Austin. It was probably one of the safest topics they could focus on. Definitely preferable to prodding the ghost of Officer Drake again. 

“It started as a joke,” he said. “His mom was trying to set him up with someone for Valentine’s…”

“I can’t believe you called me while you were at a scene.”

Buck stuck the tamales from Isabel, each one wrapped in foil, into the oven to be reheated. Eddie had arrived with them just as he promised, and Buck practically tore them out of his hands. He hadn’t even remembered to actually greet his boyfriend until he was halfway across the apartment, where he turned and went back to kiss him hello.

“Hey, Chimney called Bobby about the guy stuck in the chocolate,” Eddie reminded him. He’d taken a seat at the table, spreading himself out like he owned the place. “And no one else was coming up with any ideas.”

“I ain’t complaining about my genius being recognized,” Buck said, chuckling at Eddie’s scoff, and set a time on his phone for the tamales. “So, did you get a new probie?”

“No, that was some kid that worked at the bowling alley,” Eddie answered. Buck nodded. “Hey, uh… How’s Josh?”

A few days ago, Josh had been attacked and mugged while on a date with a guy he’d met online. Even worse, it had been the guy he was on the date with that had done it. Maddie told Danny and Buck, and Buck, of course, told Eddie. According to her, Josh never did give the cops much of a statement. He was apparently embarrassed and simply wanted to put it behind him.

“He’s fine, already back at work,” Buck answered.

“So, was it just a mugging?” Eddie asked. He sounded kinda hesitant. “Or…?”

“Pretty sure it was just a mugging. This wasn’t like Timothy.”

Timothy was a kid that went to the same high school as them in El Paso, for all of maybe three months. Buck didn’t even remember his last name, however much he sometimes thought to look him up and see how he was doing. Timothy was homeschooled and sheltered, something that already offset him from the rest of the student body in ways not entirely dissimilar to skinny fourteen year old Evan.

Unlike skinny fourteen year old Evan, Timothy knew that he liked the other boys the same way that the other boys liked girls, and he hadn’t been shy about admitting it. Unfortunately, the other kids had not been kind about it, and he ended up transferring to another school by Halloween. What happened to him was a huge reason why Eddie, and by extension, Buck, had been so reluctant to come out as a teenager. That, and his parents.

“Good. That’s good,” Eddie said, and then, “Not that being mugged is good, I mean…”

“Usually it’s me tasting my own foot,” Buck teased.

“Shut up. Hey, did you guys get called out for anything fun?”

“There was a guy that got impaled by his toilet.”

Eddie stared at him, and then slowly tilted his head.

“Explain,” he requested.

“Okay, so he was uh- He was sitting on his throne, right? Holding court.” Buck ignored his boyfriend’s amused snort at the euphemism. “And the whole thing just shattered beneath him.”

Eddie blanched in horror and he let out a emphatic,

“Qué chingados.”

“When we got there, the poor guy was lying on the ground with his pants still around his ankles. And there was this giant piece of porcelain sticking out of his left ass cheek,” Buck continued, indicating the size with his hands. “Mehta made me check all the toilets in the station  afterwards.”

“Probably a good thing,” Eddie said. “I like your ass too much for it to be stabbed by a toilet.”

“You just say the sweetest things.”

Chapter 6

Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

“But am I happy?” Chimney’s question sounded rhetorical to Eddie. The two of them, along with Hen, were in the locker room and pulling on their uniforms for the start of their shift. “Albert’s annoying, but maybe he’s right.”

Apparently, the night prior, Chimney interrupted Albert and a lady guest on the couch. Hen found it absolutely hilarious, much to Chimney’s displeasure and Eddie’s embarrassment, because months ago, Danny had oh-so-graciously shared with her the story of when he walked in on Buck and Eddie in the same situation as teenagers. But somehow, Chimney finding Albert mid-coiitus led to a conversation with his brother about his relationship with Maddie.

“Things with me and Maddie are great,” Chimney continued. “But we’re not exactly lighting the world on fire.”

“Does it matter what he thinks?” Eddie asked him, shrugging on his button-up and smoothing out the collar. “Only you know how you feel about Maddie.”

“I really care about her.”

The statement got a groan from Hen, sitting on one of the benches.

“The dreaded C-word. I really care about good arch support,” she said, with a demonstrative gesture to her boots that she had been lacing up. “That is not how you feel about your significant other.”

“Obviously, I care about her more than good footwear,” Chimney said.

“Okay, how much more?” Hen asked him.

“A lot,” he answered, straddling the other bench.

“Do you love her?” Eddie asked.

Chimney gave a small nod and an even smaller,

“Yeah.”

“Does she love you?”

“It’s unclear,” he said. Eddie paused in the process of doing up the buttons of his shirt to share a look with Hen. “I mean, I feel like she does. But neither of us have actually said those exact words out loud.”

Hen scoffed and said,

“You’ve been together for, like, a year.”

“Technically, we have been dating for ten months and three weeks.”

“So you’ve been together for, like, a year,” she repeated, making them laugh.

“With everything she’s been through, y’know, that we’ve been through,” Chimney said. “We just wanted to take it slow.”

This time it was Eddie’s turn to scoff at the man.

“Glaciers move faster, Chim,” Hen said.

“They’re also melting,” Chimney shot back. “So maybe fiery is overrated.”

Austin stepped into the locker room then, face as inscrutable as ever.

“Reynolds wants us to do a lineup,” he told them.

“Are you actually going to be there?” Chimney asked. The driver-engineer just shrugged and left. “He never showed when I called for lineups.”

“He’s probably not going to show for this one, either. He knows how to disappear in this place.” Hen got up with a sigh and headed for the door. “I can’t believe Cap left us with this guy.”

“I wasn’t gonna do it again.” Chimney got up to follow Hen to where everyone else was waiting, right outside in the truck bay. But when Eddie called his name, right when he reached the door, he stopped and turned. “Yeah?”

“I get wanting to take things slow,” Eddie said, walking up to him. “I didn’t tell Buck how I felt about him, the first time around. I was too scared. And after he left, after I ruined everything, I didn’t think I’d ever have the chance. Maddie’s here today, but you don’t know about tomorrow. So if you love her, tell her.”

Chimney was just kinda staring, so Eddie gave him a nod and a pat on the shoulder before going out to join the lineup. Somehow, in that short window of time, Austin did very much manage to disappear. He didn’t show back up until they were dismissed, reappearing almost instantly and looking for all the world like he’d been there the entire time.

Eddie was sorely tempted to ask him for pointers.

“I love you.”

Buck paused in the motion of washing the engine, dropping his arm to his side and the sponge into the bucket. He could feel the smile stretching across his face.

“I love you, too,” he responded. “Did you call me just to say that?”

“Not just,” Eddie said. “I’m also sharing gossip with you. Maybe complain a little.”

“Oh, then please.” Buck leaned against the engine, careful to stick to a dry portion. He felt warm all over, and it had nothing to do with the California sun shining down on him. “Go ahead. Gossip and complain away.”

“Okay, first. Where the hell does Austin go when he disappears?”

Buck burst out laughing.

“I don’t actually know,” he admitted. “I never really paid attention before. Why?”

“Reynolds had us do a lineup at the start of shift-”

“And Austin was magically nowhere to be found.”

“Yup. There one moment, gone the next.”

“Well there’s your complaining.” Buck glanced about, making sure no one - making sure Danny - wasn’t about to come over and get on him about not doing his chores. “What’s the gossip?”

“Chimney walked in on Albert and a guest on the couch,” Eddie said, laughing along with Buck. “And then Chimney started questioning his relationship with your sister.”

That had Buck straightening up and looking around anxiously.

“Should… Should I be worried?” he asked. “Do I need to hide the bat?”

“Nah, he asked her out on a date. I think.” Eddie sounded unsure. “He came out of the ambulance covered in blood and immediately called her, so… I don’t really know what happened there. I’m not sure I want to. All I know is that I just spent the last hour helping clean up the mess. And that he’s been upbeat ever since.”

“Okay, good.” Buck relaxed back against the truck again. “I don’t think Danny would go off, but…”

“Yeah, no. No repeats, please.” Eddie chuckled a little. “Hey, uh. You’re not doing anything when you get off shift tomorrow, are you?”

“Nope. Why?”

“Wanna get lunch? Chris’ll be there, so it won’t be anything too fancy. Some place that offers chicken tenders.”

“I’m always down for chicken tenders,” Buck said. “But are you sure you won’t need a nap after work, old man?”

“Respect your elders.”

They were both still laughing as they said their goodbyes and their I-love-yous. Buck let out a happy sigh, staring at his phone. And then someone cleared their throat behind him, making him jump and screech. It was absolutely a manly screech, though. Very masculine.

Danny did not seem very impressed with him when he turned around.

“Lookin’ real busy there, squirt.”

“I’ve been working,” Buck lied, bending back down to pick up the sponge.

“Oh, yeah. Totally.” Danny ran his finger down the side of the truck. “You’re supposed to be making the lady shine. Making her glitter. There’s still dirt on the wheel well, c’mon.”

Buck glanced over and spotted what his brother was talking about.

“I just haven’t gotten to that yet.”

“This lady deserves your respect and your full attention, Buck,” Danny lectured. “You shouldn’t be neglecting her to flirt with your boyfriend, you’ll hurt her feelings.”

“You are so weird.” Buck rolled his eyes at his brother, bending down slightly to scrub at that spot of dirt. “Do you want me to leave you and the lady alone? Because I can. I might tell Austin that you’re cheating on him with a municipal vehicle, though.”

“Austin’ll understand. He knows not to get between a man and his fire truck. That’s a sacred bond, right there.”

“You are so weird,” Buck repeated.

“Remember, she’s a lady.” Danny gave him a pat on the back before heading off again, back inside the station. “She deserves to shine!”

“So weird!”

His brother just laughed.

The period of time in El Paso after Buck left for his Neverending Gap Year Road Trip was a special type of awful for a myriad of reasons. The fact that Daniel was suddenly and terribly alone, as he had never been before, was the biggest and most unavoidable of them. His brother’s absence at the time was an open wound, reopened every time he stepped into his apartment to find it silent and empty. 

Daniel spent many an afternoon and evening next door, at Alma’s, simply because he did not want to be home alone, where he was constantly reminded that his baby brother was so far away. Without her, he wasn’t entirely certain how he would’ve made it through those months between Christmases. Or how he would’ve made it through the Christmas that Buck didn’t come back at all.

All of that to say that Daniel was perfectly content to have Buck keep living with him, and was perfectly happy to ignore their sister’s occasional sideways remark about it. Sure, sometimes he was a pain, sometimes he acted like a puppy that hadn’t learned his manners yet, but leftovers disappearing from the fridge and wet towels left on the floor of the bathroom and the occasional dish left in the sink was entirely worth it. Because Buck was there, and not hundreds or thousands of miles away.

There were times, though, Daniel was grateful when Buck wasn’t quite as physically present as he could be. Because Buck was horribly curious, always had been, and there was no way that Daniel would manage to get out of the apartment dressed as he was - black on black on black, a crew neck under a suit jacket with matching pants - without being subjected to an inquisition. And he really, really didn’t want to explain where he was going, and with who, to Buck. Mostly because Buck would probably tell Maddie and getting the third degree from her would be several magnitudes worse, combined as it would be with sisterly concern.

Tonight, Daniel was finally taking Mehta up on his poker invitation, and he was dragging Austin along with him. Back in the day, they used to meet up at a bar to drink and talk shit, before it turned into going over to one of the other’s apartments and staying in. Austin wasn’t the type to go out much, and Daniel was perfectly fine just hanging out with him wherever. So it had been a while since Daniel went out and did something, much less dressed up to do it.

Probably that last date with Attica, which was… Best not to dwell on how long ago that was, actually.

“I don’t know why I agreed to this,” Austin said as he climbed into Daniel’s car. “I’m already regretting it.”

Daniel, too, was already having regrets. Definitely not for the same reasons as Austin, though. Because he’d never seen Austin dressed fancy before. He’d seen him in uniform and in turnouts, in day-to-day outfits, in sweats and a t-shirt that was more hole than fabric. But not in a suit and tie: the former was a light gray, the latter striped in alternating shades of the same color, and the shirt beneath the jacket was a blue so dark that Daniel mistook it for black at first.

Austin looked very, very good in it, and Daniel was very, very screwed.

“Um, yeah,” he blurted out, once he found his voice again. “Uh. You said it sounded fun. Remember?”

“No, you said it sounded fun,” Austin retorted. “I went temporarily insane.”

That made two of ‘em, Daniel thought as he started driving again. Driving was good, it meant he had to keep his eyes on the road instead of letting them linger on Austin.

The poker game was being held at Don Rivera’s Mexican Grill. He followed Mehta’s instructions, parking and leading Austin around back to the delivery entrance. When he checked over his shoulder, he saw the other man glancing about with a slight frown.

“I feel like I’m in some bad mobster movie,” Austin commented.

“Nah, everything’s on the up-and-up,” Daniel assured him. “Trust me, a restaurant run by the cartel would look totally different.”

“And you know this, how?”

Daniel shot him a grin and knocked on the door.

“I was very pretty arm candy,” he told him.

The alarm buzzed and the door opened, revealing a bored looking member of the kitchen staff. He didn’t say anything, just jerked his head at the two of them before turning and leading them inside. They had to walk through the kitchen, which was thankfully not filled with busy cooks, and walk down a very short set of steps to get to the dining area.

“This looks like a speakeasy.” Austin stepped out of the way as they guy they’d been following, his job done, returned to the back. Either to do his actual job, or because he was supposed to wait on more guests. “Are you sure your captain isn’t in the mob?”

“Fairly certain.”

The whole thing did have the air of some illegal den from the golden days, though. Daniel wouldn’t be surprised if he had been a speakeasy in a previous life. The wall by the way they just came in was taken up almost entirely by the bar, with shelves and shelves of liquors and wines. There were booths tucked away along the edges, lit up by lamps with soft glows. There were old photographs hanging up, dozens of them.

In the middle was the poker table. Mehta was already sitting at it, along with the dealer and one of the battalion chiefs, Williams. It was weird to see the captain in a suit and tie; it was even weirder to see Williams made up in a deep red dress that sparkled when she moved.

“Jones!?” A woman’s voice, sounding shocked. The owner, wearing a bright green cocktail dress, made their way towards them. An androgynous figure in a suit sedately followed. “The hell are you doing here?”

“Hey Rosen, Crawford.” Austin nodded to each of them in turn, probably for Daniel’s benefit.

“According to Wilson and Han, you’ve dodged every invite to go out for drinks after shift,” the woman, Rosen, said. “But here you are, with… Who is he? Who are you?”

“Dan!” Mehta called, answering the question. “You made it!”

“Dan,” Crawford, the androgynous one, repeated. “Oh, the guy that came in and yelled at Nash. Buckley’s brother.”

“That’s me.” Daniel stepped past them, going for the poker table and shaking first the chief’s and then his captain’s hands. “Hey Cap, Chief.”

“Glad to see you could make it,” Mehta said. “And with a friend.”

“That’s Austin. He’s convinced this is a mob thing.”

The man in question gave them both a nod as he took a seat, ignoring Rosen’s gaze burning a hole in the side of his head. The dealer was already distributing stacks of chips to everyone and Daniel was thankful that his recent misadventure with the game refreshed his memory, because otherwise he wouldn’t remember which color was which value. It was a good thing this was a low-stakes game, or else he’d be pretty screwed.

“Oh no.” Williams smiled as she picked up one of the white chips and flipped it between her fingers. “Now we’re going to have to kill you.”

“She’s joking,” Mehta said.

“Am I?”

“She is.”

Austin glanced between them and then just shrugged, appearing entirely unperturbed.

It took only two hands for Mehta and Williams to start grinning like sharks every time they glanced Daniel’s way. It would’ve had him bristling, maybe, except he came into this fully expecting to crash and burn. The glass of whiskey that found its way beside his elbow also helped. He ended up folding not too long after, bowing out as his captain crowed and Rosen jeered. 

Austin, though, was doing significantly better than him. Not because he was particularly good at the game, but because his face just gave absolutely nothing away. Daniel leaned against the back of Austin’s chair, laughing as Williams’ scowl deepened further and further as she found herself incapable of figuring out if Austin was bluffing or not. The fact that the man remained mostly silent, allowing them to talk around him but not joining in, was probably as much of a factor as the constant expression of polite boredom that he was wearing.

“The next time Maddie invites me to a game,” Daniel said, voice low and head bent down so he was speaking directly into Austin’s ear, “I am dragging you with me.”

“Only if you come with me to the baby showers,” Austin shot back, casually putting a small stack of the blue chips in the pot. “Raise ten.”

Williams stared at him, looking very much like she was about to burst a blood vessel with the strain of it, before placing her own stack of chips and gritting out,

“Call.”

The chief let out a sigh of relief when, after Mehta called as well, she won the hand. The last round, she’d folded only for Austin to reveal cards that sucked, or at least that was what Daniel gathered from everyone else’s disgusted reactions. It was just apparently really hard for them to figure out if Austin was raising the stakes because he actually had a good hand or because he was fucking with them, and that was starting to get to the other players. Or at least to Williams.

Crawford, at the other end of the table, was silently laughing their ass off. Probably because they’d figured out what Daniel already knew: that Austin was always fucking with them, and actually winning had long ago become secondary.

The battalion chief seemed entirely too happy to see the backs of them when the game came to a close, which was especially rude considering that Austin didn’t even win in the end. Daniel wouldn’t be surprised to learn that she made a beeline for the bar, because Austin just had that effect on some people. It was one of the many, many reasons that Daniel- Well.

“Y’know, back in the day, I always looked forward to nights like this.” Daniel purposely bumped into Austin as they headed for the car, trying to keep his thoughts from falling into that particular pitfall. “I’d get to dress up and go somewhere fancy and drink something fancy. On the best nights, I didn’t have to do anything, because all they wanted was arm candy. I mean, I usually ended up finding someone else, because Evan was already taken care of for the night and the extra cash helped, but still. It was nice. But none of them looked as hot in a suit as you.”

Austin frowned at him.

“How drunk are you?” he asked.

“Uh.” Daniel thought about it. After that whiskey, he’d seen the brightly colored drink that Crawford had and decided to try one, and then that one became two. And then, after that…  “...Drunk.”

The other man silently held out his hand. Daniel dutifully gave him his keys. It was far from the first time Daniel crashed on Austin’s couch, and it definitely wouldn’t be the last.

Buck had not been home for long before his brother was coming in through the door. He’d noticed the car missing from its designated spot and wondered what was up with that. Now, seeing Danny’s squinty eyed glare at the sunlight coming in through the window and the man still dressed in what had to be last night’s clothes, given the pants and the suit jacket tossed over his shoulder, Buck…Actually still had no idea what his brother could’ve been up to.

This looked like a post-date walk of pride, to him, but that didn’t really fit with the understanding he walked away with from Hen’s impromptu lecture on QPRs. Did Austin and Danny have dates? Dates struck him as rather non-platonic, so…

“Late night or early morning?” Buck asked him, going through the motions of getting the coffee machine going.

“Both,” Danny told him. He tossed his suit jacket onto the couch and then collapsed into a seat at the kitchen table, pillowing his head on his arms. “Austin got woken up this morning by his brother-in-law because Cynthia’s having a freakout about… Something.”

“When is she due?”

“Uh.” Danny lifted his head up, face scrunched up in thought. “End of May. I think. Or maybe that’s his sister-in-law.”

“Y’know, a good fake boyfriend would remember that kind of thing.”

“Shut up. Hangovers are so much worse after you hit thirty, squirt.”

“I’ll remember that,” Buck told him. His phone began to chime in his pocket and he pulled it out, not even glancing at the screen before answering it with, “Go for Buck.”

Danny snorted at the greeting, and got glared at for it.

“How come Nine-One-One doesn’t respond when I call?” Chimney asked him.

“Uh.” Buck was caught off guard by the question, and found himself stumbling for an answer. “Is that some kind of riddle? Like, ‘who watches the Watchmen?’”

“That’s not a riddle, Buck,” Danny said.

“Neither of those things are riddles,” Chimney said at the same time. Buck made a face at them both, though only one was there to see it. “Okay, I just tried calling Nine-One-One and got the high call volume message. Did I miss an earthquake?”

“No, pretty chill morning,” Buck told him. He put his phone on speaker and set it on the counter before grabbing a pair of mugs from the cabinet. “Why are you calling Nine-One-One? Is everything okay?”

“Your sister said that she loved me.”

“Okay?” Buck poured both himself and his brother their coffee, adding a small mound of sugar to each one. “The way Eddie told it, that was the whole point of the big date last night. Wasn’t it? You declare your love and she declares hers?”

He turned around to give Danny his coffee and caught him scowling. Buck just rolled his eyes and set the mug in front of him.

“But it didn’t happen last night,” Chimney said. “She made a big deal of it, saying that she couldn’t say those words. And then this morning she just blurts it out over the phone and hangs up on me.”

“Still doesn’t quite sound like an emergency.”

It definitely sounded weird, though. Maybe a little concerning. And Danny was definitely thinking the same, Buck could tell that just from the way his brows were pinched together. Or maybe that was the hangover.

“Because I sound insane. She’s at the call center, what could happen there. Right? You know what? Forget it.”

Chimney hung up before Buck could get another word in edgewise. There was silence as Buck and Danny stared at each other, and then they were both going for their phones.

“I’ll try Maddie,” Buck said.

“I’ll try Josh,” Danny said.

But much like when Chimney had tried, neither one of them answered.

Chapter End Notes
