Chapter 7

Chapter Notes

Happy (maybe late) Halloween!

See the end of the chapter for more notes

The longer that Maddie went without texting anything as little as an emoji, the more anxious Buck got about the possibilities. Danny, too, was feeling it: Buck lost track of the number of times his brother tried calling their sister, Josh, even Sue. When Buck’s phone rang, they both jumped like startled cats, feeling slightly disappointed that it was just Chimney.

“She still hasn’t replied,” the paramedic said. “I’m gonna head to dispatch.”

“Okay, hold on-”

“Do not try and talk me out of this,” Chimney told him, sounding understandably testy. “I need to go down there for myself and make sure she’s okay.”

“Yeah, no, I- I get that,” Buck hurried to assure him. “She hasn’t picked up for us either. Josh is going straight to voicemail.”

“Now I’m definitely going.”

“What if something is wrong? Maybe we should call the police.” Buck rolled his eyes at his brother when the man scoffed. “Or at least Athena.”

“...better.”

On the other end of the line, he could hear Chimney opening his door. And then Chimney said,

“I think someone already beat you there, Buckaroo.”

“What does that mean?” Buck demanded to know, but the other man didn’t respond. Not to him, anyway, because he was talking to someone. To- “Is that Athena? Chimney, is Athena there?”

When Danny made sharp gestures at him with his hands, obviously wanting to know what was going on, Buck put his phone on speaker once more. Now they could both hear Chimney and Athena and the explanations being bandied about. Athena was telling him that she was sent there because some lady called about a restaurant putting onions in her omelet when she specifically said she didn’t want any.

Obviously, she’d been sent to the wrong place. Normally, Buck could safely say that it was nothing more than an error somewhere. But to have Athena sent to Chimney’s apartment, on the same day that everyone they knew at dispatch were concerningly radio silent? This was no funny coincidence, this was a flashing neon sign that something was terribly wrong.

“Okay, so, I told her what’s going on,” Chimney finally said, coming back to them.

“And?” Danny demanded.

“And she said she’ll call her captain.”

Buck and Danny shared a scowl.

“And!?” Buck asked this time. “Is she still there?”

“Yeah, yeah, she’s on the phone. She’s waiting for her captain to answer… And now she’s talking to her captain.”

Buck tried to wait patiently, he really did. But as Danny and Eddie and literally everyone else who knew him would say, patience was never one of his strong suits. He broke within only a couple minutes.

“What is she saying now?” he asked.

“She’s making her case,” Chimney answered, and then, “And now she’s folding like a cheap suit.”

“Yeah, no.” Danny was glaring at the phone. “Put her on.”

There was the sound of footsteps, Chimney’s maybe. Athena was talking, her voice getting closer to the receiver.

“Captain needs to make some calls,” the sergeant was telling Chimney. “As evidence goes, an I love you is less than convincing.”

“But they sent you down to my apartment for an assault with a deadly onion,” Chimney pointed out. “That feels more convincing.”

“She’s gonna talk to Operations, see if they can get eyes in the building, figure out if anything’s wrong.”

“No, no, no!” Buck shouted it into the phone, making his poor brother cringe at the volume. “You can’t just send in SWAT. If there is someone inside the call center doing something, they’ll know we’re onto them.”

They hadn’t actually discussed the possibilities for what was going on, but Buck thought a third party doing something nefarious was a good guess. It would explain why dispatch briefly went offline and why they were once again handling 9-1-1 calls now, even as other avenues of communication were failing. It would explain the weird turn in Maddie’s phone call with Chimney. And, most importantly, it would also explain why Athena had been sent to Chimney’s for a nuisance call that had nothing to do with him.

There was no way to know which dispatcher was responsible, but Buck was willing to bet it was either Maddie or Josh. Because there was no way that they just randomly sent Athena, out of the entire police department, to the person who Maddie had been talking to when everything went sideways.

“Let’s go for a drive,” Athena said. “Talk to you later, Buck.”

“What? No, no, Chimney, don’t-” Buck cut himself off as his screen flashed to tell him that the call was dropped. The urge to throw his phone at the wall was very strong, but he managed to crush the impulse.

He looked at Danny; Danny looked at him. And then, together, they rushed for the door, with Danny making sure to grab his bat on the way out.

Buck remembered when Danny taught both him and Eddie how to drive. There’d been times, several of them, where his older brother looked legitimately afraid for his life as he screamed for them to hit the brakes. And he was now starting to understand how his brother felt in that moment, because Danny had thrown all ideas of cautious driving out the window.

They took a sharp turn at an intersection, and Buck was certain that they went up on two wheels for a couple seconds there. He grabbed the oh-shit handle, which was a very apt name for it at the moment, as three different other cars blared their horns at them. His brother just ignored them, eyes focused on the road as he did his best to make the poor little car they were in go a little bit faster.

There was a cop ahead, the space between them quickly eaten up. Buck narrowed his eyes as they got closer, because while it looked like every other LAPD patrol from the back, he’d seen the back of this one often enough to recognize the number decals.

“Pretty sure that’s Athena,” he said, pointing. Like his brother was liable to miss the car right in front of them.

“She needs to drive faster,” Danny said. And then he swerved around and cut her off.

“I don’t think she’s gonna like that.” Buck twisted around in his seat as sirens came to life behind them, audible over the wind that whipped through their open windows. He could see Athena and Chimney through the windshield of the other vehicle, better and better as she caught up to their speed, and the expression on her face made him shudder. “Yeah, she’s not happy.”

He waved at them. Chimney waved back. Athena, Buck was pretty sure, started glaring at them even harder from behind her shades. He looked over to his brother, who was showing no signs of slowing down.

“Um. Are you going to pull over?” he asked Danny.

“Wasn’t planning on it. Why?”

“Because I think she might start shooting at us if we don’t.”

Danny glanced into the rear view mirror and let out a sigh, like what was being asked of him was some great imposition. He hit the blinkers and casually came to a stop on the curb. Athena parked not far behind them, getting out and stomping to the driver’s side window. Her presence, when she reached them, was more imposing than it would’ve been if they were in the jeep, since the car was so much lower to the road.

“What can I do for you, officer?” Danny asked, resting one arm on the door and the other on the steering wheel.

“Get the hell out here before I arrest you both,” Athena snapped. “You can join Chimney.”

Buck threw open his door and scrambled to do as she ordered. Danny was a bit slower with it, taking the time to roll up the windows and turn off the car before stepping out. When he went to the back, to no doubt go for his bat, the sergeant stopped him,

“Oh, I don’t think so,” she said, blocking his way. “I can guess what’s in there, and you’re not bringing it.”

“Do we really have time to be arguing about this?” Danny asked, moving around her to open the door. Athena slammed it shut again before he could get it open very far.

“No, we don’t,” she said. “So you should get moving.”

Buck watched as his brother glared at the sergeant for one moment, then two, before throwing his hands up and marching for Athena’s cruiser, using his keyfob to lock the car. When they reached Athena’s cruiser, his brother stopped just short of opening the door, expression twisted into something that Buck couldn’t quite identify. Then, with a glance at Chimney in the front, Danny climbed into the back. 

“Did you tell anyone else what’s happening at the call center?” Athena asked, once she was back behind the wheel. Chimney and Buck both shook their heads; Danny was looking out the window, posture stiff. “Good, ‘cause I’m not sure we can fit anyone else back there.”

They got back on the road, no one speaking as they got closer to the dispatch center. Buck found his leg bouncing with nerves, though he was careful not to jostle the back of Athena’s seat with it. The last thing he wanted was to annoy her even more.

When they arrived, the sergeant pulled them into a little bay area not far from the front door.

“Okay, we’re here,” Chimney said, turning slightly to look at Athena. “Now what?”

“If everything’s normal, I’ll be able to walk through the front and go inside,” Athena said, unbuckling. “Take a look around, see if everyone forgot to change their damn cell phone.”

“And if it’s not normal?” Buck asked her, leaning forward a bit.

“I guess we’ll find out,” she told him, setting her shades on the dashboard before getting out.

The silence that followed her departure was heavy, and it did nothing good for Buck’s nerves. He unbuckled as well, twisting around and sitting up in his seat to watch Athena as she left the little bay, turning the corner to go for the front door. Even then, he didn’t turn back around.

“So.” Chimney was not doing any better with the silence. “Dan. You’re looking dressed up.”

Right, Buck had forgotten about that. Danny was still wearing the clothes he’d walked into the apartment in that morning, though he’d left the suit jacket behind. He didn’t answer right away, not until Buck poked the side of his face.

“Oh, yeah,” Danny said, batting at Buck’s finger. “I went to a thing last night.”

“A thing,” Chimney repeated.

“Are you okay?” Buck asked him, managing to worry about two different things at once.

“Yeah, I’m fine,” his brother answered. “Hangover.”

Buck narrowed his eyes and stared at him for a moment, before deciding to take his answer at face value. It was a decision helped by the fact that Athena was returning. She seemed unbothered, not exactly hurrying like someone with a gun was on her heels. But the moment she got back into the cruiser, her face dropped into a mask of seriousness.

“Well?” Chimney nudged, when the sergeant didn’t say anything.

“Sit back, Buck,” was all Athena said as she pulled the cruiser out and put them back on the road. Her words were clipped, and Buck had the horrible feeling that they were all right to be worried.

“Athena, what happened?” Danny asked.

She shook her head at him in the rearview mirror before pulling out her phone. Buck wasn’t certain who she was calling, until she was greeting her captain. And then she was informing her captain that the dispatch center was being held hostage.

“I’m sure. They knew I was downstairs,” she said into the phone. “They’re using the CAD to monitor our locations… That was Sue Blevins on the radio giving me the code seventy-seven. Whoever's running this, they’re doing it from the inside.”

Buck wondered what Athena’s captain said to that, because she was hanging up shortly after that ominous statement. She didn’t look angry or frustrated, though, or at least no more than she did before the call. He was choosing to believe that it was a productive conversation, even if he could only hear one side of it.

“What’s a code seventy-seven?” Chimney asked the moment the phone was lowered.

“It’s the code for an officer in danger,” Danny answered. “I think.”

“Possible ambush,” Athena corrected, gazing at him curiously through the rearview mirror. “Proceed with caution.”

“Okay, so- so- so what are we gonna do?” Buck asked, pushing forward to stick his head between the front seats. 

“We aren’t going to do anything,” the sergeant told him. She took a turn, pulling into the parking lot of some store. “Right now, I’m going to disable the GPS.”

She reached down and popped the hood, before hopping out. The rest of them scrambled to do the same as she went and opened the car hood entirely. Danny went to join her, looking genuinely curious about what she was doing.

“I’m guessing it’s something similar to what they use for the fire engine,” he said, bent down a little to look. “How are you gonna turn it off?”

“By yanking out something important,” was Athena’s simple answer as she reached in, furrowing her brows as she blindly felt around. “Buck, keep an eye on the screen in there, tell me when it does something.”

Buck nodded, and went to lean against the driver side door so he could look through the window. The screen that Athena was talking about was the screen for the on-board computer, which allowed her access to her end of the CAD system. And probably did other stuff, Buck wasn’t sure. At the moment, it showed a map of the city streets with their current location and the recent calls that she’d been sent on.

“So what’s the plan?” Chimney asked. Buck glanced over to see him hovering anxiously over the sergeant. “There’s gotta be a plan, right?”

“It’s probably the same plan that they always come up with,” Danny said. He sounded frustrated, probably with the entire situation. “Storm the place with SWAT and just start shooting blindly.”

“No, that- that can’t be the plan,” Chimney protested. “Right?’

Athena didn’t say anything. When Buck looked over, she was glaring at the engine of her cruiser, arm moving around inside it. 

“‘Thena.” His voice was shaking. “That isn’t what they’re gonna do, is it?”

“I don’t know,” the sergeant finally said. She grunted quietly, and then she was pulling a small gray block out of the engine. “Buck?”

Right, his job. He glanced at the screen, seeing that it had thrown up an error message on a blue background.

“It’s off,” he reported.

“Good. Get in,” she said, slamming the hood closed. “I’ll ask Maynard if they’ve decided on a staging area.”

They were all quiet as they got back into the cruiser. Chimney kept shooting Athena anxious looks, while Danny was glaring a hole into the seat in front of him. Even as Athena called her captain again, to ask where they were meeting, the silence remained heavy enough to dampen her words.

The staging area was not too far from the dispatch center itself, just a few blocks away. It was empty when they got there, but it quickly filled up with first responders, both police and firefighters, as well as construction workers. Athena spent much of the time at first on the phone with - or so Buck gathered - other units, since the radios were compromised, sharing how to disable the GPS on their vehicles and where to go after that.

At least Athena, and Captain Maynard, when she arrived, were bothering to keep them mostly in the loop. Enough to tell them that whoever was holding the dispatch center hostage got in because they were pretending to be LAPD that were scheduled for sit-alongs. Enough to confirm that there was a plan, not that they told them about it beyond the fact that they didn’t like it.

The presence of SWAT, though, told Buck that his brother was probably, horribly right.

One of the additions to the staging area that didn’t fit in with everything else was a bus full of random people. He and Danny, along with Chimney, had been tasked with checking in with the fire stations that had arrived, probably to keep them out of Athena and Maynard’s hair. Buck paused on the way to update the two women with the super important information, though, to stare at the bus in confusion.

“How are we doing with those RA units?” Maynard asked when she spotted them, leaving Athena to talk to the guy from one of the neighboring dispatch centers.

“The One Twenty-Two and the One Thirty-Three just got here,” Chimney said, gesturing where their engines and ambulances were parked. Buck didn’t know anyone from the 122, but he recognized Captain Shore and some of the others that were currently on shift from the 133. “There’s two more houses en route.”

“Who are all the people on the bus?” Buck asked.

“Off-duty dispatchers,” Maynard answered. “They’ll handle call response once we take back the building.”

“Take it back?” Chimney asked. “You’re not gonna negotiate, see if they surrender first?”

Danny’s scoff was as derisive as Buck had ever heard it. Maynard scowled up at him for it before responding to Chimney’s questions.

“They haven’t asked for anything or made any demands. They don’t even want us to know that they control the building,” she said. “If we reach out to them, we’ll lose the element of surprise. If we do this right, if we hit ‘em fast, we can take the building before they even know what’s happening.”

“Or,” Danny said, “you fuck up and a bunch of people get shot. Including my sister.”

Maynard’s mouth was drawn into a flat line.

“Yes,” she admitted. “That’s why we asked for as many RA units as we did.”

And then Buck was watching her walk off, like she hadn’t just dropped the worst bomb into their laps. Athena, he’d noticed, was also gone. He had no idea where to, though.

“I fucking hate cops,” Danny spat, filled with so much venomous vitriol that it made Buck and Chimney both flinch. “And I really hope Maddie and them have a better plan.”

With all of the SWAT around, the ambulances that had been called in, and the busful of replacement dispatchers waiting in the wings, Buck found himself hoping the same thing.

Daniel was a mess of nerves by the time that Maynard gave the green light for SWAT to storm the building. He watched, from across the way and behind the yellow caution tape, as they swarmed through the front. They went in, and then a few minutes later paramedics were being requested, with the relief dispatchers just behind them, and he just knew things hadn’t gone the way that they were all hoping.

He held his breath, watching and waiting, as they released everyone that had spent the morning as hostages. People in blue and maroon shirts coming out in a line, hands behind their heads like they were the suspects and not the victims. He spotted Maddie at the same time Chimney, having taken a spot closer to the action, did. He could hear him shouting her name as he ran for her.

Sue had found her way over while Daniel was so focused on the entrance. She was talking to Buck when he went to grab him, saying,

“I’m surprised you’re not over there.”

And Buck, he started to reply, saying,

“She already has-”

But Daniel didn’t particularly care what his brother thought their sister already had. He grabbed him by the arm as he went by, not breaking his stride and making Buck stumble for a bit before he managed to match his pace. Their sister, when they reached her, was hugging Chimney. But Daniel also didn’t particularly care about that, either, as he tugged them apart to hold her at arm's length and look her over.

“Are you okay?” he demanded.

“Yeah, yeah.” She nodded, reached up to wipe at her face. “I’m fine, Dan.”

He let out a breath that trembled. And then he pulled her in close and hugged her tight enough that she was soon complaining about her ribs and her lungs.

Chapter End Notes

Daniel cares not for the narrative's insistence that Maddie's hoes take precedence over her broes.

Chapter 8

Chapter Notes

Listen, guys. I am posting this as polls close and I am Not Okay. Hopefully you're reading this from a beautiful future where everything is rainbows and unicorns, but I am not there right now.

My nerves cannot handle today.

The first sign that the day was not going to be a good one was that Eddie woke up to the other side of the bed being empty and cold. Not that it was an unusual occurrence. In fact, it used to be that he was always waking up that way. But since he and Buck had reconciled, since Buck got out of the cast, since the tsunami, half his mornings had him waking up to… Well, to the other side of the bed being empty, but warm.  

Buck was one of those disgusting, godless people that greeted the start of a new day with a smile. Eddie, meanwhile, always wanted the morning sun to go screw itself while he buried himself under his blankets for another hour or five. Sadly, though, that hadn’t been an option for many a year.

Buck hadn’t stayed over the night before, returning to the apartment just after they had dinner. Because he hadn’t packed an overnight bag as he usually did. Or, more specifically, because they’d argued about the fact that he was still needing to pack an overnight bag before spending the night, about the fact that Buck left barely a trace of himself here. A toothbrush, the occasional clothes that got mixed in with Eddie’s laundry that were inevitably gathered up and taken back.

It hadn’t been much of an argument, their voices barely raised with how conscious they were of Chris in the house. The seeds of it were planted by a comment Carla had made to Eddie the other day, about how Buck hadn’t spread himself all over the place in the same way he had Abby’s. Something about Abby’s medicine cabinet being taken over by hair products. Carla was laughing about it at the time, because to her the comparison was funny.

It hadn’t been much of an argument, because they both knew why Buck always left with almost everything he brought over. But it still kinda sucked to have it thrown into his face as yet another example of how Buck’s trust in him, in their relationship, was still shaky and hesitant. Eddie didn’t know what he could do to prove himself to Buck beyond what he had already done. 

Anyway, waking up alone was the first sign that the day wasn’t going to be a good one. An easily dismissed sign, at that, especially since it wasn’t like the universe was a conscious entity that threw out warnings like that. Buck would disagree with that statement if Eddie said it aloud, but it didn’t make it any less true.

The second sign - if there were signs, of which there weren’t - came with Carla and Chris’ surprise visit to the station, after they just got done testing the radios.

“Five-alarm school emergency,” Carla explained when Eddie met them in the middle of the bay, between the trucks and the space under the loft. “He’s supposed to tell Ms. Flores what he’s presenting for show and tell on Friday.”

“And so he sucked you into stopping here on the way,” Eddie guessed, shooting his son a mock glare. Chris grinned up at him, innocent as could be.

“You know I can’t resist a cute face,” Carla said.

“Okay. Show and tell.” He hunched down a bit to be closer to eye level with his son. “I thought you were bringing your new hamster.”

Buck had campaigned for Chris to bring in the skateboard set-up that he and Danny had put together. Because Eddie’s boyfriend could be a very petty man when he wanted to be. Eddie was kinda thankful that Chris decided against that, because he wasn’t certain how they’d get the thing into Ms. Flores’ classroom. Nor did he particularly want to provoke the woman like that while she was still his son’s teacher.

“The hamster is old news,” Carla informed him, reaching into her large purse hanging from her arm. “Somebody’s been snooping in your closet.”

She pulled out a small box that he was unfortunately very familiar with. He didn’t need to open it to know what was inside, though he did anyway. The Silver Star seemed to mock him.

“This is what you want to bring to show and tell?” Eddie asked.

“‘Cause you’re a hero,” Chri said, smiling up at him.

The words made Eddie’s gut clench.

“We don’t need jewelry to know that,” Carla said, squeezing Chris’ shoulder.

“You’re sure this is what you want to bring to school on Friday?” Eddie tried.

“Yeah!” Chris nodded, curls bouncing. “And you can tell the story.”

“I’m…” He looked to Carla, and got no support from that corner. “I’m not sure that’s a story I can tell a bunch of fourth graders, Chris.”

“Please, Dad,” Chris begged. “Please?”

Someday, Eddie would have to ask for pointers from Danny on how to be strong and say “no” in these instances. Or, on second thought, maybe not Danny. He remembered the way the man would cave to Buck each and every time, just like Eddie was about to do now with Chris.

“Okay,” he sighed, prompting his son to cheer. “I’ll figure something out.”

“You promise?”

Above, the alarm let out its shrill ring and the entire station burst into motion, everyone sprinting for their gear.

“Yes, yes, I promise. You and me, Friday morning, telling fourth grade appropriate war stories.” Eddie headed for the engine, turned slightly so he was walking backwards. “Love you, Chris! And Carla! Remember-”

“To Buck’s after school!” Carla cut him off. “I remember!”

The pair waved as Eddie pulled on his turnouts and then climbed into the cab, and they kept waving until the trucks were out of the bay and on the road.

The call was the third of the signs that the day was not going to be a good one. Bobby didn’t give them many details as they sped off, heading for a farm. What he did share was that it involved a child, and that they were meeting Athena there. 

They pulled up into the yard of the farmhouse, dirt kicked up into the air by the wheels of two fire trucks and an ambulance, their sirens breaking what would otherwise be tranquil silence. Athena’s patrol car was already there; when they jumped out, Bobby made a beeline for the farmhouse proper, the others close on his heels. The sergeant met him halfway.

“What do we got?” the captain asked her.

“Missing boy. Two kids playing in an open field. Mom calls them home, only one shows up. It sounded like an abduction - the road’s not too far, so it made sense.” Athena led them into the house. The mother was huddled in a chair, young daughter in her lap. “But then I’m interviewing the mother, asking the usual questions, and then I saw this photo that came with the house.”

The photo was an old one, sepia toned, displayed on a table with various other photos depicting the small family. In the photo was an antique truck, which was probably fairly new at the time the picture was taken, in front of a windmill.

“The windmill was torn down years ago,” Athena said, pointing at it. “But it used to power a water pump.”

There was a collective in-take of breath at the statement. Because none of them were idiots, because they could all connect the dots. Because suddenly they understood what had happened to the smiling boy in the family portrait.

They dispersed from the farmhouse immediately, spreading out in all directions as they looked for the old, abandoned well that the kid must’ve fallen down. As everyone shouted out the boy’s name - “Hayden! Hayden!” - in the hopes of receiving a reply, Eddie went to the small fenced in garden just on the other side of the trucks.

The gate was ajar, he noticed. Like someone went through and carelessly pulled it behind them, not paying attention to whether or not it latched. And there, too, in the dirt: a tiny little toy tank, looking lost and neglected by itself. There was another gate in the fence on the other side of the garden, this one also ajar. 

Eddie went through it, after making a stop to pick up the toy. It looked like the farm’s personal junkyard. There were scrap parts, wheels and shelves and even an engine of some sort.  There were metal barrels, empty, with one tipped over on its side. There were boards of plywood.

There was a shoe print on the plywood. A small one, child sized. There was another one, the other foot. And then something circular sticking out of the ground.

“Guys!” Eddie shouted as he dropped the tank and started clearing the detritus out of the way. “Over here! Give me a hand!”

The others came sprinting over, and Eddie heard Chimney giving Bobby an update over the radio. Together, they managed to get all the junk cleared away, giving them a better view of what they were working with. The well was a metal pipe just barely sticking out of the ground. There was no way, Eddie thought, that it was big enough for a kid to fall down.

And there was no response when he called down.

Space on both the engine and the ladder was at a premium, reserved for gear that they needed on the most common of calls and some of the uncommon ones. Rarely did they require a camera that could snake down a hole, and so they didn’t have it on the trucks. Bobby radioed for it, and it arrived in the back of a captain’s truck.

Once they got the set-up going, with a wheel of cable attached to a screen in the back of the truck, Eddie huddled around the screen with the others as Chimney and Austin lowered the camera. Chimney called out the distance every five feet, their hopes diminished as the number increased.

“We’re at forty feet, Cap,” Chimney said. “We’ve only got fifty feet of cable.”

“Can a boy even survive a fall that far?” Athena asked, peering over Bobby’s shoulder with the rest of them.

“The well’s narrow, so there’s lots of friction to slow a fall,” Hen said. “But if he’s really down there…”

“There!” Eddie struck his arm out, pointing at the screen. He could make out the top of a head blocking the camera’s way. The kid, Hayden, looked up and allowed them a view of his dirty, tear-streaked face. “There he is.”

“Look at the way he’s pinned.” Hen pressed into the space for a closer look at the screen. “Arms forward, chest constricted, shallow breaths.”

“Forty-five feet,” Chimney announced. Eddie didn’t look away from the screen, from Hayden’s frightened face, to look at him. “At that depth, oxygen’s an issue. We’ve gotta get a line of compressed air down there ASAP.”

“You found him!?” Hayden’s mother rushed into them, pushing people out of the way with a ruthlessness that, if he were there, would’ve undoubtedly earned Danny’s respect. “Is he-!?”

“He’s alive.” Athena had her arms wrapped around the frantic woman, holding her back. “Okay? He’s alive.”

Eddie wasn’t sure that the woman - he didn’t even know her name - even heard the sergeant’s words. Her gaze, much like his own had been, was fixated on the video feed of her trapped son. He recognized the relief on her face, to see her child alive, and he recognized the heartbreak and the terror at the knowledge that he was so far away. She reached out a hand, like she wanted to reach through the screen and comfort her son, and her voice trembled as she whispered,

“Oh, my baby…”

The sound of knocking - small, uneven, but very enthusiastic - had Buck just about leaping off the couch. Danny, sitting on the other end from him, rolled his eyes as he, too, got to his feet. When he reached the door and opened it, Buck was greeted by a smiling Carla and a grinning Chris.

“Superman!” Buck stepped out of the way, letting the pair inside. Chris immediately pressed his side, and he reached down to run his hand through the kid’s hair. “And hello to you, too, Carla.”

“Well, I know where I stand,” Carla said with a laugh. She handed him Chris’ bookbag, along with another that was filled with clothes. “We stopped by the house for him to change and to get a fresh uniform for tomorrow.”

“You were going to tell Ms. Flores-” Buck did his best to keep his distaste for her out of his tone as he said her name. Danny’s scoff and Carla’s eye roll told him that he wasn’t quite successful. “-what you were doing for show and tell on Friday, right? What did you decide on? The skateboard?”

“It was the rat, wasn’t it?” Danny said.

“Hamster,” Chris corrected.

“The rat,” Danny repeated with a nod. The kid groaned at him.

“He found Eddie’s Silver Star,” Carla told them. “So he’s taking that and his father in with him.”

That Silver Star was buried deep in Eddie’s closet. Deeper than Eddie had buried himself, even. Buck had never even laid eyes on it, and only knew of its existence thanks to Bobby’s introduction on the day Eddie started at the 118. His boyfriend did not like to talk about it, not even to brag.

Buck didn’t understand. If he had a medal like that one, he wouldn’t ever take it off. Catch him walking into the grocery store on laundry day in his rattiest clothes with it pinned to his chest. Hell, he’d find a way to shower with it on.

Carla didn’t stay for very long, eager to get home to her husband. Buck carried the bags over to the dining table, depositing them both there. Chris was already making his way to the couch, and the controllers that were sitting out on the coffee table, and Buck was about to join him when Danny cleared his throat. He was also making pointed glances at the bookbag.

Buck let out a sigh.

“Hold on,” he said, like the killjoy he had to be. “What homework do you have?”

Chris let out a groan, head flopping back.

“I have a packet for science,” he admitted, moving instead to take a seat at the table and start digging things out.

“That’s not too bad,” Buck said. “We can get through that in no time.”

“And a math worksheet.”

Ah. That one would be a tad bit more difficult. But luckily…

Buck turned to give Danny his best puppy dog eyes. His brother, in turn, rolled his own.

“I’ll help with the math, I guess.” He sounded so very grumpy about it. “We don’t want him to flunk the class.”

Buck blew a raspberry at him, though any proper rebuttal was cut off by his phone ringing. He snagged it off the end table and answered it with a smile, putting it on speaker.

“Hey, Eds. Chris just got here.”

“Hey. I figured it was about time.”

“Are you still stuck at the farmhouse?” A glance around and Buck located his laptop, sitting beneath the coffee table for some reason. He went and grabbed it, so he could use the almighty internet for the homework. 

“We’re waiting on people from the city to get here,” Eddie said. “At the moment we’re just… Twiddling our thumbs. Is he working on his homework?”

“Just getting started. Danny’s gonna help with the math.”

“Gracias a Dios,” Eddie said, and then laughed when Buck blew a raspberry through the phone. “Lemme talk to him?”

“Sure.”

It was a request easily agreed to, because Buck understood Eddie’s need to talk to his kid at the moment. Finding another little boy stuck in a well would not have been easy for Buck; it was undoubtedly harder on Eddie. Who, for some reason, Austin kept calling Lassie in his texts to Danny and then just replied with textual disappointment when they asked for an explanation.

“Hi, Dad!” Chris chirped as he clutched at Buck’s phone. “Yeah, I am… I promise.”

Buck left him to it, pulling up the website for his favorite pizza place on his laptop. 

“Get me garlic sticks,” Danny… Well, it wasn’t so much of a request as it was just an outright demand. Buck rolled his eyes, even as he added garlic sticks to the order first thing.

Chris didn’t stay on the phone for very long, just long enough for Eddie to reassure himself. Buck took the phone back and chatted with Eddie for a bit, until the kid came to a problem that he needed help with. They said their goodbyes, both a bit reluctantly, and Buck pulled the packet to himself.

“So what do- Oh, hey, the mitochondria. It’s the powerhouse of the cell, y’know.” That just had Chris staring at him blankly. “Okay, so let’s see here…”

The city official finally arrived early in the evening, with mostly useless maps and grim information. Hayden was stuck five feet above a water table, and they didn’t have a good way to get to him. Bobby came up with the plan of drilling a parallel tunnel, wider and deep, before sending someone down to access the well by punching through it. The difficulty with that, their only plan, was that they couldn't dig the tunnel too close to the well without risking its integrity.

It could collapse right on top of the kid, and anyone else that was down there.

With the drill rig came the news channel vultures. With the evening came storm clouds. The pressure of time was felt by them all, and they moved with brisk efficiency to get things ready. As the rig got into position to start drilling, they stuck a radio down the well in the hopes of talking to Hayden.

“So I’ll be able to talk to him?” Hayden’s mother was clutching the mic like it was a lifeline.

“You might not be able to hear him,” Bobby told her. They were all gathered in front of the video screen and the live feed of Hayden. “But hopefully he’ll hear you. Just let him know you’re here and help is on the way.”

“We hit forty feet,” Austin reported, crouched over the well and feeding the radio down.

“Everybody off,” Bobby ordered. “All channels.”

The air was filled with various clicks at every shut off their radios. Hayden’s mother took a trembling breath before raising the mic to her mouth.

“Hayden? It’s Mommy.” There wasn’t a reaction at all, and the woman’s face scrunched up like she was about to burst into tears. Bobby had Jones raise the radio, and she tried again. “Hayden, can you hear me? Hayden, please. Please, look up!”

When he did, finally, look up at the camera, Eddie was surprised that she didn’t start crying.

“Hayden, baby.” Her voice wobbled a little. “I know it’s scary down there, but it’s gonna be okay, baby. They’re coming to get you, I promise.”

“Mom!”

“Baby, I’m so sorry. I’m so-” There were the tears, now. She dropped the mic a little, thumb no longer on the button. “I can’t-”

“I got it.” Eddie reached out and plucked the mic from her hand before Hen could. He tried to remember what he knew Buck had done with Chris during the tsunami, regretted not keeping a copy of Alice in Wonderland on the truck. He wondered if Chris had been as scared during that awful day as Hayden looked now. 

“Hey, Hayden,” he said into the radio. “I’m Eddie, I’m a firefighter. I’m here with your mom and a lot of other people, and we’re all working to get you out. You’ve been so brave today, and I just need you to be brave a little bit longer. Okay? There’s gonna be a loud noise, and it’s gonna be scary. But it’s just us making our way to you. We’ll be there soon.”

The storm reached them before they reached Hayden. Rain came pouring down in heavy sheets, and lightning lit up the sky. It slowed them down further, the added difficulty in ensuring their tunnel didn’t fall in on itself taking precious time. And the commissioner, who was officially Eddie’s least favorite person at the moment, tried to pull the plug on the plan before Bobby convinced him not to.

He had a point, because that drill rig was a lightning rod and a disaster waiting to happen, but Eddie had no intentions of leaving that little boy buried in the earth any longer than he had to be. That was why, when the time came, he was the one to volunteer to go down.

“I’m the one that was talking to him on the radio,” he told Bobby. “He knows my voice. It makes sense that it’s me.”

Buck had dove head first into the raging ocean to rescue his kid. The least he could do was go down into the depths of the earth and rescue someone else’s.

Chapter 9

The rain did not show any signs of slowing down by the time they approached depth. They got the winch set up, and the harnesses out. Eddie changed out of his turnouts and into the safety gear for climbing, transferring his St. Christopher medallion from the pocket of his coat to the overalls he put on. He was making sure everything he needed once he got to the bottom, to get to Hayden and to get Hayden out, was in his bag when Bobby entered the tent he was getting ready in, an oxygen tank in his arms.

“Extra oxygen, in case you need it. The water’s rising fast down there,” he told Eddie, angling everything so he could show the attachment to it. “Green light, full supply. Yellow light, two minutes. I wanna see you topside before you see red.”

“Copy that.”

“Alright, then let’s go.”

Bobby led him outside, into the pouring rain. The tent wasn’t too far from the well and the hole they’d dug, The captain briefed him as they walked.

“We’re gonna lose comms,” Bobby said. There wasn’t much doubt there; the radio they’d used to contact Hayden lost signal at forty feet. “So here’s the plan: You have thirty minutes to dig yourself across, not one minute more. After thirty minutes, you’ll feel two strong tugs on your line, and then we’re pulling you out. The same goes for you. You find that boy, you tug twice.”

The flash of lightning and the crack of thunder interrupted him just as they reached the drill site. The city official overseeing everything immediately jumped in to say,

“That’s it, we’re done.”

“We’re close enough,” Bobby declared, turning to catch the drill operator’s attention. “Bring it up!”

The operator nodded, reversing the controls. The giant drill stopped, and then began to rise. When the rig was out of the way, they set up the tripod with the rope and pulleys. Bobby himself made sure everything was secured, before the others helped him climb into the hole.

“Thirty minutes,” Bobby reminded him, pressing the start button on the timer he wore on his wrist. Eddie had an identical one, and he started it at the same time.

“See you then,” he said.

The whir of the winch joined the sound of the rain and the thunder. Eddie was thankful that he wasn’t claustrophobic as he was lowered down, the walls of the hole looming on all sides. As he was lowered, he used the radio to give updates to the others for how far down he was.

“Thirty feet,” he reported. And then, “Thirty five.”

There was a reply, but it was garbled.

“Cap, can you hear me?” he tried. Another garbled message was the only reply as his feet hit the bottom of the hole. “If you can hear me, I’ve reached depth.”

There wasn’t any reply this time. Eddie wasn’t surprised, he knew - they all knew - that he would lose communications down here. Even so, on the off chance that it was only on his end, he radioed that he was going to start digging through. And then he pulled out the small shovel out of his bag and got to work breaching through the compacted earth.

It was hard work, in this cramped space. Messy work, too, with the rain turning everything slick and the mud clinging to everything it could. He very purposefully did not look at the time on his wrist, though the glimpses of it that he could not avoid told him how much time was passing.

Too much. Too much time was passing.

Eventually, he hit clay instead of mud. Clay like the old pipes were made of. He pulled a shard of it out of the way, tossed it behind him with the mud that he had shoveled. Putting his head in, he noticed two things: that he’d dug into where one of the feeder pipes intersected, and that Hayden was not where he was supposed to be.

Hayden was below him. Soaked through, trembling. And he looked so very afraid when he raised his head.

“Hey!” Eddie did his best to smile down at him, even though he doubted Hayden could see it with his headlamp pointed right in his face. “It’s me, Eddie. Remember? I told you we were coming for you. Are you doing okay down there?”

“Cold,” was the quiet, shaking answer.

“I bet.” After a second’s debate, he reached for his radio, just in case. “Cap, I have eyes on Hayden. He’s fallen about five feet. Partially submerged, water’s rising fast. I need more time.”

The timer on his wrist showed he was almost down to one minute. One minute to get Hayden out of there. 

“I’m gonna reach down for you now, okay?” Eddie told the boy. “Try not to move, let me do all the work.”

He reached down, he grabbed the kid’s hand. He was pulling him up, as gently and as quickly as he could. And then-

The timer on Eddie’s wrist went off. At almost the exact same time, the rope attaching him to the surface above yanked hard. It tore him away from that tiny hand, and it dragged him out of the hole he had dug. He frantically clung to everything he could, the mud slipping through his fingers.

He’d been close, he’d been so close. They couldn’t take him away now. In a moment of franticness, where his only thought was that Hayden had been so close, he pulled out his knife and cut through the rope.

Eddie fell, sliding down the walls of mud, and came to a sudden stop in a pool of water, the wind leaving him.

He wasn’t sure how long he laid there, catching his breath, but it was the sound of Hayden calling for his mom that made him move. Every movement was met with aching protest by his body, but he ignored it as he dragged himself back into the hole he had dug. 

Hayden was just where he’d left him, clinging to the side of the tunnel. Eddie wasted no time pulling him out all the way and into the interconnecting tunnel. In the bag was a foil blanket, and he wrapped it around the boy.

“Is that better?” he asked.

Hayden nodded and then his attention was caught by something on the ground. He reached down and picked it up, holding it out for Eddie to see.

“What’s this?” he asked.

Eddie’s heart skipped a beat. It was his St. Christopher medallion. It must have fallen out when he was got yanked.

“Thank you, buddy,” he told him, taking it and tucking it away in his pocket once more.

“Eddie!” That was Chimney’s voice. “Are you down there!?”

Chimney’s feet came into view first, splashing down in the water. The rest of him came into view with a relieved laugh.

“Thank God,” he said. “I was afraid I was gonna have to save your life.”

“Nah, Hayden and I are just fine,” Eddie informed him. “Right?”

Hayden gave a short little nod.

“Well let’s get you both out of here. Hayden, I’m gonna take you to see your mom, okay?” Chimney bundled Hayden up in his arms, the kid going eagerly with the promise of see his mother. “We’ll lower another line down. Try not to cut this one.”

With that final jab, Chimney reached up and tugged on his rope. Once, twice. And then he and Hayden began their ascent. Eddie moved so he could watch them go, as they got farther away and closer to the surface. From below, he could see them reach the others, and then they were both out of the hole.

And then, something happened. Eddie wasn’t sure what, at first. There was just a noise that came from above, a noise that sounded suspiciously like an explosion. He tried to radio up, to ask what was going on, but he got nothing but interference.

Then the tunnel collapsed inward, mud and dirt falling around his ears, and Eddie was trapped in darkness.

The screen flashed as Buck’s avatar died a gruesome death once more. He groaned and threw himself back into the couch, while Chris made no effort to conceal his laughter. Neither did Daniel.

“I swear, you cheat,” his baby brother complained.

“I’m just better than you,” Daniel retorted, and then frowned at his phone when it began to ring. That was Austin’s ringtone. “I’ll get us more popcorn.”

He grabbed the bowl and his phone, taking both across the room to the kitchen. Digging through the cabinets for the popcorn, he answered his phone and pinned it between his head and shoulder.

“Where’s Buck and Chris?” was the way he was greeted. “Are you all watching the news?”

“Uh.” Daniel turned to look at the two in question: Buck was in the middle of tickling Chris, no doubt revenge for reveling in his losses. “We’ve been playing video games. Why?”

There was a sigh on the other end of the line.

“We lost Eddie.”

“What-?” Daniel cut himself off, glanced at Buck and Chris once more, and then lowered his voice. “What does that mean?”

“Eddie went down to get the kid,” Austin explained in his ear while he threw the popcorn bag into the microwave and hit the buttons. “He had a time limit, because the radio hasn’t been working down there. He ran out of time, Cap gave the order to pull him up, and Eddie…. Eddie cut the line.”

“Fucking dumbass,” Daniel grumbled.

“Cap sent Chimney down. He came back up with the kid,” Austin continued. “We were about to send down a new line for the dumbass when lightning struck the drill rig. It fell over, and everything collapsed.”

“Everything collapsed?”

“The well, the hole we dug. All of it. He’s buried, Dan.”

Daniel was struck speechless at first. It was not quite like that awful day of the tsunami, nothing near the all-encompassing shock and horror. But there was shock and horror. He braced himself against the counter and gripped the phone in his hand.

“Wh- What?” he managed to get out, the words hushed. “What is Nash doing? Why are you on the phone with me instead of digging him out?”

“We don’t have another drill, and it’s raining too hard to dig by hand.”

“So what are you doing!?” Daniel snapped.

“What we can,” was the irritatingly calm response. “I have to go. Try to remember that you hated him.”

The screen on his phone flashed to tell him that Austin had ended the call. He glared at it until he heard Buck’s worried voice behind him.

“What’s going on?”

“Um.” Daniel looked at his baby brother, and then past him to Chris. “Hey, Chris? Why don’t you pick out a movie for us to watch?”

“Okay!” was the kid’s eager response as he got up and headed for the stand of DVDs by the TV.

“Danny?”

He’d promised that he would do better about not keeping things from his baby brother. At the moment, he kinda hated that.

“Something’s happened to Eddie,” Daniel told his baby brother, keeping the words hushed. 

Buck’s face went from worried confusion to heartbreak as Daniel explained what Austin had told him. He blindly grabbed for one of the dining chairs, pulling it out so he could collapse into it. He shook his head and kept shaking it, as if he could simply will the denial into reality.

“They’re doing what they can,” Daniel said, repeating what Austin had told him, crouching down in front of him. “Eddie’s going to be fine. Okay? He’s going to be fine.”

After a bit of hesitation, he raised his hand, pinky out. Just like what Maddie and him used to do, so long ago. Buck stared at it, and at him, for a moment before raising a shaking hand and wrapping his own pinky around Daniel’s.

“I picked a movie!” Chris called out, as loud as ever. The sound of his voice had Buck jumping in his seat.

“What do I- Danny, what do I tell him?”

“You don’t have to tell him anything right now,” Daniel answered. “Not until we know. Not until he has to know.”

Buck blinked at him several times in a row, understanding blooming in his eyes, before leaning forward and laying his forehead against Daniel’s shoulder.

“I’m sorry,” he said into Daniel’s shirt.

“Go see what movie we’re watching, squirt,” Daniel told him, because there wasn’t anything to forgive. 

He felt Buck nod, felt him draw in a breath. Then Buck stood up, a fake smile across his face.

“Okay, Superman, what’ve we got?”

Daniel dragged his hand down his face as Buck went over to Chris, exaggerating his shock and awe over the movie the kid chose. He got up, tucked his phone into his pocket, poured the popcorn into the bowl, and went to go pretend like everything was hunky-dory for as long as they could.

“I’m still alive down here!” Eddie shouted into his radio, ignoring the futility of it. “Does anyone copy? I’m alive down here!”

There was no response. He wasn’t surprised, but that didn’t make the crushing disappointment any better. He was stuck down here, with no idea if rescue was coming or if he’d been written off for dead, and the water was still rising. It was going to be up to him to escape.

How, though? The way up was sealed, and the intersecting pipes were too small for him to fit through. But the city official, he remembered, had mentioned there might’ve been drainage tunnels, that the water table was fed by the reservoir half a mile away. He was almost to the water table, Eddie knew that much from how first Hayden and now himself were half-submerged.

What did he have? The shovel, to break through the mud. The extra oxygen that Bobby had given him. Glowsticks, for when his headlamp inevitably died once submerged. That was what he had, and so he got to work.

Eddie did not have to dig far, at least, before he was hitting water. A little more digging, and then feeling around, confirmed that there was a tunnel, heading in the direction of the reservoir. He pulled out the glowstick and snapped it, the green light casting an eerie glow, readied the oxygen, and he dove.

The headlamp, as predicted, died not long into the swim. The long, cold swim.

The extra oxygen did not last the entire journey. He wasn’t entirely certain how far he’d gotten, or how much farther he had to go, when he noticed it thinning. There was a gap between the water and the ceiling above, and he took the opportunity to surface and confirm what he already knew: the oxygen tank was empty, light flashing red and beeping in warning. It was just useless weight now, and he shrugged it off to sink to the bottom. He took a breath, held it, and submerged again. 

There was no actual way to tell if Eddie was going in the right direction, other than the faint current that he was pushing against. He was freezing, and his lungs were burning. It would be so easy, he thought, to just give up now. When he was surrounded by darkness, the glowstick clutched in his fist barely enough to light his way. When it was taking all his strength to keep going.

But he couldn’t leave Chris. He couldn’t leave Buck. And so Eddie kept swimming forward.

Eventually, the walls that were pressing in on him opened up. The floor dropped, the ceiling disappeared. Above him was light, glorious light. With a burst of renewed energy, Eddie kicked upwards and upwards, until he broke the surface and took a breath of fresh air that had never tasted sweeter.

The rain had stopped, was what he first noticed after he tossed off his helmet and let the glowstick sink. That and the fact that he somehow ended up in the middle of the reservoir, and that all the floodlights that had been set up were so far away. But he’d made it this far, he was almost to the finish line.

He dragged himself forward, through and then out of the water. Then he dragged himself to his feet, and kept dragging himself. Until he crossed that half-mile, to where his friends were waiting. That was when he let himself fall, and that was when he was caught.

It felt like hours, long, anxious hours, before Danny’s phone broke the silence again. They’d sat through two movies, Chris eventually dozing off in the middle of the second. Buck would’ve joined him, but he was too busy worrying and fretting.

The moment the phone rang, the moment his older brother got up to answer it, Buck was getting up, too, easing Chris down onto the cushions.

“Okay,” Danny was saying. “Okay… I’ll tell him. Thanks, Austin.”

“Tell me what?” Buck asked, the moment he hung up, a bit terrified to know.

“Eddie’s at LA General,” Danny told him, sounding almost as relieved as Buck felt. “Hypothermic and exhausted, but he’s okay.”

If not for the arm of the couch, Buck might’ve hit the ground when his knees gave out. He pushed himself back up, took a step towards his shoes and his keys and the door, and then stopped to look back at Chris.

“I’ll watch him,” Danny told him, and that was all the permission that Buck needed before he was rushing out the door. His brother shouted after him to “Tell Eddie he’s an idiot!”

The journey between the apartment and LA General took entirely too long. So, too, did it take too long to find out which room Eddie was in. But finally, finally, he was coming to a squealing stop just outside the open door. 

The others were there, Bobby and Hen and Chimney, but Buck did not pay them much attention. He zeroed in on his boyfriend, ignoring the others as he crossed the room to his bedside. He wrapped his arms around Eddie, who still felt entirely too cold, and didn’t let go for the longest time.

“Danny says you’re an idiot,” he said into Eddie’s shoulder. “I think he’s gonna yell at you.”

“I think I’ll live,” Eddie said, pulling him closer.

Chapter 10

See the end of the chapter for notes

“Who all knew about Officer Drake?” Dr. White asked, sitting across from him. She looked all prim and proper, hair up in a bun and nails lightly tapping against the back of her notepad.

Daniel stared at her, lip curling a little.

“What?” he snapped.

“Before you left El Paso, who knew about Officer Drake?” she asked again. “The way you talk about it, he seems to have been a prominent figure in your life in Texas. Who all knew about him?”

“He was a cop,” Daniel said, trying to keep his tone polite. Trying and failing. “I assume a lot of people knew about him.”

“I mean about him and you.”

He huffed out a sigh.

“Alma. She was our neighbor, kept an eye on Buck when I had shifts at the station or, y’know… Worked.” Daniel shrugged, irrationally annoyed that the doctor seemed entirely unphased everytime he brought that up. “Single parent like me. Her girls graduated high school last year. She knew about the, uh. The hooking, too. Caught me sneaking out the first night I ever… Immediately clocked it, told me she’d stay up in case Buck needed anything, told me to be safe. Insisted that I told her every time I went out for it afterwards, didn’t matter how late, and that I let her know when I got back.”

“She sounds like a good friend.”

“She is. We bitched about our parents, hers might suck more than my own.”

“And after you moved here,” Dr. White said, moving on. “Besides Austin, who else have you told about Officer Drake?”

Daniel just shrugged again.

“No one.”

“No one?” the doctor repeated. “Not even your sister?”

“Why the fuck would I tell Maddie?”

“Why wouldn’t you?” she asked in return. “The two of you have both escaped from abu-”

“Yeah, no. Don’t insult her by comparing this to that dead fuck, may he burn in hell”

“You don’t think your experiences were similar?” Dr. White tilted her head as she looked at him, mouth turned into a curious frown.

“No.” What sort of stupid question was that? “Not even close. Officer Drake and I, that wasn’t a relationship. He was just… He was a cop on a power trip. Look, do we really have to keep talking about him? He doesn’t matter any more. He’s in Texas, he can’t bother me or Buck. It’s all in the past.”

“Just because it’s now in the past, it doesn’t mean it’s not still affecting the present,” the therapist said.  “It still leaves scars. It still leaves trauma.”

Daniel would like to be able to tell the woman that everything was fine, that there were no scars or traumas. But he’d already told her too much for her to ever believe that blatant of a lie. Sure, maybe she didn’t know about the literal scar, but she knew enough to label him with PTSD. Sorry, complex PTSD. Honestly, it seemed rather simple to Daniel, but what did he know? He wasn’t the one with the fancy college degree.

“Look, could we just talk about something else?” he asked, and hoped it didn’t come across like he was begging. “I could tell you about the joint baby showers that Austin dragged me to yesterday. That was traumatic.”

Austin’s sister, Cynthia’s pregnancy hormones were leaving the poor woman a mess. Daniel had never seen someone’s mood flip from joyful to raging to crying and back again so fast before. His sister-in-law, Irene wasn’t having nearly as rough of a go of it, but at one point they seemed to synchronize. Which had been utterly terrifying, especially since it was directed at him after he made the wrong comment at the wrong time.

Austin, the asshole, magically disappeared with his niece and nephews, only reappearing when the coast was clear.

“I’m sure,” was Dr. White’s dry response. “Fine, if you don’t want to talk about Officer Drake any more-”

“I don’t!”

“Then let’s talk about Captain Nash.”

Daniel’s sneer was entirely on reflex.

“Why?”

“Two sessions ago, you bragged about how you ‘handled’ him.” She raised a hand to do air quotes. “By intentionally bringing up his personal traumas. Not to mention how you threatened him with physical violence the year before.”

“Is there a point to this?” he asked her. “Because you’re sounding like Maddie now. Like yeah, fine, I shouldn’t have done that. Mea culpa or whatever.”

“Do you actually feel remorse for those actions?”

“It worked, didn’t? He got out of Buck’s way, and he hasn’t laid a hand on him again.”

From the sigh alone, Daniel thought that statement did not meet whatever unknowable criteria Dr. White was judging him on.

“Maybe,” she said, “we can try to come up with possible alternatives you could have gone with, instead. Ones that weren’t quite so… Extreme.”

That sounded awful. Still better than talking about Officer Drake, though.

It wasn’t the biggest apartment fire that Daniel had ever been to, but it definitely wasn’t small. A three alarm fire, with both the 133 and the 118 arriving shortly after the 153. Mehta was with the incident commander, Buck was inside helping clear everyone out of the building, and Daniel himself was with the other paramedics, triaging the injured. 

“Mayday, mayday,” the incident commander said over the radios. “Building is unstable, we’re calling for immediate evacuation.”

The glance Daniel sent to the burning building, with Buck and Eddie both inside, was purely reflexive before he focused back on his current patient. It was a tiny little girl in an oversized shirt. She was covered in soot and crying, and she whimpered when he finished dressing her burned hand. Somehow, he always ended up with the children. He was beginning to think it was a conspiracy.

“Okay, darlin’, I’m done. That wasn’t so bad, was it?” The little girl sniffled and shook her head, hair flopping around with the motion. He stood from where he’d been kneeling in front of her and looked about until he spotted who he was looking for. “Nola! Her mom ready to go?”

The other paramedic didn’t even bother glancing his way, too busy doing the last touches of whatever she needed to do for the girl’s mom. Instead, she raised a hand and gave him a thumb’s up.

“Go on over there and Ms. Nola will take you and your mom to the hospital,” Daniel told the little girl. He nudged her shoulder a little and she hurried off. When she reached them, she hovered anxiously as her mother was loaded up into one of the 133’s ambulances and then allowed Nola to carefully lift her up inside.

“Possible airway burns,” he heard Chimney reciting as he hurried past, towards one of the other ambulances with a patient on a gurney. “Let’s get her to Sunset General.”

Right behind him, heading for Daniel - and Hen, he hadn’t even noticed she was there - was Nash and Eddie and a couple others, the four of them using a thermal blanket as a sling to carry someone. They rushed over and carefully lowered the guy onto the ground, where both paramedics dove into checking him over. Daniel noted the blood smeared over the side of his head, looking like it came from somewhere past his hairline.

“We found him on the bathroom floor, he must’ve slipped and hit his head,” Nash reported. 

“He passed out as soon as we got him up,” Eddie said.

“Sir?” Hen had removed the oxygen mask they stuck on him and was waving smelling salts under his nose with one hand and rubbing at his sternum with her other. “Sir, can you hear me?”

“Did you get her?” the man mumbled, still sounding out of it. “Please, tell me…”

“I got her.” Buck was, for some reason, carrying a cat. Daniel would ask him how he’d ended up with a group of people from his old station, except he figured the answer was obvious: Buck had probably followed Eddie, because duh. “I got Gladys.”

The man’s eyes blinked open and, though he looked elated at the sight of the cat, he did not look very much relieved.

“No, that- that’s Hoover,” he said, reaching for the cat. He immediately cuddled it to his chest when Buck handed it over, the furry beast purring up a storm. “Thank God, but where’s Gladys?”

“Atwater Street incident, this is Metro Fire Command.” Maddie’s voice, from Nash’s radio. “Please respond.”

The 118’s captain grabbed his radio, thumb it on.

“Go for Captain Nash.”

“I have a deaf woman trapped in apartment 10G.”

As a group, the four of them - Daniel, along with Buck and Eddie and Nash - stepped out of the medical tent to look up at the tenth floor of the burning building. As they watched one of the windows shattered outward, glass falling to the pavement before like twinkling snowflakes. They didn’t need Buck voicing the obvious to know where the missing Gladys was.

The ladders converged as best they could. They extended a hundred feet, but they had to be angled, so in practice they only really reached eighty. That put them two stories below where they needed to be, far too short to be of use. Plus,

“The end of her hallway is engulfed,” Nash said.

“There’s no access to the stairwell, either,” Eddie said.

Buck, though, wasn’t looking at the burning building. He was looking at its neighbor, separated by an alley. Rather intently, too, and Daniel wasn’t sure he liked that.

“The building next door isn’t on fire,” he pointed out.

“Please, do not tell me…” Daniel wasn’t begging, but it was a close thing.

“The rappelling kit’s got a hundred-fifty feet of rope,” Buck argued. “That’ll get me down to the street with her.”

“He wants to do a rope rescue.” Eddie threw up his hands. “Of course he wants to do a rope rescue.”

“Did you miss the part where the building is on fire and unstable?” Daniel spat. It would probably defeat the purpose of keeping his baby brother safe if he strangled him to death right here and now. He opened his mouth to tell Buck just what he thought of this plan, but then he spotted Nash watching him. “Fine! Eddie!”

Eddie didn’t even need to ask for clarification, he just nodded and hurried for the trucks with Buck to grab the gear they needed for this monument to stupidity. How ruffled the captain looked to have Daniel giving one of his people orders was something he couldn’t help but savor for a moment. Only for a moment, because then Daniel was grabbing his radio and barking into it.

“Flowers, I need the cushion.”

“Got it.”

The time spent getting the air cushion into position and inflated was a suitable distraction. It didn’t last long enough, however, because he was soon looking up just in time to watch first Buck and then Eddie take a running leap to cross the space between the two buildings. He lost sight of them for a bit, but then Buck was soon abseiling down to the tenth floor, stopping at one of the unshattered windows. Buck gestured to someone, presumably Gladys, to get out of the way before he kicked off as the gathered crowd of onlookers gasped, swinging backwards and then forwards like a pendulum, crashing through the glass and into the apartment.

Long moments later, Daniel could hear him radioing to Eddie that he was coming back out. But Buck was barely a floor down, the woman clinging to him like a koala, when there was an ominous roar and crash from the burning building.

“Cap!” Eddie shouted across the line. “The roof is gone!”

“Secure the rope and get out,” Nash ordered. “Buck can lower himself the rest of the way.”

He probably would’ve been able to. Except, well, the building was on fire, and fire tended to spread. Daniel only knew something was wrong when Buck stopped again, head swiveling frantically between the inflated airbag below him and his rope above him, which seemed to have caught from either an errant spark or just the heat and was smoking as a flame ate through it. It snapped, sending Buck and Gladys plummeting the remaining distance to land on the cushion.

Daniel was the first one to them, hurriedly passing Gladys off to Chimney and Nash so he could get to Buck. He hauled him to his feet and wasted no time checking him over, making sure he didn’t land funny or that the woman didn’t land on him too hard. Once that was done, once he’d contented himself with the knowledge that Buck was fine, he reached up and held his brother’s face between his hands and asked, as seriously as possible,

“Why do you two insist on doing stupid things?”

“But I did good, though,” Buck said. “Right?”

Daniel shook his head and stomped off for the triage tent, ignoring his brother’s continued attempts to fish for praise.

“Whoo!” Buck tossed his balled up towel into his locker. “That was something, huh? A fire that big and no fatalities, we have to celebrate.”

It was the end of the shift, and everyone was in various stages of changing to leave. Except Buck was still running on the high from rescuing Gladys, not quite ready to go home for the night. He wanted to go out and do something.

“He’s like a puppy,” Jon commented, sitting on the bench and doing up the laces of his shoes. “All excitable and energetic.”

Buck scrunched up his nose at him, trying to figure out if he was being insulted or not.

“Try living with him. At least he’s mostly housetrained,” Danny told the paramedic, and then asked Buck, “Why not go out somewhere with Eddie?”

“He’s working a double.” Buck couldn’t help but pout as he said it, which had the others sniggering at him. The addition of new car payments to the budget found Eddie working more than a few doubles. “And Chimney and Hen have date nights.”

“Wow. He’s cheating on our sister with a married woman.”

“Not together.” Buck rolled his eyes at his brother. “C’mon, what about you guys?”

“Sorry, squirt. Austin managed to talk his nephews into playing that game of his and somehow I got dragged into it, so I’m gonna spend the night rolling dice, apparently,” Danny said. He looked up from zipping up his bag and glowered when he saw everyone staring at him. “Not one goddamn word from any of you.”

“Nerd,” one of the other paramedics, Aiden, called out from the other end of the locker room. Danny threw someone’s boot at him. “Ha! Missed!”

“None of the rest of you want to go somewhere?” Buck asked, looking around. “That bar on Pico has loaded fries. Come on.”

“My place has a very comfortable bed,” Flowers retorted, closing his locker. “And a very beautiful woman who will be very upset with me if I get drunk the night before our anniversary.”

“No one said anything about getting drunk.”

“Then what’s the point of going out?” Jon asked, throwing his arm around Buck’s shoulder. “How ‘bout this. I’ll talk to Nola, see what her plans are. She’ll probably be up for some loaded fries.”

“Yes!” Buck pumped his fist.

“Try not to lose him,” Danny said, reaching for Buck’s bag. They’d come into work together again that morning, and Buck hadn’t thought that far ahead yet. “He tends to wander off after a couple drinks.”

The bar on Pico was a bit more country themed than Buck’s usual tastes, even after four years spent in Texas, but it had the added benefit of being a bar that he hadn’t worked at. Nola made a face at the twangy music when they entered, and Jon made fun of the deer’s head hanging on the wall. The bar proper was empty except for an older guy that was exuding grumpiness.

Buck bought the first round, along with loaded fries for everyone. Nola bought the second, and Jon the third. He was feeling extra loose and giddy by that point, swaying in his seat at the corner booth they’d claimed to themselves.

“You really are like a puppy,” Nola said, chin propped on her fist. “I don’t even remember any of the probies being this energetic.”

“Do you even remember the last couple of probies' names?” Jon asked her.

“Point.” She lifted her head to look past and above Buck. “Hey, you’re on the news again.”

Buck twisted around to face the TV above the bar. The channel 8 news was running a story about the apartment fire, and was including footage someone had taken of him on their phone as he rescued Gladys.

“I’m gonna get another round,” he told them, getting to his feet. “Do you guys-?”

“No.” Jon shook his head, as did Nola. “I’ve learned my limits the hard way.”

Buck shrugged, unperturbed by their refusal, and went up to the bar. The bartender was busy, so he stood around waiting to catch their attention. The older guy glanced at him, then at the television, and let out a pointed sounding,

“Idiot.”

“Excuse me?” Buck blinked at him.

“Running straight into a hellfire like that, pulling rope stunts.” The old guy shook his head. “Only a moron would do something that reckless.”

Oh, wow. It was like he’d somehow got his hands on Danny’s lecture notes.

“Those morons,” Buck said, “are saving lives.”

“Damn straight.” The old guy raised his beer in a toast. “LAFD, best and bravest on God’s green earth. Right?”

He let out a laugh and Buck shook his head, understanding now.

“You used to be a firefighter.”

“I’m still a firefighter,” was the immediate correction. “Just ‘cause you retire, it doesn’t mean you forget who you are.”

He held out his hand.

“Red Delacroix.”

“Evan Buckley. Buck.” He took the offered hand, gave it a firm shake, and took the seat next to him. “Here, what are you drinking?”

“No, no.” Red waved him off. “After what you pulled there, this round’s on me. But I still think you’re an idiot.”

Between one round and another, they somehow moved from the bar to one of the tables. Buck sat there, engrossed as Red told him one story after another. The last one was about a guy named Mac and the time the two of them rescued a mother bobcat and her litter from a bushfire. Red finished it with a sigh, slumping in his seat.

“He bought it in Two-thousand Two,” he said, mostly into his drink. “Power lines. Chatsworth.”

“Oh, man, I’m sorry.” The words sounded lame even to Buck’s own ears. “What about the others? Still in touch with them?”

“At first,” Red said with a shrug. “Y’know, there were barbecues and parties and swapping war stories. Then there were Christmas cards and emails about the grandkids.” he let out a sigh. “Nowadays, we only ever get together when there’s a funeral.”

Buck wrinkled his nose.

“Morbid,” he said, taking a sip of his drink.

“It’s the truth!” the older man shot back. “We’re all gonna go eventually, kid. You just don’t want to be the last one left.”

Like Buck said: morbid.

Chapter End Notes

A couple hours later -
Nola: "hey, where did Baby Buckley go?"
Jon: "...ohshit."

The fun thing about Red being introduced here is that this version of Buck isn't suffering from crippling abandonment issues. He's always had at least one person - Daniel - who was there for him and never left. In fact, Buck's the one who's done the leaving on more than one occasion. So I just think it'll be neat to have him focusing on Red because he's a good person and not because he's partially projecting with his fears for his future.

Chapter 11

Buck paid for the Uber that got them both to Red’s apartment. The old man complained and grumbled about it the entire time, but Buck, even with his good sense fogged up by alcohol, wanted to make sure he got home safe. It was probably a good thing, too, because Red tripped over his feet when he first got out of the car, laughing it off like he hadn’t nearly gotten intimate with the pavement. The Uber driver certainly didn’t care, because he was taking off as soon as the car doors were shut.

“I didn’t need an escort,” Red complained again as Buck walked with him up the sidewalk to the front door.

“Just didn’t want you to end up in a ditch,” Buck said, which had the other man scoffing.

“I’ve been finding my way home since I was thirty,” he said, which for some reason Buck found really funny. Maybe it was the overly dramatic flip that Red did with his keys when he pulled them out of his pocket.

It wasn’t a really big apartment. It was smaller even than the one in El Paso, but it was clearly lived in. Red hit the light switch when he let them in, going through the entry room to the next one and turning on more lights as he went. There were a lot of framed pictures and news clippings on the walls, most of them related to firefighting.

“Alright, there you go,” Red said as he turned on another lamp. He straightened up and started taking off his coat. “Enough good deeds, you can get home, now.”

Buck barely listened to him. His attention was caught on an old photo on the wall, above a large landscape portrait. It showed a bunch of firefighters lined up in rows in front of an engine and ladder truck. There was a caption, reading “The Fighting 134” - 1983.

“This is them, right?” he asked, getting the other man’s attention. “This is your house.”

“Yeah, that’s my family.” Red came over and started pointing at people. “That’s our cap, Al Prescott. And then Phillie, I told you about him. And then there’s Arno, Mac, and that’s me. We were about your age around then, I think.”

Buck smiled, though it dropped with confusion when his eyes landed on a certificate of commendation for-

“John Delacroix,” he read aloud.

“You didn’t think Red was actually my birth name, did you?” the other man asked, laughing at him. Buck shrugged, because his sister’s legal name was Maddie. “The guys used to call me Code Red ‘cause I was a bit of a hothead when I was young.” Red smirked at him and then nudged at his side. “You’d know about that, wouldn’t ya?”

They were both laughing as Buck let himself be bullied, before he spotted another picture. This one depicted a much younger Red, not much older than he was in the group photo, with a woman in his arms.

“Who’s this?” Buck asked, picking it up.

“Cindy. The one that got away.” The words were laced with old hurt and wistfulness. “We were gonna be married.”

“What happened? Why didn’t you?”

“Our jobs keep us pretty busy.” Red shrugged. “It’s hard for someone not to feel like they’re always coming in a distant second.”

“You broke up over the job?”

Red shrugged, waggled his head back and forth.

“World Series, Nineteen Eighty-eight,” he said. “She got tickets to see the Dodgers play Oakland, home game. And I’d already scheduled a shift, and I figured nobody was gonna beat the A’s anyway. So I told her I’d make it up to her later.”

Buck grimaced, already mentally filling in the blanks there.

“But there was never a later,” he guessed.

“Gibson hit that homerun in game one, and by the time the fifth game came along, she was gone.” Red’s gaze, which had been set on the middle-distance as he spoke, suddenly focused on Buck. “You got anybody, kid?”

“Yeah, I- I do, actually.” Buck ducked his head with a smile as he thought about Eddie. Red laughed at him and nudged him again. “We, uh. We met in high school.”

“That’s a long time to be together.”

“We weren’t together the whole time. Things… I left. And then we ran into each other again.”

“Kid, lemme tell you something.” Red reached out to grip Buck’s arm. “You can be the hero, save lives, but don’t neglect having your own. Last thing you want is to be at the end and holding nothing but regrets. Trust me.” He squeezed Buck’s arm before letting go. “I know.”

“Well, on the bright side, we’re both firefighters,” Buck said with a shrug. “So we both understand when the job gets in the way.”

Red tilted his head as he stared at him, before letting go an almost silent “Huh” and giving his arm a pat.

“Like I said, you’ve done your good deed.” He pushed at Buck’s shoulder. “Get on home. Go. And get them flowers or… Whatever.”

Buck laughed as he allowed himself to be pushed towards the door, pulling out his phone to arrange for a ride. 

“Look, I’m just saying,” Buck said, still going on about this. He could admit that he had maybe not shut up about this particular topic. “The guy’s a forty year veteran of the department with two citations of bravery. Now he’s living alone in a one-bedroom apartment that he pays for with his pension.”

They were out on a call. It was actually a rather serious one, but not a scene that really required his skills. Apparently, a pair of idiots got into a shootout in the middle of the street like it was the OK Corral, blindly firing at each other. Luckily, they were the only ones who got shot. Unluckily, a bunch of other people still got injured by debris flying through the air or while trying to escape the violence. The woman that Danny was currently treating, for example, had several slivers of glass sticking out of her arm and face.
