“Did it seem like he was bothered by this?” Danny asked, using tweezers to pull out the glass. Buck was holding a little plastic jar for him to put the pieces into. “I can’t believe you ditched Mendoza and Nola for some old guy. I’m never trusting them with you again.”

Jon and Nola, along with the other two paramedics, Aiden Huff and Leon Ryerson, were focused on the two that shot each other. They were far enough away that they couldn’t hear the slight against them, not that it mattered. Buck had been taking shit from them all shift for ditching the pair of them like he had, which… He couldn’t really blame them for it.

But in his defense, Danny had warned them that he tended to wander off after a couple drinks.

“I don’t know. Maybe? I know I’m bothered by it.”

“I think that’s the last of the glass,” Danny said. Buck screwed the jar shut and started pulling out what his brother needed to patch the woman up. “Some people don’t mind living alone. Some people like living alone. Look at Austin, the weirdo.”

“There’s a difference between living alone and being alone, though,” Buck pointed out. “Austin still has his family, and he has you. Red doesn’t have anyone. No friends, no family. All the guys he knew from the One Thirty-four, they either don’t talk anymore or they’re dead.”

“That’s so depressing,” the woman chimed in. Buck gestured at her excitedly, glad that someone was agreeing with him.

“You should save that for the hospital bill,” Danny told her, taking off his medical gloves and gathering up the mess of supplies he’d made. “A trip to the ER would definitely be for the best, a couple of those might need stitches, but I can’t force you.”

The woman made a face at that, which turned into a wince when the motion pulled at the cuts. There really wasn’t anything else they could do for her beyond what Danny already had, because the ambulances were taken by the two gunshot victims. With everything packed back up, they made their way to the engine so Danny could stow his medical bag.

“I don’t talk to anyone from my old station, y’know,” Danny said as they walked. “Pretty sure Austin doesn’t talk to anyone from his old one, either. I think the only reason Mendoza stayed in touch with him is ‘cause Mendoza’s like herpes. You just can’t get rid of the guy.”

“You’d know all about STDs you can’t get rid of.” Buck stepped to the side to avoid the elbow that his statement earned. “It’s just… I dunno. It just isn’t right.”

They stopped when they reached the engine, Danny tugging open one of the compartments to shove the medical bag into it.

“Why do you care, squirt?” he asked, slamming the compartment door closed again. “You didn’t even know the guy last week.”

“Because I just do,” Buck said. “Because he doesn’t have anyone. Not like I have, like I always have. Even when Maddie chose Doug, and when Eddie chose Shannon, I always knew I had you. Always, the entire time I was growing up and even afterwards, and I know that’s not gonna change. But Red doesn’t have anyone like that and it… It just isn’t right.”

His brother sighed, face softening as he gripped Buck by the shoulders.

“You have too much heart,” Danny said, giving him a squeeze before letting go. “We’re not inviting the old man to dinner.”

He rounded the engine, probably to go speak to Captain Mehta and see what else needed doing before they headed out. Buck started to follow him, only to pause and look around. There was the unsettling feeling of being watched, of eyes digging into his back. It took a moment, but he spotted the culprit on the other side of the street and down the sidewalk a little.

It was one of the detectives. The cops showed up a couple minutes after them, but Mehta refused to let any of his people out to treat and triage until the scene had been cleared. The detectives arrived not long afterwards, a pair of them pulling up in their unmarked cars. Buck hadn’t paid them any mind, too focused on doing his job. And Danny, he knew, purposefully went out of his way to ignore them, which was much better than the overt hostility he probably would’ve shown if he was out of uniform.

Buck’s brother did not like the police, with Athena as the one and singular exception, which was something that became quite clear over the years.

This detective had been in the middle of getting a statement from someone, judging from the notepad he was tucking away into his pocket. He was chewing gum and he was smirking in Buck’s direction. Something about it, about that smirk, made his skin crawl. It had him hurrying to catch up with his brother while doing his best to make it seem like he wasn’t running away.

There was the nagging, niggling thought that the detective looked familiar, somehow. But Buck just shoved it away and did his best to move past it, to ignore how creepy the guy was. Mehta was telling them to pack it up and move out, anyway, so that was a good enough distraction.

“I found her!”

The sudden exclamation startled Eddie a little in his seat on the couch. He turned slightly to face Buck, who’d spend the entire evening on his laptop as he hunted down some old woman on the internet. He’d been subject to the texts and the rants about some old firefighter named Red and how he was all alone, and while he didn’t really understand his boyfriend’s current obsession about this, it hadn’t really been much different from any of the other times something caught his focus. By this point, he just rode the wave and tried to make sure Buck didn’t get lost at sea.

“Red’s Cindy,” Buck clarified, as if he needed to. “I found her, where she’s living.”

“Okay. Good. I guess,” Eddie said, a bit uncertain just what the appropriate response to his boyfriend’s successful bout of stalking should be.

“It is good,” Buck said, eyes flitting across the screen. “Even better, her husband’s dead.”

“Buck.”

His boyfriend paused what he was doing, lifted his head up, and then cringed.

“Yeah, okay. Not better, but…” He shook his head. “But this means that I can reintroduce them! She’s alone, he’s alone. It’s perfect, they can have their redo. Like we did.”

“Are you sure that-” Eddie stopped, peering over as Buck pulled up another website. “¿¡Qué carajo!? Buck, what are you doing?”

“Buying two tickets to the Dodger-Mets, for Red and Cindy,” his boyfriend explained, like that made any more sense. “I told you about the World Series he missed, right?”

“Yeah, you- Okay no.” He reached out and grabbed Buck’s hands before he could actually buy the tickets. “Slow your roll, there.”

Back in high school, he’d somehow fallen into the role of Buck’s guardrails, the person who kept him from going off track and crashing into a fiery blaze. He didn’t mind it much, honestly, because it really wasn’t that hard to do. He just had to recognize the signs of when it was getting out of hand, like now, and make him stop and take a breath. Give him time to actually think everything all the way through.

“You have no idea if this is a good idea or not,” Eddie told him as he moved the laptop to the end table on his other side. It wasn’t out of his boyfriend’s reach, because he absolutely would just climb over Eddie to get it, but it would do.

“Why wouldn’t this be a good idea?” Buck asked, offended and confused.

Right, his boyfriend was a romantic.  

“You don’t know if Cindy wants to see him, for one. You could get Red hopes up, only for it to be… Only for it to be like an us situation.”

“I’d like to think we’re doing okay.”

“You were just about to buy baseball tickets for an old man and his ex,” Eddie pointed out, some of his feelings about that leaking through his tone. Buck opened his mouth, only to close it and shrink in on himself a little. “You don’t know what this Cindy feels about everything. What if she hates him and wants nothing to do with him? What if she’s moved on? What if she doesn’t even remember him?”

“They were engaged, Eds.”

“Over thirty years ago,” he shot back. “That’s a lot of time. That’s longer than we’ve been alive.”

Buck grimaced.

“Yeah, okay, you’re- you’re right,” he said, sighing. “I just… I want to do something good for him, y’know?”

“What if we talk to her first?” Eddie offered. “Feel her out. If she’s still holding a torch for him, good, then we can go with your plan. Or, maybe not with your plan. I can’t believe you were going to buy baseball tickets for other people-”

“Sorry, sorry, I wasn’t thinking.”

This time it was Eddie’s turn to sigh.

“I’ve been meaning to talk to you about something,” he said. Buck’s expression immediately turned guarded. “And since we’re talking about two old people and a dead husband, this almost seems like an appropriate time.”

“For what?” Buck tentatively asked.

“I nearly died not too long ago,” was the blunt way that Eddie started the discussion. Buck looked away from him, but not before he got to see the pain flash across his face. “It wasn’t the first time. With our jobs, it probably won’t be the last time. So it got me thinking about the what-ifs. If I hadn’t managed to get out of that well, Chris would’ve gone back to my parents in Texas.”

Even just thinking about that made Eddie’s stomach clench. His parents would swoop in and take Chris away from Buck and from Danny, and then they’d smother him while calling it love. It was the absolute last thing Eddie wanted for his son, not after he put so much effort getting them both this new start.

“But,” Eddie continued. He reached over, used his fingers on Buck’s chin to turn his head and make him look. “I was going to go meet with my attorney, get my will updated and everything. Make it official where I want Chris to go if something happens to me.”

“O- Okay…”

“I haven’t gotten it notarized yet,” he said. “And even after, you can still refuse-”

“Wait,” Buck interrupted, wide-eyed. “Me?”

“Well. Yeah.” Eddie shrugged. “One of my biggest regrets, from the moment he was born, was that he grew up without you. And the only other person I’d trust him with as much as I do you would be Danny. So it’s gonna be in my will: if something happens to me, you get custody.”

“But… Me?”

“You kept him safe when the ocean tried to kill everyone,” Eddie reminded him, hand cupping his cheek. “You wandered through Santa Monica for I don’t know how long while you tried to find him, bleeding the entire time, and then you only stopped when you did. You went out and found a way for him to skateboard like he wanted, when everyone else tried to convince me to discourage him from trying. You sit there and you listen to him talk about the most random shit, and you actually care about what he’s saying. Why not you?”

“I’ve only ever been good for a couple things,” Buck whispered. “There wasn’t a point to me otherwise.”

As always, Eddie found himself struggling for what to say when his boyfriend spoke of himself like this. Having held his own son in his arms, having rocked him to sleep and held him through nightmares and listened to him laugh, Eddie could not fathom what could have gone through the Buckley parents’ heads that led them to raise Buck to think of himself like this. He could not grasp nor comprehend even the idea of teaching Chris that his purpose in life was to be useful for someone else.

Sometimes he marveled at Danny’s self-control, that he didn’t simply murder their parents with that baseball bat of his.

“That has never been true,” Eddie told Buck. “Not for a single second. And even if it was, then… You have something else to add to the list.”

Buck sniffed and reached up to rub at his suspiciously wet eyes, and then he nodded.

“I wouldn’t refuse,” he said.

“I know.”

“Give me my laptop back.” Even as he spoke, he was already climbing across Eddie to grab it. “I’m buying baseball tickets.”

“Please don’t tell me it’s for the old people.”

“No.” Buck rolled his eyes. “It’s for us. I hope you’re okay with nosebleeds.”

“Eh.” Eddie shrugged. “I’ll live.”

Chapter 12

Chapter Notes

CW for the end of the chapter: derogatory language; abusive and controlling behavior; implication of past nonconsensual sex
(and probably more that I simply don't know how to phrase appropriately.)

They went to visit Cindy together the next day, after seeing Christopher off to school. Eddie rode in the passenger seat of the jeep, stuck listening to Buck as he sang along with the pop music on the radio. Change the songs, put them into a different vehicle, and it wouldn’t be much different from when they were in high school. Especially since his boyfriend’s singing talent had not improved in the intervening years.

He made a point of telling him so at a stop light, and then leaned across the center console to kiss away the offended pout that the statement got him.

Cindy lived in La Crescenta, on the other side of Glendale and Griffith Park. It was a longer trip than when they took Chris to the zoo, especially with the city’s morning traffic. Her house was picturesque. A bungalow that was painted a blue that bordered on gray, with a porch that ran along the entire front and a white picket fence that stretched from the row of hedges on one side to the driveway on the other, with vines trailing along it and over the trellis that arched the gate.

“It’s a nice place,” Eddie commented as they got out.

“Her husband was some sort of doctor,” Buck said. “And I’m pretty sure there’s a homeowner’s association.”

“This entire neighborhood is hideous.”

Buck’s laughter carried them through the gate and up the sidewalk. He bounded up the steps ahead of Eddie and rapped at the door, bouncing on his toes as they waited. The woman who answered the door was definitely not the woman they were looking for, not unless Red was literally cradle-robbing.

“Hello.” The woman looked between them warily. “Can I help you?”

“Yes, ma’am,” Buck said. “We’re here to see Cindy.”

The woman opened her mouth when another lady, much older, popped up behind her. The newcomer - Eddie figured it was fair to assume that this was Cindy - looked between them curiously.

“Who is it, Doris?” she asked.

“We’re- Well, I’m a friend of Red’s,” Buck said, though the statement sounded more like a question at the end. “I was wanting to surprise him, help the two of you… Reconnect, you know?”

“I knew a Red once,” Cindy said, almost absently. Eddie caught Buck’s smile drop into a quick frown, there and gone again.

“Y- Yeah, Red Delacroix. You were, uh. You were engaged,” Buck said. “Back in the eighties…”

Doris looked conflicted, but she stepped farther back and opened the door wider.

“Cindy doesn’t get many visitors,” she said. “Come on in, it’ll be nice. Right, Cindy?”

“Yes.” Cindy nodded, hesitant at first and then with more feeling. “Yes, yes. Come in.”

The two women led them into the house, to the dining room with a large table. The visit went okay at first. Or, mostly okay. As always, Eddie allowed Buck to drive the conversation. He talked about Red and how he met the old man, urging Cindy to talk about him as well. And she did, in fits and spurts.

But the lines coming out of her mouth were disjointed, not quite connected to the topics they were talking about. It got worse as they went along: a story about a snake had her mentioning, out of the blue, how they were terrible pets; mentioning children led to her telling them, very seriously, that they had to be folded very carefully before putting them in the box; there was a throw away comment about “those damn birds” that she didn’t seem to even realize she had said. Every time it happened, Eddie watched Buck’s face drop before he pulled his bright smile back up again.

When Doris went into the kitchen to get them drinks, Eddie offered his assistance. Mostly, he just wanted to get away from the increasingly uncomfortable atmosphere of the dining room.

“Cindy, she’s…”

“Alzheimer’s.” Doris pulled out a pitcher of iced tea from the fridge and placed it on a tray. “Whatever your friend was wanting to do, I don’t think it’ll go the way he was hoping.”

“Yeah, I -”

He was interrupted by Cindy’s suddenly raised voice, the woman shouting,

“Who let you into my house? Doris!”

Eddie and Doris both rushed into the dining room, finding Cindy on her feet, looking absolutely terrified. Buck, meanwhile, just looked pained.

“I think it’s getting late,” Doris told them, though it wasn’t even midday yet.

“Right, you’re right.” Buck got out of the chair, giving both women a wobbly smile. “We didn’t mean to bother you, we’ll just… We’ll just go. I’m really sorry.”

They let themselves out, guiltily leaving Doris to calm Cindy down. Unlike the walk up to the house, there was no laughing as they went back to the jeep. Instead, they were grimly silent as they climbed into the jeep. Buck, despite sticking his key into the ignition, didn’t start the engine right away. He just laid his head on the steering wheel, looking dejected.

“Abby’s mom was like that,” he said, the words quiet. “She kept mistaking me for Abby’s ex, some guy named Tommy. The first time I saw Abby in person, the first time I met Carla, was because she got up and wandered outside one day. One of the guys who found her, he warned us that it would only get worse. And it did. Abby was relieved after her mother died, and I couldn’t really blame her.”

Eddie reached over and laid his hand on Buck’s back and began to rub aimless circles against it. He heard his boyfriend sigh, a quiet and sad little thing.

“What are you going to do?” he asked him.

“I don’t know,” Buck admitted. “Tell Red, I guess. Give him the choice. It’s only fair, isn’t it?”

Buck lifted his head and looked at Eddie in question, and Eddie’s only answer was to shrug. It wasn’t like he knew what the right thing to do here was. All he knew right now was that he wanted to call his Abuela up and just be thankful that she wasn’t like that.

“At least you stopped me from rushing into it,” Buck said. He sat up and turned the key, the jeep’s engine rumbling to life. “I would’ve just brought Red over and I don’t know how bad that would’ve gone.”

Eddie glanced out the window to look at the bungalow again before they were pulling away from the curb.

“I hope we didn't upset her too much.”

“She won’t remember,” Buck told him, and that might’ve been the most heartbreaking statement that Eddie had heard in a very long while.

Buck went alone to talk to Red, after hanging out with Eddie for a bit longer. Somehow, in the full light of day, the building he was in looked smaller and sadder. At least he didn’t have to wait long after knocking before Red was answering the door, still drying a kitchen pan. He must’ve been washing whatever dishes a lonely old man could go through in a meal.

“What are you doing back here, kid?” was how he greeted Buck.

“I, uh. I found Cindy,” Buck answered, nervously tucking his hands into his pants pockets.

“I didn’t know she was lost,” was Red’s reply, which only served to confuse Buck. “Last I heard, she was living in La Crescenta with that dentist husband of hers.”

“Wait.” Was he understanding this correctly? “You knew where she was this whole time?”

“It wasn’t like I was stalking her, but… Yeah.” Red shrugged, going back into the kitchen just off the entryway while he talked. He didn’t tell Buck to go away, so he stepped inside and followed him, closing the door as he did. “From time to time, I’d learn some stuff. Did you hear the part when I told you she was married?”

“Not anymore, he died,” Buck told him, which caught Red’s interest.

“When did he die?”

“A few years back.”

“So she’s been alone all this time…” Red’s word trailed off with the thought. He sat the dried pan on the counter by a rack full of dishes and picked up a mug to start wiping down.

“Yeah,” Buck agreed, because it really did seem to be the case. “But…”

“But?” the old man prompted.

“She has Alzheimer’s,” he said, because he did not know of a way to soften that truth. He watched Red’s face twist with heartbreak.

“How bad?”

“Bad. She remembered you, when we told her and her nurse why we were there,” Buck told him. “But she also… She forgot who I was in the middle of talking to me. Got upset because a stranger was in her home.”

“Oh, Cindy,” Red whispered, clutching at the mug and the towel.

“She’s still there,” Buck told him. “She’s alone except for her nurse, and like I said, she remembered you when I told her why I was there. If… If you wanted…”

“No.” The old man shook his head. “I have these great memories of her. The girl that started bar fights, the girl who was terrified of snakes. The girl who knew me. I’m not sure if I could take it if I went there and she…”

“Yeah, no. I- I get it.”

And Buck did, was the thing. He remembered getting a front row seat for it with Abby and her mother, Patricia. He remembered seeing firsthand the toll it took on Abby, every time she was viciously reminded that her mother - while still right there in front of her - was taken away a little bit more every day. He’d told Eddie that Abby had been relieved when her mother finally passed and as awful as it sounded, it had been very true. Buck didn’t blame her for it one bit, either.

He was dragged from his thoughts about Abby and Patricia by Red suddenly putting a hand on his arm.

“Listen, kid,” the old man said. “Thank you. You wanted to do something kind for me, and your heart was in the right place.”

“My brother says I have too much heart.”

“And you should keep it that way.”

Buck stuck around, hanging out with the retired firefighter that was more than triple his age. Red seemed to appreciate it, however much he might’ve tried to deny how lonely he was. Unfortunately, he couldn’t stay too long, because he’d promised part of his time to Chris and he had a shift the next day. He left with the promise to visit Red again soon, which the old man took with obvious skepticism. 

The promise was kept much sooner than Buck expected, and not in the context he’d hoped. In the early evening, Red called him, which was initially an unexpected delight, considering Buck assumed he’d have to inflict himself upon the man’s self-imposed exile. It soured quickly, though, when the reason for the call became evident. 

Red’s hospital room was easy enough to find, after a quick talk with a nurse. He reached it in a rush, finding the old man looking small in the bed, an oxygen cannula beneath his nose.

“Hey, I came as soon as I could,” Buck told him, slowing to a stop by his side. “What’s going on?”

“I’m sorry.” Red sounded miserable. “I didn’t know who else to call.”

“No, no, I’m glad you called.” Buck wasn’t sure there was even another option for Red to have called besides him. “You said you needed some help getting home?”

“I should be so lucky. These-” He cut himself off with a frustrated huff. “I’ve been arguing with these doctors for the last hour. They won’t release me, so I think you wasted a trip down here.”

“They- They probably know what’s best,” Buck said. He took a look at the vitals being tracked on the nearby monitor, which didn’t seem to show anything concerning. A low O2 count, but that was what the oxygen was for. “They’ll release you when you’re better.”

“Oh, kid, there is no better,” Red said. “This escalator is only going in one direction. Mesothelioma, got diagnosed last year. I wasn’t even supposed to survive this long, but you know me. Stubborn, never wanna quit. Not that I’m getting the choice now.”

“No.” Buck shook his head in denial. “There must be some kind of treatment, something they can do.”

“You’re forty years too late to save me. Stop trying.”

Buck ducked his head and swallowed down the protests that clogged his throat. 

“I’m sorry,” he said, the words coming out quiet. “Is there, um. What can I do?”

“Sit with me for a while?” Red asked, patting the bed. “Unless you’ve got something else to do.”

“No, no, I’m good here.” Buck glanced about, spotted a stool on wheels and tugged it over to sit down. Eddie would understand, and so would Danny. “You, um. You never told me about Arno. How did he break his nose?”

“That’s a good one,” Red said, laughing a little. Buck settled in to listen. “The call comes in, and it’s in an abandoned warehouse downtown on Fifth. Smoke coming out of every window. So Arno, pretty clumsy…”

“It looks good on you,” Eddie told Hen. “The doctor’s coat, I mean.”

Their previous shift before, Hen went, maybe, a little bit off the rails. He wasn’t entirely certain what happened in the ambulance, but he knew most of the important details. There was a contestant on a cooking show, who got a piece of shrapnel in his chest - very near to his heart - after a canister of whipped cream exploded. Something happened in transport that led to Hen doing a thoracotomy, reaching in and manually pinching the aorta, staying like that all the way up to and through the surgery.

It was Chimney’s idea to surprise her with a doctor’s coat in place of her turnout at the start of their shift. Eddie took plenty of pictures, mostly because he knew he wouldn’t hear the end of it from Buck if he didn’t.

“It fits,” Hen commented, tugging on the lapels of the coat. She hadn’t taken it off yet, even though they were now elbow deep in doing inventory for the ambulance. “I do like the sound of Dr. Wilson.”

“Aren’t you married to a Dr. Wilson?”

“She’s a rocket scientist, it’s not the same thing,” she said, waving away the semantics, her words lined with the fondness that always crept up whenever Eddie heard her talk about Karen. “How goes the adventures of Buck and the old guy?”

Hen and the rest of the 118 had been keeping up to date with it, mostly thanks to Buck's continuous texts and Edde’s commentary. 

“The old guy is dying,” Eddie said with a shrug. Hen blanched. “Mesothelioma.”

“Oh, God. I’m…” She shook her head. “Seriously, then, how’s Buck doing?”

“If I told you he was doing okay, I’d probably be lying,” he told her. “He’s going full Buck about things, spent all of yesterday making phone calls.”

“To who? Miracle cancer clinics?”

“Captain Mehta, Chief Williams, whoever he could get ahold from Red’s time at the One Thirty-four that might still be around. He’s big on the grand gestures, I think he’s trying to get some big sendoff for the guy.”

“Karen and I will have to drag him over for a visit, it’s been too long since our last get together,” Hen said, and then nodded to herself before pulling out her phone. “I’ll tell him to clear a day. He’s not getting a choice in the matter.”

“He’s not gonna say no.” A question popped into Eddie’s head, and he was too curious not to ask. “Hey, do you still talk to anyone from before? Buck’s the only one I know of that you make the effort.”

“Not really,” she admitted, not that it looked to be a hardship for her. “Most of the guys that were here when I started, I was glad to see the back of. The atmosphere wasn’t really conducive to bonding, especially when it came to me and Chimney. Our first captain was…”

“Old fashioned?”

“A racist, sexist prick,” Hen said, and that had him barking out a laugh.

The apartment was silent. Buck sat at the old dining table, slumped in on himself. Maddie had come over, declaring it an impromptu Buckley Sibling day, and sent their brother out to get what Buck needed to eat his feelings in an unsubtle maneuver to monopolize their time for a bit. The evening before, after spending a lot of time on the phone, he managed to get department approval to give Red the sendoff he deserved. The 133 lined up, along with retired members of the 134, from the hospital doors to the engine, which Red got to ride home.

“He passed away at Five Twenty-three this morning,” Buck told Maddie, wiping at his face. It felt stupid, to be this upset about someone he only knew for a few days. “The department’s gonna pay for the funeral.”

“At least he wasn’t alone in the end,” Maddie said, reaching over to gently place her hand over his. “You were a good friend to him.”

“Did I just make it all about me?” he asked. “I mean, I was the one who was upset about him being lonely. He was perfectly fine before I barged into his life.”

“Did he seem upset with you being there?” Maddie asked him.

“No. He liked telling me all his old work stories,” Buck said. “That was all he wanted to talk about. It was practically his whole life, it was all he had.”

“He had you at the end, too,” his sister said. “I know we all like to tease you, but you really are a good person and a good friend. Simply being there so he could tell someone his stories might’ve been the best thing you could’ve done for him.”

“Yeah, maybe.” He was still left with the unshakable feeling that he should’ve been able to do more. “I’m, uh. I’m thinking about… Not asking to move in with Eddie, but claiming a drawer, maybe.”

“The two of you have been together for…” Maddie scrunched up her nose. “Are we counting the high school years?”

Buck just shrugged.

“Red told me not to reach the end holding nothing but regrets,” he said. “But there’s Chris to think about, and I… I trust Eddie, I do. I want to trust Eddie. So this is, y’know. A baby step towards that. Plus, there’s Danny-”

“I’m sorry,” Maddie interrupted, not sounding very sorry at all. “How does our brother relate to you moving in with your boyfriend?”

“I’m not moving in, I’m gonna ask him for a drawer,” Buck reiterated. “But I don’t really want to leave Danny alone again. I don’t think he does well.”

He remembered the manic, frantic energy that surrounded Danny, when he came to Buck that Christmas after he spent two years without visiting El Paso even once. The desperation that dripped off of him was part of why Buck hadn’t argued when his brother bluntly informed him that they were moving to Los Angeles. It was why, even when he felt guilty and a bit ashamed to be encroaching on his brother’s space again, he kept coming back to do it even after he moved in with Connor and the others.

“The two of you are the definition of codependent.” Maddie rolled her eyes and, after a thoughtful pause, raised her hand between them, pinky out. Buck stared at it, uncomprehending. “We’ll both make sure that Dan isn’t wallowing alone. How about that?”

“Deal,” Buck agreed, wrapping his own pinky around hers.

“Where is he, anyways?” Maddie pulled out her phone to check it. “He should be back by now with my ice cream.”

“I thought the ice cream was for me to eat my feelings.”

“I can eat your feelings, too.”

Daniel Buckley loved his siblings, and that was the only reason he allowed himself to be ordered out of his own apartment to do a store run for ice cream. He’d also stopped for pizza, guessing that his brother wouldn’t be up to cooking anything and that neither of them would complain about it. Juggling everything between the car and the apartment building took some work, though, and it was a welcome distraction from the clinging smell of cigarette smoke that was filling the evening air.

He nearly dropped everything, though, when he heard his voice.

“If it ain’t my favorite whore.” 

It was a slow, reluctant turn that brought Daniel around to face him. The man was just behind him, having stepped out from wherever he’d been lying in wait. Back in the day, Daniel would’ve been more vigilant about it, but time and distance lowered his guard.

The man didn’t look all that different from the last time that Daniel saw him. His dark hair was still cut close to his scalp, the drawl and the smirk was the same, the cigarette was probably even the same brand. The suit was new, though, and maybe his face was a little thinner.

“Officer Drake.” Daniel hated how his voice trembled, hated how his hands shook. “What are you doing here?”

“It’s Detective Drake, now.” He walked closer and Daniel scrambled backwards, until he hit the wall of the apartment building. He’d forgotten how much shorter than him Drake was, because he always seemed to loom over him in his memories. “Got a promotion, transferred over. Imagine my surprise when I ran into a Buckley, of all people, durin’ a case. And then I saw you and lil’ Evan the other day. Small world after all.”

Horror crawled up Daniel’s throat. Drake had been around, had been watching them, and he hadn’t even noticed. How hadn’t he noticed?

“What do you want?” he managed to ask, stupidly proud of himself that the words didn’t shake too much.

“To catch up,” Drake said, like he was actually interested in catching up. “We left off on a sour note, after all.”

That was an understatement. There’d been more than just Buck’s refusal to return to El Paso that had led to him deciding to move, even if his brother had been the biggest drive behind it.

“I told you we were through.”

“And I told you that whores don’t get to say no,” Drake told him, getting into his space. Daniel pressed himself into the wall and wished he could just fall through it.

“I’m not a whore anymore,” he said. “I’m telling you no. Evan’s an adult now, remember? You can’t threaten me with CPS anymore. There’s nothing you can threaten me with anymore, so just fuck. Off.”

His heart pounded in his chest as he watched Drake’s face twist into a snarl. The man never did like being told no, and he hadn’t been happy the first time Daniel drew the line in the sand. He raised the cigarette and Daniel could not help but flinch as he snubbed it out on the wall right beside his head, close enough that the man’s hand brushed against Daniel’s ear.

“Well I’ll be around,” Drake said, the words deceptively calm for all that Daniel knew enough to recognize the undercurrent of anger and danger. “For when you change your mind.”

Daniel meant to tell him to fuck off again, meant to tell him that there wasn’t a chance in hell that he’d change his mind. But his words were caught in his suddenly too-tight throat, and it took all he had to keep from dropping everything with the way he shook. The moment Drake took enough steps back to give him the space, he was running through the front doors of the building.

The elevator ride to the third floor was far too short, but it gave Daniel the chance to calm his racing heart and the shaking of his hands. By the time he was walking through his door, he was pretty sure neither of his siblings would be able to tell that anything was wrong.

“I come bearing gifts,” he declared, beelining for the dining table that Buck and Maddie were sitting at to set his cargo down.

“About time,” Buck said, diving for the bag with the ice cream. He dug a tub out and immediately tore the lid off.

“Try to remember that we taught you manners.” Maddie rolled her eyes at their little brother. She glanced Daniel’s way, her mouth turning into a frown that he did not particularly like. “Are you okay?”

“Peachy,” Daniel lied. “I’m gonna go take a shower real quick. Make sure he doesn’t eat all the pizza.”

At least Buck was too busy being offended to question anything.

Chapter 13

Firefighter funerals for line-of-duty deaths were big affairs, full of pomp and circumstance. People from other departments travelled halfway across the country to pay their respects, and it seemed like half the city would shut down for them. They were thankfully also rather uncommon: Daniel had only been to a couple by this point, one in El Paso and one since moving to Los Angeles. 

The first line-of-duty funeral he went to, the one back in El Paso, Buck went with him. Daniel hadn’t been doing the job for very long at that point, had yet to even finish his first year. Buck spent that service unusually silent and still, all solemn in the new clothes bought just for the occasion. He’d clung to Daniel’s side afterwards, and it wasn’t long before a secondhand police scanner appeared in his room.

Daniel was fairly certain that his brother hadn’t quite understood what the risks inherent to the job actually entailed until that first funeral. It had not been an open casket.

The funeral for Red Delacroix was not nearly as extravagant as those two. There was no procession, no final tone out, no speeches made by public officials. The venue wasn’t packed to bursting with people that came all the way from places like Washington and Ohio. There was just a sad old man in a casket and the few people that bothered to show up to pay their respects.

Obviously, Buck was one of those people, and just as obviously, so was Daniel. Eddie would’ve been, if he hadn’t been stuck on a shift. Not because either of them particularly cared about Red - Eddie never met the man, and the only time Daniel spent with him was when they gave him the ride home from the hospital in the engine - but because Buck did. So Daniel dragged out the funeral clothes and sat through the service, from the opening prayer to the internment.

When that was done, when even the other retired members of the 134 were dispersing, they got back into Daniel’s car to leave. Buck was silent as they drove, and was so lost in his head that he didn’t appear to notice that they weren’t heading back to the apartment.

“Why are we in Los Feliz?” he finally asked, looking up to frown out the windshield at the houses surrounding them.

“We’ve been in Los Feliz, squirt,” Daniel informed him, taking a turn. “Not my fault you weren’t paying attention to your surroundings.”

“Okay, but why?”

“Reasons.”

Buck did not seem to appreciate that answer, going by the glower he now wore. Daniel ignored his pouting, though, to pay attention to where he was going. He’d never been to this particular destination before, after all, and relaxed when he spotted Austin’s car on the curb down the street, parking behind it.

“So do I get to know anything?” his brother complained. “Whose house is this? Why do you keep doing this to me?”

“It’s Ethan and Irene’s.”

“Austin’s brother, right?” Buck peered out the window as he unbuckled and they hopped out. It wasn’t a very tall house, with an enclosed front porch, along with fencing and walling that surrounded the property. Though there wasn’t much actual yard in the front, a symptom of the city’s constant drought conditions, the little of it there was, was claimed by shrubs and flowers. There was even a climbing vine of some sort using the screen around the porch as a trellis. “It’s a nice house, I guess.”

“Ethan’s an electrician,” Daniel said. “I have no clue what Irene does, something in an office. I dunno.”

“None of this answers why I’m here, though. I don’t know why I’m getting dragged along to the Joneses family gatherings.”

“You’re not.” Daniel stopped just short of the porch. “Ethan’s an idiot and doesn’t have the new baby’s room ready yet-”

“Isn’t the baby almost due?”

“Like I said, idiot. And Austin got dragged in to help, which means I’m getting dragged in to help.”

“So I’m, what? Being forced to put together a crib or something?” Buck made a face. “Am I at least getting fed?”

“No to the crib, yes to the food. You’re keeping Irene and the little brat company.”

Buck looked, if possible, even more confused at that statement. Daniel ignored it as he went onto the porch and knocked on the front door. There was from the inside the sound tiny pitter-pattering of feet running across the room, the wiggling of the door knob, the sound of a tiny little girl shouting for her mom. A couple minutes later, the latch was undone and the door was opening.

“Oh, thank God,” Irene said when she saw them. She was very heavily pregnant, looking fit to burst, but Daniel wasn’t going to say anything. Not after her and Cynthia’s colorful threats involving forks being stabbed into places they should never go the last time he made a comment without thinking. “I haven’t seen the mess they’ve made of everything, but it sounds like it’s going awful.”

“You remember Buck, right?” Daniel gestured at him, and then looked down to greet the tiny little girl standing just behind her mother’s legs. “Hi, Rose.”

“Hi!” Rosemary shouted and waved, her dark hair tied up in pigtails.

“Seriously, Danny, what am I doing here?” Buck asked, doing his best to keep his voice to a whisper as they stepped inside.

“Hanging out with the kid,” was Daniel’s answer, and then didn’t wait to listen to his brother’s confused sputtering as he headed down the hall, leaving Buck behind with Irene and Rosemary.

The room he was looking for was easy to find, he just had to follow the cursing. When he stuck his head through the doorway, there was a mess of parts scattered across the floor with a barely put-together crib in the middle of it. Ethan, who looked very much like his older brother, was staring at the instructions in clear confusion. Austin was just sitting off to the side, beer in hand. He raised it in greeting when Daniel came inside.

“Did you come straight here?” Austin asked, pulling another beer from the six pack beside him and holding it out.

“Neither of you do anything straight,” Ethan immediately replied, still focused on the instructions. “This makes no sense, the spacers and the supports look the exact same!”

“Things are going well here, then.” Daniel took the offered drink and twisted the cap off. “Didn’t make sense to go to the apartment only to have to turn around and come back. And Buck needs cheering up, figured Rose could help with that.”

“My baby girl is a perfect angel, ‘course she can!” Ethan declared, and then threw the instructions across the room. “Screw it, we’ll figure it out. Austin, hand me that screwdriver.”

Austin handed the tool over, rolling his eyes at Daniel as he did. Daniel got settled onto the floor, reaching to drag the instructions over to himself, along with one of the parts, and got to work trying to prevent the thing from turning into a death trap for an as yet to be born infant.

When Buck decided to take a (very minor) leap of faith and ask Eddie for a drawer to keep clothes, he knew the man wouldn’t say no. What he didn’t expect, however, was for the man to immediately go to his bedroom, yank a drawer out of his dresser, and dump all of its contents onto the bed. The Diazes had a flair for the dramatics, that much Buck was well aware of, but he had a suspicion that it wasn’t just that. Or more than a suspicion: he remembered the argument they’d had, the evening before Eddie was buried alive in the mud. 

Carla’s innocent, joking comparison between how Buck was with Abby, practically moving into her place, and how he was with Eddie had upset the latter. They both knew why that was, too, even though they only spoke around the reasons. Chris made for a nice excuse, the insistence that it was his home, too, but he very much wasn’t the real reason for why Buck was holding himself back.

Red had told him not to reach the end holding nothing but regrets. So here he was now, taking a very minor leap of faith and a drawer in the bedroom. And some space in the bathroom medicine cabinet. 

“I don’t remember you using all this back in school,” Eddie remarked, watching him from the bathroom door. When Buck glanced back at him over his shoulder, the man’s smile was nearly splitting his face.

“I couldn’t afford it back then,” Buck told him, nudging a can of shaving cream aside to make room for a thing of pomade. “Not the good stuff, anyways. Now I can.”

“There’s space for you to put clothes in.”

“That didn’t take long.”

Buck shut the medicine cabinet and caught sight of his boyfriend’s reflection. The man was, for some reason, embarrassed. His cheeks were flushed, continuing down his neck beneath his shirt, and he was suddenly looking at his feet. The reason why became readily apparent when Buck took his bag into the bedroom, finding an empty dresser drawer on the bed with all of its former contents dumped out around it.

“Seriously?” Buck picked up a pair of balled up socks and turned to fix an incredulous stare on Eddie.

“I didn’t want to risk you changing your mind,” Eddie mumbled with a shrug. “I’ll find somewhere to put everything.”

Buck rolled his eyes, even as he smiled at his boyfriend’s antics.

“You’re adorable,” he drawled, and started emptying his overnight bag. 

He’d never been very particular about how his clothes were put away, something which only got worse with his years spent on the road. More often than not, if they weren’t going to be hanging in the closet, they just got bundled up and stuffed somewhere. There was usually a system, pants going into their own drawer, for example, but there wasn’t ever anything neat about it.

Apparently, watching Buck just carelessly stuff everything into his designated drawer was a bit too much for Eddie, because he was soon marching over with grumbled complaints. He grabbed a shirt, neatly folded it crisply and placed it back, and then repeated the process with a pair of sweats.

“Well if you want to do it for me,” Buck teased. It earned him a dirty side-eye, but his boyfriend grabbed the bag and dragged it towards himself.

“I know Danny and Maddie taught you to fold your clothes,” Eddie said.

“That shirt was folded! I watched you unfold it!”

“It wasn’t folded very well.”

Everyone was a god damn critic. Buck let out a huff and sat on the bed, grabbing one of the balled up pairs of socks to toss between his hands. He hadn’t brought much with him, barely more than what he usually packed to spend the night. The point wasn’t to bring enough to practically move in, after all. The point was that little leap of faith and trust that they were both committed to this. The point was the soft, contented smile on Eddie’s face as he put away the proof that Buck trusted him.

“What’s this?” Eddie suddenly asked, patting around the inside of the bag. When he pulled out the old, tattered copy of Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland, he looked to Buck for an explanation.

“I stole them both off Danny’s bookshelf, the day I left. I always pack 'em whenever I go somewhere,” Buck explained with a shrug, reaching in to pull out Through the Looking-Glass, which was in the same battered shape as the other book. Danny had gotten both books when they were still in Hershey, at some yard sale, back when Danny himself was still a kid. Buck figured it was an act of desperation from how tired he was of reading The Stinky Cheese Man so damn often. “Maybe I should give them back to Danny, I dunno.”

He slid the book back into the bag. After a moment, Eddie did the same with the one he was holding.

“We do have that copy you bought Chris for Christmas,” Eddie said, sounding a bit hesitant. 

“Which I guess means I don’t have to bring these copies here with me, at least.” Buck got to his feet and picked up the now half-filled drawer. He took it back to the dresser and slid it into its proper slot, after a bit of wiggling and some elbow grease. “We should find somewhere to put those at.”

He pointed at what was still on the bed as he said it.

“Probably,” Eddie agreed easily, before grabbing a nearby (empty) laundry basket and using his arm to sweep everything off the bed and into it. “There.”

Eddie looked so proud of himself, Buck had to kiss the smile off his face.

Back in El Paso, when everything was at its worst, Daniel would creep through the parking lot of their building like it was enemy territory. He’d constantly look around, checking for ambushes, and didn’t relax until he was inside their apartment. Drake liked to lurk, to wait and catch him when he was just coming home. Probably got a thrill out of how stressed it made Daniel.

He would probably get a thrill out of knowing that a single encounter sent Daniel right back into that headspace. The officer- the detective hadn’t made a reappearance since Daniel told him to get lost, but Daniel knew that it was only a matter of time. “No” had always been more of a suggestion for the man, and he always got off just as much on the tormenting as he did from the actual sex.

The knowledge that Drake was out there and knew where he lived, again, was partly why Daniel started finding reasons to not be home alone. That mostly meant that, in the days since, he was bothering Austin even more often, either making up excuses to have him come over or going to the other man’s apartment. He’d actually accepted his coworkers’ invitation to go out somewhere without the usual reluctance or complaint, even though, or rather because Buck had plans to be with Eddie that day.

Tonight, though, Daniel found himself at Michael’s again, of all places. Worse, he ended up crashing Michael’s time with his kids. He’d only meant to try and set up the time for their next two person support group, since he knew Michael would be going in for a scan that week. But something must have come across in Daniel’s tone to have Michael inviting him over.

Dinner at the Grant apartment turned out to be Chinese takeout and it very much felt like Daniel was intruding, however much Michael assured him that he wasn’t. It helped that he was familiar enough with both of Athena’s kids from that summer he watched them while she went off on illicit rendezvous with Nash. Still though, this was Michael’s time with his kids and Daniel was almost certain he was here only because the man had caught that thread of desperation in his voice while trying to make plans.

Knocking at the door interrupted their conversation, which was mainly Daniel entertaining them with embarrassing stories of Buck and Eddie. Michael frowned at the door in confusion, glanced at his phone for the time, and then got up to answer it.

“Bobby, hey!” was how he greeted the person on the other side, and Daniel nearly strained something with how hard he rolled his eyes. May caught him in the act and did a poor job of stifling giggles. “I thought Athena was doing the pickup.”

“She took an extra shift and I’m subbing in.” Nash looked past Michael into the apartment. Daniel knew when he was spotted sitting at the table with the kids, because the fire captain made a face. May giggled even harder. “And I’m early.”

“Are you hungry? We’ve got plenty of food.” Michael stepped aside, already welcoming Nash inside. “Come on in.”

It was amusing to watch the conflict play out over Nash’s face. It was with some reluctance that he made his way to the table, Michael closing the door behind him. The captain went the long way around to a free chair, giving May and Harry quick pats and squeezes in greeting, and it was surely a mere coincidence that it meant he didn’t go anywhere near where Daniel was sitting.

“Athena’s been picking up a lot of overtime lately,” Michael commented as he grabbed a plate to set in front of Nash, before he retook his own seat.

“Yeah, lately, I’ve been feeling like all our communication has been through text messages and Post-It notes,” Nash complained. “Ever since she caught this case.”

“Which case?” Harry popped up to ask. Michael and Nash fell into awkward silence, so it was May who answered him.

“The Realtor Rapist. Mom’s on the task force,” she said, sounding proud and not a little excited. When she noticed her father’s disapproving stare, her tone turned defensive. “What? I saw it on the news.”

“Realtor Rapist is a stupid name, though,” Daniel couldn’t help but comment, which had Michael’s turning his disapproval his way. Daniel was completely unbothered as he stabbed a piece of chicken with his fork. “It’s true. The only thing it has going for it is the alliteration.”

“It’s not exactly polite dinner table conversation, so let’s just leave it there, okay?” Michael said. “Happier subjects please.”

“Okay,” May agreed. “So let’s talk about the schedule for Saturday.”

“What’s on Saturday?” Daniel asked, curiosity getting the better of him.

“Prom,” she answered.

“Oh.” He scrunched his face up. “I never went.”

“Why not?”

“Better things to do.” Better things, in this case, being a part time job to earn the money needed to get Buck the hell out of Hershey.

“What did Buck and Eddie do for their prom?” Michael asked, because by now they’d all heard an abridged and sanitized version of the pairs’ high school romance.

It was clear from Nash’s face - eyes wide, lips flattened and drawn into a long line, gaze focused on the table instead of any of them - that he had a more complete idea of things. He might have even gotten a version of the prom story specifically.

“Um,” Daniel said, and then smiled as a thought came to him. He wasn’t a very nice person at times. “You know what? The next time you see Eddie, you should ask him that.”

Nash let out a noise that was most definitely a laugh, no matter how much he tried to play it off as coughing. Michael just looked confused, but he let it go as May grabbed the metaphorical pulpit.

“Mom’s gonna take me to get my hair and makeup done at twelve,” she informed them. “We should be done by three-”

“You’re not getting ready at the house?” Bobby asked, clearly unaware of this. Neither was Michael, apparently. Daniel, meanwhile, was much more concerned with why it was going to take three hours to get her hair and makeup ready. Not even Buck took that long when he was primping. “When did this happen?”

“It happened after May guilt-tripped Mom because she didn’t go with her to pick out her stupid dress,” Harry said.

“I did not guilt-trip her,” his sister protested. “I just said it would have been nice for her to be there when I picked it.”

“You guilt-tripped her.”

“Good for you,” Daniel told her, nodding in approval. He’d taken Buck to get the suit he wore to that disaster of a prom, and didn’t really understand why Athena would let something else take precedence over dress shopping with her daughter.

“Darius is coming to pick me up at four,” May continued as she rolled her eyes at the both of them. “Dad will have forty-five minutes for pictures, so-”

“That’s it?” was Michael’s offended question.

“We have to go take pictures at Darius’ house, too. Everybody gets forty-five minutes.”

“Don’t you think your old man should have a little extra time?” he asked, before gesturing dramatically at his head. “On account of the brain tumor.”

May glared at her father, lips pursed.

“Not funny,” she told him, and then threw up her hands. “Fine. I’ll tell Darius to come early, you’ll get an hour.”

She got out of her seat as she pulled out her phone, walking to the other end of the apartment to have her conversation. Daniel silently bumped fists with Michael.

“I don’t think you’re gonna get to play that card much longer,” Nash said, very obviously amused. “Your scan is tomorrow, right?”

“And Dad’s gonna crush it,” was Harry’s optimistic statement.

“Hopefully,” Michael said. “I’m feeling good. No headache, no dizziness, but, you know, I just…”

“You don’t want to jinx it,” Nash finished for him.

“Right. Last time was nothing but bad news. I’m just preparing myself for the worst.”

“Do you have anyone going with you tomorrow?” Daniel asked him.

“Athena and Bobby both work, but it’ll be fine,” Michael answered with a shrug. “But seriously, what happened with Buck and Eddie’s prom?”

For the first time in a very long time, perhaps for the first time ever, Daniel and Nash agreed on something as they worked together to hurriedly change the subject.

Chapter 14

Chapter Notes

Content warnings in this chapter for: off-screen physical assault (that the characters can hear); the aftermath of physical violence; sexual coercion; threats regarding the misuse of authority; and a slur directed Chris' way for added seasoning.

People were idiots, this was a fact that Eddie was already fully aware of. Still, though, it never failed to surprise him whenever someone proved how true it was. It was mostly the ways that they did, honestly. People could be very creative with their stupidity.

Apparently, a woman took issue with tree trimmers doing their jobs. Which, fair, they weren’t exactly arborists, closer to butchers in how they went about their job at times. Still, though, stealing their truck while they were working was a bit overboard. The tree trimmer ended up taking a dive into an Amazon delivery van when he saw that the bucket he was in was about to be driven right into a powerline.

When they arrived, the woman was trapped in the cab of the truck. Its engine was on fire and there was electricity crackling in the air. So much electricity, in fact, that her hair was rising from the static as she looked about rather grumpily.

“These lines are still hot,” Bobby said, gesturing at the power lines that were draped over the truck and across the road. As if to emphasize his point, there was a small explosion of sparks that had them all flinching back. “Grab dry chem and CO2 from the truck.”

While Eddie jogged back to the engine to do just that, he heard the captain radioing witha  request for the power to be shut off. The fire was put out with clouds from the fire extinguishers. It did nothing for the electricity, though, which made it still too dangerous to try and extract her from the vehicle. A squad car pulled up, its sirens giving a final whoop as the pair of officers got out.

“You came for the tree murderers,” the woman called out the window when she spotted them, seemingly quite happy at the sight. Eddie didn’t have the heart to tell her that it was most definitely her that they were there for.

“I can see subdermal tissue damage from the strike,” Eddie told Bobby when the captain returned from checking on the fallen tree trimmer. Said tree trimmer was being looked over by Hen and Chimney. “We need to transport her. Any update on when they’re gonna get the power off?”

Bobby shook his head with a frown as he reached for his radio. Just as he did, though, the transformer above them exploded in a shower of sparks and debris, smoke wafting up. The low level hum of electricity that had been a constant presence in his ear - and on his skin - went dead silent.

“There’s your answer,” Bobby said. 

Eddie hurried to yank the door open and get the woman out, now that it was safe to do so, as the captain thanked dispatch for getting the power off. He didn’t really pay attention to the conversation, more focused on his patient. Not until he heard Bobby say,

“If you didn’t shut the power off, who did?”

A moment later, there was a squeal of tires and then the crunching of metal. At the intersection down the street, beneath traffic lights that were just as dead as the powerlines that Eddie was helping the woman step over, a pair of cars had t-boned. No one had turned the power off, it seemed - the woman, in her attempt to save the trees, had caused a minor (or perhaps a major) blackout.

It was going to be a very long day.

It had been a very long day so far. And a crappy one, at that. Which was very unfortunate, because it had started so well, with Buck waking up in Eddie’s bed after spending the night. He got clothes out of the drawer he’d filled the night before, unable to resist stealing one of his boyfriend’s shirts. He had a fresh uniform hanging in the closet, right beside Eddie’s own, and he tucked it away in his work bag so he could change at the station.

The beginning of the shift was fine, even though he had to suffer through Danny’s teasing in the locker room about claiming a drawer at Eddie’s. Worse, the others were soon joining in on the fun, like sharks converging on a hapless seal after getting a whiff of blood in the water. They were emboldened every time they caught him texting Eddie, too, even though they already knew all about their relationship.

(Buck may or may not have spent a shift shoving pictures of Chris, strapped into that contraption he and Danny put together so he could skateboard, into the faces of anyone who stayed still for too long.)

Partway through the shift, while they were in the middle of helping a well-meaning husband get themselves unstuck from the hatch to the attic, the power suddenly went out. It was still middle of the day at that point, early afternoon, so they weren’t just abruptly thrown into darkness. Still, though, the suddenness was disconcerting, the lack of the sounds of electronics that Buck got used to and filtered out was jarring.

It turned out, according to Eddie and Austin, anyway, that the blackout was caused by some random woman taking a cherry picker for a joyride in protest against the butchering of her neighborhood trees. Except she stole it while the trimmers were getting ready to work, the arm and its bucket raised, and that meant she ended up bringing down a powerline or two. And then half the city’s powergrid with it.

The shift was an awful mess afterwards. They’d get done at one scene - usually a motor vehicle accident, because apparently no one in this city was taught the rules of what to do when the traffic lights were out - and get back to the station with enough time to start restocking. And then the alarm would ring and they’d get sent right back out. It seemed to only worsen as the sun set and night fell.

Currently, they were at the scene of yet another MVA. It was one of the nastier ones, involving three different cars. They were trying to extract the driver from the middle car, which had been T-boned and then rear ended, with Buck barely paying attention to the radio chatter. It would burst into life on occasion, other units and dispatch conversing. It was something that Buck learned to block out usually.

Whenever he recognized the people talking, they would snag his attention for a moment or two. Usually whenever it was Maddie, sometimes when it was Bobby or one of the others. Occasionally, as now, it was because he recognized Athena’s voice and her unit number.

This time it wasn’t anything special, Athena doing a business check somewhere and Maddie acknowledging it. Then the sergeant began requesting back up and detectives, only to be interrupted by something.

There was a pained grunt.

There were sounds of struggle.

There was Maddie trying to get her to respond.

Buck stood, frozen in place and holding the Jaws, as he listened. As everyone around him listened. Even one of the drivers from the car, getting checked for a concussion by Nola, sat staring at her radio with his mouth open as the sound of Athena fighting for her life played out for all of them to hear.

“All units, police and fire RA, clear channel two,” Maddie said to the soundtrack of Athena’s grunts and yelps and smothered screams. “Switch to Tac Channel Fifty. Officer on open mic in distress at Studio Self Storage. Needs assistance.”

Mehta was the first to switch over, followed by Nola and the other paramedics. One by one, their radios stopped playing the god awful sounds. All of them except Buck, who could not bring himself to reach up and turn it off, who could not stop listening no matter how awful it was.

It was Danny who did it for him, stepping in front of him and changing the channel on his radio. Athena was cut off mid-yell and Buck stared at him.

“Pack it away,” his brother told him. It was the advice he had given him so long ago, after the rollercoaster and Devon. 

“Danny…” This was not a loss on the job that Buck needed to learn how to let go. This was a friend in need of help and they were just standing there.

“We have a job to do,” Danny reminded him. “And people who need us here.”

Buck swallowed back the argument at the tip of his tongue, because he knew his brother was right. It galled and it ached, but he was right. So Buck did his best to pack it away for the moment, to push to the back of his mind all the horrible visions he was coming up with of what was happening to Athena, to push through the worry and the anxiety. He did his best to focus on the job in front of him, on using the Jaws to pry open the car door and then helping Danny extract the driver.

It was difficult, though. Back in school, it was often difficult - sometimes impossible - to keep his attention focused on the work in front of him. It was better as a firefighter, with the physical activity and the people in need. But now, every time their radio burst to life, he would pause and he would listen in the hopes for an update, any update at all, until Danny or one of the others nudged him back into the here and now.

After the MVA was cleared up and the patients carted off, they were sent to a clinic to free someone stuck in an elevator. On the way, Buck desperately checked his phone in the hopes of Eddie or Austin or anyone having left him a message with any news. There was nothing, though, and it made him worry what that could mean.

Getting the elevator open was easy. Finding Michael, of all people, stuck inside with someone else was not.

“Finally!” the man cried. “I’ve had enough of this place. No offense.”

That last part was directed to the man he was stuck with, who shook his head.

“None taken.”

Buck looked to his brother, all grim faced. Danny took a breath.

“Michael-”

“Oh! Dan.” Michael turned to actually look at them. “I didn’t realize it was you guys.”

“Michael,” Danny tried again. “Listen-”

He was cut off by Michael’s phone. The other man pulled it out, an apologetic expression on his face, answering it with,

“Hey, Bobby.”

Buck’s heart dropped as he watched Michael’s face fall. The man barely paid them in mind as he sprinted past them, leaving his elevator friend behind. The man looked rather dejected to be abandoned so suddenly. It was probably why Danny took pity on the guy.

“His ex-wife is hurt,” he told him. Because that was undoubtedly what the call had been about. Buck wondered if Bobby had been called, as Athena’s emergency contact, or if the 118 had been the ones to respond.

“Oh,” the man said, frowning in the direction of Michael’s exit.

“C’mon, squirt.” Danny slapped Buck on the arm. “Let’s get going.”

“Yeah.” Buck followed him absentmindedly, jumping as he felt his own phone go off. A quick check showed that it was Eddie, finally, with a not-very-informative text. Buck barely paid attention as he texted back. “Yeah, okay.”

Eddie came over the next afternoon with Chris and pizza. Both the child and the food got warm receptions in the Buckley apartment, Buck stealing away the former - literally picking him up and carrying him over to the couch - while Danny took the latter.

“This definitely tells me where I rank,” Eddie complained without an ounce of real heat. He set Chris’ book bag on the dining table. “He has homework, Buck.”

“Lame.” Buck drew the word out, making Chris giggle where he was hanging over his shoulder. Even so, he turned and course corrected, dropping the kid into one of the dining chairs. Chris dragged the bag over to himself and started pulling out everything he needed while Danny sat a plate down at his elbow with a couple slices of pizza on it.

“Thanks, Danny!” the kid chirped.

“You’re welcome.” Danny gave Chris a pat on the head, grabbed his own slice of pizza, and then jerked his head in a gesture for Buck and Eddie to follow him across the apartment. After checking to make sure Chris was paying more attention to his homework, he asked, “Austin said something about Nash grabbing an ax?”

“Yeah, when we got there,” Eddie said. The 118 had indeed been the station to respond to Athena’s distress the night before. Buck highly doubted it was because for any other reason than that Bobby decided they would be. “Pretty sure Bobby was gonna murder the guy if he had to. Do you know how she’s doing?”

“Michael said she’s pretty beat up,” Danny answered. “He ran off to see her after we rescued him from the elevator he was stuck in.”

“Well I’d say she’s doing better than the guy who attacked her. She-” Eddie paused, glanced over at Chris, and then lowered his voice before saying, “She shot his damn verga off.”

Buck choked on the piece of pizza he’d just swallowed. Danny thumped him on his back as he coughed, dislodging it enough for it to go down.

“She shot him in the dick!?” he whisper-screeched.

“Good for her,” Danny declared. “Who was he, anyways?”

“That Realtor Rapist guy they were looking for,” Eddie said.

“Good.” The word came out of Danny’s mouth viciously, a bit bloodthirsty, even.

“I know Bobby’s with her right now,” Buck said, pulling out his phone to pull up his message thread with the man. “And Hen mentioned something about going to see her.”

“I was thinking about it,” Eddie said. “Don’t really want to drag Chris with me to the hospital, though. Especially with, y’know. The news and all.”

Buck grimaced. The news had been full of grim, borderline apocalypse movie level tidings. He was sincerely hoping things were just being exaggerated for shock value.

“I’ll watch him,” Danny offered with a shrug. “He’s easier than Buck was at that age.”

“Hey!”

Eddie didn’t have any problems with that. They ate their fill of pizza and then told Chris they were visiting a friend that had gotten hurt, not wanting to give him too many of the grizzly details, and that he was gonna stay with Danny. Specifically, Eddie told him he was going to stay with Uncle Danny, and Buck got the chance to witness his older brother being utterly taken aback for a few moments.

They made the drive in the jeep, bickering over the radio. Eddie already knew which hospital they were going to, First Presbyterian, and it wasn’t that long of a drive to get there. It took longer to find the room when they arrived, getting instructions from a nurse that kept her distance from them and spoke to them through a mask. All of the nurses and doctors were wearing masks, Buck noticed.

Any uneasiness the sight of that might’ve provoked went out the window when they got to Athena’s room. She looked horrible, half her face bruised and swollen, an arm casted up and in a sling. Bobby, sitting in the chair by her bedside, did not look much better. There was a rollaway bed tucked against the wall, presumably where the fire captain had spent the night, and Buck doubted it was very comfortable.

“Athena,” he breathed. “You look-”

“Absolutely beautiful,” Eddie said, cutting him off before he could accidentally stick his foot in his mouth.

“Thank you, Eddie.” It looked like it hurt for Athena to smile. “C’mon, take a seat. Michael told us you rescued him from an elevator.”

“Yeah,” Buck confirmed. “Pretty sure the guy he was stuck with was disappointed to be freed.”

Athena raised an eyebrow with a smirk, though it disappeared with a wince. The movement must have pulled at one of the cuts on her face.

“How crazy was the blackout for the One Thirty-three?” Bobby asked.

“A lot of MVAs, mostly. One person who nearly broke their neck trying to walk down the stairs without a light.”

“Did Eddie tell you about the guy in the freezer?”

“No.” Buck smacked his boyfriend on the arm with the back of his hand. The dramatic goof made a show of wincing and rubbing at the spot, like it actually hurt. “He didn’t.”

“Well,” Bobby said. “I had Hen and Chim use the defibrillators on the lock…”

Doing basic maintenance on the fire engine was actually one of Daniel’s favorite things to do. He didn’t have any real love for auto mechanics, not enough that pulling apart an engine just to put it back together again was ever something he’d be interested in. All the same, he was interested in how some of them worked. That was how he’d fallen into the role of driver engineer back in El Paso, just like his interest in how human bodies worked - and failed - led him to thoughts of being a doctor as a kid.

But none of that was why he liked doing basic maintenance. He liked it because it was an excuse to get away from the others for a bit, because he wasn’t all that different from Austin in that regard. He’d pull out the creeper and whatever tools he needed and hide away under the engine for a bit. Sometimes he had an actual reason to use as an excuse, too.

Even better at this moment, the truck bay was entirely empty of people except for himself. Everyone else was farther inside the station as they waited for dinner to be done. Which meant there was no one around to hear as he talked to Austin over the phone.

“You remember I don’t know how to play this game, right?” Daniel dug into the tray of tools he’d brought with him. Buck was busy on cooking detail, and when Daniel left him he was slapping Mendoza’s hand away with a wooden spoon, so he wasn’t there to hand him whatever he needed on request. “We spent an hour with you just talking me through making that character.”

“Dean and Sam don’t know how to play it either,” was Austin’s reply. The phone was set to speaker and was laying on Daniel’s chest.

“They’re five.” Actually, they were eight and six, respectively, but that was beside the point. “That doesn’t make me feel better.”

“It’s not that difficult, Dan. You roll dice, you say what you wanna do, I throw monsters and puzzles at you. Simple.”

“I already regret agreeing to this,” Daniel complained, even though he hadn’t needed much convincing and was going along with it regardless. “Almost as much as I regret ever letting you come up with a name.”

“My suggestions were fine.”

“You came up with Conan for my barbarian guy. And that was the better idea.”

“Barb wasn’t bad.” Austin sounded as offended now as he did the first time the idea was shot down.

“I really hope no one ever asks you to name a child,” Daniel told him.

“Didn’t you get Buck’s name out of a book?”

“I was seven, it was two books, and it’s better than anything you would come up with now.”

Austin would probably have named him Spot.

Their conversation, or rather their fond bickering, didn’t last for much longer. The alarm rang on Austin’s end, the 118 getting sent out, and so he had to hang up. This left Daniel to continue doing the minor maintenance, or at least pretending like he was, in silence. At least until he heard someone walking towards him, footsteps loud in the quiet bay.

He let out a sigh as he realized that he was about to be bothered, debated telling them to fuck off when they kicked at his foot, and then rolled out from under the engine. His breath caught instantly when he saw just who was now standing above him and he scrambled to his feet.

“What are you doing here?” Daniel spat, putting distance between them.

“I can’t visit you at work?” Drake’s smile was a facsimile of friendly and made Daniel’s skin crawl almost as much as that lingering odor of cigarette smoke.

“No. I told you to fuck off.”

“You did.” The detective nodded, that smile unwavering. “Hey, when did the Diaz kid get a Diaz kid of his own?”

Daniel could swear that his heart stopped beating.

“What?”

“Y’know, the kid that little Evan was so buddy-buddy with back in the day,” Drake continued. “Still buddy-buddy with. Really close buddies, from the looks of things. Is that new, or were they always that close?”

Daniel did nothing but stare at him and shake his head.

“You remember how hard it is to be a single parent.” Drake’s smile took an edge of mocking cruelty. “Must be even harder for him, since he’s stuck with a retarded cripple for a brat.”

“Shut your fucking mouth,” Daniel snapped, the flare of anger overtaking everything else.

“A single phone call,” Drake said. He reached into his pocket and pulled out a card. “You remember, right? A single phone call is all it would take.”

“You wouldn’t.” Except that he would.

“I don’t know if you still have my number.” Drake held the card out until Daniel took it with trembling fingers. “Can’t wait to hear from ya. Remember, a single phone call.”

Drake tipped an imaginary hat at him and walked away, the smile never slipping from his face. Daniel watched him go, the man pulling out a carton of smokes from his shirt pocket as he stepped out of the station and out of sight, and could not tear his eyes away until he heard someone shouting for him.

“Dan!” Mendoza, on the other side of the truck bay, at the door leading into the rest of the station. “Your brother says that dinner’s ready!”

Daniel opened his mouth to reply, choked on the words, cleared his throat, and tried again.

“O- Okay!” he shouted back. “Tell the squirt I’ll be right there.”

His fingers were still trembling as he tucked away the detective’s card, with all his contact information.

One single phone call was all it would take.

Chapter 15

Chapter Notes

Just gonna be blunt here: content warning at the beginning of this chapter, for allusions to sexual assault and the aftermath thereof. Nothing's shown, just heavily implied.

The years and the distance had not softened Drake’s demeanor. In fact, where most people’s hearts might grow fonder with time, Drake’s might have actually grown crueler. That was very apparent the first time Daniel dragged himself to the detective’s place to present himself like a dog returning to its owner after slipping its leash. The phone call preceding it had been humiliating, even more so because Daniel had been the one to call Drake. It was supposed to be humiliating and degrading for Daniel, a nice little appetiser for the bastard. A form of foreplay, even.

But what was the alternative? Drake had been very clear with his threats, which weren’t all that different from before. The only real difference this time was the target of them. Maybe it would take more than a single phone call to have CPS snatching Chris away from Eddie, maybe a cop’s “well-meaning concerns” wouldn’t be enough for that to happen, but Daniel did not particularly want to take that risk. So he swallowed his bile, dialed Drake’s number - a number that had not changed and which he still knew by heart - and sold himself again.

Having their rendezvous at Drake’s place was a change. Back in El Paso, before Buck fled the state, before Daniel drew the line in the sand and told him no for the very first time and then put up with all the harassment that followed, they always took place either in cheap motel rooms or in the back of Drake’s police cruiser. The former was usually much preferred, because Daniel could drag his aching self - he was always left aching when they were done - through a shower and get as clean as he could ever be after the fact, before going home to face Evan. 

Daniel wasn’t being given that chance this time. When they were done, when Drake got tired of him for the time being, he kicked Daniel out the door with his pants still undone and his shoes untied. He laughed as he did it, too. Daniel was left to make his way to his car, refusing to make eye contact with anyone that drove by, while finishing getting dressed.

What he meant to do, once he started the engine and pulled away, was go home and take the hottest, longest shower imaginable. Hopefully Buck wouldn’t be home and he could just get through his own apartment without needing to come up with an excuse for why he looked so awful. Buck would ask, too, because he’d gotten into the habit of eying Daniel like a hawk ever since the cancer scare that turned out to be mono.

Wait, shit. Buck was going to notice the new marks, there was no way he wouldn’t. This hadn’t been a problem the first time around, and wouldn’t be a problem now if Buck was still at the 118. But now they shared a locker room and his brother was going to see every single bruise that was currently covered up. The others wouldn’t ask too many questions, would accept a joke that was closer to the truth than they’d realize and let it go.

Not Buck, though. Which meant Daniel needed to come up with something before their next shift.

He was losing time and driving on autopilot. It was something he only noticed when he realized what street he was turning onto. Daniel had meant to go back to his own apartment and his own shower, but while he was lost in the panic of how he was going to hide this from his baby brother, he’d ended up driving himself to Austin’s. Realizing where he was had him hesitating at the turn, toying with the idea of going on home as intended, but he ended up pulling into the parking lot and one of the guest spots he parked in all the time.

The apartment was empty when he let himself in. Austin was out, though Daniel had no idea where. There was probably a text waiting on his phone that could tell him, either directly or through whatever Austin was making snide comments about.
