The apartment was empty and the lack of the other man made it seem cold. Daniel didn’t really think about what he was doing as he crossed the living room and collapsed to curl up on the couch, not even bothering to take off his shoes.

There was one of Austin’s sweaters on the back of the couch. Austin had the habit of putting them on when he was chilled and then tossing them onto the nearest piece of furniture when he got too hot in them. Which was always convenient for Daniel whenever he came over after a particularly harsh session with Dr. White - God, what was he going to tell her? How was he supposed to sit through a session of her badgering him to talk about Drake after this? - and he could simply worm his way into whichever sweater was laying discarded that day. Much like he did now.

Daniel laid there, curled up on the couch in Austin’s sweater and with Austin’s striped throw pillow clutched to his chest, for he wasn’t sure how long. It could’ve been as little as a couple minutes or maybe a couple hours. When the apartment’s door suddenly opened, it caught him by surprise.

“-stop watching the news,” Austin was saying, phone pinned between shoulder and ear. He stopped just inside when he saw Daniel on the couch, mouth dropping into a deep frown. After a moment, he closed the door behind him. “You’re just scaring yourself, Dad… I’m fine and I’ll be fine. No one-... No one’s sick at work.”

That wasn’t true, Daniel thought as he closed his eyes and let Austin’s voice drape over him, as comfortable and warm as any blanket. He’d heard Austin and Eddie both mention someone from the ladder coughing and being treated like a leper by the others. But Daniel wasn’t about to speak up and contradict what Austin was saying, not only because he didn’t feel like speaking right now - his voice would probably come out hoarse and scratchy, anyways, and he wasn’t sure how to explain that away - but also because he was no stranger to telling loved ones comfortable lies.

He almost fell asleep like that, as exhausted as he felt. Even as dirty and disgusting as he felt. It wasn’t until Austin had stopped talking and was laying a gentle hand on his shoulder that Daniel opened his eyes. The other man was kneeling in front of him, that frown from earlier still present. It had grown deeper, more severe.

“You look like shit,” was Austin’s blunt statement. “Did you have therapy today?”

Daniel shrugged. It was as good of an excuse as any.

“You reek of cigarettes, too,” was Austin’s next observation, nose scrunching up at the smell. That would be because Drake was a goddamn chimney when he was off duty. “C’mon, get up and take a shower. You’ll feel better when you smell better. I’ll find you clothes to change into.”

The instinctual joke about Austin trying to get Daniel’s pants off shriveled and died on Daniel’s tongue. It didn’t feel right, not at that moment. Not with Austin. Instead, he just nodded and gamely allowed himself to be prodded to his feet.

The shower he took was long and scalding and he did his best to scrub his skin off. He still stepped out feeling just as dirty as he went in.

“What the hell is this?” Buck blurted out, staring at the brochure in his hand. “Summer camp?”

“It’s all Chris can talk about.” Eddie took a seat on the couch beside him and handed him an already open beer. “Some of the other kids from school are going. It’s only two weeks.”

“Okay, no, hold on. Two weeks away from home?” Buck mindlessly set the beer down on the table, still focused on the atrocity he was just now hearing about. “Isn’t Chris too young for that? What if something happens? What if he gets homesick?”

Eddie gave him a flat stare.

“You were supposed to be making me feel better about him going,” he said.

“Why would I want to do that?” Buck asked, flipping through the brochure. “This is- What the hell is this farm-to-fork thing?”

“The kids pick veggies and cook ‘em for dinner.”

“Child labor!” Buck tossed the brochure onto the coffee table in disgust and then picked up his drink. “He’s nine! They’re going to make a bunch of nine year olds grow their own food?”

“Pretty sure they aren’t growing anything in two weeks,” Eddie pointed out. Buck just waved the logic away. “Chris is excited to go. He didn’t stop talking about it when he got home. He’ll probably chat your ear off about it when he gets the chance.”

“Well I’m not excited about it.”

“Clearly.” Eddie’s eye roll was not appreciated by Buck. “What would Danny do?”

The question caught Buck off guard.

“What would what?”

“What would Danny do?” his boyfriend repeated. “If you went up to him as a kid and told him you wanted to go to summer camp?”

Buck glared, because that was not a fair hypothetical to ask him. He knew damn well what Danny would do. Danny had stood there and let him pack up the jeep to drive off into the sunset by himself and supported his every action. Danny would absolutely support Chris going to some god awful summer camp for two weeks.

Judging from the way Eddie was grinning at him, his stupid boyfriend knew he’d won the argument. Buck let out a huff and took a long draw of his drink.

“How much does this stupid thing cost?”

Eddie winced at the question.

“It’ll be fine,” he said. “I can cover it. Just might be tight for a bit.”

Buck let out a sigh and threw his arm over the other man’s shoulder, pressing close to him.

“Eds, c’mon. Three loving parents, remember? That’s what you told me Shannon wanted for him,” he reminded him. “You named him after me. You put me in the will for him. Let me help pay for this.”

“Buck…”

“Eddie,” he mocked. “You’re still paying off that truck, and you’re renting a house in Los Angeles, and you’ve got the tuition for that fancy pants school.”

“Most of that’s paid for thanks to Carla.”

“Most, not all. And! There’s Carla.” Buck shook him a little. “Insurance covered most of my jeep and I took care of the rest before Christmas. I don’t have much in the way of expenses. Let me help.”

“Fine,” his boyfriend said with a sigh, very grudgingly. 

Buck grinned and slapped a wet kiss on the side of Eddie’s head.

He ended up staying the night, shooting Danny a text to let him know. Chris, when he came out of his room and spotted Buck, did indeed seem to be only able to talk about the camp and how cool it sounded and how all his friends were going. Buck listened and nodded along and did his best to act like he hadn’t just been vehemently arguing against Chris going. Eddie blessedly didn’t call him out on it.

The next morning, Buck made breakfast for the three of them and listened to Chris’ continued chattering about the summer camp, before they all went their separate ways for the day. Danny’s car was in the station’s parking lot when Buck pulled in, though he was just getting out. When he got out, Buck saw that he was already in uniform. Which was odd, because they normally changed at the station.

“Did you not have clean clothes?” Buck joked, pulling his bag - which contained his own uniform - out of the backseat of the jeep. He remembered how often his brother got on him for letting his laundry pile up as a teenager, and it was funny to imagine the roles being reversed.

“Just wanted to save some time this morning.”

Danny’s voice sounded rough, and a horrible thought flashed through Buck’s mind. He darted forward and felt his brother’s forehead with his hand, which was slapped away.

“You’re not running a fever,” Buck said, peering intently at Danny.

“I’m not sick.” Danny tugged at the end of the sleeves of his button down; he’d gone with the long-sleeves today. “Stop looking at me like that.”

“Excuse me for being concerned,” Buck sniped, sticking his nose in the air, and followed after his brother into the station. “It was only a few months ago that you thought you had cancer.”

“Yeah, yeah. Love you, too, squirt.”

They both went to the locker room, but Danny only stuck around long enough to stash his bag before leaving again. It was as he was exiting the room that Buck noticed that he was walking differently, almost stiffly. Buck suppressed the sniggering, because he recognized that gait.

He wondered how Austin felt about Danny having sex with other people, but quickly decided that it wasn’t any of his business.

The entire shift had been a rather slow one. All the emergencies they were sent to were minor things, quickly and easily solved. The kind of call-outs where they spent more time in the trucks than they did with their boots on the ground. At the moment, though, they were taking advantage of the downtime. Bobby was fixing dinner, with Chimney assisting him. Hen, though, was taking a practise MCAT test; she was approaching her newfound desire to be a doctor very seriously.

“Summer camp, huh?” Bobby remarked, peering at the brochure laying on the kitchen counter. Eddie had brought it in with the hopes of the others making him feel better about letting his kid go. Better than Buck did, at least.

(His trusted maxim of ‘What Would Danny Do?’ only went so far.)

“Yeah, he’s been talking about it nonstop.” Eddie kept an eye on his watch, tasked with the important job of timing Hen. “Two weeks away from home. Buck’s not a fan of it. You’d have thought I was letting them ship Chris off to a work camp if you’d heard him. Time, Hen.”

He sat down at the round table Hen was doing the test, taking it from her and grabbing a pen and dragging the workbook to himself as he started marking the answers for her. Hen sat and anxiously watched him, rubbing at her hands.

“Is it the distance, the length, or Chris’ age?” Bobby asked, hands moving as he prepared their dinner. "I started going to sleepaway camp when I was 8. I loved it, looked forward to it every year. Camp Weegeewagen - Edeee-idee-odee-ooh-hoo!”

The three of them stared at the captain for a moment, even Hen. Eddie sincerely hoped Chris didn’t come home as a fan of… Was that yodeling?

“Yeah,” Chimney said. “But Christopher’s a city kid.”

“So was I.” Bobby sounded vaguely insulted. “St. Paul is a city.”

“If you say so.”

“Isn’t it two cities?” Eddie asked, looking between the answer key and the test.

“We don’t talk about Minneapolis in this station,” Bobby sternly told him.

“I’m just trying to imagine trying to sell Denny on the idea of two weeks without the internet,” Hen said. 

“Chris is excited for it, they have a farm-to-fork program. Buck called it child labor.” Eddie laughed, marked the last answer, marked down the grade, and handed Hen her test back. “There you go.”

Her face fell at the number he’d scrawled and circled at the top.

“Damn it,” she said. “I gotta get above a Five Eleven.”

“Five Oh-Four is pretty good,” Eddie pointed out.

“Getting into medical school at this point in my life is hard enough,” she argued. “I can’t afford to be an average applicant.”

“Hey, there is nothing average about you,” Bobby told her. “You just started studying this, give yourself a break.”

“Yeah,” Eddie agreed. “And besides, you’re not an average applicant. You’ve been a paramedic for however many years, that’s gotta count for something.”

There was an awkward silence as one of them failed to speak up. Eddie turned in his seat to stare at Chimney in expectation, seeing Bobby doing the same. Chimney looked between them until he got the message.

“Hen, you’re brilliant,” he said. “You don’t need a test to prove that.”

She seemed partly mollified by their words, at least. Her phone, laying face down on the table, chimed and she picked it up to check it. Her face immediately twisted into confusion.

“Bobby, why is your wife asking me if she could hold May’s graduation party at my house?”

“Our living room is kind of under construction right now,” the captain sheepishly explained, which only served to raise more questions.

“Well there is not enough room at mine for all the guests to park,” Hen informed him, typing away at her phone.

The slowness of the shift lasted long enough for them to sit down and eat dinner when it was ready. It didn’t last much longer than that, the alarm screaming at them almost as soon as their plates were empty. They rushed for the trucks and sped away towards the county line.

They arrived at a mess of a scene. A train had gone off the rails, resulting in wreckage and debris everywhere. As they pulled to a stop, Eddie could see walking wounded dazedly wandering around and spot fires putting off smoke. The captain of the 153 met them as they all hopped out, going straight for Bobby.

She introduced herself and explained the situation, which mostly amounted to utterly FUBAR. Besides the people in the cars that came crashing to the ground, there were passengers trapped in the part of the train still on the rails. There were more houses on the way, along with USAR, but for the moment they were on their own.

There was a woman arguing with a pair of firefighters from the 153, trying to convince them to let her into the train wreck. She wore a pair of large glasses and her hair was the shade of blond that bordered on being red. Eddie sent the other firefighters on to deal with the more pressing matters, deciding to handle her himself.

“Ma’am, I’m sorry, we can’t let you inside,” he told her. There was a cut on her temple, trickling blood. “It’s too dangerous.”

“I know it’s dangerous,” she said. “I need to get up in that car.”

“I hear you, but I’m sorry-”

“Wait, are you from the One Eighteen?” she suddenly asked, staring at his helmet.

“Yeah?” Why would that-

“Abby?” Buck’s voice had them both turning. The 133 must’ve just arrived; Buck was standing just a few feet from them, Danny at his shoulder. The older Buckley did not look particularly pleased. “Wait, were you on the train?”

“Yeah.” Abby said. It was weird for Eddie to realize he’d somehow run into his boyfriend’s ex here, of all places. Probably as weird as it was for Buck to run into her here. “Listen, I’ve gotta-”

“We need to get you checked out,” Buck insisted, marching up to her. Behind him, Danny not-so-subtly rolled his eyes.

“No, no, I’m fine,” she argued, stepping around them all to get to the wreckage. “I need to get up there.”

“What? No, that’s crazy.” Buck tried to catch her and ended up getting in front of her. “Abby, stop.”

“I’m trying to find someone!” the woman screeched, sounding distraught and close to tears.

“So tell us who, we’ll-”

“My fiance!” she said. Buck blinked but didn’t seem bothered by the revelation. “He fell asleep and I went to the bar car and…”

“Okay,” Eddie said. “Can you give us a description?”

Abby pulled out her phone and pulled up a picture of her curled up with a guy.

“That’s him,” she said, holding it up for the three of them - Danny had come over as well - to look at. “We were in that top car right there, all the way in the back.”

She gestured at the car; it was, of course, the one standing almost on its end, kept from falling only by the way it was propped against one of the other train cars.

“We’ll find him,” Buck told her. “What’s his name?”

“Sam. Sam Egan,” she said. “Thank you.”

“Don’t worry about it, we’ll bring him back to you,” he said, and then, “I promise.”

Danny’s displeased look morphed into a scowl that held as they left Abby behind. Eddie couldn’t blame him, because he was feeling the same. They all knew better than to make those kinds of promises.

“Too much damn heart,” he heard Danny mutter under his breath.

Buck must’ve heard him, too, because he ducked his head with a muttered “sorry.” Danny just sighed and clapped him on the shoulder and reached for his radio to loop in Mehta. Eddie did the same, grabbing his own and thumbing it on.

“Hey, Bobby…”

Chapter 16

Climbing up the tilted train car brought back memories of the earthquake for Buck. They had to use the seats and tables as hand- and footholds, pulling and pushing themselves up. Eddie and Danny were keeping pace with him, or at least Eddie was. Danny was a couple rows below. Both of them had med kits hanging off their shoulders.

“Hurry up, old man,” Buck taunted, shining his headlamp down the aisle. His brother squinted back up at him, too busy gripping a chair to shield his eyes. “Maybe next time I invite you out to go rock climbing with me, you’ll actually come.”

“Oh, shut it, squirt.”

“Cap.” Eddie was paused at a seat with an unmoving blond woman, radio in hand. “Be advised, another black tag up her about halfway.”

“Copy that.”

Buck grimaced, the small amount of levity evaporating from the air. She wasn’t the first casualty they’d come across, the second one in this car alone, and although he’d been expecting it to be bad - there was no way a trainwreck of this severity wouldn’t be bad - it was still a little bit soul crushing each and every time they made the discovery.

They were quickly approaching the top of the car, what had been the observation deck for passengers to look out as the train sped down the tracks. It was where Abby said her fiance was supposed to be, and none of the black tags that he’d seen so far resembled the man in the picture she showed them. Hopefully that meant only good things.

Maybe not so good things; there was a man pinned to a chair at the end of their climb.

“Sam?” Buck tried. The man groaned in response and tried to raise his head. “Sam, can you hear me?”

He climbed up the last little bit and propped himself against the seat right before the man. It was Sam, if far more beaten up. A living Sam, too, which was half the load off Buck’s shoulders.

“Hey, Sam.” Buck peered at him, grimacing at the way the man was struggling to breathe. “How’re you feeling?”

“It hurts… hurts to breathe,” was the disheartening answer.Eddie and Danny had both caught up to him, faces getting grimmer by the moment. “Please, my fiancée… She’s on the train…”

“Hey, Abby’s okay,” Buck told him. “She’s the one who sent us up here for you.”

“Be aware,” Danny said into his radio. “We have a passenger pinned at the top of the car. A support beam from the observation deck broke through the floor. We need the jaws.”

“Copy that,” Bobby replied. “Coming right up.”

“Hear that, Sam?” Buck moved slightly to give Eddie and Danny room to work. “Help is on the way.”

Help could be faster, though. Something shifted, sending the whole car tilting sideways. Metal groaned and glass shattered somewhere as the three of them - Sam was wedged too tightly by the beam to be moved; Buck was unwillingly drawing comparisons to butterflies pinned in a display case - were sent tumbling against the side.

“Motherfucker,” Danny spat. “You two okay?”

“I’m fine,” Buck answered. “Eds? ¿Estas bien?”

“Estoy bien,” Eddie grunted as he climbed back to check on Sam. “Someone really needs to secure this car before it topples over.”

“Pretty sure that was our job, before we got sidetracked.” Danny placed a pulse-ox to Sam’s finger. Seconds later, he was grimacing at the readout. “Eddie, I’m not liking his O2. How’re his lungs sounding?”

Eddie, who’d put on a stethoscope and was pressing the head to the parts of Sam’s back and chest he could reach, made a face at whatever he was hearing.

“Not good,” he answered. “We need to get him out of here.”

It took far too long before help, in the form of a grunting and groaning Bobby, arrived with the jaws as well as the ram. Buck managed to catch his brother’s lips thin in displeasure at the sight of the captain, before he managed to wipe it away and replace it with a mask of professionalism. Buck rolled his eyes and reached out to grab the jaws, before moving to try and free Sam.

“He’s got a collapsed lung from the blunt force,” Eddie informed Bobby as Buck jammed the jaws into place and turned on the hydraulics.

“And his O2 stats are dropping,” Danny added.

“We can relieve the pressure,” Eddie continued. “But we gotta move this beam off him.”

That was going to prove a problem. A piece of the seat came off, reaching its breaking point long before the beam might deign to move.

“Still too heavy,” Buck complained. “It’s not gonna budge.”

“Alright, let’s try the hydraulic ram,” Bobby suggested, holding out the tool. 

Buck sat the jaws aside in one of the seats, where it wouldn’t fall down to the bottom of the car and kill someone with its weight, before taking the ram from his former captain. He wedged the ram beneath the beam, close to the end that was crushing Sam, and turned it on. And then a girl somewhere began to scream.

He stopped the ram as everyone else began to yell. The source of the screams turned out to be a few seats below them. Eddie and Bobby slid down, moving the debris that was covering the new patient to reveal a young woman with a bloodied face. The beam was laying on top of her.

“How are you doing?” he heard Eddie ask her.

“My side really hurts,” was her answer.

“I’m gonna take a peek.” Eddie reached down and lifted up her shirt. Buck couldn’t see what it uncovered, but the look on his boyfriend’s face told him it wasn’t good. “Force of the crash pushed her leg up into her torso.”

“What!?”

“This is gonna hurt a little bit,” he warned and then did something that had the girl crying out in pain. “Alright, there’s still a pulse in her foot. Blood’s still pumping to it.”

Eddie looked to Bobby, who jerked his head and started lowering himself down. Buck followed with Danny to where they were apparently holding an impromptu conference, clambering carefully over seats and table and beam.

“What’s going on?” he asked when he reached them.

“They’re both trapped by the same beam. We take the pressure off of him and we’re squeezing her,” Bobby summarized, before turning to Eddie. “Which has the better shot?”

Eddie looked to Danny, who simply gave him a shrug.

“Injuries are different,” Eddie answered. “The risk is the same.”

“No, no, wait, hold on. What are we saying?” Buck demanded to know. “We gotta pick who we save?”

“I’m saying I don’t think we can save ‘em both,” Bobby said.

Buck was not exactly pleased with that statement. He figured his feelings were obvious from the apologetic glances that Eddie shot him and the way Danny clapped him on the shoulder before climbing back up to Sam. Buck followed after him and watched as Danny got the man hooked up to an IV with fluids. Then he took out one of the limited doses of morphine they carried in the medical kits and filled a syringe.

“Alright, this’ll help with the pain,” he said, shouting out to Eddie how much he was administering. He used the syringe to gesture between Buck and Sam. “Make friends with the guy, people like you better than me.”

Buck scoffed at the excuse, but didn’t get to say anything before Sam himself was speaking, voice hoarse and weak.

“It’s her or me,” he said. “Isn’t it?”

“No. No, that isn’t what we do,” Buck told him, shaking his head. He ignored the almost pitying gaze his brother fixed him with. “Tell me about your fiancée. When’s the wedding?”

“June,” Sam answered. “She wants to wait… ‘til the girls are done with school.”

Buck’s heart dropped. Danny was silently cursing as he tracked the man’s vitals.

“You’re a father.”

“Yeah. Tess and Natalie…”

There was a moment of silence that Buck didn’t quite know how to fill after that. Luckily (or perhaps unluckily) Danny had an idea.

“He dated your fiancée for a while,” he said. “Right before she flew to Europe.”

Buck turned to gape at him.

“Danny!”

His brother just shrugged, entirely unbothered.

“Right before…” Sam lifted his head and squinted his eyes at him. “Are you Buck?”

“Uh. Yeah?”

“You helped her with her mother,” Sam said. “Thank you.”

“Um.” Buck blinked, taken aback. “You’re… Welcome?”

“Buckleys,” Bobby called.

He was below them again, with Eddie. When Buck climbed down with Danny, he knew from the grim faces both of them were wearing that he was not going to like what he was about to hear.

“I’m calling it,” Bobby declared, keeping his voice quiet so it didn’t carry. “We start with the girl, we get her out.”

Danny let out a sigh.

“Okay,” he said, at the same time Eddie said, “Copy that.”

“No.” Buck shook his head. “That’ll crush Sam’s other lung, it’ll kill him.”

“I’m aware of that,” Bobby said. “Protocol dictates we save whomever has the better chance, and that’s the girl.”

“No,” Buck said again and looked to his brother for support.

“He’s starting to decompensate,” was what he got from Danny instead.

“Her vitals are still strong,” Eddie added, sounding apologetic. “If we have to choose…”

“We do,” Bobby said. “We can’t move that steel beam.”

The car rocked again, throwing Buck into the side. The girl screamed, and he heard Sam groan in pain.

“Okay, okay, fine, you’re right,” Buck admitted, scrambling to sit up again. “The beam is steel. But- But the skin on this thing.” He thumped his fist at the wall of the train car. Gently, because he did not want to cause them to tip over. “The skin is stainless, that’s much thinner. I could go outside, cut a piece out, pull the girl through. That’ll buy us enough room to save Sam.”

“No!” Danny said at the same time as Bobby, though the captain’s was not nearly as vehement. Danny scowled at Bobby like it was a personal insult that they agreed on something. In any other situation, Buck would find his brother’s attitude funny.

“This car hasn’t been secured, that’s why we’re working on the inside,” Bobby said. “If this thing topples, we can ride it down. But if you’re on the outside…”

“Yeah, I know, I’ll be crushed by a hundred tons of train car and that’s a lot heavier than a fire truck.” Buck kept his focus on Bobby, ignoring the way he could feel Danny’s gaze boring into him. “But Bobby-”

“Buck, stop,” Eddie snapped, cutting him off. “I know you made a promise.”

“What promise?” Bobby asked. Eddie ducked his head sheepishly, obviously not having meant to blurt that out in front of the captain.

“He promised Abby he’d rescue the guy,” Danny said, gesturing at Sam with his thumb.

“What does Abby have to do with this?”

“She’s his fiancée,” Eddie said, grabbing his kit again and climbing past them to the girl.

“Look, no, it’s not just about her,” Buck argued as Bobby shook his head. “He’s a father, he’s got two daughters-”

“Stop,” Bobby interrupted. “You’re too close, and this is too risky.”

“Well, I’m willing to take that risk.”

“It’s not yours to take. You can’t just rush into any dangerous situation and assume it’s gonna be okay. ‘Cause sometimes it’s not and I am tired of being on the wrong side of those hospital visits.”

“Hey!” Danny barked. It sounded angry and it made Buck jump a little, even though it wasn’t directed at him. “He’s not your kid, Nash. Remember? And you ain’t his captain, either.”

Bobby glared at him, face twisting in anger.

“We don’t have time for this,” Eddie reminded them, sounding annoyed.

“He’s right,” Danny agreed, and then grabbed his radio. “Mehta, we need this car secured ASAP. We’re gonna have to cut into it from the outside so we can extract a victim.”

“Copy that, Buckley,” Mehta replied.

“Thank you, Danny,” Buck said. 

His brother shook his head and scowled at him.

“Don’t thank me,” he told Buck. “I’d rather use the beam to squeeze that guy until his guts pop out his mouth than risk having to watch you be crushed again.” Buck winced, feeling himself shrivel a little. “Go get what you need.”

“Yeah. Yeah, okay.”

Buck started the delicate journey down the car and back to the ground, shuffling past Bobby as he did. The captain was still glaring at Danny, but he followed Buck a moment later.

“I can’t believe you’re letting him do this.”

Daniel glanced over at Eddie, who was checking over the girl, and shrugged. The disbelief was fair, because he was not nearly as okay with this plan as he pretended to be. He hadn’t been lying when he said that he would much prefer to lose one of the patients than risk his brother’s safety. In fact, if forced to choose between Buck or one of them, he knew how much morphine they had on hand and how much he’d need to cause an overdose in someone whose oxygen levels were already approaching rock bottom.

But his brother had too much heart, always had. Daniel knew that Buck wouldn’t be able to live with himself if he didn’t at least try to save them both. He remembered the utter mess Buck had been after the guy dropped to his death from the roller coaster. Plus, he didn’t really feel like forcing his brother to watch and listen as they brutally killed Sam in order to save the girl. Because that’s what they would’ve been doing. It wouldn’t just be letting him die, lifting up the beam to free the girl would mean them actively causing Sam’s death.

If he could protect his baby brother from that, he would.

“Danny,” Sam breathed out. “You’re Daniel?”

“Yup.” He checked the guy’s O2 levels to see they were just as low as before. Perhaps lower.

“You threatened Abby with a bat. And got her fired.”

Daniel snorted.

“Is that how she’s telling it?” He could hear the saw chewing into the metal skin of the train car, though he couldn’t see Buck. “I guess it’s not wrong. How’re you doin’?”

“Okay. How’s the girl?”

“Eddie! How’s the girl?” Daniel saw him lift up a hand and give a thumbs up, still focused on tracking the girl’s vitals. “She’s good.”

“I’m really sorry,” the girl said. Daniel wondered if Eddie had gotten her name at any point.

“For what?” Sam asked, doing his best to be heard.

“That you got hurt. You were really nice to me.”

“Sorry you’re gonna miss your gig.”

The girl weakly laughed.

“Neither of you are missing anything,” Eddie told them, which was a nice sentiment. But Danny had seen the girl’s leg, and the bone that was sticking out of her side. She was definitely going to be missing her gig, plus a lot of other things. “We’re getting you out.”

The car rocked again and Daniel hurriedly reached to grab hold of a seat. He glanced to the wall beside the girl, where he knew Buck was working on the other side. The saw had stopped, no doubt as Buck waited for the car to settle again, and Daniel didn’t look away until it started back. 

“You care about him,” Sam said, catching his attention. “Buck.”

“‘Course I do, he’s my baby brother.”

“Was that what the fight was about?”

“Maybe. A little.” Daniel shrugged as he used a pen light to check Sam’s pupillary response, not entirely bothered that the patients had heard them arguing. “Nash sometimes gets the idea in his head that he’s Buck’s dad. And then I have to remind him that he isn’t.”

“Abby called you a psychopath.”

“That’s rude.” 

Though Dr. White had called him “antisocial” and “borderline,” so maybe his brother’s ex-girlfriend wasn’t far off the mark.

The sawing stopped again. Daniel looked over to see a rectangular piece of the train car’s frame getting pulled out, the metal grinding and scraping, and tossed away. Buck peeked through to grin at them before shouting down at the people below to,

“Send up the basket!”

With where Buck had cut through, it was a simple matter of arranging the girl so they could pull her out from under the beam and through the hole. Daniel ignored the occasional cry of pain as they jostled her broken leg, focusing on getting her transferred over to the basket as quickly (and as safely) as possible.

“Alright, your turn, Sam,” Eddie said as they started lowering the basket, and the girl, down to the firefighters waiting below.

While Buck scaled farther up the car to pop out the window across from Sam, Daniel took the hydraulic ram and started moving the beam out of the way. This part was easy, now that the girl wasn’t at risk. Sometimes, brute force simply was the best course of action.

The basket was ready and waiting by the time Eddie was sliding Sam out from behind the seat. Daniel removed the ram and let the beam fall back with a hard thump to go help him. When Sam was safely secured, he and Buck both were lowered down.

“Grab the jaws,” Daniel told Eddie, slipping his medical kit over his shoulder and hefting up the ram. “I want to get out of this death trap before it decides to take us all with it.”

“Yeah, I can get behind that plan.”

“Kinda figured.”

They moved down the aisle carefully yet quickly, very much in a hurry to get onto solid ground and far, far away from the car. The patients were both already untethered and transferred onto gurneys to be loaded up onto ambulances. Daniel spotted Buck, helmet in hand and his curls starting to come free from the product he slathered on them, talking to Abby and Sam. Eddie had also seen them, and now he was scowling in their direction.

“Oh, God,” Daniel scoffed, putting all of his disgust into it.

“What?” Eddie demanded, tearing his eyes away to direct that scowl towards him.

“You’re being an idiot, that’s what.” Daniel pointed at Buck and Abby. “That is dead. She practically told him he wasn’t worth sticking around for and he’s told me about how she was basically using him as a distraction from her mom. Don’t get your tighty-whities in a bunch over them breathing the same air.”

Eddie looked suitably abashed over the admonishment, so Daniel rolled his eyes, handed him the hydraulic ram, and left to find Austin in the midst of all this mess. Because he did not want to be this involved in his brother’s romantic life, thanks very much. Unfortunately for him, his plans were soon waylaid as an angry fire captain intercepted him shortly after he started his search.

“Daniel!” Nash snapped out, marching towards him. Daniel sighed and came to a stop, patiently waiting for the man to catch up to him. “We need to have a talk.”

“Oh. Do we?”

“Yes. Your behavior back there was unacceptable!”

“You’re not my captain, either,” Daniel reminded him. “And you’re not the IC. So, I don’t really give a shit.”

That seemed to incense Nash further.

“I do not understand you!” he spat. “There’s no way that you were okay with him doing something that needlessly risky.”

Daniel shrugged rather than admit that the man was right. Because he very much was not okay with Buck’s plan. His breath had caught in his chest each and every time the car shifted while Buck clung to its side, and he didn’t feel at ease until he saw his brother with his boots firmly on the ground and untethered from the death trap they’d been in.

“The math was better,” was what he said instead. “I mean, you didn’t want another corpse on your conscience, did you?”

A few months ago, that kind of jab had the captain shutting down. Today, it simply had him grinding his teeth and clenching his fists.

“Buck should never have been allowed to take a risk like that,” Nash gritted out. “He was too close to the situation.”

“And you weren’t?” Daniel scoffed. “Get off your high horse. If it was anyone else, you wouldn’t have had a problem with them doing it. That’s why he transferred stations. And honestly, if you actually cared about him at all, and not just how you felt, you wouldn’t have asked him to just accept that one of ‘em had to die. ‘Cause we both know that ain’t Buck.”

Nash didn’t seem to have a response to that, and Daniel didn’t bother to wait for him to find one. As he stepped around the captain, he idly wondered if the man would file a complaint for the way he spoke to him, before deciding that there were many things in his life he cared about more than a write-up in his file from Captain Nash, of all people.

Chapter 17

Chapter Notes

A Merry Christmas and a Happy Hanukkah to everyone who celebrates.

See the end of the chapter for more notes

“I got written up by Nash,” was how Daniel opened his next therapy appointment.

Dr. White, sitting across from him, raised an eyebrow in surprise. It usually took a lot of poking and prodding from her to get him to open up like that. But Daniel figured that there was less of a risk that she’d try to talk about Drake today if he tossed her a bone.

“Your brother’s previous captain, right?” She shifted in her chair, notebook resting on her knee. “What for?”

“Guy’s got issues with objectivity, and I snapped at him during a rescue,” Daniel said. “He keeps thinking Buck’s his kid.”

Mehta was the one who told him about the complaint lodged against him, taking him aside at the start of their next shift. The 133’s captain actually found it funny, and told Daniel not to take it too seriously once he gave his side of everything. After all, as Daniel had told the man himself, Nash’s behavior during the train rescue was a good example of why Buck transferred stations. The guy needed to figure his shit out.

“Other people besides yourself are allowed to care about your brother,” Dr. White told him, almost chiding.

He sneered at her for it.

“I know that. But he doesn’t need another parent trying to smother him in cotton. He’s already got two of those in Hershey.”

“I distinctly remember multiple instances that you have told me about where you did something similar,” Dr. White said, almost casually. “Like when you kept Buck from going after your sister and brother-in-law with you.”

“That one was different.”

“How so?”

“Seriously?” Daniel rolled his eyes and then told her to, “Stop trying to make me empathize with Nash.”

“At least you’re aware of that much.” Dr. White said it under her breath as she wrote something down in her notebook, so it probably wasn’t meant for him to hear. Her next words were louder. “What, exactly, led up to Nash having anything to write you up for?”

“That train crash,” he said. “Both our stations got called out to it. We ran into Buck’s ex, the dispatcher-”

“The one you intimidated and then got fired.”

“Yes.” Daniel drew the word out as he rolled his eyes again. “Her fiancé was on the train and Buck promised to rescue him, like an idiot. We don’t make those promises, he knows that.”

Dr. White let out a little hum and wrote something down. Daniel glared at her notebook, before he went back to telling her what happened in the train car. Finding Sam pinned by the beam, the injured girl stuck by that same beam, the choice they had to make. The argument that ensued.

“Do you think Buck would’ve been less adamant if it wasn’t his ex’s fiancé?” Dr. White asked him. “If he hadn’t made her that promise?”

“No,” Daniel scoffed. “It’s Buck. He would’ve argued to try and save them both no matter who they were. Nash, though, the only reason he was against the plan was because it was Buck wanting to do it.”

“And how much of why you supported your brother was based on Nash arguing against it?”

Daniel glared at her.

“Buck’s ex apparently thinks I’m a psychopath,” he said, instead of giving that question the courtesy of an answer. “Her fiancé mentioned it while we were waiting for Buck to cut into the car.”

“The woman that you intimidated and then got fired,” Dr. White said, repeating herself from earlier. “Psychopathy hasn’t been a recognized official diagnosis since the DSM-II. Like insanity, it’s a term that tends to be used more in the field of criminal justice these days.”

“I notice you’re not actually disagreeing.”

“It got replaced with Antisocial Personality Disorder in the third edition.”

Daniel gave her the flattest look he could possibly manage.

“Now,” the doctor said, crossing and recrossing her legs as she shifted in her chair. “You said you got a write-up, but described the argument as being mostly between Captain Nash and your brother.”

“He confronted me once we were all on the ground again,” Daniel said. “We had another spat. I might have pointed out that he should’ve been glad for Buck’s idea, since it meant there wasn’t another dead guy on his conscience.”

His therapist let out a terribly large sigh and pinched the bridge of her nose.

“What?” he demanded.

“I would like to direct us back to another conversation we’ve had before,” Dr. White said. Daniel made a face, because he knew what was coming. “About your last argument with Captain Nash…”

It managed to ward off any possible discussion of Drake, at least. Which meant that, at the end of the session, he didn’t leave her office feeling quite as wrung out. He still ended up going to Austin’s, both because he knew Buck was out of the apartment (as was so often the case again these days) and because he didn’t feel like taking the risk that Drake would be lying in wait for him. And also simply because he wanted to.

Austin, for once, had guests over when Daniel let himself in. Short guests.

“Hi, Dan!” Dean, the oldest of the two, waved at him from Austin’s dining table. He and his brother, Sam, had a bunch of dice dumped out in front of them.

“Cynthia’s popping,” Austin explained from the kitchen area, where he was pouring out a bag of pretzels into a bowl. “So they dropped the brats off here.”

“Hey!” Sam complained.

“I tell it as I see it.”

Daniel laughed at the insulted expressions on both kids’ faces as went to grab a handful of pretzels.

“Emmett’s freaking out,” Austin told him, keeping his voice hushed. “They’re not letting him into the delivery room.”

Daniel grimaced.

“I probably just had my last therapy appointment for a while,” he said, words just as quiet. “We talked about it at the end of the session. She’s gonna try to figure something out, but…”

No one at the department had said anything definitive yet, but people were definitely starting to circle the wagons. There was a very ominous feeling in the air now, whenever he went outside.

As Austin went to set the bowl of pretzels in front of his nephews, there was frantic knocking at his door. Since Daniel was closest to it, he just shrugged at the other man and went to see who it was.

“Oh, thank God,” Ethan blurted out. Austin’s brother looked very harried as he practically shoved his daughter inside and then a bag into Daniel’s chest. “Rosie, be good for your uncles. Bye, thanks, Austin! Dan!”

And then he was gone, sprinting down the hall and bypassing the elevator for the stairs. Rosemary, hair once again up in pigtails, giggled at him.

“Mommy said the baby’s coming,” she said, sounding delighted by that fact.

“What would he have done if I wasn’t home?” Austin asked, shaking his head as Daniel closed the door behind the little girl. “Leave her on my doorstep with a note?”

Daniel shrugged, still a bit thrown by Ethan’s casual reference to him as an uncle, and set the bag down by the pair that presumably belonged to the boys. Then he pulled out his phone, because this undoubtedly called for several pizzas.

The last time Buck had been at the Grant-Nash residence, it had been for the dinner that went horribly south. The one where he learned that it was Bobby who was holding him back from returning to active firefighting. It wasn’t quite as awkward as it could have been, being in the house again, since there were so many people crammed inside.

It was a party for May’s graduation, with guests that included people from the station, friends of the family, and other kids from her class. There were decorations put up, balloons and streamers and banners. There was cake and food. There was even a professional photographer, of all things. But what really stood out to Buck was the minor renovation that had occurred in the time since that dinner.

Apparently - or so Buck heard secondhand, from both Danny and Hen - Bobby and Michael decided to vent their frustrations in regards to Athena being attacked out on the fireplace that used to separate the living room from the kitchen. Now, in its place, was what was supposed to be a fire pit. Athena wasn’t too happy with it.

Personally, Buck kinda liked the whole open plan concept.

“What did you guys do for yours?” Maddie asked him as they posted in the photobooth - really a section of the living room in front of a black curtain - with props. Hers was a pink leopard print hat and inflatable guitar. His was an inflatable microphone and what he was fairly certain was a pink pompom, its plastic strands shiny and metallic looking, that he was using for a wig. “When you and Eddie graduated, I mean.”

“Eddie’s family basically used it as an excuse to get together. Ramon even managed to be home for it,” Buck told her. “And Danny took us both out to eat.”

Speaking of… He took a quick look around the crowded room and spotted their brother talking to Michael. They were both laughing about something. Michael was in very good spirits that day, buoyed no doubt by the news of the brain tumor having shrunk by a lot.

“Danny!” he hollered, making Maddie, the photographer, and several nearby partygoers cringe at his volume. “C’mere!”

“The lungs on you,” Athena commented as she went by. She was looking better, with time after her attack, but her arm was still in a sling.

Danny made his slow way through the crowd towards them, clearly in no hurry. Buck huffed at him.

“What do you want, squirt?” he asked.

“Pictures!” Buck said, reaching out to grab his wrist. Or he tried to, anyway; Danny managed to lean out of reach, so all he got was the fabric of his sleeve. “C’mon, you, me, and Maddie.”

“Just go with it, Dan,” Maddie advised, grabbing a random prop from where they were laid out and holding it out to him. “Here, have a mustache on a stick.”

“Better than what Buck can manage to grow,” Danny quipped, stepping up to Maddie’s other side. 

“Hey!” Buck complained, even as he made a face at the camera. “What were you and Michael talking about?”

“He went on a date with Elevator Guy.”

“Good for him,” Maddie said.

After a few pictures together, Maddie meandered off for more cake. Eddie was going by at the same time, so Buck dragged him in for pictures with Danny. Eventually Danny fled, too, leaving just Buck and Eddie.

“Gimme those beads,” Buck demanded, tossing the pompom and microphone over and making grabby hands. His boyfriend rolled his eyes but acquiesced, before grabbing a smoking pipe on stick for himself. “Oh, that’ll look very classy.”

“Thank you,” Eddie said, holding it up and pretending to smoke from it.

“Are you ready for Chris to be gone for two weeks?” Buck asked him, slipping the large collection of beaded necklaces on, leaning past him to grab a yellow inflatable guitar. “‘Cause I’m not.”

“Um.” They struck a pose for the camera. “Actually- Hey!”

“Oh, I’m sorry.” Buck had jumped with a bit too much enthusiasm and spirit and whacked his boyfriend in the face with his beads. Eddie was a little cross eyed. “I am so- You okay?”

“No, you might’ve just ruined my future modeling career.”

“I think you’ll be fine.” Buck rolled his eyes before pecking a quick kiss to the spot between Eddie’s eyes. “What were you saying?”

“The summer camp got cancelled,” Eddie said. “They told me this morning. I haven’t told him yet, though.”

“Oh, man. Want me to be there?”

“...Please?”

Hen and Chimney joined them in the photobooth for a few group pictures, before Buck got shoved out to let other people use it. He mingled through the crowd a bit while Eddie abandoned him to get some cake. Bobby was out on the patio, where some of the other guests had drifted, and so Buck took a breath and made his way over.

“Hey, Bobby.”

The other man turned, smiled.

“Hey, Buck. Enjoying yourself?”

“Yeah, it’s been fun. But, um…” Buck wet his lips. “I wanted to, y’know. Apologize for what happened on the train.”

“It’s fine,” Bobby said, shaking his head. “We both got a little hot, and… Well. It was pointed out to me that I was just repeating the same mistakes again.”

He glanced behind them, into the house. Buck followed his gaze and spotted Danny in a conversation with Denny and Harry. Hopefully whatever happened between Bobby and Danny this time around wasn’t as bad as the last.

“How are you doing?” Bobby asked him. “Running into Abby again like that. Finding out she had a fiancé like that.”

“Fine,” was Buck’s simple answer.

“Just fine?”

“I mean, yeah. Am I not supposed to be?” Buck asked with a shrug. “We talked before her mother died, about what we were both wanting. She wasn’t looking for anything serious then, just something to make her feel like she was more than her mother’s caretaker, and I was cool with that.”

Bobby's face twisted into an odd expression, though Buck had no idea why. Not until he remembered the conversation he’d had with Bobby about stepping into the mess with Abby.

“‘Sides, I have Eddie now,” Buck said, pushing on. It might’ve been more accurate to say that he had Eddie again, but this time around was far different from when they were teenagers, and far better, besides.

“That’s true,” Bobby agreed, and then, “Where are those two rushing off to?”

He was talking about Maddie and Chimney, who were making a mad dash through the partygoers for the front door. Buck, just as lost as the captain, didn’t have an answer to give him. Not then, anyway.

A couple days after the party, however, Maddie came by the apartment. After making sure that Buck was there instead of at Eddie’s. It was a weird request, and a vaguely worrisome one. Neither he nor Danny could figure out a reason that their sister would need to talk to the both of them like this.

“You don’t think something happened with Mom and Dad, do you?” Buck asked, pacing a little.

“I’d know if it had,” Danny answered, sitting on the couch and flipping through channels on the television. “Probably.”

“Is- Is she sick, do you think? Like…”

“I…” Danny frowned. “I hope not.”

Their sister didn’t knock when she arrived. She simply let herself in, striding with forced casualness. Buck was on her before she even got the chance to put down her purse, invading her space to feel her forehead.

“What are you doing?” Maddie snapped as she batted his hand away.

“He’s worried,” Danny told her. He’d gotten up and followed Buck. “Pretty sure that everything going on has made him even more paranoid about everything.”

Buck huffed.

“Excuse me for being concerned,” he said, crossing his arms and scowling. “You both hide things when something’s wrong.”

There was an awkward moment where Maddie and Danny both shifted awkwardly where they stood, because they couldn’t argue against his observation. Maddie spent years hiding everything with Doug, and Danny managed to hide the cancer scare from him until he got the phone call that it was mono. Could Buck really be blamed for being a bit paranoid about these things?

(Speaking of, Danny was wearing long sleeves again. But he wasn’t running a fever, and he wasn’t looking pale, so Buck didn’t think he was getting sick again…)

“Nothing’s wrong,” Maddie said. “I mean… I have been sick recently. Every morning, just about.”

“Every morning?” Danny repeated. He was standing stock still and staring straight at her, a smile forming on his face.

“Yes,” she said with a nod, returning the smile.

“What?” Buck demanded, looking between them. “What does that-”

And then the penny dropped.

“You’re pregnant!?” he shouted.

“Yeah.” The word trembled a little as it left Maddie’s lips. “I haven’t gone to the doctor yet, getting an appointment right now is painful, so I don’t know how far along, but… Weeks, at least.”

“That’s wonderful!” Buck wrapped her up in a hug, squeezing her tightly and lifting her off the ground. And then he nearly dropped her as a thought occurred to him. “Oh God, you and Chimney had sex. Gross.”

It was a statement that earned him a smack from both his siblings.

“Grow up,” Danny told him, rolling his eyes. He was smiling as he said it, and it stayed as his phone buzzed on the coffee table. When he went over to check it, however, the smile slid off his face like an ice shelf crashing into the sea.

“Everything okay?” Buck asked, setting Maddie back on her feet.

“Yeah, everything’s fine,” Danny told him. “Just makin’ plans for tonight.”

“You and Austin going out?” Maddie asked, and then, “Is there anywhere to go out to right now?”

It was a fair question. It wasn’t just summer camps that were closing - Chris had thrown an almighty tantrum when he was told, and was still giving the world the cold shoulder - but everything else seemed to be, too.

“Uh, no. I’m, y’know.” Danny waved a hand in the air. “Other people besides Austin exist, Mads.”

“I know. And I’m glad that maybe you’re moving on,” Maddie said, going over to squeeze his arm. “I don’t want you setting yourself up to be hurt.”

And though Buck didn’t really understand what she meant by that, he was even more confused by the way that their brother seemed to find her statement funny.

Chapter End Notes

When I was developing the bones of this installment, I debated having COVID progress the same way it did in reality. Except that I quickly realized that if it had, then 3b would simply not have happened, even though the writers in season 4 want us to believe that it actually did happen the same way. So easing into it months later than it should've was my compromise.

(So basically what I did in my other two series, but with more ominous foreshadowing thrown in.)

Chapter 18

Chapter Notes

And we're officially in the pandemic era.

See the end of the chapter for more notes

It truly did feel like they were staring down the end of the world. Never before had Buck seen the city streets so ominously empty as everyone stayed safely tucked away within their homes. Even the skies were empty, with the airports closed and the planes grounded. The beaches and the pier, the theaters, the restaurants, the hotels - everything was closed as people cowered away from each other.

Going to work was an exercise in patience. They were stuck waiting in their cars until someone came out to check them for a fever, and only then were they allowed into the station. The alarms, once a source of adrenaline and excitement, were now dreaded by everyone. Especially once it became apparent that, as the city and the world and life itself shut down, the nature of the emergencies had shifted. Where once they would be sent out for traffic accidents or cooking disasters or the consequences of foolishness, they were faced with the harrowing reality of what was ravaging the populace.

Worse still, it became very obvious that they were not properly stocked for this. Unless it was a fire, everyone put on the disposable face masks and the nitrile gloves before interacting with the public. Even for the simplest of calls. But this meant they were going through what they had on hand far too quickly, as were the other stations, and the supply chain was straining under the burden of demand. They couldn’t just not cover up, however, not when every stranger they met could spell disaster for everyone. 

Not just strangers, either. A week after May’s graduation party, one of the 133’s paramedics - Aiden Huff - called in to work. Then Theo Gray, who usually rode the engine with them, and then Flowers, the apparatus operator for the ladder. Everyone on their shift held their breaths for days afterwards, waiting to see if anyone else would be joining them. It was a problem plaguing the entire department, how many of them were falling sick. There were floaters, but there were too few of them for as many positions needed filling. And they brought with them the dangers of exposure and spread.

The trucks and the ambulances were disinfected after every call. After every call they washed their hands in hot water and soap, and at the end of every shift, they scrubbed themselves raw in the station showers. Some of them, Buck knew, did it all over again when they got home.

The year before, Buck and Eddie had celebrated their birthday together for the first time since everything went to shit between them. Buck, with his leg in that clunky cast, stood next to the other man as they both blew out the candles just as they had as teenagers. This year, there was no cake. This year, Eddie was miles away at his home while Buck was in the apartment. This year, they wished each other happy birthday through the screen of Buck’s tablet.

They hadn’t seen each other in person since Aiden got sick. It had been that long since Buck had seen any of his friends, at least the ones he didn’t work with, in person. The same was true for Danny, though he didn’t seem nearly as bothered by it as Buck felt. He actually seemed to get happier as their world narrowed down to the apartment, the station, and the quick and tense trips to the grocery store.

“I don’t know what I’m going to do.” Eddie looked awful, hair in utter disarray and face drawn.  He was one of the ones who scrubbed themselves down at the station and then did it again when he got home, before he even thought of greeting Chris. “I don’t blame Carla, a couple of her other clients are Abuela’s age. But this means I don’t have anyone to stay with Chris.”

Carla had, apparently, sat Eddie down after his last shift and regretfully informed him that she was having to let certain clients go to protect the others. Buck, like Eddie, couldn’t blame her one bit. It still made life that much more difficult.

“Maybe…” Buck rubbed at his neck as tried to think, pacing along the length of the apartment. “What about Isabel? Or- Hey, isn’t Pepa working from home at the moment?”

“She’s helping Abuela,” Eddie said. “If Carla can’t watch Chris because it’s too dangerous for the other people she helps, then I can’t expect the same of Pepa. And…” He looked around, leaned in closer to the screen, lowered his voice. “Shit, Buck. I’m afraid of hugging my kid.”

Buck felt his heart break at the same time that Eddie’s voice did. 

“What if… What if he stayed with one of them?” he offered. “Until this all blows over.”

Whenever that would be. God, he hoped it would be soon.

“That… Maybe. It would make it easier for them, too, everyone together.” Eddie sighed and leaned back. He was sitting on the couch in his living room. “He’s already so upset about everything, though. I don’t want to make it worse by uprooting him in the middle of all of this.”

“Then- Then… Then what if you uprooted yourself? What if you go somewhere else? That’s what Hen’s doing, right?”

Hen, as she’d mentioned to Buck the last time he spoke to her, was moving into Athena and Bobby’s guest room. May and Harry were staying with their father, who was just as out of work at the moment as Karen and Pepa were.

“Maybe,” was Eddie’s begrudging agreement. “Who, though? Austin?”

“No.” Danny was sitting at the dining table, bathrobe wrapped around himself and a bowl of cereal in front of him. It was the middle of the afternoon. “Does your boyfriend want to die? ‘Cause that’s how your boyfriend’s gonna die.”

Buck rolled his eyes at his brother, which was at least enough to make Eddie laugh.

“What, are you the only one allowed to crash on his couch or something?”

“Austin likes his space,” Danny said, the closest thing to an authority on what Austin Jones would or would not like that they had. “Why doesn’t he just… Shit, Eddie, just stay here.”

“I… I think that kinda defeats the whole, y’know. Bubble thing. Since we work at different stations.”

“Maddie lives with Chimney and works at dispatch,” Buck pointed out, feeling excitement bubbling up in his stomach at the process of actually seeing his boyfriend again without a screen between them. “We’ve ended up at the same scenes together, anyway. And…”

He glanced at Danny, turned around so his back was to him, and whispered,

“And I really, really miss you, Eds.”

Danny loudly and obnoxiously cooed, because while he was the best big brother, he was still a big brother. Buck flipped him off over his shoulder without bothering to turn around.

“Well, since you miss me…” Eddie’s face had gone soft, no longer quite as marred by the worry and the stress.

“I can give you a drawer here,” Buck told him. “It’s only fair. Right?”

“Yeah, okay.” The relief was evident even through the screen. “I’ll talk to Pepa and Abuela. And with Chris, definitely. But… Yeah.”

They stayed on the call for a little bit longer before Eddie said his goodbyes and got off, to go have that conversation with Chris. Buck didn’t envy him for it one bit, because he knew it wasn’t going to be an easy one to chart a course through. The last time Buck had spoken with Chris, the kid had been more than a bit sullen, the normal sunshiney attitude having gone decidedly cloudy.

“He’s not sleeping in your bed,” was what Danny said the moment the call ended.

“Seriously?” Buck rolled his eyes at him. “I’m an adult, I’m closer to thirty than I am twenty-five.”

“We share a wall,” his brother said, pointing at their bedrooms. “I’m still traumatized from the times I walked in on you two-”

“It was just the once,” he protested.

“It was more than once, but once was enough. I don’t want to get woken up because you’ve decided to relive being randy teenagers,” Danny said. “He’s sleeping on the couch. Or you’re sleeping on the couch. Hell, I’ll sleep on the couch and he can take my bed. Either way, you two are not sharing a room. I don’t want another reason to need therapy.”

“You’re just jealous you can’t convince Austin to move in and sleep in your bed.” Buck stuck his tongue out at his brother, unbothered by his glower. “How is that going, anyway?”

“What? Austin?”

“No, therapy.”

Buck hadn’t really meant to ask about it, but his curiosity had the words leaping off his tongue before he realized it. Neither of them had really talked about therapy since their discussion just before Christmas, where Danny tried to convince him to give it another go.

“S’okay,” Danny said with a shrug, getting up to dump his bowl into the sink, along with the spoon. “Nothing's happening right now ‘cause everyone’s dying-”

“Danny!”

“But she mentioned figuring something out so we could, y’know. Do it over the phone or the computer or whatever.”

“And you’d want to? Keep doing it?” Buck asked, not really sure why he was asking. Curiosity, definitely, but also… “You’re actually… You like therapy?”

“Absolutely,” Danny said, without a moment’s hesitation. “Love it, look forward to it every time.”

Buck wasn’t certain if he actually believed that. Before he could decide whether or not to call his brother out, however, the tablet still in his hand came alive again with an incoming video call. Answering it led to Maddie’s face filling the screen.

“Happy birthday!” she shouted at him. Albert and Chimney both echoed her from off-screen. “Sorry it’s late, I just got home.”

Her hair still looked wet. The firefighters weren’t the only ones scrubbing themselves clean after every shift. As much as being a dispatcher meant she was more insulated from the outside world than them, she still came into contact with all of her coworkers, and whoever they came into contact with.

“It’s fine,” Buck told her. “And you texted me this morning, remember?”

“Not the same,” she insisted. Tia Alma had said the same thing when she called. “Have you heard from Mom and Dad, yet?”

“Um.” Buck glanced at Danny, who’d gone all scowly at the mention of their parents. “Dad texted, too.”

Or rather, Dad had texted Danny to have him pass the happy birthday wishes along. Neither of them had Buck’s number, thank God; he did not want to know how much his mother would have screamed at him after the ladder truck for being selfish again and getting hurt. Or after the embolism. Or the tsunami.

“Any big plans for the day?” There was a hint of sarcasm in his sister’s words. It was impossible for that question to not be sarcastic these days. “Did you at least have a cake?”

“Nah.” He shrugged at Maddie’s frown. “Didn’t feel like running the gauntlet through the grocery for a store-bought cake.”

“You could have sent Dan to do it for you,” she said, which had the man in question rolling his eyes where he was leaning against the counter. “And a candle to go with it, so you could blow it out.”

“Not that it matters, I’m gonna get my wish anyway,” he told her. At Maddie’s questioning eyebrow, he explained, “Eddie’s probably gonna be staying here for a bit. He’s worried about getting Chris sick.”

“That’s-”

Maddie got interrupted as the tablet she was using was suddenly yanked out of her yanks. The image became a dizzying blur before it settled on a manic looking Chimney.

“Can I stay with you!?”

“Um.” Buck blinked, a little taken aback. It took a moment for his brain to catch up, and then when it did, he wanted to kick himself. Chimney was probably, undoubtedly, just as terrified of carrying something home to Maddie as Eddie was with Chris. “Sure, you can sleep on the couch.”

He grinned at Danny’s scowl.

The world felt like it was ending, the sky falling down around their ears, and yet Daniel was the happiest he’d been in weeks. It wasn’t going to last, he had learned his lesson about believing that kind of foolishness. While the fear of the pandemic and the enforcement of social distancing meant he could keep Drake at bay for a time, he was well aware that the man would undoubtedly be itching to make him miserable once more. That it was inevitable Drake would be calling him to heel sooner than he wished.

Still, he was enjoying the break while it lasted.

Unfortunately, his little sanctuary was about to be invaded. Eddie staying was one thing, that was tolerable. As long as they both lived like cloistered nuns, at least. But no, Buck just had to go and extend that offer to their sister’s boyfriend-slash-baby daddy. Four people in their two bedroom apartment were absolutely going to be pushing it, and he would resort to murder if he got screwed out of the hot water.

That meant Chimney’s life expectancy was entirely dependent on him switching over to cold showers for the duration of his stay. Daniel liked Eddie far more than him, and couldn’t ignore Buck’s pouting as well as he could their sister’s annoyance. Maddie would get over it, eventually, and being a single parent really wasn’t that hard once you got the hang of it and people to help.

“Stop grumping,” Austin told him. “You’re always complaining about the apartment being empty when Buck’s gone.”

“It’s not my fault I’m a people person,” Daniel shot back, leaning back on his bed. 

“You’re a freak.”

“How’re the new niblings?”

“Fine, I guess. Ethan keeps sending me pictures of Rosie with Robin,” Austin said. “And the boys were complaining that Adam cries a lot. God, if Cynthia has any more, I don’t know what she’ll name them. Cassie, if it’s a girl?”

“This is another Supernatural thing, isn’t it?”

“That reminds me. Cynthia wants me to tell you-”

“Oh, Jesus Christ.”

“-that you don’t have an excuse not to watch it, now.”

“Can my excuse be that I just don’t want to?”

“She’s going to keep being insufferable to both of us until you do. And what’s the alternative? Watching your brother make out with the other kid you adopted?”

Daniel could feel his face scrunch up in disgust.

“Don’t be gross.”

“I notice you aren’t denying the adoption bit,” Austin remarked. It wasn’t like Daniel could really deny it, he’d shown up for Eddie during those four years more often than Ramon did his entire childhood. Well, he actually could and definitely would be denying it. “Any word on therapy?”

“Is it something in the air? Something besides death, I mean. Buck asked about it, too.”

“Maybe that means he’s thinking about it,” Austin offered. “That’s not answering my question, though.”

“She sent an email earlier,” he said. “Apparently she wants to switch to doing it over Skype or Zoom or something. Maybe it was FaceTime. Actually…”

Therapy through a screen might be just what Buck needed, now that Daniel thought about it. It was very clear that one of his biggest issues was the prospect of being in the room with them, of being alone with them, thanks to the bitch that Daniel still wanted to take his baseball bat to. Maybe Buck would be more willing to talk to one if he knew he could do it at a distance.

“Actually?” Austin prompted, once Daniel was quiet for too long.

“Nothin’,” Daniel said, because even though it was Austin, he still didn’t feel right gossiping about this particular trauma of his brother’s. “Supernatural is on Netflix, right?”

“You’re really leaning into the Golden Retriever comparison, squirt,” Danny said, from where he was lounging on the couch.

“Shut up.” Buck was standing in the middle of the room, gaze fixed on the door in anticipation. “I haven’t seen Eddie in-”

“The two of you video chat almost every day.”

“Fine, I haven’t touched-”

“Gross.”

“Would you just shut up!” he snapped, which just caused Danny to laugh at him. “I miss my boyfriend, okay? Lay off me.”

Today was the day that Eddie would be coming over to stay. Hopefully only until everything blew over and he could go back home to Chris. Buck missed them both immensely, and felt their separation like a physical wound. 

When the door opened, Buck practically leaped across the space. He managed to hold himself back from tackling his boyfriend, since he didn’t want the man to drop anything. Eddie was weighed down with bags and had a box in his arms, which he went to set down on the dining table.

“Abuela made us a cake,” he explained, after dropping his bags by his feet and taking off the disposable mask he was wearing. “She sent us her love through Pepa.”

“That’s sweet of her,” Buck said, and then asked, “How was Chris?”

The way Eddie’s face fell at the question was answer enough.

“About as well as we thought he’d be,” he said, tone morose. “Spent half an hour hugging me before I left.”

Abuela was going to stay at Eddie’s, to keep from throwing Chris’ life into any more disarray than it already was. The plan was to keep the two of them in a nice little bubble, while Pepa got them their groceries. It wasn’t perfect, but it was the best they’d be getting right now.

“It’ll be okay,” Buck whispered, wrapping his arms around Eddie. Eddie hugged him back, tight and desperate.

“Alright, you two,” Danny said after a minute. When they pulled apart, Buck turned to see he was perched on the coffee table and gesturing at the now vacated couch. “Take a seat.”

“Oh, God,” Buck groaned, at the same time Eddie let out a quiet, “Ay, Dios.”

“I just flashed back to being sixteen,” Eddie complained, even as he moved to sit at the couch. “What is it, Danny?”

“We need to go over the rules,” Danny said. “Mostly just the one rule, really.”

“He wants us to be nuns,” Buck told Eddie, flopping down next to him and pressing into his side.

“I don’t want to hear you two having sex.”

“We’ll put a pillow behind the headboard,” he said, even as Eddie covered his face with a groan. “And I’ll buy you earplugs, it’ll be fine.”

There was knocking at the door before Danny could tell him how not fine he thought the whole thing was. He got up, still glaring at both Buck and Eddie, and went to answer it. Chimney came bursting through with his bags, just as manic as he’d been when Buck talked to Maddie on his birthday.

“Thank you so much for this,” Chimney gushed, the words muffled by the multiple masks he had on.

“Whatever,” Danny said, waving it away. He went back to the couch and, with another scowl at Buck and Eddie, grabbed the remote before sitting at the far end. The home screen for Netflix was pulled up on the television a moment later.

“Make yourself at home,” Buck told Chimney. “Don’t mind Danny, he’s a grump. He’ll get over it.”

There was no way this would last very long, anyways.

Chapter End Notes

And thus begins Daniel Buckley's Huge Gay Crush on Dean Winchester.

Chapter 19

Chapter Notes

We are still firmly in the Pandemic Era. Also, there are spoilers therein for Supernatural, although they are older than some people that are currently driving on the roads.

The living situation in the apartment took some adjusting to get used to. It was not a space necessarily meant for four grown adults, and there were inevitably squabbles around the use of the shower and the food in the kitchen and who got to watch what, when. Actually, the last bit was an argument that was swiftly preempted with Danny reigning supreme, which meant they were marathoning that Supernatural show between shifts.

For some reason, despite having been so adamant against watching it for so long, Danny couldn’t get enough of it now. Buck enjoyed it, at least well enough that he didn’t actually mind the binge-fest, and it turned out he’d been to a couple of the locations shown during his Neverending Gap Year Road Trip. Eddie scoffed loudly and often at everything happening on the show, while Chimney had already seen it once. Buck didn’t think Danny actually appreciated the audience commentary that they all provided, but only Chimney was getting dirty looks for it.

It probably helped that, at times, Eddie and Danny were in full agreement in their opinions on what was happening in the show.

“-I told you not to leave this room. I told you not to let him out of your sight-”

“¡Eres un ojete!” Eddie threw a piece of popcorn at the screen. “He’s a kid. Why did you leave them alone with a monster on the loose? That eats kids!?”

“Please tell me he dies,” Danny asked Chimney, reaching over Buck - somehow, despite starting off on the end of the couch, Danny ended up plastered to Buck’s side for this particular episode - to get a handful of popcorn from the bowl that Eddie was hogging. “I know I snapped at you for spoiling the bit about the psycho hillbilly family, but please tell me this asshole dies.”

“And goes to Hell,” Chimney confirmed with a nod. He was sitting in the arm chair.

“Thank God.”

“Then he gets freed and goes to Heaven.”

“Motherfucker.”

“Wait, if he knew a guy who was only three hours away,” Buck said, as the characters on the screen talked about being taken to someone named Pastor Jim. “Why didn’t he leave his kids with him and then go hunt the kid-eating whatever?”

“Shtriga,” Chimney helpfully told him.

“The kid-eating whatever.”

“He’s an asshole,” Eddie and Danny said at the same time, with the exact same dark tone. Eddie, without looking over, held out the bowl for Danny.

“Pretty sure he was using them for bait,” Chimney answered, stretching to grab some of the popcorn for himself. “Can’t kill it unless it’s eating a kid.”

“No, seriously.” Danny was glaring at the screen. Buck recognized the particular scowl his brother was wearing, and the twitching fingers that accompanied it. “Why doesn’t he stay in Hell?”

“God’s plan or something.”

“Fuck God.”

That had Eddie breaking into laughter. It was the full body kind, which meant Buck had to rescue the bowl of popcorn before it spilled across the floor. They watched the rest of the episode, Danny making an odd noise as the kid that was about to be monster bait talked about doing anything for his younger brother. The monster was killed, the day was saved, mullet rock played as everyone drove off into the sunset.

Danny looked suspiciously teary-eyed.

Before Buck could speak up, to either ask if something was wrong or to leap on the opportunity to take revenge for all the times Danny had embarrassed him, Eddie’s phone began to ring where it lay on the coffee table. Eddie lunged forward to grab it as Danny paused the show before it could play the next episode. They all recognized the ring tone by this point, so they all knew who was calling. The time was the only surprise.

“Hey, bud,” Eddie said, waving at his son through the small screen of his phone, pacing away from the rest of them. “You’re a bit early, is everything okay? Anything wrong?”

By this point, a few days into it, they’d fallen into a routine when it came to Chris on the days they weren’t on shift. There’d be a video chat in the morning, while he was having breakfast, that was mostly Buck and Chris making fun of Eddie for being a zombie. There was another video chat in the afternoon, and a third one around bedtime. They’d had the afternoon one already, and bedtime for Chris wasn’t for a couple hours yet.

“No,” Chris answered, voice small. “I just missed you.”

Buck felt his heart clench as Danny and Chimney exchanged identical grimaces.

“I miss you, too,” Eddie replied, tone just as soft. This time, it was less of a clench that Buck felt in his heart and more of a general shattering. “Have you two had dinner yet?”

“Yeah. We had enchiladas.”

“Ugh, lucky,” Buck said with a played up whine, getting up to peer at Chris over Eddie’s shoulder. “Hey, Chris.”

“Hi, Buck!” Chris glanced away from the screen. “Abuela says hi, too.”

“I have an idea,” Buck whispered into Eddie’s ear, tugging him into his bedroom. 

Eddie didn’t question it, instead simply going along with everything. He sat on the bed at Buck’s urging as he chatted with Chris, propping himself against the headboard. Buck, meanwhile, popped over into Danny’s room. Just as he said he would, he’d stuck the two tattered copies of Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland and Through the Looking Glass back on his brother’s shelf years after stealing off with them before his roadtrip. Danny hadn’t said anything about their reappearance, nor did he say anything as he watched Buck carry them off again.

He jumped onto the bed beside Eddie, making the other man bounce a little.

“Hey, Superman, go get your copy of Alice,” Buck instructed, holding up the one in his hand where he could see. “We’ll read it together, yeah?”

Chris tilted his head, clearly considering it, before he nodded and scrambled away. They were left with a not-so-interesting view of the ceiling in Chris’ room as he abandoned his tablet on the bed. When he got back, the screen bounced around as he picked the tablet up again and propped it up.

“I got it,” Chris announced to them, waving it to show it off. It was too close to really see, but Buck could recognize the bottom of the spine of the book he gave the kid two Christmases ago.

“Awesome.” Buck nudged Eddie with his elbow. 

His boyfriend turned his head to him, and raised an eyebrow when Buck held out one of the books. Eddie took it with a shrug, after another nudge, and handed him the phone in return.

“Okay, mijo.” Eddie opened the book, cleared his throat. Danny peered in at them and then eased the bedroom door closed. “Alice was starting to get very tired of sitting by her sister on the bank, of having nothing to do…”

Daniel loved and adored his baby brother. If tortured for long enough, he might even admit to having positive emotions for Eddie. And he was learning to tolerate his sister’s boyfriend. But God above, with all three of them stuffed into the apartment together, he was on the verge of earning a manslaughter charge. Again, it was Chimney whose life was truly the most at risk. Luckily for Maddie’s baby daddy, though, Daniel had a place to run away to when the urge to grab his bat and start blindly swinging became a bit too hard to resist.

Austin was in the middle of talking to someone on his laptop when Daniel let himself in, and though he glanced up, he didn’t pause the conversation at all. When Daniel threw himself onto the couch like Buck in the middle of his angsty teenager phase, he saw Cynthia’s face on the screen. She looked like an older, softer, girlier version of Austin. And a tired one, too.

“And Uncle Dan has joined us,” Cynthia commented. She smirked as he grabbed one of Austin’s discarded sweaters - there were two of them tossed onto the back of the couch, this time - and pulled it on. “I’d have Adam say hi, but he’s a bit preoccupied.”

She adjusted the blanket that was covering her chest, and Daniel realized it was blocking the baby from view as she fed him. Daniel was thankful for that, because he wasn’t sure what the protocol was when it came to seeing your fake boyfriend’s sister’s boobies. It probably broke some sort of moral code or something.

“Is this a visit or are you hiding?” Austin asked him.

“I’m trying to avoid needing to hide a body,” Daniel answered. “I don’t know what Maddie sees in the guy, sometimes.”

“How is your sister?”

“She’s driving Albert-”

“Chimney’s brother,” Austin helpfully supplied.

“-insane by making him run across the city for her weird cravings,” Daniel told her. “She woke him up at three in the morning for Skittles. Then she only ate the red ones.”

Speaking of. He got up and headed for the kitchen, finding the resealable bag of Skittles in the cabinet.
