“Apparently she could’ve just called up Austin.” Cynthia sounded like she was laughing when he came back.

“These are mine,” Daniel firmly told her, leaning into Austin. “They’ve got my cooties on ‘em and everything.”

“Gross.” Cynthia’s nose scrunched up. “The boys are wanting to know when you’re having the next nerd session.”

Austin rolled his eyes at his sister, and then turned to look at Daniel. Because he’d gotten dragged into this, too. It had been a few times now that he had to sit through playing a game that did not hold his interest at all, but he’d done it without complaint. Maddie was split between teasing him for it and tutting in disapproval, as she remained firmly in the camp of “you’re only going to get yourself hurt, Dan.”

The concern was funny, all things considered, except for all the ways that it wasn’t funny at all.

“I get to cover for a paramedic on B-shift,” Daniel said, answering the unspoken question. “So I’m pulling a double the next two days.”

“After that,” Austin told her. “Sometime in the afternoon, so this one can get a nap.”

“I’ll let them know,” Cynthia said, and then her eyes cut over to Daniel. He didn’t like the way they were already laughing before she even said anything. “So, Austin wouldn’t tell me. How much did you cry at the end of season two?”

“Shut up,” Daniel grumbled, which had her cackling. “We’re halfway through season three, now, anyway.”

“Uh-huh. You should tell me how much you cry at the end of that one.”

“No, seriously, shut up,” he said, and then, “Wait, so they don’t save Dean!?”

“Sorry, toots.”

“Mother-” Daniel remembered there was an infant right there and cut himself off, contenting himself with angrily shoving a handful of Skittles into his mouth while Cynthia laughed at him more.

Back in the day, during high school, it wasn’t unusual for Eddie to end up alone with Danny. Usually, it was while they sat in the bleachers as they watched one of Buck’s football games. Other times, it was because Eddie showed up at their apartment while Buck was working one of the part-time jobs he had as a teenager.

Eddie always liked hanging out with Danny. From the moment he turned ten and his father took him aside, told him it was time to step up and be the man of the house, he’d felt the crushing weight of responsibility bearing down on him. He had to grow just so his shoulders were big enough to carry it. But being with Danny was always a break from that, a break from helping his mother run the house and look after his sisters while his father was off on his constant work trips, God only knew where. Eddie certainly wasn’t keeping track.

These days, Eddie ending up alone with Danny was a rarity. For several reasons, not the least of which was that a couple years ago it probably would’ve resulted in Eddie’s murder. That singular night with Shannon had made such a mess of everything and destroyed so much of his life, with Chris the only silver lining coming out of it.

This time, they’d ended up alone in the apartment because Chimney was covering a shift and Buck was running off some of that near perpetual energy of his. Eddie was perfectly content to leave him to it, even though Buck had tried badgering him into joining. He regretted it somewhat, though, when the awkward silence fell over the apartment in Buck’s absence.

“So.” It was Danny who broke it, sitting in the armchair. He looked very much like he’d just rolled out of bed. He was also sipping a beer, despite the fact that five o’clock was a couple hours away still. Not that time felt like a real concept these days. “How’re you holding up?”

“Um. I’m holding up,” Eddie answered, drawing his legs up onto the couch. The blanket and pillows that Chimney used were all piled up at the other end. “Wishing this would just… End, y’know?”

No one had thought this would last this long. Buck sounded so confident when he assured Eddie that this would all blow over soon. That was weeks ago, now, and everybody’s patience with it was growing short. For some reason, though, the possibility of their self-enforced isolation ending had Danny grimacing. A small thing, there and gone again, but Eddie spotted it.

“How’s Chris?”

It was Eddie’s turn to grimace.

“He’s, uh… Holding up. He was upset last night.”

Chris had asked when he was coming home, a question that was becoming more and more common when they talked. He didn’t like that the answer hadn’t changed, that Eddie hadn’t promised to come home right there and there, and ended up throwing the mother of all tantrums. It had probably been building up, his displeasure at his father being gone - again - becoming more and more apparent each day. And though Eddie had weathered his share of Chris’ meltdowns since being discharged, it was far more difficult to do when they were separated by a screen and he couldn’t actually do anything to help.

“It’s like I’m back overseas,” Eddie complained. “I moved here with him and joined the department so I could actually be with my kid, not… This.”

“It’s why we moved here, too,” Danny said, bottle dangling from his fingers as he avoided looking at Eddie. “Went two years without actually laying eyes on Buck in person, ending up flying all the way to fucking Peru to tell him we were moving to Los Angeles.”

“Are you telling me to bring him here?”

“What?” Danny turned his head to fix him with an incredulous glare. “No, you idiot. I was trying to... Sympathize, empathize, whatever. You can’t hug your kid, it sucks.”

“Yeah.”

A part of Eddie couldn’t help but feel a little jealous of Danny through all this. The man was basically treating this like some sort of vacation retreat, perfectly happy for this to last as long as it needed to. Except for when Chimney’s cracks and quips became a bit too much for him. Usually when they were aimed at Buck, although it also happened when a particularly barbed one was thrown Eddie’s way. Then the easygoing attitude was replaced with ill-temper, which usually led to Danny storming out to go to Austin’s.

“Is Austin in our bubble?” Eddie blurted out.

“I guess, maybe.” Danny shrugged. “Pretty sure I’m the only person he’s spending time with outside of work. Not that that’s much of a change from before.”

The apartment’s door was thrown open and Buck came bursting in with all his usual enthusiasm. He was sweaty, his shirt sticking to his chest and his hair sticking to his forehead. He stumbled over to the couch to drape himself over the back and on Eddie.

“Gross,” Eddie complained, squirming to get away. “You need a shower.”

“I do,” Buck agreed with a hum. “You should join me.”

“Your brother is right there,” Eddie pointed out, gesturing to where Danny sat looking rather ill.

“He can go to Austin’s,” Buck retorted. Then his head shot up with a grin. “Hey, Danny, you should go to Austin’s.”

“This is my apartment,” Danny argued, even as he got up. He went to the kitchen sink and poured out his drink, which turned out to be mostly full, still, before tossing it into the recycling.

“And my boyfriend and I are about to have sex in it,” Buck retorted. “So unless-”

“Yeah, yeah.” Danny cut him off with a wave and an eye roll. “I’m going.”

Buck at least had the decency to wait until Danny was closing the door behind him before he pounced, yanking Eddie off the couch and manhandling him into the bathroom to take that shower together.

Afterwards, they lazed on Buck’s bed together in the afterglow, both of them in terrible need of another shower. Eddie’s head was half-hanging off the end of the bed, comfortable despite the fact that they’d somehow managed to pull the sheets mostly off in the midst of their activities. Buck was tracing lines on his skin, the shapes meaningless yet familiar.

“I think this one might be my favorite,” Buck said, which was just random enough that Eddie roused himself to figure out what context he was missing.

“Your favorite what?”

“Of your moles,” Buck clarified. He tapped a spot high up on the back of Eddie’s thigh. “This one.”

“Why?” Eddie asked, craning his neck in an attempt to see the mole he was talking about.

“Dunno, it just is.”

“Weirdo,” he teased, reaching out and dragging Buck into his side. “I think I might go back home soon.”

“Oh.” Buck’s voice was small as he buried his face into Eddie’s shoulder. “Yeah, makes sense. Everything’s opening back up. Hen mentioned thinking about doing the same, when I talked to her earlier.”

“I miss him,” Eddie said. “I know you do, too. And he misses us both.”

“Yeah.” The sigh tickled Eddie’s skin. “It’d be good to hug my Superman again.”

Buck checked the time on his phone and glanced at the closed door of Danny’s bedroom. An hour ago, his brother secluded himself in there with his laptop. After giving it a couple more minutes, and making sure Chimney was focused on his conversation with Albert, gesturing dramatically even though the younger Han obviously couldn’t see it over the phone, Buck eased the door open.

Danny’s laptop was sitting beside him on the bed. It was closed, which meant he was definitely done.

“What’s up, squirt?”

“I just… I just wanted to ask you something,” Buck said, closing the door behind him. “Do you- Um, do you remember last year, before Christmas?”

Danny swung his feet onto the floor and sat up, patting the spot next to him. Buck hesitantly took it.

“About the therapy? ‘Course I do,” Danny said. “What about it?”

“I was just- I was thinking about, maybe… Trying it? Again?” Buck said. “Since- Since, you know, everything’s over Zoom or Skype or FaceTime, now. It sounds… Convenient.”

For the briefest of moments he remembered the feel of a skirt brushing against his thighs, fingers curling into his hair, a touch on bare skin that felt like a brand…

“I mean,” Buck continued, shaking the memory off. “You’re doing it from your bedroom.”

“It is certainly that,” Danny agreed, eying him. He slung an arm over Buck’s shoulder. “You want me to ask Dr. White for some names? I’m sure she could help find one that you might like.”

Buck didn’t miss how he didn’t suggest Dr. White herself. He wondered how much he came up in their sessions.

“Yeah, yeah. That would be… Yeah. Thanks.”

“Don’t-” Danny cut himself off as his phone buzzed a short pattern where it sat on the nightstand. He scowled when he checked it, before tossing it back down, going back to Buck like nothing happened. “I’ll shoot her an email or something.”

“That would be great, thanks,” Buck told him. “Everything okay?”

“Yeah,“ Danny lied. Buck knew he was lying. “Absolutely.”

Chapter 20

Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

Chimney’s life expectancy was shrinking by the day, not that the man seemed to have realized that quite yet. Eddie was back at his own home with his kid, and had been for some weeks now, and Buck seemed to be spending just as much time there as he did at the apartment. Daniel himself hadn’t gone over since lockdown started, however nice it would be to see Chris in person instead of through a screen. And also to get away from the house guest that just would not leave, even though it was well into September now.

Cohabitating was perhaps the absolute worst thing that the two of them could have done, or at least that was what Daniel decided mid-way through the lockdown. He was also forced to come to the conclusion that his sister’s taste in men just simply sucked. To be fair, Daniel’s opinion of Chimney was already colored by what he’d heard from both Austin and Buck, how he spent the entirety of his last relationship lying to his girlfriend about everything and how he apparently thought it was acceptable to threaten suicide in order to get laid, plus everything about his tenure as interim captain. But these months stuck together had allowed another character flaw to come to light, that being just how often Daniel’s baby brother was the target of the man's jokes and barbs.

It was easily overlooked at first, because the man’s brand of humor was a bit on the caustic side and while Daniel could be more than a bit hypocritical at times, he wasn’t about to throw a stone at that particular glass house. Everyone got at least three witty quips aimed their way in a single conversation, which was entirely fair. But what caught Daniel’s attention and drew his ire was how often Chimney would, without prompting, insult Buck. Usually about his perceived lack of intelligence or his history of promiscuity.  The only thing that kept the bat from being swung was that Buck seemed to just laugh it off.

Thankfully, Chimney was capable of learning, or at least was capable of realizing how thin the ice was that he was treading, as he’d started cutting way back on the comments. At least within earshot of Daniel. A change in behavior that was encouraged, no doubt, by the death glares that Daniel started shooting the man whenever he let loose another volley, which would have him flinching every single time.

(Buck had to put up with too much bullying growing up, even if Daniel always made sure to thoroughly quash it whenever it came to his attention. He’d be damned if Buck would have to deal with it in his own home.)

On this morning, instead of getting ready to leave for his shift, Chimney was at the kitchen table trying to helicopter parent an unborn child over FaceTime. Buck was at Eddie’s, and while his day started earlier - Eddie was apparently taking Chris to the Wilsons for his shifts, since Karen was working from home, which meant a longer commute - it was probably far less annoying and came with better food for breakfast. Even if it was nice to be able to see and talk to Maddie, through a screen or not. 

“You know what I miss? I miss caffeine,” Maddie was complaining. “I mean, we’re sleeping great, the morning sickness is gone. We’re in the sweet spot, but I really need my cup of joe in the morning.”

“Well that is no longer part of your complete breakfast,” Chimney told her. Daniel didn’t even bother to hide the way he rolled his eyes as he leaned against the kitchen counter behind him, already in uniform for the day, with a bowl of off-brand Fruit Loops in hand.

“Peppermint tea.” Albert appeared on-screen, leaning in to set a mug down in front of Maddie while clutching at his own, whose nostrils flared before her expression went flat. “Delicious.”

“Yours is coffee, I can smell it,” she said, and turned her head just enough to snap out, “Give it!”

“Don’t do it, Albert!” Chimney demanded.

“If you value your life, Al, give her the fucking coffee,” Daniel told the younger man. Chimney twisted around to glare at him. “Trust me, you don’t want to piss off a pregnant woman. The only reason I didn’t get castrated with forks was because Irene and Cynthia were too big to squeeze past all the chairs in their way.”

The biggest betrayal was how Austin had started to clear the path for them before Daniel managed to talk his way to safety.

“Dan!” Maddie admonished with a laugh.

“I’ll make you a coffee,” Albert said, smiling nervously as he left again with the tea.

“Smart,” Daniel commented.

“Maddie,” Chimney said with a slight whine.

“The doctor said one cup a day.” Maddie held up a finger to make it clearer.

“She’s the doctor, not the parent.”

“Did you miss what I said about the castration and the forks?” Daniel asked him, slurping the left-over milk in his bowl as obnoxiously as possible. 

“Go stick your face in your own FaceTime.”

“Y’know, you could be bickering about this there, right? I mean, I understand why you’re not, you’re safely out of fork range here.” Daniel wiped at his mouth with the back of his hand. “But Buck said that Hen went back to Denny. And Eddie went back to Chris, and he has as many reasons to be worried and paranoid as you do. Yet here you are, hiding in my apartment from my sister.”

“I’m being cautious. And we’re not bickering, we’re bantering. Playfully,” Chimney argued, and then turned slightly to face him. “Why don’t you go banter with whoever you keep locking yourself in your room to talk to?”

“Excuse me?”

“You know, whoever it is you talk to for hours at a time through a webcam,” the other man said. “I know it’s not Jones, ‘cause I heard a woman’s voice.”

“And why am I just now hearing about this?” Maddie asked. Daniel made a face at his sister’s nosiness.

“He also keeps going out to meet someone,” Chimney told her, even though at no point had Daniel ever told him that was what he was doing. “He’ll get a text and then off he goes.”

“Danny’s getting booty calls in the middle of a pandemic?” Albert suddenly popped up on the screen again, shoving his face in front of Maddie’s. “What’s your secret?”

“Ain’t got a secret,” Daniel lied, shrugging at them. “I’m just hot.”

“Sometimes it is very obvious that he’s Buck’s brother,” Chimney told Maddie.

“Buck imprinted on him like a baby duckling,” she replied, shoving Albert’s head out of the way. Daniel ignored them as he went to the sink, turning on the water to rinse out his bowl. “He’s not wrong, though. The point of moving in together was to live together. We could be having our pillow talk on actual pillows.”

“I know,” Chimney sighed. “But hello, global pandemic. We need to be safe.”

Daniel rolled his eyes - it felt like he was doing that a lot that morning - as he set the bowl on the drying rack along with the spoon he used.

“So we take precautions like everyone else,” Maddie replied. “I mean, would it be so bad if we both had to strip down at the end of the day?”

“Gross,” Daniel loudly crowed, sticking his face right by Chimney’s. The man cringed away from him, or maybe his volume.

“Grow up,” his sister snapped, and then leaped in her seat a little. “Oh! Good morning.”

“What? What, oh?” Daniel asked, peering at her. “Wait, did the baby just kick?”

“Every morning like clockwork.” Albert reappeared on the screen to place a new mug in front of Maddie, this one lacking the tail of a steeping tea bag. “Maybe the kid likes coffee.”

“The kid’s the size of a mango,” Chimney argued, bullying for space in front of the screen. “The mango doesn’t get a say.”

“Well, Mango misses Daddy,” Maddie said.

Daniel glanced between his sister on the screen and Chimney, able to feel the mood turning maudlin with her words.

“And on that note, I’m gonna head on out. I have time to get coffee on the way. Because I’m not limited to a single cup.” He grinned at Maddie’s glare. “Tell May I said hi.”

“Yeah, yeah, I will.”

“I should get going, too. Shift starts in less than an hour,” Chimney told Maddie. “I love you. Both.”

He reached over and pressed the button to end the call just as Albert finished saying it back. The man sighed and sat there instead of getting up.

“You know.” Daniel couldn’t help himself. “If you went back home-”

“Shut up, Dan.”

“Fine, fine.” Daniel rolled his eyes and grabbed his bag from where it sat on the couch, and then his keys and phone on the table. “Lock up on your way out.”

He didn’t wait for a reply from Chimney before stepping out into the hall. When he turned on his phone’s screen to text Buck and ask if he wanted anything from the coffee place, he found that his brother had sent him a bunch of messages about microquakes, for some reason. So that was probably going to be a thing all day.

The world still felt like it was ending all around them, but Eddie was more content waking up in the morning now than just a month or two ago. Even if he was waking up far earlier than before. The commute to the Wilsons’ house was not exactly the kindest, timewise, since Eddie needed to get Chris there in time to be set up for school. But it was the best solution he had, with Pepa once again focused on helping Abuela and Carla unavailable for the foreseeable future.

It was tolerable, though, because he got to walk down the hall again and gently wake up his son. And half the time, he’d do it to the smell of breakfast being cooked in the morning because Buck stayed over, such as he did now. After making sure Chris was roused, he shuffled through the dining room and into the kitchen. Buck, standing at the stove in his pajamas still, turned his head a little to smile at him and give a quiet,

“Hey.”

Eddie gave a grunt as he got behind him, letting his head fall forward to rest on his boyfriend’s shoulder, which shook a little with laughter.

“A decade and a half later,” Buck’s voice was laced with fondness, “and you’re still such a zombie.”

Not yet awake enough to come up with a proper response to that, Eddie gave another wordless grunt. And then he (lightly) bit Buck on the shoulder.

“Hey, hey, no chewing on the chef,” Buck protested, though it sounded more teasing than anything. Eddie heard something crack and opened an eye enough to see that Buck was breaking eggs on the edge of a skillet that Eddie did not remember buying. “Breakfast is almost ready, ya animal.”

Eddie grumbled at him, content to stay leaning against his boyfriend as he woke up a bit more. He didn’t move until he had to, which was a few minutes later when Buck was pressing a couple plates loaded with food into his hands and directing him to take them to the dining table. Chris came trundling in when Buck called for him, looking far more awake than his father. He cheered at the sight of breakfast, which Eddie echoed when Buck set down mugs of coffee along with Chris’ glass of OJ.

After breakfast, after both Eddie and Chris got ready for the day together, they said their goodbyes to Buck, who didn’t have to go just yet, and headed out the door. The Wilsons’ house was not simply a stop on the way to the station, unfortunately. They lived on the other side of the city from Eddie’s house, which meant he had to drive past the station to drop off Chris and then turn around. But it was what he had to do, so he did it without complaint. Well, without much complaint.

It was Karen who greeted them at the door when he arrived, smiling widely and warmly as she let them in.

“Hen’s almost ready,” she told Eddie. “Chris, go on and get set up at the table with Denny.”

“Okay!”

Eddie followed along behind his son, placing his bag with the school-issued chromebook onto the table for Chris to dig out. Nia, the little girl that Hen and Karen were fostering, came running out of the hall and Eddie managed to catch her before she collided with his legs.

“Careful now, chiquita,” he tutted, steadying her on her feet. She barely paid him much mind before sprinting off for Karen, who scooped her up.

“Okay!” Hen came jogging out from the same direction as Nia, duffel bag hanging from her shoulder. “I’m ready. Sorry for the wait, Eddie.”

“It’s fine,” he told her, waving it off. “Chris-”

“Behave for Ms. Karen, I know,” Chris said, rolling his head with his eye.

“I was going to say to have a good day,” Eddie teased, pressing the most obnoxious kiss he could to Chris’ curls and laughing at the kid’s groan. “See ya tomorrow, mijo.”

“Bye, Dad.”

Eddie waited for Hen to say her own goodbyes, and then they were both heading for his truck. The car ride to the station had fallen into a pattern since they started this routine, with a stop for gas that Hen paid for and the both of them catching up on gossip. At some point, the rides to and from work turned into her fishing for more stories about going to high school with Buck, which was a topic that, for one reason or another, neither he nor Buck had talked about with the others much.

The overall shape of it, mostly, and some of the more bare details and a couple embarrassing stories, those had been shared. But the topic had been nearly taboo before Eddie found his courage at his shield ceremony, and then usually brushed over in the year after with more current events taking priority. 

“Hot chicks love athletes.” Hen’s voice was filled with scathing judgment, and he didn’t need to look at her to know her expression was the same. “That was seriously what you said?”

“It was not my proudest moment,” Eddie admitted. “But the last thing I wanted was for the other guys on the baseball team to, y’know. Know.”

“No, no, I get that,” she said. “Buck’s mentioned Timothy before.”

He winced at the name.

“Yeah. And then Buck thought it would be funny to surprise me with a dinner date at Denny’s.”

Hen was still laughing as they pulled into the station’s parking lot.

Unlike earlier in the summer, they didn’t have to wait for someone to come to them. Instead, they got out and headed for the front entrance, where there was a member from C-shift standing by to take their temperatures, along with a stand with a dispenser for hand soap. When they were cleared, they went to the locker room and changed and stowed away their civvies.

Bobby was in the bay, and Eddie and Hen followed him up the stairs to the loft. Eddie because he wanted more coffee, Hen because Bobby started talking with her about Athena’s return to work that day. It would be her first shift since being attacked.

“I don’t know what to do,” Bobby complained to Hen. “I don’t think she’s ready.”

Eddie paused in the process of pouring himself some coffee to look at the captain. He opened his mouth but didn’t get a chance to voice his thoughts before Hen, sitting at the island, shook her head at him. Eddie rolled his eyes and went to get the creamer from the fridge.

“Michael says he’s seen her go through rough patches,” Bobby continued, oblivious to the silent conversation. “But never like this.”

“What happened to Athena was devastating,” Hen said. “It made her question everything, her ability to do the job. That can’t be an easy thing for a woman who counts on nobody but herself.”

Bobby gave a noncommittal grunt to that statement.

“There’s a reason she drives the L-car, Bobby.”

“No partner.”

Hen nodded.

“And I’m not saying that she doesn’t need you,” she said. “Or me, or Michael. I’m just saying that for this particular thing, she has to figure it out by herself. And if I know Athena, she is tired of talking about it. In her mind, there’s only one thing left to do.”

“Get back out there,” Bobby concluded with a sigh.

“And we’ve seen what happens when you try to keep someone from going back to work because you think they aren’t ready,” Eddie said, unable to keep quiet on this for too long. He ignored Hen’s chiding scowl. “It wasn’t pretty.”

Although he knew Athena was more than capable of yelling at Bobby herself.

“No, it wasn’t,” Bobby agreed with a grimace. “I don’t suppose I need to ask you how Buck’s doing. He’s been texting me about earthquakes for the past half hour, in between asking about Athena and May.”

“You too?” Hen laughed and her head. “Eddie’s phone went off every minute on the way here with text-to-voice reading them out. But earthquakes are better than some of the other things he’s sent Eddie that I had to hear.”

Eddie flushed when Bobby looked at him.

“I don’t want to know,” the captain said, shaking his head.

“I wish I didn’t,” Hen told him, laughing at Eddie’s increasing discomfort. “How is May? I know Athena wasn’t happy with what she’s doing.”

“She was excited to start an actual shift at dispatch,” Bobby answered.

“Here’s hoping it’s a boring one,” Eddie said, to the agreement of the other two.

The earthquake struck a couple hours into their shift. Buck was helping - well, “helping.” He was mostly just stuck to his phone - Danny and Flowers do the daily maintenance checks on the trucks. It wasn’t a particularly big one, just enough to shake things up and give everyone a jolt. Buck didn’t even look up from his phone.

“There goes our morning,” Danny complained, rolling out from under the engine.

“We’ll have to finish this up when it calms down,” Flowers agreed, glowering at the floor. Or maybe at the earth itself.

“Caltech’s been tracking microquakes the last few days,” Buck said, attention stuck to his phone. “Thousands of them.”

“We know.” Flowers sounded amused, not annoyed, but Buck still felt himself flushing in embarrassment. He really had been pestering everyone too much about the microquakes that morning, he knew that. “What do they say about that not-so-micro quake?”

“Uh.” Buck checked. “It was a three-point-two, apparently.”

“That’s a baby,” Danny said, getting to his feet and sending the crawler rolling away with a shove of his foot. It bumped into the bay wall and bounced back a bit before coming to a stop. “People are gonna freak out anyway.”

“Fingers crossed that it’s nothing too stupid,” Flowers said, holding up his crossed fingers.

Above them, the alarms began to wail.

“And so it begins,” Danny dramatically intoned as he and Flowers headed for their gear.

Buck sighed and tucked his phone away to follow after them.

Chapter End Notes

Part of this chapter brought to you by me watching 8x04 and getting caught on Chimney just out of the blue calling Buck stupid.

Chapter 21

Chapter Notes

I almost added this to the wrong story. Woops.

“That does not go there.”

Eddie silently agreed with Chimney’s statement, even as he rolled his eyes at the obviousness of it. Above them, sticking out of the side of a tall office building, was a bus. Somehow, despite the bigger quake that morning having been more of a dud than anything truly earthshaking, it had resulted in the dam for the Hollywood reservoir busting open. And that, in turn, somehow launched a Metro bus into a building.

“Alright, Chim, Hen, we’ll go directly to the bus and start triaging who we can there,” Bobby explained to them. “Eddie, Jones, you’ll go to the roof so one of you can rappel down and secure it. And remember, while Metro is phasing them out in favor of electric, they still have buses that use natural gas. Dispatch said this was one of them, so keep that in mind.”

Eddie nodded along with the instructions, noticing a quick grimace that made its way across Austin’s face. It was there and gone again before Eddie could think to ask him about it. They gathered the gear they would need and trooped inside, crowding into one of the elevators. Eddie pulled out his phone when it went off on the way up, snorting and rolling his eyes at the messages waiting for him.

“Buck’s wondering where all the water is gonna go,” he informed the others when they turned to look at him.

“My mom survived the Baldwin Hills dam break in the Sixties,” Hen said, turning back around. “Water only ever wants to go in one direction: out to sea.”

There was a soft ding as they reached their first stop. Bobby and the paramedics hurried to pull up their masks - the LAFD had issues reusable one a few weeks into the pandemic, which helped a lot with PPE supplies - as the doors opened, revealing visions of destruction. The entire office space in the room beyond was wrecked, with furniture overturned and light fixtures sparking and remnants of the wall scattered across the floor.

“This is definitely our stop,” Chimney commented as he followed Bobby and Hen out of the elevator.

“Hey, so.” Eddie glanced at Austin as the doors closed and they started rising again. The man was looking increasingly discomforted. “Buck said your brother lived somewhere close to Hollywood.”

And Danny once commented that Austin’s parents lived in “suburban hell,” but that description could cover a lot of the city. Eddie wasn’t even certain how the man defined it. Maybe it was just whatever reminded him of the house in Hershey as opposed to that rather dingy apartment building in El Paso.

“Los Feliz.” Austin’s hand twitched with an aborted motion for his pocket. “Should be out of the way.”

“Yeah. Like Hen said, the water’s headed for the ocean, it shouldn’t go that way.”

“Yup.” There was the faint sound of buzzing and Austin hurriedly reached into his pocket, pulling out his own phone. He looked at first disappointed and then amused at what he saw. “Dan’s other brat just asked if I’d heard from Ethan. Seems you’re sharing the braincell today.”

“Dan’s other brat? Do you mean Buck? Wait, who else…?”

“You, obviously,” Austin tapped away with his thumb and then tucked his phone away once more.

Eddie wasn’t sure how to respond to that, even as hearing it made something warm bubble up in his belly. The elevator doors opened again as they reached the top floor, and then they had to carry all the gear they needed for this - the winch and the ropes and everything else - out into the hall and to the stairwell that gave them roof access. They burst into the sunlight, the sound of traffic and sirens muffled by distance. Austin grimaced as he looked around, similar to the face he made when Bobby gave them their marching orders, and dumped the gear not far from the stairwell entrance.

“Are you okay?” Eddie couldn’t help but ask as he unpacked everything.

“Peachy,” Austin answered. “I’d just really rather Buck be here for this one. Or that Cap would hurry up and find someone to fill his spot.”

“Why?” He ignored the talk about filling Buck’s empty spot, because he knew it was necessary even if he didn’t like the idea. “Don’t want to be doing this with me?”

“No.”

Eddie didn’t realize what was bothering the other man until they both went to the wall lining the roof’s edge to judge where the winch needed to go in relation to the bus. Austin leaned over and then immediately pulled back, shaking his head as he took quick steps away.

“Are you afraid of heights?” he blurted out. Austin waved the question away like an irritating fly. “Guess I’m going down, then.”

“Obviously.”

It didn’t take long for Eddie to strip out of the gear he had on and put on the helmet and climbing harness, which was never quite as comfortable these days as when it was Buck checking the straps for him. With the winch set up and the ropes hooked to him, he threw a leg over the roof’s wall and started rappelling down.

“Diaz is on his way down, Cap,” Austin radioed. Eddie looked up and saw the man watching from above, expression tight. “I’ll send down the webbing when he’s got boots on the bus.”

“Copy that,” Bobby replied.

It didn’t take very long for Eddie to touch down on the bus’ roof. The vehicle creaked and groaned under his weight, wobbling enough to have him freezing. But it didn’t tip over and send everyone hurtling to their deaths below.

“Boots on target. Just waiting on the webbing and I’ll get everything secured,” Eddie relayed, and then sniffed the air. “And the automatic exfil for the natural gas tanks are working.”

“Sending down the webbing,” Austin radioed.

The webbing was more like a series of tie-downs and hooks on ropes. They were tethered to the roof up above and would anchor to specific hardpoints on the bus to hold its weight. It required that Eddie swing around the air a bit so he could attach everything to where they needed to go on the frame of the bus, which meant that, if Austin was bothered enough by heights to have him looking like he did just peering over the edge, it was definitely a good thing that Eddie was the one doing this.

“Gentlemen, where are we at?” Bobby asked.

“Got the second tie-down secured, heading for the middle,” Eddie answered, already half-swinging, half-crawling to the next spot. He grabbed the large hook where it dangled right above him and stepped just inside the entry wound on the building, dragging the hook down as he knelt and slotting it into place. “Second hook secured, Cap.”

“Everything’s good up here,” Austin radioed. His voice didn’t even have a twinge of the uneasiness that Eddie had seen on him.

Eddie was just about to stand back up when he saw something beneath the bus that demanded his attention. Or rather, someone, another victim previously unaccounted for.

“Cap!” He shouted, forgoing the radio since they were all right there. “Got a vic under the bus!”

It summoned the others to him, with Bobby rushing over and falling into a crouch beside him. One of the other victims, a woman in business wear and her arm in a sling, knelt down to peer as well.

“Oh my god,” she exclaimed. “Is that Keith?”

“Let me in,” Chimney said, moving both Bobby and Eddie out of the way. He crawled under the bus and felt around, before looking back at them. “He’s got a pulse. We’ve got a live one, Cap.”

Eddie looked between Keith, pinned beneath the bus, and up at the windows of the vehicle, where he could just barely make out the top of a passenger’s head. He wasn’t sure how they would manage to get the passengers off the bus with the man trapped as he was, and he couldn’t see a way to get him out with them in it. For a brief moment, he was reminded of the train crash back in the spring and was for once thankful for Buck’s absence.

“Probably a fractured pelvis.” Chimney had maneuvered himself around to take stock of the patient. “Pulse and BP aren’t great, but he’s holding up.”

The woman from before came to their side of the bus, and Keith was awake and aware enough to talk about… Eddie didn’t really care what they were talking about. Something about a meeting, a sexist asshole, and Keith having less spine than a slug. It wasn’t really the time or the place, but it wasn’t like Keith was going anywhere. The way the bus creaked and groaned and shifted simply made the danger more apparent.

“Maybe you guys can have a sidebar after we get the thirty-thousand pound teeter-totter off you, okay?” Chimney advised.

“That’s it,” Bobby suddenly said. “It’s a seesaw.”

“Also known as a teeter-totter,” Chimney quietly quipped. Bobby either ignored him or didn’t hear it as he reached for his radio.

“Jones, we have a patient under the bus,” he relayed. “We need it to rock backwards a little bit so the front end lifts up and we can get him out.”

“Cap? The bus is secured to the building. It’s stable, it’s not going anywhere.”

“I know, but I need it to move. Put it on the heavy winch.” Bobby dropped his hand and turned to the rest of them. “Meantime, we get everyone off the bus, let it rock back, and then we pull Keith out from underneath.”

“As plans go,” Hen said, sounding uncertain, “it is one.”

They set up anchoring ropes from the ceiling, to keep them from being dragged down with the bus if things went pear shaped. Eddie transferred from the rappelling rope he was on, and it was left to dangle outside as Austin did whatever he needed to for Bobby’s plan. The captain used a Halligan to force the bus doors open and then they were rushing in.

Eddie listened to Hen as she gave them information on the people inside the bus, only half paying attention to the words as his mind ran a mile a minute. He’d done triage in far more dire circumstances, and already he was ordering the patients in order of priority. Vanessa the driver, with a probable dislocated shoulder but pinned by a beam, was low priority. The people in the far back, with just lacerations and maybe a fracture, were all near the bottom of his list. The kid sitting in the middle with some scratches to his face and rocking slightly in his seat? He seemed almost perfectly fine, physically, and wasn’t even worth the mental space at the moment.

The woman laying in the middle of the aisle with a visible dent on her skull? At the top of the list, but simply moving her could be dangerous without proper precautions.

Zeke, with a laceration to the head along with a wound to the thigh that meant he was liable to just bleed out? The highest priority victim that they could also immediately treat and get out of the way.

Eddie knelt down, grabbing the tourniquet that Chimney handed to him. There was already a DIY one in place, a belt neatly tied off just above the wound, which was absolutely the only reason this guy wasn’t already dead. Eddie placed their bright orange tourniquet in the same spot, tightening it until he was satisfied. Then he worked with Chimney to get the man to his feet and heading for the doors, pausing when the guy addressed the kid that Eddie had mentally dismissed as a non-priority earlier and thanked him for saving his life.

Apparently, the kid was the one who tied the belt.

“Forward seating is reserved for mobility-challenged passengers,” the kid said, eyes focused on the back of the seat in front of him and his head twitching as he spoke. “And members of the elderly community.”

“It won’t happen again,” Zeke promised, finally allowing them to escort him off the bus.

They passed Bobby, who was carrying what he needed to move the beam pinning the bus driver. Eddie passed Zeke off to other paramedics that were waiting with a gurney, leaving Chimney to give them the brief rundown as he went back to the bus. The driver was already freed, and Eddie directed her towards the paramedics.

On the bus, Eddie paused just inside the doors as he listened to Hen and Bobby talking, the pair of them huddled together.

“If she’s not in surgery in the next twenty minutes,” Hen was saying, “the swelling’s gonna start pushing her brains out of her eye socket. We need to extract her, but not on a bodyboard. We gotta keep her at thirty degrees.”

Eddie was moving before Bobby even turned to him, already jogging across the room to where Chimney and the other paramedics were.

“I need a gurney at a thirty degree angle,” he barked at them. “Now.”

The paramedics hurriedly adjusted the bed of the gurney, lifting the headrest up, and then they rushed back to the bus as Hen anxiously called for them. The gurney was parked just outside the bus doors as Eddie and the paramedics hopped on. He slipped his arms under the woman as one of the others grabbed her legs, being careful to keep her head slightly elevated compared to her torso.

“Everyone else, off the bus!” Bobby shouted out. “Come on.”

The gurney was out of the way as they laid the woman out on it, allowing the low priority passengers to make their way off and then away. Hen got off the bus as well, unclipping herself from the tether and following the gurney to the exit. Chimney had gone back to Keith, beneath the bus, and apparently they were pressing for time since he soon radioed,

“Cap! We need to do this now.”

“Jones,” Bobby radioed. He was still on the bus, along with the kid. “Be ready to tilt the bus on my signal.”

“Copy that, Cap,” Austin replied.

“Cap.” Eddie peered into the bus, to find the captain seemingly having a stare down with the kid. “Pretty sure the bus is supposed to be empty before we do this.”

“I got it,” Bobby said, stretching his hand out to the kid. “Just come a little closer, CJ.”

The kid, CJ, took a step back and shook his head, muttering something about Pink Apron Day. Eddie decided to trust that Bobby knew what he was doing, going instead to where Chimney was crouched down by Keith. A minute later, he heard Bobby give Austin the signal, even though he knew neither the captain nor CJ had gotten off the bus.

The bus creaked and groaned as it rocked, sounding suitably ominous, but Eddie ignored it as he joined Chimney in hurriedly clearing everything off of Keith. There was nothing particularly gentle about the way that they first dragged him out and then pulled him onto the waiting backboard, which made the man’s silence that much more worrisome. That was Chimney’s problem, though, along with the other paramedics.

“Bring it back, Jones,” Bobby radioed.

“Copy.”

There was more creaking, more groaning. There was also suddenly the very concerning smell of rotten eggs filling the air. Eddie’s eyes went wide and he rushed for the bus, only to find himself instinctively ducking as the leaking gas ignited in a short-lived ball of flames that took out whatever windows on the bus weren’t already shattered.

“Cap!” he called out as he practically leaped through the bus doors. “Cap, sound off!”

“I’m fine, Eddie!” Bobby was on the aisle floor, having apparently tackled the kid and covering him. He got to his feet now and held his hand out. “You okay, CJ?”

“I would like to get off the bus now,” he heard the kid reply.

Eddie was just thankful he didn’t have to tell Buck that something had happened to Bobby.

“Where’s the H?” Buck asked, peering up at the Hollywood sign. Or, the parts of the sign that were still there.

Part of Mt. Lee in the Hollywood Hills had collapsed, its stability eroded by first the quakes and then the flood from the burst dam. That meant that LAFD resources were being diverted from flooded streets to the neighborhoods now buried beneath mud and dirt. The Mobile Command that had been set up was a flurry of activity, with people coming and people going, helicopters buzzing overhead as they dropped off supplies and picked up patients. 

He knew the 118 was here somewhere, too, had seen and greeted some of them as they rushed by, but he’d yet to lay eyes on Eddie.

“With the rest of the mountain,” Danny answered. He was facing away from the mountain, past Buck, and Buck saw his face light up. “Austin!”

Buck turned and spotted Austin heading their way with Chimney at his side. Like himself and Danny, they had gear bags on their backs and the shorter pike poles in hand. He rushed to them, already speaking.

“Hey, Austin, have you-”

“Ethan and everyone else are fine,” Austin interrupted. Buck slumped in relief.

“Good, good. That’s good.”

“We’re being sent out to help search for survivors,” Danny said as he ambled up to them. “You guys?”

“Same.”

“Where’s everyone else?” Buck asked.

“Bobby’s taking Hen and Eddie to find a group of hikers,” Chimney answered.

Buck huffed in disappointment. Danny shoved him for it.

“C’mon, squirt,” he said, pushing his shoulder to get him moving. “We’re running out of golden hour.”

“Yeah, okay.” Buck turned to head out, paused, and glanced over his shoulder at Austin and Chimney. “Are you guys coming?”

“You know what?” Chimney started forward, getting ahead of them and leading the way. “Why not? I can use you guys to workshop some dad jokes as we go.”

Buck didn’t have to look at Danny to know he rolled his eyes, ‘cause he was doing the same.

Chapter 22

Chapter Notes

A longer than usual chapter because I couldn't find a good cut-off point.

It was disconcerting, Buck thought, to be walking along what was now ground level with roof tops peeking out of the mud. This had been a neighborhood just that morning, these had been people’s homes. Now they were all buried, now it was silent as a grave except for their shouting.

“LAFD!” Buck called out, his voice carrying over the desolation. Chimney echoed him a moment later, in the other direction. “Anybody out there!?”

The sound of laughter had Buck looking over his shoulder to see Danny laughing at something that Austin had said, their heads bent close together as they walked just a few feet behind them. They were both perfectly content to let himself and Chimney do the shouting, it seemed. Buck wondered for a brief moment if this was how he and Eddie looked to everyone else before turning forward again.

“I don’t understand what’s up with those two,” Chimney commented. He had his neck craned to look back at the pair as they walked. “They aren’t dating, but they’re like that.”

“Yeah, it confused me, too, until Hen explained it to me.”

Chimney’s brow furrowed, like he was about to ask what, exactly, Hen had explained. But then he shook his head and a different question came out of his mouth, the words hushed.

“Do you know who he’s been talking to and seeing?”

“Do I- What? Who?”

“That’s my question!” Chimney asked. A bit louder than he meant, since he glanced back at Danny and Austin again. “Dan’s been talking to someone over FaceTime, some woman. And he keeps going out for booty calls.”

That first half sounded like Chimney had overheard Danny’s sessions with Dr. White, but thankfully not enough to realize what they were. The other half had Buck making a face at the man.

“Why would I know?” he asked in return.

“Because you’re his brother!” Chimney hissed. “You’re closer to him than Maddie is, he’d-”

He cut himself off, throwing out an arm to slap Buck in the chest and then using that same hand to point over at a half-buried car. No, not the car. Chimney was pointing just beyond it, at the man sticking out of the mud. They both broke into a jog, Chimney heading for the man while Buck went for the car, dropping to his knees to clear off the passenger-side window and peer in.

“Anyone?” Austin asked. A quick glance up and Buck saw both he and Danny were hovering just behind him.

“No, no one inside,” Buck told him.

“I’m not getting anything,” Chimney grimly announced from where he’d been checking for a pulse.

“There’s bound to be others,” Danny told them as he dug into the bag on Austin’s back and pulled out a beacon. He slapped it down on top of the car and activated it. It began trilling and flashing. “We should keep moving.”

It was with heavy silence that they restarted the marching, shouting out for anyone that might’ve been able to hear. They received no response except for their own echoes, though. It was reminding Buck far too much of the last time he marched through devastation, fruitless calling out and getting no response. The scenery was not at all the same, and it was earth instead of water, but it might as well have been.

“I’m gonna have so many nightmares tonight,” Buck grumbled, thrusting the pike pole he was using as an impromptu hiking stick into the mud with enough viciousness that he had to tear it out.

Danny, walking next to him now, frowned first at him and then at the remnants of the neighborhood around them. He scowled at it for a bit before clear concern replaced it.

“The tsunami?”

“Yeah.” Buck glanced at one of the roofs sticking out of its grave and grimaced. “It’s not the same, but…”

Danny didn’t say anything. He just clapped Buck on the shoulder and squeezed, shaking him a little. His eyes flickered up to Chimney, a few feet ahead with Austin, and he lowered his voice to ask,

“How’s Copeland?”

“She’s…” Buck shrugged. “It’s been okay.”

Dr. Copeland was Buck’s new therapist, whom he’d started talking to just weeks ago. She was on the list of names that Danny had gotten from Dr. White, and the only ones who knew he was even talking to a therapist were Eddie and Danny. Maybe Austin, if Danny had mentioned it to him. One of the only benefits from the apocalypse was that everything had gone virtual, which meant that therapy appointments were being held through a screen. Buck hadn’t really let himself think about how anxious he’d been that he’d do something again that would lead to a repeat of Dr. Wells until he was being offered a way to make it an impossibility.

He’d mentioned that to the good doctor during their first session, tucked away at Eddie’s kitchen table with Eddie and Chris just on the other side of the door. That had led to a harrowing conversation that he still wasn’t sure about. It had included words that he didn’t want to even think about in regards to himself.

“Just okay?” Danny asked.

“Yeah. It’s… It’s better than last time.”

Danny stared at him real hard, like he was trying to peel away at Buck’s skin with his eyes, and then he nodded.

“Good.”

“Hey.” Chimney had stopped in his tracks, head cocked like he was listening for something. “Do you guys hear that?”

They all stood around in silence. Buck strained his ears, trying to hear whatever the other man had noticed. And then, from not too far away-

“Is that a baby?” Austin asked, turning in place. “Where is that coming from?”

“Over there,” Chimney said, already moving. They hurried to catch up, following him to a bunch of debris that had gotten caught on the side of one of the houses. The baby’s wailing got louder as they got closer. “It’s under here.”

There was a large tree branch, or maybe a tree trunk, that Buck and Danny grabbed together and hauled out of the way. Chimney reached into the debris, but instead of an infant he pulled out the receiver for a baby monitor.

“The baby’s not here,” he said with a frown. “So where is it?”

“Can’t be too far,” Austin told him. “I think that’s the same kind of monitor Ethan and Irene have. A few hundred feet, maybe? A thousand?”

“A few hundred feet that way,” Danny said, pointing uphill where all the mud had come from. “In one of the houses? We’d hear the baby crying if it was out here. Plus, well.”

He did an odd jerky motion with his head, eyebrows bobbing, that managed to convey exactly what he meant by the “plus, well.” 

“Too bad we can’t just ping the monitor,” Buck said. “Y’know, like- Like Find My Phone!”

“I don’t think that’s a thing,” Chimney told him.

“It should be.”

“Maybe you’ll invent it for when I misplace my kid.” The words earned the man three incredulous stares. “You know it’s gonna happen! I lose my phone at least three times a week.”

Chimney glanced around, eying the helicopters in the distance.

“I’m gonna call for backup, we need more people out here searching. Do we know which channel Mobile Command is on?” He reached for his radio and started flipping through the channels, all four of them wincing when one was just a high-pitched squeal. “Not that one.”

“Wait, no, go back to that one,” Buck told him. Chimney frowned at him as he did it, settling on the squealing channel. “The mudslide knocked out the power on the cell service, there shouldn’t be any interference.”

“You’re thinking it’s the baby monitor causing the feedback,” Danny guessed.

“Yeah! So if we follow the feedback to where it’s loudest…”

“That’ll be where the transmitter is.”

“And the baby,” Chimney concluded. “Find My Baby!”

Buck tugged the radio off his chest and switched it to the channel receiving feedback. Chimney was already marching off in the direction they were assuming they needed to go, but Danny was clapping Buck on the shoulder before he could follow

“Good catch, squirt,” his brother said, giving his shoulder a squeeze before letting go.

Buck preened.

They followed the radio like a dowsing rod, the volume turned up as far as it would go so they could hear when the feedback changed. The baby had fallen silent on the monitor, and Buck was choosing to believe it was because the poor thing had exhausted itself and not for any other reason. Chimney, as bad with the silence as Buck was - neither Danny nor Austin seemed to be taking issue with it - spoke up a few minutes into their search.

“You know, I only heard a baby, not an adult,” he pointed out. “Before, when we heard the crying.”

Buck paused, thought about it, and realized that Chimney was right.

“The parents could be unconscious,” he said. “Or, y’know…”

“Dead?” Chimney said. Buck stared at him. “Poor kid might be an orphan.”

“Or maybe they just got separated,” Buck argued. He glanced back at Danny and Austin, scowling when his brother just shrugged instead of agreeing with him. “You really do just go to the worst-case scenario, don’t you?”

“Is that judgment I’m detecting?”

The radio squealed, higher-pitched than before. They all froze as Buck lifted the radio in the air a bit, like that was actually going to do anything, and turned to retrace his steps.

“Yeah, it is,” he told Chimney. “‘Cause you’re having a kid with my sister, but you’re living on my brother’s couch.”

“To protect her,” Chimney replied with a sigh similar to what he’d heard from his grade school teachers when he asked a question or two too many. Buck wasn’t certain why, but for some reason it had Danny bristling where he stood. “And your niece or nephew-”

“Nibling,” Danny offered, even as his eyes bore into the side of the man’s head.

“The world’s gone to crazy town, in case you missed it,” Chimney continued, like he hadn’t been interrupted. “I’m just trying to keep them safe until…”

“Until what? The world goes back to normal?” Buck scoffed. “What if it never does? What if this is normal, now?”

“Then I’ll be a crappy dad over video conferencing. That’s actually something I got experience with.”

“Wow.” Danny was giving Chimney a flat stare as he rested his weight on his pike pole. Austin was a silent presence at his side. “Kid’s not even born yet, and you’ve already decided to abandon ‘em.”

“Woah, hey, that’s-” Buck tried, only for his brother to interrupt him with,

“Keep lookin’ for the baby.”

Buck huffed. He could very well do that and keep his brother from being an asshole.

“I’m not abandoning anyone,” Chimney tried to argue, but Danny scoffed at him. Loudly.

“No, you’re just gonna force my sister into being a single parent and not have anything to do with my nibling except, what? Over FaceTime? I mean, Christ’s sake, fuckin’ Ramon did more than that.”

Chimney puffed up, ready to defend himself, but then Buck’s radio let out an ear piercing squeal of feedback. The building argument was dropped in an instant and utterly forgotten as the other three rushed to Buck’s side, where he was standing next to a roof sticking out of the mud. It wasn’t much different from its neighbors, a little flatter maybe.

“This has gotta be it,” Buck said. His radio was still screaming at them, so it turned it down.

“How do we get in?” Danny asked. “Can’t exactly dig down to the door. Not by ourselves, not with this much mud.”

Buck looked around, and then spotted a possible way.

“Chimney,” he said.

“What?” the paramedic asked. Buck looked at him and then shook his head.

“No, that chimney,” he clarified, pointing with the radio. There was a chimney towards what might’ve been the end of the roof, it was too covered by mud to know for sure, made out of brick with a metal cap.

They used their pike poles to tear off the chimney cap, and then crowded around to peer down into its depths.

“So,” Buck said. “Who’s going down?”

“You’re the senior paramedic,” Danny said to Chimney. “I don’t think I’d fit, anyways.”

They had rope and a harness in one of their bags. While Chimney slipped into the latter with Buck’s help, Danny and Austin tied the rope off to a lamp post sticking out of the mud. They didn’t have a wench, but the three of them would be able to lower the man down just fine.

“Okay, when you get to the bottom,” Buck told him as he perched on the edge of the chimney’s mouth. “We’ll drop the medical bag and tools down after you.”

“Copy that,” Chimney said, swinging his legs over and down. “And in the future, if anybody asks, this is how I got my name.”

They lowered him down, carefully feeding the rope through this hands and making sure it didn’t go all at once to send him plummeting to the bottom. It didn’t take long before the tension suddenly went away and Chimney radioed up that,

“I’m in.”

Buck pulled the rope back up and attached Chimney’s discarded bag to it, before lowering that down as well. After that, there wasn’t much left to do other than gather around the chimney and wait.

“Should I be worried that you’re going to murder my coworker?” Austin asked, leaning against the brick.

“I haven’t murdered Nash yet, have I?” Danny retorted.

“Danny,” Buck sighed.

“I’m not gonna murder our sister’s baby daddy,” his brother said, and then muttered something that sounded very much like “today,” though Buck couldn’t be sure. “I might boot him out of my apartment, though. If he’s gonna be a crappy dad on purpose, he can do it from someone else’s couch.”

“He’s not- He’s just scared,” Buck argued.

Danny did not look as if he took that argument very seriously. Thankfully, though, the man in question took that moment to radio back up again.

“I got ‘im. Can’t be more than a few days old, not a scratch on him,” Chimney said. All three of them standing around topside let out a breath of relief at the news. “Found the mother, too. Deceased, looks like blunt force trauma to the head.”

Damn it.

“We’ll notify Mobile Command and tag the house,” Buck radioed back. “Let’s get the both of you outta there.”

“Copy-”

And then Chimney suddenly cut off. Buck frowned at his radio in confusion, noting the other two wearing similar expressions.

“Chim?” Buck tried. “Chim, do you copy?”

“Did he lose signal?” Danny asked, peering down into the house as best he could. “I don’t see him.”

“Chim, come in.” Buck paused, waited, tried again. “Chim?”

“I’m here,” Chimney finally replied. “But uh, we’re gonna need reinforcements.”

“Why?” Danny was the one who asked.

“Well...”

Apparently, it was not just the baby and a dead woman in the house. Apparently, there was a locked room with mothers-to-be trapped inside, because the dead woman, who Daniel was going to mentally call That Vile Cunt from here on out, lured them in and then sold their babies to hopeful parents wanting to adopt a kid. One of the trapped women gave birth a few days ago, to the infant that they’d heard on the monitor, but the earthquake, flood, and mudslide happened and That Vile Cunt got whacked by karma.

Daniel hoped it was slow.

The requested reinforcements came in the form of the rest of the 118, including Nash. Daniel ignored the captain as they worked to uncover the skylight that Chimney reported, and he ignored his baby brother and said brother’s boyfriend as they acted like they hadn’t seen each other for days instead of mere hours. At least Hen and Austin were both there to roll their eyes at them, too. And he thankfully didn’t have to deal with Nash’s presence for too long, as he went off to take care of something else shortly after Battalion Chief Williams arrived.

“Okay, I’ll go down and help Chimney with the one about to pop,” Daniel said as they finished setting up the tripod for the wrench and pulley over the now accessible skylight. “And Buck-”

“It’ll be like a relay,” his baby brother said, and then looked to Eddie and Hen. “I’ll get ‘em in the harness and send ‘em up to you two.”

“You ready?” Eddie asked, holding out an ax.

“Yup.”

Buck knelt down and motioned for the women visible through the skylight to get out of the way before using the ax to shatter it. Daniel went down first, with a better stocked medical bag than the one they set out with earlier and a pair of face shields. Once his feet hit the mud-covered floor, he undid the harness and helped get it onto one of the women, who was promptly lifted up before he went onto the bedroom-turned holding cell that Chimney and the fourth victim were located, the pair of them on one of the beds.

“How are we doin’?” Daniel asked as he handed Chimney the bag and one of the shields, tugging the other one over his own face.

“Close,” Chimney answered, putting on the shield. He’d be taking point while Daniel kept track of her vitals. “But no baby yet.”

“Alright. Buck’s getting the others out.”

Daniel tugged on a pair of nitrile gloves as he looked the woman over. She was young, he couldn’t help but notice. Probably younger than he was when he took Buck and ran for Texas.

“You’re doing so good, Amber,” Chimney assured her.

“I can’t believe I’m having a kid down here,” Amber panted out. She raised her arm when Daniel tapped it, allowing him to put a blood pressure cuff on her. “Alone.”

“What about the father?” Chimney asked, shaking out and putting down a powder blue blanket between her legs.

“He doesn’t know, I didn’t tell him,” she said. “He- He wasn’t a good guy.”

She let out a long, whining groan. Daniel frowned as he tracked her BP, which was probably exactly where it could be expected to be in this situation. He pulled out a stethoscope to check her heart rate and then the baby’s, pressing the head of it to her belly.

“Is that how you ended up here?” Chimney asked.

“Yeah, I didn’t have anybody.”

“No one?”

“My parents kicked me out.” Amber’s voice broke as she said, and Daniel hissed. “I had nowhere to go. Then I met Carol, and she- she made it seem like the best option. My only option. She promised I wouldn’t be doing this by myself, that my baby would be better off. And I believed her, like an idiot.”

“No, no, hey.” Chimney squeezed her knee with a gloved hand. “You were scared. And we don’t always make the best decisions when we’re operating out of fear, right?”

Amber gave an uncertain, jerky nod, and then grimaced as she let out another moan of pain.

“I feel like I’m afraid all the time, though,” she said, once she’d caught her breath. Daniel immediately checked her and the baby’s heart rates again. “I’m gonna be a terrible mother.”

“You know,” Chimney said. “I heard that ninety percent of being a good parent is just showing up.”

“It is,” Daniel said.

“Do you have kids?” she asked.

“Yes,” was his immediate answer, ignoring the look Chimney shot him.

“My girlfriend’s pregnant,” the other man said. “Our first.”

“You’re lucky,” Amber told him. “You don’t know how many times I wished I had someone there with me. All those first, those ultrasounds and when the baby started moving and then kicking. Just to be able to reach out and have someone take my hand.”

Daniel felt he should be commended for the way he didn’t say anything about that. He wanted to, though. He wanted very much to point out that there was nothing stopping Chimney from being there with Maddie for all that now except himself. But he didn’t, he packed it away for the moment and moved on.

“I was so lonely,” Amber sobbed. “That’s probably how I ended up here. I thought I would feel safer with someone by my side. I was so, so wrong.”

“Hey, you are about to have someone by your side for the rest of your life,” Chimney said.

That statement had Daniel physically biting his tongue, thankfully his cloth mask covered most of his expression. Maybe Chimney was just thinking about his dead mother, and not his father half a world away. But Daniel barely spoke to his own mother, however much he loved her still. Maddie didn’t talk to Margaret much more than that, Buck hadn’t since that surprise visit to El Paso. 

But none of that would do any good for Amber to hear.

(See, Dr. White? He had empathy.)

“Yeah,” Amber said. “I guess I- I- Oh! Oh! Ow!”

The first time Daniel ever helped deliver a baby was just a couple months into the job. He’d been left as the man behind while everyone else, including EMS and the paramedic captain, was out. A woman came stumbling into the station, having been driving herself to the hospital only to realize that the baby would be arriving before she did. Daniel had been utterly unprepared and absolutely terrified. She’d ended up telling him what to do.

It went much better this time. Chimney coached Amber through it while Daniel tracked her vitals. Much like the first time, once the baby decided it was ready to make an appearance, everything happened quickly. One moment, Amber was letting out a cry of pain. The next, there was a little bundle in Chimney’s arms making her displeasure known to the world as he wrapped her up in the blanket from earlier.

After that, it was simply a matter of getting the new mom and her daughter both topside.

Daniel wasn’t entirely certain what part of everything led to Chimney finally, finally, moving back in with Maddie. He was even less clear on how that led to Albert ending up on his couch, instead. But he wasn’t about to file any complaints on either point.

“How do the uncles like living together?” Maddie asked. They had a laptop open on the kitchen table to FaceTime her and Chimney.

“They have a lot of rules,” Albert complained. Daniel scoffed as he poured himself some cereal, but it was Buck who beat him to any comment as he leaned in next to him to ask,

“Are you really complaining that we’re gonna split chores evenly?”

“Hate to break it to you,” Chimney said. “Albert doesn’t do chores.”

“He’s gonna,” Daniel said, loud enough for his sister and her boyfriend to hear, and eyed Albert. The younger Han quailed a bit. “I got Buck to do ‘em, after all.”

Actually, somehow, Buck had trained himself into doing them. For the most part. But it happened after Daniel took them both away from Hershey, so he was taking all the credit for the achievement.

“I contribute in other ways?” Albert said, shrinking where he sat. “I make a great cup of coffee.”

“I can attest to that,” Maddie said.

“I thought you weren’t supposed to be drinking coffee,” Buck said, ignoring Daniel’s motions for him to shut up.

“It’s one cup a day, people. Back off!”

Buck jumped a little in place and pulled out his phone, before absently waving goodbye to their sister and Chimney and taking off for his bedroom.

“Guess he wanted to talk to Eddie alone,” Albert said, scrunching his nose up a bit. “I do not want to know why.”

Daniel snorted in amusement, because he knew that was probably the alarm for his session with Dr. Copeland.

“Have you ever watched Supernatural?” he asked Albert.

“Uh.” The kid screwed his face up in thought. “A couple episodes?”

“Good enough, c’mon.” He clapped Albert on the back on his way to the couch. “Talk to you later, Mads!”

“We’re being abandoned for your crush on a fictional character,” his sister scoffed.

“He’s prettier to look at.”

He ignored his sister’s outraged squawking as the call ended, and then patted the spot next to him.

“Alright, Al,” Daniel said as he grabbed the remote. “The first thing you need to know is that John Winchester is an asshole, and so is God…”

Chapter 23

Chapter Notes

Hello everyone. It has been, uh... -checks dates- Let's just not worry about how long I've neglected this story for the other one, alright? Alright.
Content warning for Drake, and all that he entails, at the beginning of this chapter. It's not quite explicit, but a bit more in your face in some ways than I've been before. If you'd much prefer, skip down to "Albert was out" and you'll be fine.

See the end of the chapter for more notes

Daniel panted into the mattress, arms aching from where they were held up by handcuffs to the headboard. He winced as the body on top of him pulled out far too quickly and roughly, felt the bed dip as the other man rolled to the side, and then grimaced at the sound of a lighter clicking and the acrid smell of smoke that followed.

Before Drake, Daniel thought that someone lighting up a cigarette after sex was simply a cliche. Something that happened in movies, old ones at that, but not something that anyone did in real life. And yet, that’s what the officer - the detective - did whenever their rendezvous happened when he was off-duty. He’d roll off Daniel, grab the pack of Marlboros he seemed to always have with him and turn into a chimney. He also started to yap.

It wasn’t the worst part of the experience, it actually ranked pretty low in that aspect. But it was very much like having salt rubbed into the wound, being a trapped audience for the man. Luckily, he never seemed to actually care if Daniel replied or even listened. It was more akin to telling your dog about your day, the way that Drake talked to Daniel. But it gave Daniel time to catch his breath.

A sudden touch to his bare skin had him twitching.

“I remember when I gave you this,” Drake casually remarked, tracing the small, circular burn scar on Daniel’s ass. “You squealed.”

Daniel lifted his head just enough to weakly glare at him. Drake just laughed, which turned into a hacking fit.

“Maybe-” Drake started when he was done, pausing to clear his throat. “Maybe I should give you another one. Y’know, to remind you that whores don’t say no.”

“I have to see my sister after this,” Daniel reminded him, words quiet and voice rough. He clenched his fists in an effort to hide the trembling.

“That’s what you said. And I told you I didn’t care.”

Drake put the cigarette out in the ashtray, though, and Daniel allowed himself to relax. There was a jingle of keys and then the detective was looming over him as he undid the handcuffs. His hands fell to the mattress, tingling slightly as blood flow returned. He jolted when Drake’s hand came down on him, hard enough that the sharp crack of it resounded in the bedroom and left his skin throbbing..

“Get dressed and get out, then,” Drake told him, then grabbed him by the hair to tug his head up. “And next time I want to see you, don’t make me ask twice.”

Daniel was still feeling wobbly when he left, pants barely done up, but he wasn’t going to stick around longer than he had to. He was going to be late getting to Maddie’s, he knew, but there was no avoiding it now. He was just lucky that Drake hadn’t decided to keep him longer out of pique. The man wasn’t above it, had done it before in the past and left him scrambling to show up on time to more than one of Buck’s games.

Albert was out when he got to the apartment, thankfully. The last thing he needed was for the younger Han to notice the scent of cigarettes that was clinging to him. Daniel pulled his clothes off, throwing them into the wash, and then hopped into the shower to scrub himself until all he could smell was eucalyptus and coconut. It was only then that he fully relaxed under the spray.

When he got to Maddie and Chimney’s, in fresh clothes and hair still slightly damp, his sister opened the door with a glare and a,

“You’re late.”

“Sorry.” Daniel shrugged at her, stepping inside. He left his mask on, so the apology was slightly muffled. “How’s it going?”

“This thing is looking like a death trap.” Chimney was standing next to a crib.. He gave it a shake and frowned and looked down at the instructions in his hand. “I think we mixed up the spacers with the supports.”

“Yeah, but they look the same,” Maddie complained.

“Let me look at it,” Daniel offered. “I helped Austin’s brother put together their crib.”

“Yeah, okay.” Chimney handed him the instructions when he came over, and then looked about in search of something. “Buck, did you steal the screwdriver again?”

“Yeah, and it is all yours. I am finally finished babyproofing the place.” Buck stood up from where he’d been messing about with one of the bottom cabinets in the kitchen and tossed the screwdriver to Chimney. “I wonder if we should put some alarm sensors on these windows.”

“You know we live on the second floor, right?” Chimney pointed out, kneeling by the crib and disassembling it.

“And what if the baby tries to get out?”

“Buck.” Maddie’s tone was fond exasperation and Daniel huffed in laughter. “I said you could babyproof the apartment, not turn it into an inescapable fortress.”

“I just don’t wanna underestimate the curious interiority of my nephew.”

“Nice vocab, squirt,” Daniel teased. Buck stuck his tongue out at him. “Also, Mads, he’s got a point. Remember how that one was the moment he could walk?”

Maddie’s face dropped and her hands went to her stomach.

“Oh God,” she intoned, and then shook his head. “We don’t know if it’s a boy, though. It could be your niece.”

“The last ultrasound, the baby was in the wrong position to tell the sex,” Chimney explained while Maddie went to the fridge. “She said it looked like the baby was mooning them.”

“Definitely yours then.” Buck gave Chimney a mocking slap on the back as he joined him and Daniel at the crib. “If it is a boy, I had some name ideas. You know, there’s Buck or Buckley. Kid could be an Evan.”

“Really dug deep for those, huh?”

“Can’t blame him, I got his name from a book,” Daniel said. “Hey, Mads, do you know what happened to that?”

“Not sure. Maybe it got thrown away.” She went to open one of the kitchen cabinets, or tried to anyway. She ended up just yanking at it without success before turning to glare at their younger brother. “Seriously, Buck!? It’s an upper cabinet, how’s the baby gonna reach that?”

“One again, remember when Buck was… I don’t even think he was two. That time he somehow managed to climb up onto the counter.” Daniel turned to Chimney, who was looking more than a bit worried, and explained, “He was rambunctious. Hand me that screwdriver.”

He reached out for it, sleeve falling down a little. Any hopes that he could pull it back up before the marks from the handcuffs were spotted went up in smoke when his precious baby brother exclaimed,

“Jesus, Danny! What happened?”

“Do you really want to know about my sex life?” Daniel shot back, which was enough to make Buck recoil with a grimace. Maddie echoed the sentiment, letting out a loud,

“Gross.”

“That wouldn’t be related to that woman you’ve been seeing, would it?” Chimney asked. At Daniel’s blank expression, he expanded with, “The woman you were talking to on your laptop with the door closed, when I was staying on your couch.”

Ah, right. This

“Wait, is she why you were late getting here?” Maddie asked, sounding very judgmental as she finally managed to get the cabinet open and grab a couple glasses. “Off having sex with some mysterious online girlfriend? In the middle of a pandemic.”

Daniel let out a sigh and waved Buck into silence when his brother opened his mouth.

“Don’t got a girlfriend,” Daniel told them. “I have a therapist.”

“You’re seeing a therapist?” Maddie glanced up from the glasses that she was filling up with water from the fridge. “Why would you lie about that?”

“I didn’t lie. You all just assumed, and I didn’t correct you.”

“Why are you seeing a therapist?”

“We’ve all had our turn in the hot seat,” Chimney said, shrugging up at Maddie when she brought him one of the waters. “It’s the cost of doing our jobs, it’s not a big deal.”

“I’m seeing a therapist, too,” Buck blurted out. Daniel threw him a grateful smile. Or tried to, anyway; it was covered up by his mask. “Not a department one, not because of the job.”

“Why are you both seeing a therapist?” Maddie asked, head swivelling between them.

“I don’t know, stuff.” Buck shrugged at her. “Everyone has issues, right?”

“We all fled Mom and Dad for a reason,” Daniel pointed out.

His sister huffed.

“They’re aren’t bad people, just-”

“Bad parents, yeah, yeah.”

It was the same line she always tried feeding him, whenever the topic came up.

“Hey, maybe instead of college funds,” Chimney said, “New parents should start therapy funds.”

Buck snapped his fingers and pointed at him.

“There ya go,” he declared “I know what I’m getting you guys for a baby gift.”

Maddie did not look very satisfied with the topic, even as the conversation moved on. They got the crib disassembled and then reassembled, this time with all the parts in the right place. He and Buck stayed a bit, to spend time with their sister, before leaving. They’d barely gotten home, Buck telling him all about how, after the 118 responded to someone in distress at a “smart home,” Eddie was apparently freaking out about technology and robotic revolutions, with Buck in the middle of telling Daniel that he was gonna make Eddie watch an old Disney Channel movie on Disney+ just to torment him, when there was knocking at their door.

When Daniel answered it to find their sister on the other side, he was not very surprised. He stepped back to allow her in, giving her a wide berth because he’d left his mask sitting on the coffee table.

“Didn’t we just leave your place?” Buck asked.

“Yeah, I just, you know.” Maddie said, taking off her own mask. “Wanted to come and talk about the therapy thing.”

“Okay.” Buck shot Daniel a look of pure confusion. Daniel just shrugged as he closed the door. “But we were just at your place.”

“Yes, I know. I just thought that maybe you didn’t feel comfortable talking about it in front of Chimney, so.” She threw out her arms. “Here I am. We’re alone now, just us Buckleys, so, you know. You guys can tell me the truth.”

Yeah, like that was gonna happen. Daniel was barely telling the truth to his therapist these days, which was causing problems, and hadn’t said a damn thing even to Austin. He was not gonna tell his sister anything.

“There’s nothing to tell,” Buck told her, then, “It’s Danny’s fault.”

“How?” Maddie asked.

“He sat me down before Christmas- Last Christmas, the one at the station. All, ‘I’m going to therapy, Buck, so should you.’” He wagged his head and dropped his voice as he said it.

“That is not at all how I sound,” Daniel protested. “Is it?”

“Little bit,” Maddie said, raising up her hand with her finger and thumb out, bare space between them. 

“Rude.”

“Is it helping? The therapy?” she asked, the question directed at both of them. The brothers shrugged at each other.

“I guess,” Buck said. “I mean, I’m fine. I just wanna be finer.”
