Daniel, who still vividly remembered his baby brother saying that maybe the embolism should have killed him, just because he couldn’t be used as a donor at the time, bit his tongue. There wasn’t any need to get into that in front of their sister, or at least not that he could see. He didn’t know why Maddie was hung up on this like she was, but the last thing he wanted was to make it worse.

“Have you talked to Mom and Dad about this?” she asked, and Buck actually laughed.

“Maddie, I haven’t talked to them since my Junior year of Highschool,” he told her. “They don’t even have my number.”

“What?” She blinked uncomprehendingly. For all that she had been the first of the Buckley children to fly the nest, for all that their parents had cut her off entirely after she married Doug, she still never lost those rose-tinted glasses when it came to them. “But… What?”

“I talk to Mom a couple times a month or so,” Daniel said with a shrug. “But no, I didn’t see the point in telling them about therapy. They’d just worry.”

And then maybe get the stupid idea to come visit or something. 

Their sister let out a sigh, shoulders slumping, and looked more than a bit lost.

“You know that I’m here for you, right?” she told them both, glancing between them with a hint of desperation. “Whatever you need?”

“I’m not sure this is something you know how to fix,” Buck told her.

“Why not?”

There were a multitude of answers that Daniel could’ve come up with. There were a dozen right there, on the tip of his tongue. The answer that Bcuck gave her was probably the kindest:

“‘Cause I always felt like you were sad, too.”

A couple days ago, the 118 responded to a man who’d fallen in his shower. He also lived in a fancy smart home, everything hooked up to Siri’s competing cousin, Hildy. It had, evidently, whigged Eddie the fuck out, because he was still going off about it. Apparently, the house addressing him by name was simply too much for him.

Buck found it hilarious, and made him sit through that Smart House movie on Disney+. Which may or may not have been a mistake, because now he was pacing around the house collecting all the electronics while Buck and Chris played a video game. Or rather, Buck was trying to play while Chris kept jostling him.

“I’m beating you!” Chris crowed, knocking into his arm.

“You’re cheating,” Buck complained.

“Come on.” This time, Chris snaked his hand under Buck’s arm and yanked at it, causing him to fumble the controller. Eddie, not saying a word, went to kneel in front of the television.

“Hey, Eds.” Buck tilted away from the little cheat. “I think you need to talk to your kid about playing…” The game suddenly froze on the screen, a message popping up saying that the connection was lost. Eddie had just unplugged one of the cords. “Fair. Or you can just do that.”

“Dad,” Chris whined. “I was beating him.”

“Well, we’re taking a little break from the internet, right now,” Eddie declared.

“But how am I supposed to talk to my friends?”

That was enough to set Eddie’s fight-or-flight instincts into motion, apparently, cause he was looking very distressed as he exclaimed,

“You’re talking to people on this thing!?”

“Danny, sometimes,” Chris said. “We have the same games.”

Eddie let out a huff, barely mollified by the answer.

“Is this about the smart house thing?” Buck eyed his boyfriend warily. He noticed that all the loose electronics, all of them, from remotes to the house phone, were piled up on the dining table. As he watched, Eddie picked up Chris’ headphones, which were probably destined for that pile. “This seems like it might be about the smart house thing.”

“Ever since that call, every time I go online, there’s an ad for coffee makers,” Eddie said, volume rising as he spoke. “Read the news, coffee maker. Check the weather, coffee maker.”

“Yeah, it’s, uh, it’s called ‘targeted advertising.’”

“I don’t even want a new coffee maker! The one I have is fine! I only mentioned it in front of Austin and…” He lowered his voice and glanced about, like he was certain there was someone behind the floor lamp, eavesdropping on the conversation. “And Hildy.”

“Hildy? Are we getting a Hildy?” Chris excitedly asked.

“No, we are definitely not.”

“Buck, can we go play video games with Danny?”

Buck opened his mouth and paused, catching the expectant expression on his boyfriend’s face. His arms were crossed, his eyebrows slightly raised, his head tilted just so. There was very much a right answer here, and there would very much be consequences for the wrong one.

“Sorry, kiddo.” He didn’t feel very sorry, because he was not going to tempt his boyfriend’s wrath, not with him in this mood. “I think we’re gonna be playing it old school for a while.”

“What’s old school?” Chris asked. Eddie nodded in approval and marched off to ransack the rest of the house of its electronics, depositing the headphones on the table with the rest.

“Have you ever heard of Scrabble?” Buck asked in turn, already mentally planning a shopping trip in the near future. He severely doubted there were any board games in this house.

And maybe he could plot out some sort of prank, because he was not a good person.

Maddie was not certain how late it was, when Chimney finally came out of the bedroom in search of her. She just knew that she’d been curled up on the couch, feeling sorry for herself, instead of going to bed for too long.

“Is the baby keeping you up?” Chimney asked. She didn’t immediately reply, just sat there as he shuffled from across the living room. She must’ve looked miserable, though, because his face dropped in worry when rounded the couch and he hurried to her side. “Oh, hey, what’s wrong?”

“I think I’m scared,” she quietly confessed.

“About the baby?”

“You know, right now, everything is great. And the baby’s safe and sound in here.” She laid hands on her stomach, over the little life growing within her. “Probably safer than he or she will ever be. And then they’re born and everything changes.”

She remembered, far too vividly, the sight of Dan, small and pale, in the hospital bed. She remembered, too, little Buck, constantly rushing towards the next best way to earn a scar. How their mother got through it, she would never know.

“Yeah, but in a good way,” Chimney argued. “We finally get to meet our kid, hold them in our arms, see their face, hear their voice. Get to know this person we made.”

“But we’re not done making that person yet,” she said. “They go out into the world, and that’s when everything gets harder. Every decision, every choice we make, it impacts who they become.”

“But we’re gonna make good choices.”

“What if we get it wrong?” she asked him. “What if everything you do to protect someone only ends up hurting them?”

She remembered, so very vividly, how often her baby brother got himself hurt. And she remembered, too, how their mother reacted to it. Overreacted, maybe, because that’s what people did when they cared too much, and then they felt bad for it. Their mother just cared about Buck so very much, just wanted him to be safe.

Buck was their mother’s favorite, after all.

(Had it really been so long since he’d spoken to either of their parents?)

“Are you talking about Buck and Dan?” Chimney asked her. “You think your parents might’ve…”

He let the question trail off into silence between them, but the unspoken words were so very loud just the same.

“I said that my parents weren’t bad people, alright, just… They’re just bad parents,” she told him. “What if I’m more like them than I think?”

Daniel had been so very insistent that one of them had to stay at home for Buck. He had been so very insistent that he had to get Buck away from their parents, for whatever reason. He’d always been attached to Buck, which made sense with how Buck had literally been made for him. No matter how much she tried to tell him that Buck would be fine without him, he was convinced otherwise. Like he thought their parents would hurt Buck or something.

“You’re not,” Chimney immediately replied. “Look, I don’t know them. But I know you, I know us, and… Yeah, we’ll make mistakes, but they’re gonna forgive us because they’ll know how much we love them.”

Would they? Would they forgive them? Would they know? She didn’t think Buck knew, and neither he nor Daniel seemed in any hurry to forgive.

“I think you’re gonna be a really great dad,” she whispered, instead of voicing those doubts.

“I’m gonna try,” he said. “Maybe that’s all we can do.”

And it really was, wasn’t it?

Chapter End Notes

Chapter 24

Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

The news was playing on the TV when Eddie climbed up the stairs to the station’s loft, Chimney the only person there watching it. It had been a slow day - he almost said it was quiet, but about ten different people dogpiled him to shut him up before he could finish getting the word out, with even Austin joining in - and they were taking advantage of the downtime to take care of everything that needed to be done. Eddie’s assigned chores were all finished, so he’d planned on grabbing some snacks and vegging out for a bit.

“These wildfires could not come at a worse time for firefighters in Texas,” the unseen news anchor reported, pulling Eddie to a stop. “You may recall that, just a week ago, the Pilot Knob volcano erupted-”

“Holy shit, Pilot Knob erupted?” Eddie blurted out. “It hasn’t gone off in like, seventy-nine million years.”

Chimney turned his head to frown at him from the couch.

“How do you know that?” the paramedic asked.

“Buck and I did a presentation on it for our earth science class. I can’t believe it erupted, that’s crazy.”

“So crazy,” Chimney agreed. “Still can’t believe it didn’t happen here.”

“All surrounding departments, including surrounding counties and even states, are being contacted-”

“Hey, um.” Chimney picked up the remote and turned off the TV, cutting the news anchor off. “Speaking of Buck, can I ask you about something?”

“Ominous.” Eddie hesitated for a moment, and then sat down in the closest arm chair. “Alright, shoot.”

“This might actually be none of my business, so you can totally tell me to go to hell-”

“Just spit out, man.”

“What’s the deal with his parents?”

Eddie blinked. That was not at all the question he was expecting.

“What do you mean?” he asked in return.

“He never talks about them, not really. Dan has, a couple times, but it was mostly as an insult,” Chimney said. “Maddie barely talks about them, either. Or to them, for that matter. The other night, I found her all freaked out like something was wrong. Said she was scared of screwing up with our kid the way their parents screwed up with them.”

“She said that?”

“Kinda.” Chimney shrugged. “She wasn’t specific, but she never is. She said that they’re not bad people, so I’m guessing they weren’t abusive.”

Eddie drew in a breath to bury the scoff he wanted to let out.

“I thought they were dead,” he said.

“What?”

“When I first met Buck and Danny, I thought their parents were dead,” Eddie explained. “They didn’t talk about them, they didn’t have any pictures of them. I mean, Danny was- God, he was younger then, than I am now, raising his kid brother. So it made sense that their parents would be dead, right?”

“Right.” Chimney gave a slow nod. “So you’ve never met them.”

“Once,” Eddie said. “Just before Thanksgiving, eleventh grade. They just showed up while Danny was on shift.”

“What were they like?”

That was a very loaded question. Eddie remembered how quiet and small Buck became in their presence. He remembered how every word that Margaret shot at Buck was somehow cutting. He remembered the conversation at the park, after Danny showed up and started yelling at their parents and Eddie fled with Buck in tow. Eddie remembered Buck telling him that their parents had him just to make Danny better. That Margaret wanted him to be safe just in case he needed to make Danny better again. That it was fine, because at least he was useful.

(“I’m useless, Eddie. What’s the point of me?”)

He remembered, too, listening to Buck talking to that woman, Lola, on the overpass. He remembered listening as Buck confessed to a total stranger how he would accidentally-on-purpose get himself hurt just so his mother wouldn’t ignore him anymore. How those were the only times she would fuss over him, how the rest of the time Buck might as well have been part of the scenery.

“Um.” Eddie tried to figure out how to answer that question truthfully, but not too honestly. “Their mom was really concerned about Buck being safe. She and Danny got into a shouting match over it.”

“That tracks with some of what Maddie said.” Chimney’s tone was absent, the statement more for himself than Eddie. “So there’s no deep, dark, Buckley family secret being hidden from me?”

Was there? Did the fact that they made Buck count? Probably not, because Buck didn’t exactly keep it a secret. He didn’t introduce himself to everyone with it, but he also didn’t shy away from talking about it. Bragging about it, somewhat.

“Nope,” Eddie finally said, shaking his head. “Not that I know of, at least.”

At least that answer seemed to put Chimney at ease.

“Los Angeles Fire Department.” Bobby pounded on the door of the apartment while Eddie and Hen brought up the gurney. “We got a call from this address?”

“I’m coming! I’m coming!” the woman inside shouted. It was followed by the sound of things being knocked over, of something crashing, and a small “ow.” 

Bobby turned to Eddie. Eddie held out the portable battering ram that they’d brought up with them. Dispatch had reported that the woman had called in a panic about losing her eyesight. They’d decided to work with the assumption that she wouldn’t be able to let them in, which seemed to have been the correct one.

“Ma’am, step away from the door,” Bobby warned, hefting the ram in his hands and aiming. “We’re coming in.”

The captain swung and the door opened, the wood splintering around the latch. The inside of the apartment was small and somewhat crowded with its furniture, the aesthetics vaguely New Age-y. The woman was on the floor by the couch, crying and clinging to it, head frantically turning this way and that as she sought out the sources of the sounds they were making. Her eyes were hazy, rimmed with red.

Hen parked the gurney in the living room, just out of the way, and pulled out a dining chair. Eddie went to the woman’s side and gently gripped her arm to help her up.

“We’re gonna get you to a chair,” he told her as he guided her to the seat. She calmed down as he talked, the frantic fear melting away some as he told her what was going on, so he kept doing it. “There’s just the three of us- Four, if you count yourself. Hen’s right there on your right. Cap’s in front of you.”

“Can you tell us about your symptoms?” Hen asked once the patient was settled, reaching into her medical bag that sat on the gurney for a pair of disposable gloves.

“It’s really just the one symptom,” she explained, head tilted so her ear and not her eyes were directed at Hen. “I can’t see anything.”

“Have you been having trouble with your vision before today?” Eddie asked.

“No, it’s always been twenty-twenty,” she answered, turning to face in his vague direction. Her cloudy gaze was more directed at his shoulder than his face.

“And not it’s just completely gone?” Hen asked.

“I woke to greet the world and it wasn’t there.”

“Ma’am,” Bobby broke in. “Have you been using any new skin care or makeup products, anything that might cause an allergic reaction?”

“No, nothing like that.”

Eddie had gotten out the blood pressure monitor and separated the velcro on the cuff. The noise of it was loud and her head immediately snapped towards it, so he explained, 

“I’m going to put something around your arm to check your blood pressure.”

She gave a shaky nod, flinching slightly as he wrapped the cuff around her bicep and began to squeeze the bulb to inflate it. He eyed the gauge as he did.

“What about household cleaners?” Bobby asked next. “Anything with fumes or a strong scent?”

“Just some essential oils,” was the answer.

“That wouldn’t do this,” Hen commented as she peered at the woman’s eyes.

“Blood pressure is normal, so it’s probably not a circulation problem,” Eddie reported and then told the patient, “I’m taking the cuff off now.”

“You’ve got some swelling and minor irritation on the eyelid.” Hen reached into her pocket and pulled out her penlight. “I’m gonna open up your eyelid, and I’m gonna shine this light up there. Okay? Just relax.”

Hen was gentle as she did it, the woman’s unseeing eyes bouncing around to track each and every touch. The woman’s pupil contracted when the light hit it, but not as much as it should have.

“Diminished pupillary response, minor clouding on the lenses,” the paramedic reported. “Almost like they’re covered in a film.”

“Cataracts don’t just appear overnight,” Eddie argued, his own penlight directed at the patient's other eye. And there, just on the corner, movement. There and gone again. He recoiled slightly in surprise before peering closer. “What was that?”

“What?”

“Thought I saw something move,” Eddie told her.

“In my eye!?” the patient yelped.

“Something like what?”

“Kinda looked like a worm.”

“Oh, God,” the patient whimpered. “I’m gonna throw up.”

“Just try and stay calm for us,” Eddie tried.

“Let me grab a forceps and a sample jar.” Hen twisted around to dig into her bag. “Let’s see what we’re dealing with.”

“A worm!?” the patient cried. “How did a worm get into my eye?”

“Maybe it could be some sort of bug,” Hen suggested.

“Face flies,” Bobby suddenly said. 

Eddie and Hen both turned to him. 

“It’s a type of parasite that infects livestock. They feed off the tears, lay eggs in the eyes,” the captain explained. Eddie felt stupid; out of all of them, he was the one that should’ve recognized it as a possibility. Even if his family didn’t raise animals themselves. “You don’t normally see it in people, though. Mostly cattle.”

“I haven’t been around cattle,” the woman argued. “I don’t think I’ve been in the same room with a burger in a decade and a half.”

“You probably haven’t taken a trip,” Hen said.

“Everything’s closed.”

“Maybe it’s something in your workspace?” Eddie suggested. “What do you do for a living?”

“I teach yoga.”

If he were a cartoon character, a lightbulb would be appearing above Eddie’s head right then.

“Livestock is more than just cattle,” he told her as Hen approached her eye with the forceps. “What kind of yoga?”

“Goat yoga,” she answered, just as he thought. “They do the poses with baby goats standing on them.”

“And people pay to do that?” Bobby sounded more than a bit skeptical. Which was fair enough.

“People say that baby goats offer the perfect weight and resistance to hold a plank position,” Eddie said, a statement that earned him some seriously judgmental stares from both Bobby and Hen. The latter had a tiny wiggling worm clutch in her forceps, dangled just above the sample jar. “Hey! I can know weird stuff, too.”

Admittedly, a good portion of the weird stuff he knew was from listening to Buck ramble on about it. Because he liked listening to Buck ramble on.

“No, it’s not weird,” the patient argued. Hen dropped the worm into the jar and went for her eyes again. “Okay, so it’s a little weird. But people really like the class, and goat yoga’s the only thing keeping me afloat while the studio’s closed.”

“No offense,” Eddie told her, keeping the penlight steady for Hen. “But if you’re gonna stick with goats, you might wanna consider wearing goggles.”

“Maybe it’s a sign,” she said. “My sister keeps telling me to grow up already and get a real job. Maybe she’s right.”

“Or maybe she’s wrong.” Hen sounded surprisingly vehement about it. “Who cares what other people think? If goat yoga is your jam, your dream, then own goat yoga. Never apologize to anyone for that, okay?”

Maybe, Eddie thought as he watched Hen remove more worms from the patient’s eyes, he should check in on her a bit more. Ask how medical school was going. Or maybe he should just mention this to Buck and let him at her.

“I think that’s all of them,” Hen declared a little bit later, holding up the sample jar full of writhing maggots. “Or what I can get. You should go to the hospital and get looked at, just to be sure.”

None of them would be surprised if she didn’t, though. Not with the state of things at the moment.

“Thank you,” the patient said, avoiding the sight of the bugs. She was tracking them better with her eyes, now. “Do rabbits have worms? Maybe bunny yoga is the future.”

“Do rabbits have worms?” The familiar, robotic voice chilled Eddie’s blood. He whipped his head around and spotted the Hildy device on the counter. “Would you like to hear what I found on the internet?”

“No!” Eddie yelped, leaping to his feet to just about slam the electronic she-demon facedown.

This time, he couldn’t quite defend himself against his friends’ judgement.

“You’re cheating!” Albert cried. Buck, standing at the stove as he cooked, glanced over his shoulder to see him frantically smashing buttons on his controller. “You have to be cheating!”

“I’m just better than you,” Danny casually said as his avatar threw Albert’s across the screen. “Don’t gotta cheat to kick your ass.”

“Chris cheats,” Buck told them as he went back to cooking. “Little brat was hitting me the entire time we played the other night. Just kept shoulder checking me and yanking at my arm.”

There was a moment of silence, filled with almost audible contemplation, and then he heard Danny curse followed by Albert’s yelp. When Buck looked over again, the screen was paused and Danny had his arm locked around Albert’s neck as he knuckled his head. Albert was trying to wiggle out of his grip.

“That wasn’t advice, Al,” Buck chided with a roll of his eyes.

“Take this as a lesson,” Danny said as he let Albert go. He got to his feet, picking up his neglected drink as he did, and padded over to join Buck. “What are you making, anyway? It doesn’t smell like any of the usual.”

“Brunswick stew,” Buck told him. “Don’t worry, it’s not spicy. You can handle it, gringo.”

“Strong words coming from a guy who can burn on a cloudy day.” Danny shoved at him. Buck stumbled a little and glared. “Chris hasn’t been on to play recently. What’s going on there?”

“Eddie’s still freaking out about technology. The way he’s acting, you’d think he was the one who grew up in Amish Country. He unplugged all the game consoles and gathered up all the electronics in the house, so I had to go out and buy a bunch of board games just so Chris didn’t find a way to escape to an arcade.”

“Oh!” Albert jumped to his feet. “I could teach him gonggi. It’s like um- um- Jacks!”

“Might take you up on that,” Buck said. “I’m not sure how many rounds of Scrabble and Candyland he’ll tolerate.”

His phone began to ring and he dropped the spoon he was using to stir to hurriedly dig it out of his pocket. A glance at the screen, which also had the notification for a package being delivered, had him grinning as he thumbed the button to answer.

“We got him,” was the first thing Chris said, laughing.

“Yeah, we got him good,” Buck agreed, already imagining his boyfriend’s reaction. “Man, I wish I could see his face.”

“Thanks, Buck.” That was Eddie, and he sounded annoyed. “Real funny.”

The call dropped and Buck laughed to himself as he tucked his phone away again.

“What did you do?” Danny asked, eying him curiously.

“I sent him a new coffee maker.”

Daniel waltzed into Station 118, bag hanging from his shoulder and Buck at his side, and took only a little pleasure at the wary gazes he attracted from Austin’s coworkers. It may have been over a year since he stormed in to put Nash in his place, but no one here had forgotten about it. The truck bay was a flurry of activity as people readied the fire engine to leave.

“Hey!” Eddie slammed closed the door of a compartment and ran up to hug Buck. “Ready to go back to Texas?”

“The idea does not fill me with dread for once,” Buck told him, and then Daniel was stuck watching his baby brother suck face with the other man. At least until he jabbed them both in the side.

“Chris’ll be okay while you’re gone?” he asked.

“Pepa’s got him covered,” Eddie assured him. “I figured, when you told me you both got called up to be deployed, too, that you’d be taking the One Thirty-three’s engine.”

“Can’t have too many stations down a rig.”

Would the 133’s B- and C-shift driver-engineers be pulling doubles while they were gone? Or would the ones from the 118’s go cover? Daniel didn’t know. It also wasn’t his problem, so he didn’t particularly care.

He spotted Austin, just beside the driver’s door to the engine, and made his way to him.

“We are stopping at a Whataburger the moment we cross Texas state lines,” Daniel told him. “I’m gonna prove to you it’s better than that lousy In-n-Out.”

Austin just rolled his eyes, but he also didn’t argue. He just took Daniel and Buck’s bags and tucked them away in a compartment before slamming it closed.

“We’re ready to head out,” he declared.

“Oh, no.” Hen suddenly popped up, carrying a bag of her own. “I know how you guys are. You’re gonna use the bathroom before we go, I don’t care if you think you need to or not. We have a twenty-hour drive and we’re gonna make good time.”

“I didn’t know you were coming with us,” Eddie said.

“I have two kids and med school bills to pay, I’ll take all the emergency overtime I can get,” Hen said. Daniel shrugged, because he understood that very well. “Besides, it’ll be fun. I’ve never been to Texas.”

“It’s really not that exciting,” Buck told her, and then grinned at Eddie’s affronted expression.

“We have to make it through the ride there, first,” Daniel said. “Twenty hours trapped in a metal box with Buck.”

His brother’s offended noises followed him all the way to the bathroom.

Chapter End Notes

By the way, if anyone is keeping track of the timeline, OG 4x01/02 take place in September, LS 2x01/02 take place in January. Specifically, LS 2x02 takes place on the same date the episode premiered, Jan 25th. Which means 4x03 is in February. And then there's a two month timeskip after 4x09, and a five month one after 4x13, and-
Basically, the only way the timeline makes sense is if everything from 4x03 to 4x09 takes place in February. Somehow.

Chapter 25

The first leg of the twenty hour road trip to the heart of Texas started off fine. Mostly. Austin was designated as the first driver, since it was his engine, and he got them through the Los Angeles traffic with the same calm ease as he normally did. And that was pretty much when the troubles began, because while Danny might’ve been rude with what he said - very, very rude - he also wasn’t wrong.

Buck was not someone who could do twenty hours stuck in a metal box and not go stir crazy.

It was fine when he was the one driving, because that required his focus and attention. All the minute corrections, the drivers on the road with him, the signs he needed to look for. He also tended to allow his curiosity to choose the route, sometimes, a lot of times, which meant multiple hours and stops added on. Because what was he supposed to do when he saw an advertisement for an outdoor museum with life-sized dinosaurs? Not immediately go off to check it out? He could never.

As a passenger, though, it might as well have been hell. For him and for everyone stuck with him. Especially since his phone was turned off to save on the battery life: the fire engine’s cab didn’t exactly come with enough ports for all of them to charge their phones, and it wasn’t likely they’d have much of a chance when they arrived at their destination. They had portable chargers, but those were being held in reserve.

All of this to say that Buck was stuck in a metal box for the next twenty hours, with nothing to entertain himself but himself and those around him. Danny, far too aware of how his younger brother could get during a long car ride, had claimed the captain’s seat for himself at the start. Presumably in the naive hope that it would somehow spare him from the irritation ahead.

A foolish notion, because an hour and a half into the trip found Buck turned in his seat with his finger hovering just short of Danny’s cheek. Danny was doing a valiant attempt at ignoring it, talking to Austin like Buck wasn’t there, but his eye was starting to twitch and he’d made a couple aborted motions like he was about to smack Buck’s finger away. Finally, though, his patience reached its end and he snapped out,

“Would you stop that!?”

“Stop what?” Buck asked, grinning at him. He didn’t move his finger. “I’m not touching you.”

Austin and Eddie, who both grew up with siblings, just laughed. Hen, the token only child, let out a groan of annoyance. Which pleased the little gremlin in Buck’s chest that, as the youngest of three, drove him to irritate as many of his loved ones as possible. Because that was one of the many ways he showed his love.

“Seriously, Buck?” she sniped. “Is this how it’s going to be the entire ride there?”

“The trip from Hershey to El Paso was three days of this,” Danny told her. He gave in to the impulse to reach up and smack Buck’s hand away, only for Buck to immediately go back to not-quite-touching him. “It was only supposed to be thirty hours, but I needed breaks so I wouldn’t murder him.”

“Lies,” Buck confidently stated. “You wouldn’t know what you’d do without me.”

Danny slanted a glare his way, but he didn’t argue the point. What he did do, instead, was grab the bag he had sitting between his feet and toss it at Buck. Buck only just managed to catch it before he was smacked in the face.

“What is…” He opened the bag to find that it was filled with toys, of all things. “Danny, what the hell?”

Eddie, who was sitting in the jumpseat across from Buck, leaned forward to see for himself. He reached in and pulled one of the toys out with a curious scowl.

“Is this a Bop It? It’s smaller than the old ones.”

“Three days,” Danny repeated in far more of a dramatic fashion than was necessary. “Something in there oughta entertain you enough, God willing.”

“I’m not a child,” Buck complained, even as he picked through the bag of goodies. There weren’t a lot of options, but he was immediately drawn to a yellow, six limbed something-or-other. It turned out to be a fidget spinner, the limbs multi-jointed and articulated enough to be folded up in various ways. “Did you raid a toy aisle?”

“Yes,” was the blunt answer. “You’re welcome.”

Buck wanted to be offended by it, he really did. But he was too busy being thankful to have something to play with, adjusting the limbs of the toy so it looked like a bug-eyed little guy and then spinning him. Neither Eddie nor Hen were being much better than him, the former already intently following the instructions to bop or pull or twist while the latter was pawing through the bag for herself. She had school stuff spread out in her lap and in the empty jumpseat, all of which she was now neglecting.

“Maybe I should’ve stolen some of Denny’s and Nia’s toys,” Hen remarked as she set the bag aside. “I was just planning on using the time to study.”

“There should also be a little notebook in there with pens,” Danny said. “For, I dunno. Tic-tac-toe or hangman or something. Or to pass each other love letters.”

“I’ll leave the love letters to those clowns,” Hen said. Buck blew a raspberry her way.

“You tellin’ me you’re not interested in writing any for Karen? You can pretend you’re, I dunno, a Civil War soldier writing home.” Eddie pulled at the knob on the Bop It as instructed, before dropping into as deep of a Texan drawl as he could manage. “My very dear wife, I have survived the trek to the front lines. Have not murdered any Buckleys yet, but the day is young. Send my love to the children.”

“Tempting,” Hen told him, picking up her textbook. “But Karen and I prefer to keep the roleplaying in the bedroom.”

“Now tell me what the hell Icewind Dale is,” Danny said. A quick glance showed that he was talking to Austin. “Since that’s apparently the next thing I’m being dragged into.”

“It was a pair of video games in the early aughts,” Austin answered. “I have the first on Steam, along with the Baldur’s Gate ones.”

“Of course you do. Because you’re a nerd.”

The fondness in his brother’s voice was enough to make Buck’s teeth ache. He wasn’t the only one to catch it, either, because Hen turned slightly in her seat. Her head was tilted, an interested expression on her face. She hadn’t played audience to the pair of them together nearly as much as Buck had, or even Eddie. Austin normally didn’t chat with them while he drove, content to merely listen and gather all the interesting tidbits of gossip. Or at least that was how he’d been when Buck was with the 118, and he doubted the man had changed his behavior on shift much in the year since Buck transferred to the 133.

“I figured that when we’re done with Icespire Peak, we could move on to Rime of the Frostmaiden,” Austin continued. “You guys’ll probably be overpowered, but there’s only three of you, so... It’ll be fine.”

“I won’t have to make another character, will I?” Danny asked. Austin must’ve shook his head, because then Danny said, “Good. I don’t wanna know what kinda horrible names you’d suggest for the next one.”

“My names are fine.”

“You named my barbarian guy after Conan O’Brien.”

There was silence, and then Buck heard Austin let out the loudest sigh.

“Conan the Barbarian is from an Arnold Schwarzenegger movie,” he said, tone long-suffering, which set Hen off into a fit of giggles that she tried to muffle.

“The fact that you didn’t come up with it yourself explains why it was the only option that didn’t suck,” Danny said. “How many people can play the dumb Icewind Dale game at the same time?”

Buck debated to himself whether or not to mock his big brother for the flirting - because that was what this was, right? He did the same with Eddie often enough - and dug out the notebook and pens. He flipped it open to the first page and, after a moment’s thought, drew the grid for Tic-Tac-Toe and slapped an X in the middle square. Then he held it out to Eddie, who rolled his eyes, set aside the Bop It, and took both the notebook and the pen.

They stopped just inside Arizona to refuel, to switch drivers, and to, in Danny’s words, give Buck a chance to run around. Again, Buck would be annoyed at being treated like a toddler in a car seat, or maybe like a puppy that had been crated all day, or, perhaps more accurately, like he was still that thirteen year old stuck in the car with Danny on the way to Boston, but his legs really did need the stretch and he really, really needed the opportunity to move. He’d been bouncing his leg and shifting in his seat near constantly for the past forever. And while he derived joy from being an irritant, there was a difference between playful poking and people getting fed up with him for things he could not really control.

They reconvened at the engine after they made trips to the bathrooms and stocked up on snacks. When they started to climb back into the cab, Buck stopped Danny as he went to the captain’s seat once more.

“Actually, um. Could I sit up front?” he asked.

Danny paused, hand on the door handle, gaze heavy.

“Are you sure?” he asked in turn.

“No,” Buck admitted with a laugh. “But, uh. Copeland suggested it, actually? When I mentioned we were heading down. She thought it would help. Exposure therapy.”

“Alright, squirt,” his brother said after a moment, stepping back. “But if it’s too much, tell Hen to pull over.”

“Yeah, yeah.”

Danny didn’t move to climb in himself just yet, though. He waited for Buck to open the passenger door and, after a moment of hesitation and a deep breath, pulled himself into the cabin. Then Danny circled around to the other side before getting in, choosing the seat that gave him the best view of Buck.

The engine was not the ladder truck, the cab was not the same. It was similar, though, enough that Buck felt his heart start to race. He did not normally sit up here, had in fact never sat in the front passenger seat of either rig until circumstances stuck him there that night. That was part of the problem, that his first time riding in that seat was the same night that it literally exploded beneath him.

His brain had made the connection, now, enforced by the trauma of the event and then the way he went so long without sitting in that seat again, with nothing benign to counter it. Dr. Copeland’s thought was that, since he was going to be stuck in the rig for so long anyway with no imminent emergency, that he might as well take the opportunity to reset things, so to speak. Give his nervous system the opportunity to recalibrate and begin associating sitting in the front passenger seat with soul-crushing monotony instead of fear.

He took a breath as he tugged the belt across his chest, and it shook when he let it out. The smile he gave Hen when she got behind the steering wheel wobbled, but it was real enough.

Technically speaking, Hen should not have been driving the rig. Neither she nor Eddie had a Commercial B driver’s license, neither of them were certified to drive the engine. But it was a very long drive to the heart of Texas, and splitting the time between all five of them instead of just the three who were qualified was better for all of them. No one was going to pull a fire engine over and demand to see their papers.

“Hey, um.” Buck cast about for something to talk about, or more accurately for something else to keep his mind focused on, while Hen got them out on the highway once more. “How’s medical school going? I haven’t gotten the chance to ask, really.”

“It’s going okay,” Hen answered, blasting the horn at a driver that thought they could compete for space with a ten ton fire engine. “Second semester just started, most of my classes are still online.”

“I’m pretty sure I would’ve flunked out of school entirely if my classes were online.” There was the sound of a bag being opened and he blindly reached back, to be rewarded with a handful of chips. “There’s no way I would’ve stayed focused. Most of your classes?”

“Can’t learn medicine without actually doing medicine,” Hen pointed out. “I have to actually go in for the labs, which is as much of a pain in the ass as going to work these days. More so, maybe, since the labs are in the hospital and that’s practically ground zero. We put on scrubs and plastic face shields and the little booties, everything.”

Buck winced. After the pandemic started, after it became very apparent just how bad it was going to be, the 133 had started triaging their ambulance rides. If the patient didn’t necessarily need it, then they were simply advised to take themselves in. There was a whole song and dance that the paramedics went through when they did take someone in, where they did their best to limit their exposure to the doctors and nurses and other patients, and then spent forever afterwards decontaminating first the ambulance and then themselves.

Eddie and Austin both had mentioned that the 118 were doing similar, if not the same.

“Are they at least fun?” he asked.

“We dissected human cadavers the other day, trying to diagnose the cause of death.”

“...Was that fun?”

Hen barked out a laugh.

“It probably would have been,” she said. “Except I had a… Let’s call her a difficult lab partner. Type-A, showed up on my doorstep at eight in the morning because she was worried about me negatively affecting her reputation. Called paramedics, medical Uber drivers whose opinions didn’t count.”

“That bitch!” Danny broke in, interrupting the conversation he’d been having with Eddie and Austin to share his opinion on this unknown woman.

“She showed up at your place at eight in the morning?” Buck asked.

“Yeah! Worse, Deidra, the social worker, showed up to do her surprise inspection of the house for Nia, Karen was at the store, and Nia had decided to draw all over Denny’s face with a marker. So I was trying to figure that out.”

“Rubbing alcohol,” Buck said, and shrugged at the look she sent him. “This is why everyone should grow up with siblings, you learn vital life lessons like that when you wake up with a dick drawn on your forehead.”

“You drew penises on each other’s faces growing up?”

“He did it to me two weeks ago!” Buck twisted around to glare at Danny, who just smiled pleasantly.

“Hold on.” Hen furrowed her brow as she peered at Danny through the rearview mirror. “Chimney came in with a penis drawn on his forehead during lockdown, he blamed Buck and Eddie. It was you?”

“I plead the fifth,” was all Danny said.

Buck opened his mouth for a witty remark, only for the engine to hit a bump in the road. Something big enough to jolt and bounce them in their seats. Buck’s breath caught in his chest, lungs bound in iron. He’d grabbed the door handle when it happened, knuckles white with the strength of his grip.

He didn’t realize that anyone was saying his name until there was someone grabbing and giving him a gentle shake.

“What?” Buck blinked his eyes and focused on Eddie, whose hand was gripping his shoulder and looked concerned. “I’m- I’m fine. It’s fine.”

Absolutely none of them, or at least the three of them that he could see, looked very convinced by his words. Eddie glanced over to Danny, and then back to Buck.

“Chris said you memorized Alice in Wonderland,” Eddie said. “Personally, I don’t believe it.”

“Are you calling your son a liar?” Buck asked, knowing full well what his boyfriend was doing and loving him all the more for it.

“Maybe.”

Buck gave an overly dramatic harrumph.

“Alice was starting to get very tired of sitting next to her sister with nothing to do,” he recited, feeling his heart rate slow as he did. “She looked into the book her sister was reading a couple of times, but there weren't any pictures or conversations…”

“This is weird,” Buck remarked as they crossed the state border, passing the sign welcoming them to Texas. El Paso’s city limits were dead ahead, he knew. Eighteen miles away, according to the next sign. “It looks basically the same.”

He was the one driving for this leg of the trip. Eddie was in the passenger seat, but he was asleep, face tilted awkwardly in a way that could not be comfortable. It was the middle of the night, an hour lost to time zones with another doomed to the same fate. Buck was the only one awake right now. Well, Buck and Danny.

“Hey, should we tell Alma we’re here?”

“She already ordered us to stop by hers- Or, I guess it’s Iggy’s? Whatever, we’re stopping by there on the way back to LA,” Danny told him, leaning in between the seats. “She’s probably not awake now, and we don’t have the time to visit.”

That was true. But they did have time to make a very important stop, now that they were back in Texas. And though there were a multitude of options available to them, some right off the highway, Buck ended up following nostalgia as he drove through the streets of El Paso. Nothing had changed, yet at the same time, enough was different to strike him as unfamiliar.

It gave him whiplash.

When they reached their target, the sign lit up brightly, Buck had no qualms just parking the engine across a line of empty spaces. Then he reached over and roughly shook Eddie’s shoulder, until the other man woke up with a groan and the bitchiest sounding,

“What?”

 “Food,” was Buck’s simple answer.

“Food?” Eddie sat up, rubbed the sleep out of his eyes, and peered out the window. He lit up at the sight. “Oh, nice!”

“Looks like the dining area’s open,” Danny said. There was groaning from the other two as he woke them up. “I didn’t even think to check.”

“Yeah, I’m not sure the engine could make it through the drive through,” Buck said.

The roof extended out to the sides, just far enough, and just low enough, that he didn’t want to risk it.

“What’s going on?” Hen asked. “Where are we and why have we stopped?”

“El Paso,” Buck answered. “And Whataburger.”

“Evidently, Dan was not kidding about it,” Austin said with a yawn.

They found their masks to put on and then trooped into the Whataburger, half of them still bleary eyed and stumbling with sleep. The poor girl behind the counter stared at them in shock, not prepared for a bunch of out-of-state firefighters to show up at her store in the middle of the night, but took their orders gamely enough. They put in their orders and paid, and then went to the bathrooms before claiming a table for themselves while they waited for their food to be ready.

Buck took the chance when it was just him and Eddie, to ask something that had bugged him the closer they got to their destination.

“Hey, while we’re in Texas,” he said. “Did you- I mean, we’re already gonna visit Alma. Did you want to…?”

“See my family?” Eddie finished for him. Buck nodded. “I don’t know. My sisters, maybe, but I’ve barely heard from them. Birthdays, Christmases, a couple other times. Mom wanted to follow me on Instagram. That’s been it, though. I haven’t heard from Dad at all since my badge ceremony.”

Since Eddie found his courage and kissed Buck in front of everyone.

“I’m sorry,” Buck whispered, taking Eddie’s hand on the table in his own. His boyfriend gave him a shadowed smile.

“It was worth it.”

“Ma didn’t show up for my and Karen’s wedding.” They hadn’t even noticed Hen joining them until she was dropping into the seat beside Eddie and was pressing into his side. “She never really… I don’t know. It sucks, I’m sorry.”

“Why are we looking sad at a Whataburger?” Danny asked, snagging a seat from the next table for Austin before sliding in beside Buck.

“Eddie’s parents,” Buck explained. Danny let out a scoff.

“Fuck ‘em,” he declared. “They ain’t worth it, ‘specially Ramon. You’ve got us.”

Austin, for some reason, smirked at Danny’s words. Danny, when he noticed, just rolled his eyes at him.

“I missed this,” Buck blurted out, eager to get away from the gloomy topic. “Midnight Whataburger trips, I mean.”

“You guys did this often?” Hen asked. Eddie nodded.

“Yeah,” Danny said. “Once or twice a month, whenever I was between twenty-fours and Eddie was over. This is one of the few places open twenty-four seven, which is one of the many reasons that it’s better than In-and-Out.”

That last part was directed at Austin, who simply shook his head.

(Austin declared his burger “okay” when they got their food, and Danny huffed like it was a personal offense.)

Buck was startled out of a good sleep, waking up with his face pressed against the glass of his window. When he peeled himself away, he saw it was smeared with drool and awkwardly did his best to wipe it off.

“We’re here, squirt,” Danny declared, giving his shoulder another shake. “Wakey-wakey. We’re here.”

“I’m awake, I’m awake,” Buck groused, slapping at him. He threw open his door and mostly flopped out of the cab, immediately recoiling at the feel of the air. “Ugh, this is why the rest of Texas sucks.”

“Oh, God.” Austin sounded just as disgusted as him as he clambered out. “This is awful.”

“It’s like being slapped with a wet towel.”

“Welcome to Texas.” Eddie sounded so smug about it, as if he hadn’t grown up in the driest part of the state and was just as much a stranger to this god awful humidity as the rest of them.

The air wasn’t just humid, though. The sky was overcast with smoke that glowed orange in the distance, with wisps of it filtering through the trees. The base camp was a mess of motion even at this early hour. Firefighters that had been battling the wildfires switched out for fresh bodies, and others that came from far afield like they had arrived in scattered groups.

“C’mon, we should go check in,” Hen said. “Get our bags dropped off and then gather for the brief.”

“Yeah.” Buck nodded and moved for the compartment that held his. “Alright.”

Chapter 26

Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

The gathering for the brief was a hodge-podge of out of state firefighters and those that were local, of fresh faces and those who looked as if they were returning from a war torn battlefield. It was held at what amounted to the center of operations, with maps along with fliers and torn pieces of paper with hastily jotted down information, all tacked onto cork boards to keep the ever increasing winds from stealing off with them. 

It was the deputy chief of the nearby city’s fire department, De Leon, that led the briefing as acting incident commander. He wasn’t who was holding Buck’s attention in a stranglehold, however. That would be one of the firefighters who had been here for a while already, judging from the soot that dusted her face and clothes. She was familiar, somehow, and it was bugging the hell out of Buck that he didn’t know where he recognized her from.

“Stop staring,” Hen reprimanded under her breath.

“I’m not staring,” Buck immediately denied, even as he kept staring.

“You’re staring,” Eddie said from Buck’s other side. “Should I be worried?”

“I want to introduce my operations section chief,” De Leon said, stepping aside and gesturing at the man who’d been standing just behind him. “Captain Owen Strand, out of Austin.”

Hold on. Now Buck’s attention had something else to focus on for a hot second.

“Austin’s by San Antonio,” he whispered to Eddie. “Why is a captain from there in charge of anything here?”

Eddie simply shrugged.

Buck only had a vague memory of the distances, from when he and Eddie were planning their post-graduation road trip together. But he knew that San Antonio, at least, was a couple hundred miles away from San Angelo. Surely the county or the city or the nearer communities would have their own people to fill the position of operations section chief?

“The thing we were praying wouldn’t happen has happened. The wind has shifted, the fire’s now on a collision course with the city,” Strand announced to them. Buck’s attention wandered back to the earlier mystery, the identity of that lady firefighter. He was certain that he’d seen her before, somewhere. “There’s a possibility of weather coming in but we can’t rely on it, and we won’t. We have one last shot to turn the tide. Here, on Copper Ridge…”

The captain kept talking, presumably an attempt at inspiration. It didn’t really matter to Buck, he’d just go where he was needed and do what he was told. No, what really mattered was that woman. Who the hell was she?

It was gonna bug the hell out of him for the rest of forever if he didn’t figure it out.

“Buck, seriously.” Hen was glaring at him. Captain Strand had stopped talking and the gathered crowd was starting to disperse. “Please don’t make me report you to HR.”

“Seriously, squirt.” Danny laid a hand on the back of his neck. “I know Maddie and I taught you that staring was rude.”

“No, no.” Buck shook his head but didn’t look away. “I know that I know her from somewhere. It’s killing me.”

Eddie rolled his eyes and punched him on the shoulder, before wandering off somewhere. He wasn’t the only one, because Hen disappeared too sometime between then and when they went to the trucks to change out of their button downs and into their brushfire gear. She didn’t show back up until he was shrugging on the bright yellow jacket.

“Where have you been?” Buck immediately demanded.

“Took a tour of the medical unit,” she explained.

“How is it?” Danny asked.

“They could use more people,” she answered. “Where’s Eddie?”

“Hell if I know, you both ditched us,” Buck said. “Also, why did we drive the engine all the way here from LA just to park it?”

“Only way to get to that fire is by walkin’,” Danny said. He was holding the brushfire jacket in his hand, frowning at it, before tossing it back into the truck and grabbing his button up again. “Couldn’t get the engine up there if we tried, so it’ll go into the motor pool to be used when needed.”

“No, that’s my point. It’s not gonna be used unless they really need it, and if they need it, they have plenty that didn’t have to come from three time zones away. Plus, I’m not sure I like the idea of strangers on our rig.”

“Tell me about it,” Austin grumbled.

“Not your rig anymore, anyways, squirt,” Danny pointed out with a friendly shove. He’d put on his regular uniform button down again, which had Buck frowning.

“And there’s no strangers here, Buck,” Hen told him. “Just grunts with shovels.”

She grabbed one that was laying nearby and tossed it at him. He caught it easily enough.

“And where’s yours?” he asked, smiling at Eddie when he finally joined them, already changed into the bushfire jacket. “Or yours, Danny?”

“I volunteered for the base camp medical unit,” she said. Danny pointed at her and nodded.

“Have fun diggin’, squirt.”

“Are you kidding me?” Buck huffed. “Eddie, can you believe this? They’re not going up to the fire line with us.”

“Um.” Eddie opened a compartment on the truck and pulled out one of the hiking bags full of supplies. “About that.”

An ATV pulled up between the rows of trucks. Behind the wheel was the woman that Buck just knew that he knew, however much her identity was escaping him at the moment.

“You ready, soldier?” she asked.

“Be right there,” Eddie responded.

“Hop to it. Those at-risk kids aren’t going to be any less at-risk,” she said, before driving off again.

“Her? You’re going with her?” Buck stared at the empty the ATV had been in. Her voice was familiar, too. Like- Oh! “Wait, I know who she is! That’s Firefox!”

He got four blank gazes in response.

“Seriously? She’s gone viral like, five times! She’s a total badass.” Buck couldn’t believe his boyfriend was ditching him for someone cooler. He couldn’t even be properly offended, because he’d probably ditch Eddie to hang out with her, too. Or wait, yes he could, because he’d bring Eddie with him. “I follow her on Instagram. Some reason, she didn’t follow me back.”

“Uh-huh.” Hen rolled her eyes and shouldered her own bag, before heading off. “Don’t forget your shovel.”

“Austin-” Danny started, and his not-boyfriend cut him off with,

“I’ll keep an eye on him.”

“I was gonna say to be careful, but that, too.”

“Abandoners!” Buck called after Eddie and Danny’s retreating backs. He was rudely ignored.

Eddie had not initially planned on going out for a rescue mission. He’d been getting himself some water when he overheard some of the local firefighters talk about a bunch of kids that were unaccounted for, and spoke up when the need for a medic was mentioned. So now here he was, riding in an ATV as they went farther out into the fire zone, the smoke getting thicker and the heat more stifling.

The mosquitos, too, were out in force. Unperturbed by the smoke, for whatever reason, and perfectly content to feast on his vulnerable blood. He’d smack one, only for a dozen more to swarm him.

“Got you some of them critters, Hollywood?” That was Judd, a man that almost dwarfed him and with a Texan drawl thicker than even the one that was creeping in Eddie’s words the longer they were here. “Bet they don’t get that big in LA.”

“We got plenty in El Paso.”

“Oh, no way. You’re from El Paso?” Judd excitedly asked. “Where’d you go to high school?”

“La Salle.”

“No shit?” The big man laughed. “We used to whoop your ass every year at state. I was Austin Heights.”

“You’re a Bulldog? Guess we can’t be friends, then,” Eddie joked. “And you didn’t beat us every year.”

Buck had been so very proud of himself that year, considering he’d managed to run his ass across half the football field before the clock ran out.

One of the other ATVs sped past them, the driver - the Firefox that Buck had been so focused on - behind the wheel and giving a loud whoop. Her passenger, a man named Paul, looked to be holding onto the roof for dear life. Judd let out a laugh as he watched them go.

“She always like that?” Eddie asked.

“Always.”

The kids they were looking for were located at a camp for troubled youths. They apparently hadn’t been allowed cell phones, so there’d been no contact. Before the winds had shifted, the eight kids and their counselor hadn’t seen the need to evacuate. But now they were right in the path of destruction.

When the ATVs pulled into the campsite, the group of kids immediately started running for them. Eddie immediately spotted a problem, though.

“There’s only seven kids,” Eddie pointed out, doing another headcount just to make sure. “IC said there’s supposed to be eight.”

“Yup, and a counselor,” Judd agreed, before trying to herd the panicked kids into giving them space to work. “Back up, we’re here now. We’re gonna get y’all off the mountain, okay? Marjan and Eddie’s gonna check everybody out, make sure they’re okay.”

Eddie nodded to him and started digging through his bag for his stethoscope, nabbing the closest kid for the first to be checked. He kept half an ear on Judd on the others while he listened to the kid’s heartbeat and checked his vitals. Apparently the counselor, Mr. Gomez, took the lone cell phone and left last night in search of a boy named JJ, who’d been doing his solo - a mandatory two nights alone in the woods. Judd claimed that it built character and self-respect, and that it was well monitored.

Eddie was doubtful on all counts.

“No call in eight hours,” Firefox - real name apparently Marjan - said, checking over her own patient. “Could just be bad reception.”

Movement heading towards them caught Eddie’s eye.

“Or it could be something else,” he said as he yanked off the stethoscope.

A man wrapped in a blanket, presumably the aforementioned Mr. Gomez, was stumbling towards them. Eddie and the others ran to meet him, catching him as he stumbled. He was rasping, breaths labored. Paul asked where JJ was, Mr. Gomez gasped out that he couldn’t find him, and then fell unconscious.

And he stopped breathing.

They carried him to a nearby picnic table and laid him on top. Eddie started giving orders, telling Marjan to get out the IV bag so he could run a line and then shoving the bag into Paul’s hands in lieu of a stand. The kids were gathered around, worry palpable, so Judd made them back up.

“I’m not hearing any air escaping,” Eddie reported, feeling around the man. Marjan had bagged the patient and was doing her best to force oxygen into him. “His lungs are intact.”

“Then why isn’t his chest rising?” Paul asked.

Eddie had a theory about that, one that was confirmed when they unwrapped the blanket to reveal Mr. Gomez’s chest. The entire front of the man’s torso was burned, the skin stiff and unyielding. It had to have been agonizing, and it was amazing that he hadn’t collapsed before making it to them.

Adrenaline was a hell of a drug.

“We need to do an escharotomy,” Eddie told the others.

“What the hell’s that?” Marjan asked.

“The burn tissue is called eschar, it’s constricting his chest like a rope and preventing his lungs from expanding,” Eddie explained. “He can’t breathe, so we need to cut it.”

“Now?”

“Now.” Or else just let the guy die.

Escharotomy was not a pretty procedure. It was also one that Eddie had far too much experience with. They disinfected Mr. Gomez’s chest as best they could and then the scalpel, but could do nothing about the environment they were doing it in. The cuts circled the chest and had to be deep, deep enough to get through all the burn tissue, deep enough that the subcutaneous fat was visible. Then Eddie ran a finger along each incision to break the fibrous bands that might still restrict movement. At least one of the boys ducked away to puke.

When Marjan bagged Mr. Gomez again, a few pumps of air had him waking up, gasping and asking about JJ.

“We’re aware of the missing kid, sir.” Eddie took the oxygen mask he was handed and slipped it over Mr. Gomez’s face. He was careful to use the hand that didn’t have blood smeared all over the gloved fingers. “I need you to take nice and steady breaths.”

Now they just had to get the man to a hospital, and find the missing JJ.

Working the fire line was exhausting and grueling. It was a lot of raking and hatcheting and shoveling, all in an effort to create a large enough, and long enough, space of nothing in the hopes of slowing down the encroaching flames. The captain overseeing the task was shouting… Well, it wasn’t quite encouragement, but it was something close to it. In the same zip code, at least.

To be perfectly honest, Buck didn’t mind this type of labor. It was physically demanding and repetitive. He swung and pulled and swung and pulled, a pattern of motion that was easy to get lost in. The longer he did it, the more he just kinda went completely zen. At least until one of the other firefighters started a conversation.

“So LA, huh?” The guy’s name was Mateo. He and the firefighter between them, TK, were with Firefox at the briefing.

“Yeah.”

“That’s cool. I got a cousin in LA. Marvin,” Mateo said. “People say we look alike, maybe you know him.”

Buck paused in raking to glance at Austin on his other side, who was wearing a quizzical frown as he listened.

“It’s kinda a big place,” Buck hedged.

“No, I know. His last name’s Chavez,” the guy insisted.

“Yeah, I- I don’t think so.”

“He’s in jail, anyway.”

“What the fuck,” Austin hissed under his breath. Buck silently agreed.

“I bet you get some crazy calls out there,” Mateo said.

“You have no idea,” Buck told him, going back to raking.

“We get our fair share in Texas,” TK said, finally speaking up.

“Oh, I know.”

Buck’s agreement seemed to have thrown the other man a bit, because he paused in his work to blink at him.

“You ever get a call at Disneyland?” was Mateo’s next eager question.

“That’s Orange County,” Buck pointed out.

“But LA, right?”

Austin, Buck couldn’t help but notice, had stopped raking. He was instead glaring at the brush covered ground with enough heat that it might spontaneously combust.

“We did get called to an amusement park once,” Buck said, before the Los Angeles native made any murder attempts. “I had to scale the loop of a roller coaster. Guy was hanging on by his bare hands.”

“You saved a guy hanging from a roller coaster?” Mateo sounded awed. The question, though, knocked the good spirits out of Buck.

“No, um. He let go.”

“Man, that’s rough.” TK straightened up, ax gripped in his hands. “I had a woman almost drown on me in less than a foot of water last year. She was trapped in a bus upside down in the middle of the street.”

“We had to respond to a shark attack in the middle of the freeway, once,” Buck said as he went back to raking. “And I nearly drowned in an elevator, one time.”

Austin’s question of “When did that happen?” had Buck twisting around, pointing a finger at him and nearly shouting,

“You didn’t hear that!”

“We just had an active volcano last week,” TK said, sounding smug.

“I know!” Buck turned back to him. “That’s crazy, Pilot Knob hasn’t erupted in, like, eighty million-”

TK was suddenly tackling him. A flaming car came crashing into the space where Buck stood mere seconds before. It had barely come to a stop, and Buck had barely hit the ground, before Buck was scrambling to reach the vehicle and anyone that might be inside.

“It looks like just the driver!” he shouted, running around to the other side. He could only see one shape through the smoke-blocked windows, moving around in the front. Mateo and a couple of the others had extinguishers, spraying the flames until they were out. When Buck tried the door, but could not get it open. “It’s locked!”

“Heads up!” 

TK tossed his ax over the roof. Buck caught it and immediately swung it into the car’s window, shattering the glass. He reached in, careful of the shards, and popped the lock to swing it open.

And then a dog on a leash, of all things, jumped out.

A man came sprinting down the hill, in the direction the car had come from, shouting out “Clyde!” He went directly to the dog, his dog, relief obvious with every action. He’d apparently left the dog alone, and the dog had decided to go on a joyride.

“So that was weird,” Buck said.

“Right?” TK agreed.

“Nice move, by the way. Good reflexes,” Buck told him, before hurrying to Austin. “Hey, uh-”

“I am not breathing a word of this to Dan,” the man promised.

“Oh, thank God.”

Chapter End Notes

You know what I was not thinking about when I named Austin Jones? Him being here for this crossover.

Chapter 27

Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

A constant fight against a raging inferno, day in and day out, led to a lot of injuries even in the most ideal of conditions. Half of the cots in the medical tents were already filled, and that was with them doing their best to get people out of there quickly, either back to the front lines or sent to a hospital out of the line of fire. The majority of the patients were in for something minor, or as minor as things ever were in these circumstances. Exhaustion, overheating, dehydration. There were a few burns, ranging from nothing burgers to just short of severe. One man, waiting for a lift out of there, somehow managed to trip into a tree and get himself lightly impaled. He’d been brought in with the thin branch still sticking out of his arm, and they’d simply made sure it didn’t move too much until surgeons could remove it.

The main problem, as Hen had said, was that they were woefully lacking in medics. The people in charge had been very grateful when Daniel followed her inside, eagerly welcoming another set of hands, and directed him towards the nearest person in need of triaging. That was what Daniel had been doing ever since, treating one patient and then the next, going from prescribing fluids to changing bandages to covering burns.

“Keep drinking that,” Daniel ordered the current firefighter he was overseeing, forcing the cup of water the man was holding back to his mouth. “Small sips.”

The guy had overheated while digging the fire line, not the first, not the last. At the moment, Daniel was tracking his pulse, the skin of his wrist clammy beneath his fingers. Was the guy bad enough that they needed to break out some of the cooling packs?

“You’re good at this,” Hen commented. She was treating a burned hand at the next cot over.

“Thank you.”

“Why didn’t you become a doctor?”

“Christ.” Daniel rolled his eyes and dropped his patient’s wrist, deciding he’d be fine without the packs. “Who’s been gossiping?”

“It came up when I talked about wanting to become a doctor last year,” Hen admitted. “Maddie mentioned that you wanted to be one as a kid.”

“I used to, yeah,” he admitted, tugging off his gloves and tossing them. 

“So what happened?”

“Priorities.” That was always the answer, it was also the truth. “Other things were more important, so it just never happened. Being a paramedic was a good enough compromise later.”

“Why don’t you do it now?” Hen asked. “It’s never too late. I mean, look at me. I’m forty and in med school.”

“Yeah, but you already had your bachelor’s, right?” Daniel looked at her over his shoulder. She gave a small nod. “I don’t even have that.”

“There’s nothing stopping you from getting it,” Hen pointed out as she finished up wrapping her patient’s hand. Daniel just shrugged, because he knew that was true. “Alright, keep this dry. Change the dressing every twenty-four hours.”

The med tent’s radio burst into life, as it had been intermittently the entire time they were there. This time, however, it was Eddie’s voice coming through and Daniel’s attention immediately zeroed in on it.

“This is the Great Oaks strike team. Do you copy?”

The person in charge of the med tent, or at least the attendant in charge of overseeing the logistics of the triage unit, picked up the mic to reply.

“This is base med unit. Go ahead.”

“Sending seven minors your way. Mild dehydration, smoke inhalation, a few lacerations, but they’re fine,” Eddie said. Daniel floated over to the table where the radio sat, Hen right behind him. “One adult male, critical. Gave him eleven milligrams of morphine. He will need a life flight.”

Hen held out her hand for the mic. The triage attendant passed it over.

“Eddie, it’s Hen,” she said, holding it to her mouth. “You’re sending out seven minors? I thought you went up there for eight.”

“One kid’s still missing. A couple of the guys from the Austin One Twenty-six are searching for him now.”

“Alright, you got about two hours of daylight left, and the wind reports are not good.”

At this point, the wildfire itself was fueling the wind. An ever-growing, ever-hungry monster that was propelling itself forward at speed. A rough beast slouching towards Bethlehem. Or, in this case, San Angelo.

“Yeah, it’s getting a little toasty out here.”

“Eddie, you need to put a clock on this,” Hen told him.

“I don’t think any of these folks are leaving with this boy, clock or no clock,” Eddie replied. “Remind me a little of some other people I know.”

Daniel glowered and took the mic from Hen, simply yanking it out of her hand.

“They can do what they want,” he said. “But you have a curfew.”

There was a moment’s pause and then,

“Copy that, Danny.”

Daniel rolled his eyes at the younger man’s tone, somewhere between exasperation and sulking. He was not going to let the little twerp get himself killed. He’d already had to deal with Buck being all brokenhearted over him once before, he did not have any intention of going through that again if he could help it.

“What?” Daniel demanded, when he noticed the amused expression on Hen’s face.

“Nothing,” was her answer as she took the mic back from him and handed it to the triage attendant. “I’m gonna go try scrounging up some air support for them, see if we can’t find that kid faster.”

“At the very least, we can use it to scoop Eddie out of there.” His comment had her laughing. “Good luck.”

And while she was doing that, he had about a half dozen more people to triage and to treat.

It was only Eddie and Marjan - Firefox - left at the campsite. Judd and Paul took off with an ATV in search of the missing boy, JJ. The other firefighters that came with them left with the boys and the injured camp counselor. Marjan was pacing, all anxious energy. Eddie, meanwhile, was busying himself with repacking his medical kit.

“Maybe we should go out and help them search,” she said.

Eddie almost asked her how she planned on them doing that, since they didn’t have an ATV available to them. He didn’t, though, because unlike some people, he actually had tact. Instead, he reminded her that,

“Judd told us to stay here.”

“How can you be so calm under literal fire?”

“At least no one’s shooting at us,” he retorted as he pulled out his phone. 

It didn’t take much effort to find the Instagram account for Firefox that Buck had gushed over. A press of a button had Marjan’s own phone chiming in her pants pocket. She pulled it out to check the notification, and then fixed him with a flat stare.

“Seriously? You wanna follow me on Insta?”

“Heard you put a lot of effort into it,” he said with a shrug. “I was curious.”

“I’ll show you mine if you show me yours,” she said, swaggering towards him.

“I haven’t been on social media in a while. The last post is like, nine months old,” he warned. “Super boring.”

“I’ll be the judge of that.”

“Fine, deal.”

She smirked and tapped on the screen of her phone. The request popped up on his a moment later. Eddie’s first thought, as he accepted it, was that Buck was going to bitch about this so very much later. His second thought was,

“Is that a Prius in the air?”

“Tornado dropped it between two buildings.” Huh. “This is the creepy guy that was staring at me.”

Eddie winced. He’d forgotten that one of his most recent photos was the pair of them at May’s graduation party, him with that smoking pipe on a stick and Buck with that yellow inflatable guitar.

“Buck’s harmless. Mostly,” he explained, to Marjan’s almost palpable disbelief. “He was trying to figure out where he recognized you from.”

“Right.”

“He just…” He wasn’t sure how to explain it, as unused as he was to having to do it. Everyone in their life either got used to how Buck was, or they were irritated by it and simply didn’t care to learn. “He gets caught on certain things, sometimes? He knew that he knew you from somewhere, but he didn’t know where, and he got stuck on that. Last year it was some dying old man that he felt sorry for, ended up helping arrange the guy’s funeral.”

Marjan still looked uncertain, but nodded all the same.

“Is this your kid?” she asked, holding up her phone, a picture he’d taken of himself and Chris the day he spent at the station taking up the entire screen. Eddie felt the smile slowly grow as he looked at his son.

“Christopher. He’s my world,” he told her. “I practically have a whole village helping me with him, now.”

More support than he had while married to Shannon and living in El Paso, that was for certain.

She let out a little hum as she went back to scrolling through the bare bones of what parts of his life he shared online. It wasn’t much, even discounting the fact that technology was the devil, he’d always been a rather private person. Why would he want to be one of those people who’d share every aspect of his life with total strangers?

“You did not build him a skateboard,” she suddenly blurted out.

“Well. Buck and Danny helped.” Okay, so it was almost entirely Buck and Danny, but she didn’t need to know that.

“Danny, the grumpy guy on the radio?” she asked. “The one who gave you a curfew.”

“Yup.” Eddie let out a sigh. “That’s Danny. He’s Buck’s older brother.”

“Probably why he’s so grumpy.”

He scowled and opened his mouth to ask what that meant, when the radio crackled to life and interrupted him.

“Great Oaks search team, give us your current location. We’re sending air support.”

“Air support?” Eddie repeated. “Who’s crazy enough to go up in something like this?”

He got the answer to that a little bit later, when a voice he recognized as belonging to Captain Strand, the guy from Austin who was serving as the operations section chief for the firefighting efforts - and Buck did have a point on the oddness, there - spoke over the radio.

“Great Oaks strike team leader, this is air support… Judd, do you copy?”

“Cap, is that you?” Judd radioed back.

“Yeah, I heard you could use a hand. What’s your twenty?”

“We’re a few klicks west of the camp. We haven’t found this kid yet. We found his tent, but no remains, so we think he went deeper into the woods.”

“Alright, we see you.”

Eddie could see the helicopter from where he and Marjan stood around, waiting, if he peered through the trees and the smoke. It was hovering just over the treeline to the west of them, making a large, swooping arch of a search pattern, buffeted by the wind as it went.

“Judd, we’ve got something under a grove of trees. South-by-southeast of your position,” Strand said. “I’m gonna try to get over on top of it.”

“Copy, Cap, we’re coming at you.”

Eddie and Marjan listened as Captain Strand directed Judd and Paul to JJ’s location. They listened as they got to the kid’s location. And they listened, wincing, as Judd reported that,

“His ankle’s caught in a bear trap.”

And then, after a little bit of back and forth, who, of all people, got on the radio next?

“Judd? This is Paramedic Henreitta Wilson. I’m up here with your captain.”

“Oh, you have got to be kidding me,” Eddie groaned.

“I’m pretty sure you firefighters are fully equipped and capable to handle this,” Hen said. Judd was quick to radio back with,

“No, no, please, walk us through it.”

Maybe he should have gone out with them, Eddie thought as he listened to Hen walk them through keeping the kid from bleeding to death once they got him free of the trap and then giving fluids to stabilize him when his vitals apparently started plummeting. They couldn’t have expected bear traps - or maybe they should have, coyotes had been a problem even in and around El Paso - but a medical emergency was almost inevitable with the way things were at the moment.

“Miss Henrietta,” Judd radioed after several tense minutes of silence. “The fluids worked.”

“I’m very glad to hear it,” Hen responded.

“Judd, can you get him out of there on an ATV?” Captain Strand asked.

“Yeah, that ain’t a problem. I gotta pick up Marjan and Diaz.”

“Roger that, see you back at base.”

And then, suddenly, the helicopter was putting out smoke and the pilot was radioing out a mayday. Eddie and the others could do nothing but watch as the helicopter, with Hen inside it, listed and floundered. Eddie could do nothing but watch as the helicopter crashed into the middle of the raging inferno that everyone had spent days trying to put out.

Buck was exhausted as he trooped back to base camp hours after the car and the dog, with the sun long past the horizon. His muscles ached, and the back of his neck and the bridge of his nose stung in a familiar way, telling him that he was going to regret not sparing a single thought to sunscreen for this trip. He was in high spirits, however, chatting - okay, mostly arguing, but in good fun! - with TK and Mateo while Austin brought up the rear, the same constant, silent presence he always was, before he split off on his own. Probably to find Danny, if Buck had to guess.

(Hopefully he’d keep his promise to not say anything about Buck’s newest brush with danger.)

“Come on, it’s California,” TK was saying. “Of course you’re gonna have earthquakes. But you can’t tell me that that’s cooler than the One Twenty-six going up against a solar storm?”

“What even is that? You can’t see that,” Buck retorted. “And you didn’t go up against a solar storm, did you? You had to deal with the blackout it caused and, oh wait! We’ve done that, too.”

“Guys, don’t you see what you’re doing?” was Mateo’s earnest interruption of the debate. “You’re flailing into the classic, Iron Man versus Captain America trap. Is Captain America better because he’s a super soldier with an indestructible shield? Or is Tony Stark better because he’s a tech genius with a sick weaponized suit?”

“So?” TK asked. “Who’s better?”

“Captain America,” was Buck’s immediate answer.

“No!” Mateo groaned in exasperation. “Neither is better, bro. That’s the point! It’s a speeches argument, they’re both badass. And when they team up, nobody could beat them. Except maybe Thanos.”

Dead ahead of them was the group that had gone to fetch the at-risk kids. They were lazing about, sitting relaxed and pretty around one of the ATVs.

“Glad to see the strike team’s already got their feet up,” TK crowed. 

“You guys must be exhausted,” Buck taunted. “All that go-karting up and down the hill? Whew.”

Eddie lifted his face then, expression grim. As grim as the others, now that Buck was paying attention. He felt his stomach begin to twist with anxiety, with the knowledge that something was wrong.

“You didn’t hear, did you?” Firefox asked.

“Hear what?” TK asked in return.

The story came quietly and in pieces, the four of them - Eddie and Judd and Paul and Firefox, whose name was really Marjan - switching in and out to contribute. When they reached the at-risk kids, they’d only found seven of them, plus the camp counselor. The eighth kid had been missing, sent off to do some stupid solo camp in the burning hellscape around them. Judd and Paul went to go search for them, and they’d managed to get air support, too.

Air support in the form of the 126’s captain, Owen Strand, in a helicopter with Hen.

They’d manage to locate the missing kid with the help of the helicopter, and they managed to rescue him from a bear trap he’d gotten snagged in. That was the end of the good news, however. Something had happened - the heat of the flames, maybe, or the winds, or a combination of everything - that caused some sort of mechanical issue.
