“It was trailing smoke,” Eddie explained. “The pilot sent out a mayday, and then it went down. Right in the middle of everything.”

“So why are you all just sitting here?” TK demanded, and didn’t even wait for them to give an excuse before dropping everything and rushing off for the command tent. Buck followed him, after a single glance to Eddie.

There wasn’t much action happening there, either, though. Commander De Leon and the others were talking, debating, about the best course of action as they bent over maps of the area. TK was pacing like an angry tiger, vibrating with an energy that Buck sympathized with.

“What we need to do is get containment,” De Leon said, jabbing at spots along the map. “Here, here, or-”

“This is a joke!” TK slammed his palms onto the table, shaking everything that sat on it. “We know exactly where the chopper went down. Why haven't you sent out a rescue team?”

“As I said,” De Leon responded, calmer than Buck expected. “The beacon is coming from two miles inside an active burn zone. It is not safe to send anyone up in the dark.”

“Commander, with all due respect.” Judd’s tone might’ve been respectful, but Buck suspected he wasn’t feeling it. “We accept the risk and we ain’t asking anybody else to go.”

“You know I can’t authorize that.”

“You know those are our people up there,” Buck retorted.

“They could be bleeding out right now,” TK argued. “Dying.”

“Son, we haven’t had any cell or radio contact since the mayday,” De Leon said. “Nobody else is risking their lives tonight, and your father would be the first to agree with me.”

That was very much not what TK wanted to hear. He let out an angry, disgusted sound and shoved himself away from the table, to turn and march out of the tent. There was awkward silence for a moment, before De Leon and the others fell back into the discussion and the debate. Buck, however, was thinking.

And avoiding his boyfriend’s eyes, lest his thoughts be too obvious to those that knew him.

(The trucks were there to be used when they really needed them…)

Chapter End Notes

Daniel: Eddie sucks and I hate him.
Also Daniel: Eddie better stay safe. Because Buck would be upset if something happened to him. That and no other reason...

Chapter 28

It wasn’t long after TK stormed out of the tent that the others left it, too. They drifted off, the air around them as overcast as the skies above, in search of the siren’s call of food. It was actually very easy for Buck to give everyone the slip. Understandable for those from the Austin 126, insulting when it was Eddie.

Buck was almost constantly aware of where Eddie was, his boyfriend would never have given him the slip like this.

Anyways, it was all kinds of offensive, but it was convenient, especially since Buck had to make multiple stops for what he needed. The first one was the most important, but also the easiest: the firefighters who had been working their asses off all day were ravenous, so whoever was supposed to be in charge of his target was too busy stuffing their face somewhere, instead. His second stop was in the middle of the gorging horde itself, and much more difficult. Grabbing a box of pizza was almost more dangerous than anything he had done that day, and probably what he was going to do that night, an act that almost cost him at least a couple fingers.

The next destination was wherever the hell TK had stormed off to. Because TK was the person whom Buck was absolutely certain would join him with this plan, little to no questions asked. Eddie, for as much as Buck loved and trusted him, would undoubtedly rat him out to Danny the moment he caught wind of it. It was all part and parcel of serving as Buck’s guardrails.

(Not that Buck couldn’t convince Eddie to go with them without running to Danny, but this was dangerous, and Eddie was too frightened of Danny’s anger for it to be an easy matter. They didn’t have the time.)

He found TK sitting at a table all by himself, on the phone with someone. Someone important, judging from the “I love you” that he capped it with. The other firefighter looked up with a hint of irritation when Buck came to a stop next to him.

“What’s up?”

“They just delivered twenty kinds of pizza if you’re hungry,” Buck told him, setting the box of pizza down on the table before taking a seat. There were only a few slices left in that particular one, he hadn’t been brave enough to risk taking off with a full pizza.

“I’m good,” TK said, getting up. He was clearly not in a socializing mood. “Thanks.”

“They survived the crash.” Or at least that was what he was choosing to believe, with all his heart and soul. It was what he had to believe. “And your dad is with Hen, so he is in really good hands.”

“So is she,” was the quiet, confident response.

“No doubt,” he agreed, seeing no point in arguing about it. “I haven’t spoken with my dad in over a decade. But my big brother? He’s taken care of me my entire life. He’s always been there for me, doing whatever he needed to do to take care of me, no matter what. He’s never given up on me, even when I wasn’t always the best brother to him. Even when I did something stupid. And I have done a lot of stupid shit.”

“My dad’s never given up on me either. And I’ve probably done stupider things than you,” TK said. “It just sucks, you know? Just sitting here and doing nothing.”

“Well.” Buck reached into his pocket, pulling out the thing he’d grabbed while everyone was distracted. “What if we didn’t have to?”

TK stared at him in disbelief. More accurately, at the key he was dangling from his hand.

“Is that…?”

“A key to a fire truck?” Buck smirked, feeling so very pleased with himself. “Yes. Yes it is.”

Just as he predicted, TK jumped at the opportunity being offered to him. That involved a bit more sneaking around, gathering up the supplies they needed in between stuffing their faces with pizza. Because the prospect of actually doing something to rescue his father had TK’s appetite returning. Buck could understand that.

Once again, it was laughingly, almost insultingly easy for them to get what they needed without being called out. Buck didn’t even lay eyes on the others the entire time. Any other time, he’d find it offensive that Eddie had apparently found other people to hang out with and wasn’t even trying to track him down. Actually, he was still finding it offensive, it just happened to be convenient at that moment.

With a pack of supplies on his back, Buck and TK snuck about where they’d parked all the trucks. They crouched behind an ATV, peering about through the hazy air to track the people tasked with keeping an eye on the vehicles. Not that they were putting much effort into it, and why would they? No one in their right mind would steal an engine in the middle of the night to drive off into the wildfires.

“You sure it’s still here?” TK asked. He was, evidently, the Doomer of the 126, the one who went to the worst case scenario the quickest. “Maybe they deployed it.”

“Not according to the board. ‘Sides, I have the key.” Buck reminded him, patting his pocket where it was safely tucked away. “Alright, c’mon, let’s go.”

Staying low to the ground, they sprinted across the open space between the cover of the ATV and the rows of trucks. Buck didn’t feel safe until there was red metal between him and any watchful eyes, and even then he didn’t straighten up fully.

“You know you don’t have to do this,” TK said, voice hushed. “There’s no reason that both of us get fired.”

As if this wasn’t Buck’s idea to begin with. Maybe TK would’ve gotten here on his own eventually, but he seemed the type prone to wallowing in his anger for a bit longer before he got to the doing aspect of things. Which, maybe that was healthier than Buck’s tendency of letting his emotions in the moment to drive his actions. God only knew how bad things could’ve gotten if Danny hadn’t been there to catch him before he called that lawyer.

“My friend’s up there, too,” Buck pointed out. “She would do the same thing for me. I think.”

He paused, thought about it for a moment.

“Yeah, yeah she would.”

“Oh! Here it is.” TK patted the side of the 118’s engine. “C’mon, let’s go.”

“Uh, no, that is not the truck we are looking for,” Buck said, continuing on.

“What do you mean?” TK gestured at it. “One Eighteen, Los Angeles. Let’s go.”

“Yeah, no, we’re not taking the One Eighteen’s. I’m not pissing off Austin like that.” He didn’t know what Austin would do, but he had the suspicion that it would be unpleasant. Someone had stuck itching powder in his work bag the shift after he accidentally jinxed them by saying the q-word at the station, and Buck was fairly certain it had been him. Everyone else would’ve copped to it, by now. “No, no, this is the key to your truck.”

Much safer that way, much less unpleasant sensations in his unmentionables.

Of course, they’d barely gotten to the 126’s engine when the worst possible thing happened:

“Evan Christopher Buckley!”

Buck cringed and cowered behind TK, maneuvering the shorter man in front of him like a shield, as Danny stepped out into view. His brother did not look particularly pleased at that moment, arms crossed and face stuck in a glare that made him feel fifteen again.

“H- Hey, Danny.” Buck gave him his best and brightest smile as he peered out from around a bewildered TK. “What are you doing here?”

“Eddie said you were about to do something stupid.”

Shit. Also-

“Eds, you traitor! I’m breaking up with you!”

Eddie did not look very bothered by that (admittedly toothless) threat as he stepped out from behind the trucks, too, along with Firefox. Buck was also too busy feeling pleased that his boyfriend actually had been paying attention to him to be too terribly angry over his entirely predictable actions, to be fair.

“Wait.” Firefox - Marjan, that was her actual name - tilted her head as she looked at Eddie. “You named your kid after him.”

“Yeah!” Buck preened for a moment, until he caught Danny’s eye again and remembered he was in trouble. Then he was back to using TK as a shield.

“Dumbass and dumbasser.” That was right behind him, Judd coming in from the other end of the row with Mateo and Paul. It was a sign of how much trouble Buck was in that Danny didn’t even glare at the bigger man for insulting him. “Did you stop to consider the consequences of what you’re about to do?”

“TK’s dumbasser, right?”

“The answer is no, by the way,” Eddie said. Buck scowled at him. “Buck definitely did not stop to consider the consequences.”

Okay, that was only partially true. He’d considered some of the consequences.

“You two didn’t seriously think you could sneak off and drive into wildfires, did you?” Marjan asked.

“Yes?” was TK’s small sounding answer.

“Well, that ain’t gonna happen,” Paul declared, which was enough to rile Buck up.

“You think you’re gonna stop us?” he asked Paul and them.

“Shut up and get in, squirt,” Danny said, dropping his arms and rolling his eyes.

“Wait. What?”

“We’re going with you,” was Mateo’s enthusiastic explanation as he and the others started for the 126’s truck.

Oh, that was… Buck bounced on his toes, shared a grin with TK, and dashed around to the other side.

It rained on them as they drove out of base camp and into the fires. The skies opened up and it began to pour, water pelting against the windows. It slowed them in their tracks, making navigating to the crash site harder. But Buck also watched it do in an hour what they had spent so long trying to accomplish, staring out the rain streaked window as the flames were quashed with more efficiency than they’d ever accomplish with hoses alone.

By the time the rain stopped they had reached the crash site, the helicopter on its side and the tail in pieces, and there were all the signs of a firestorm having passed through: blackened vegetation, burnt dirt, and smoke so thick in the air that it might as well have been a cloud. But the fire itself was gone, put out by the rain or simply ran out of food to fuel it. The truck had barely pulled to a halt, was actually still slowing down, when TK leaped out. Buck was not too far behind.

Everyone was calling out for those missing, and getting no response. Buck used the landing struts to pull himself up onto the helicopter. TK went through the bottom, crawling into the cockpit. The empty cockpit.

“They’re not in here!” TK shouted, face turned to look up at Buck.

“Hey! Hey!” Buck called to the others. “They made it out!”

“Out and away,” Danny added. He was pacing around the crash site, head turning this way and that as he peered through the wisps of smoke. “I’m not seeing any bodies.”

He looked to Buck and gave a nod, because that was a good sign. A wonderful sign. The dead didn’t walk away from a crash. They were alive and ambulatory, at least enough to get themselves out of harm’s way. 

“Let’s fan out!” Judd ordered, using his arms to gesture at the landscape around them. “Search the area here, yeah?”

They dashed out in all directions, Buck jumping off the landing strut he was perched on and TK scrambling out from the cockpit. The silence of the desolated hills was broken by a chorus of “Cap!” and “Hen!” and “Dad!” And then, a change in the lyrics, as Marjan called out,

“Guys! Guys, over here!”

Buck dashed across the dirt and over the rise, stumbling slightly, as the others did the same. Marjan and Paul were at a destroyed pile of boards, hacking and pulling away at them. Just in front, the thing that almost certainly caught their attention: a pair of bright yellow jackets stuck on poles, burnt by the flames that had gone through the area.

It became very clear that the wood was covering up an entrance, of some sort, along with stone and dirt. A cave or a mine shaft, somewhere that would provide shelter from the inferno. What wasn’t immediately clear was why or how it was blocked like this, like an explosion had brought it all down. It also wasn’t immediately clear if it was intentional. Maybe it had been, maybe that was why the jackets were outside like they were, but the could have just as easily been to catch the attention of anyone searching.

With as many people, as many hands, as they had, it didn’t take long to get enough of it moved to see inside. When they got the hole big enough, TK was the first one through, going straight for his father. Buck was not far behind. Hen and Captain Strand were unconscious, slumped against the side of the wall. The pilot was laid out on the ground.

“I got a pulse!” TK shouted, his relief clearer than the air outside as he fretted over the captain

“They need O2.” Danny gently pushed Buck aside so he could check over Hen. “Judd, is there any on the truck?”

“There should be,” the very large Texan said from the entrance, turning slightly to nod to one of the others just out of view. “Hollywood, how’s the pilot?”

“Rough.” Eddie was kneeling by the pilot, running his hands along his body. “Cracked ribs, fractured femur. Head injury of some sort, can’t tell how severe. Looks like he was bleeding from his ear, too.”

“Get him out first,” Danny said. “Buck, go help him.”

“Yeah. Yeah, okay.”

Buck reluctantly stepped away from his friend, who was slowly waking up, eyes blinking heavily. Getting the pilot out of the mine shaft that they were in took delicate work, since they needed to keep his leg stabilized to prevent making that fracture worse. He and Eddie carried him to the hole they’d made, lifting him up to Judd and Paul as they grabbed him under the arms and dragged him out.

“He has a concussion,” Hen was saying, words coming out weak.

“The pilot?” Danny asked.

“No, no. Captain Strand. He was… He was seeing someone…”

“He’s next, then,” he said, gesturing at the captain. 

Getting the captain out was easier, and TK scrambled out behind him. After that was Hen, and then themselves. Marjan and Mateo had tanks of oxygen ready, and Judd was on the radio requesting for an air lift. But Hen was safe, Buck’s friend was safe.

And hopefully no one would be getting into too much trouble for this.

With the rains that rolled in, and the line that Buck and the others spent all day digging, the wildfires were actually contained. Contained enough that De Leon dismissed all of the out-of-state firefighters. Eddie was very much thankful for it, thankful for the chance to get home to Chris sooner. In fact, the only one of them who wasn’t thankful for it was Danny, who’d settled into a grim mood at the announcement. Even Austin, perpetually stoic as he was, seemed worried over the older Buckley’s odd behavior.

At the moment, though, Eddie was stowing away his pack of belongings in one of the engine’s compartments while he and Judd said their goodbyes.

“If y’all get hungry, there’s a great barbecue place in Fort Stockton called Rudy’s Ribs,” Judd was telling him. “Just tell ‘em that I sent you.”

“Thanks, but we’ve got plans to make a stop in El Paso,” Eddie said, closing the compartment door. “You’re all right, Judd. Even if you are a Bulldog. I don’t think Buck will forgive me for saying that, though.”

“He from Texas, too?”

“We went to high school together,” he answered, and then grinned at Judd. “He’s the reason Austin Heights didn’t whoop our ass every year.”

Judd gave a good natured harrumph at that, and then Marjan and Paul drove up in another ATV. Eddie took a selfie with them, again mostly with the intent of bothering Buck with it, before just about begging Marjan to follow Buck back on Insta. Buck himself was on the other side of the engine with TK and Eddie caught the tail end of their conversation as he joined them.

“Hey, if you’re ever in LA,” Buck said, “we should get together.”

“Sure.” TK nodded. “I gotta mention, though, I already have a boyfriend and it’s pretty serious, so…”

“Uh. S- So do I?” Buck sounded confused as he feebly pointed at Eddie. TK’s eyes flicked to him and widened slightly in surprise.

Eddie felt himself stiffen, that familiar panic surging to the fore. He caught himself just as the denial climbed up his throat and shook his head, annoyed and angry at his own reaction. A day in Texas, and he was regressing. At least he had the excuse of them having spent much of their time here separated from each other, and their time spent together being focused on Hen, for why their relationship hadn’t come up before now, and not the fact that he regressed that badly.

He still needed to make it up to Buck, though. The first step was to take a fortifying breath and drape his arm around Buck’s shoulder, invading each other’s personal space as they always did.

TK looked between them, mouth screwed up oddly.

“I’m not sure how Carlos feels about group stuff, so I’m gonna hafta turn that down, too,” he finally said. Buck sputtered. “But it was nice meeting you, man!”

“Wh- Wh- What!?” Buck managed to get out as the man walked off. “I don’t- What?”

“What the hell were you two even talking about?” Eddie asked.

“I was trying to be nice!”

“Uh-huh.”

The house they pulled up to hours after leaving San Angelo was quaint looking, Daniel guessed. It was a step removed from the type of suburban hell that Austin’s parents lived in and which made his skin crawl, but definitely in the neighborhood. The front was taken up almost entirely by the driveway, and what actual yard was left was mostly grass that had died of heat and thirst. A bunch of yard gnomes were lined up along the path to the front door, including one on a toilet, a bunch riding a flamingo and a llama, and an angry looking one with a gun. 

The door opened as their brakes squealed, Alma stepping out to cross the yard. As soon as the engine was turned off, Buck was slipping out to meet her. Daniel himself was not far behind.

“It’s a nice place,” Daniel said, eying the house up. “Better than our old one.”

“Sucks that it got torn down.” Buck bent to hug Alma, squeezing her a mite too tightly, judging from the grunt she let out. “I wanted to show Hen and Austin.”

“It’s more surprising that it didn’t happen sooner,” Alma said. “But Iggy-”

She was interrupted by a pair of shrieks as two young women came sprinting out of the house to tackle Buck. Buck, for his part, managed to keep from being toppled by Celia and Delia’s spirited welcome, helped by Eddie supporting him from behind. The man that came out behind them, slowly and cautiously, was short. Much shorter than Daniel and Buck. He was a bit dweebish looking, with a dorky mustache.

“Hi!” The greeting was nervous as he held out his hand. “You’re Dan.”

“And you're Iggy.” Daniel eyed him as he shook the man’s hand, and then smiled. It was not a friendly smile, judging from the way Iggy shuddered. “Has anyone told you about Marcos?”

“Stop that.” Alma smacked him. “The girls told the story already.”

“The first time I met them, actually,” Iggy said with an awkward chuckle.

That did explain why the guy was shaking like an anxiety-riddled chihuahua.

“Just making sure.”

“Hi, Alma.” Hen was smiling politely as she joined them. Austin was hanging back a bit. “I’m Hen. We met briefly when you came up after Buck’s…”

She trailed off, but Alma nodded all the same.

“I remember. Come on in, we have food.”

Buck cheered and started making his way inside, his journey slowed by the way that Celia and Delia were hanging off his arms like they were little girls again and not approaching twenty. Eddie laughed and shook his head as he followed, making just enough of an attempt to get the twins to let go to say that he’d tried.

“He used to babysit them,” Daniel explained to Hen as they went in, the other paramedic watching the shenanigans with bemused amusement.

His initial impression of Iggy, just from what Alma had told him over the phone, was that he was an okay guy. Better than several of the guys she’d dated in the past, certainly. Meeting him in person simply reinforced it. The man had, after all, gladly opened his home to Alma and her daughters, making no complaint at the invasion. Daniel was actually starting to wonder if the poor guy was being turned into a doormat, with the way he ran about to get Alma whatever she wanted while they sat, but that wasn’t his problem. Alma most definitely deserved that kind of doting, anyways.

Of course, the good cheer could not, would not last. It started with a text, as it always did. And when he replied to it saying that he couldn’t, that he was busy, it was followed by a phone call. Daniel hurriedly excused himself and slipped outside into the backyard before answering it.

"What do you mean, you can’t?” Drake immediately demanded, his displeasure evident. Daniel swallowed.

“I mean that I can’t,” he said. “I’m in Texas.”

“Why are you in Texas?”

“The wildfires,” he said. “I’ll be back tomorrow. It slipped my mind. I should have told you. I’m sorry.”

“Yeah, you should have.”

And then the line went dead. Daniel stood there for a moment, heaved in a breath, and then turned to go back in-

Only to find Alma standing there, arms crossed, as she stared at him expectantly. Austin, just behind her and closing the door to the house, was frowning.

“Who was that?” she asked.

“No one,” was Daniel’s immediate answer. Alma scoffed.

“Wanna try that again?” When he didn’t answer, she shook her head at him. “I saw your face when you got that text, when your phone rang. Who was it, Dan?”

“I told you, it’s-”

“Dan.”

“A bad date,” he said. “I have a social life, you know. A sex life. I-”

“You’re lying again,” Austin interrupted. “You’re always lying. Why are you lying now?”

“It’s- It’s nothing, really, I…” Daniel trailed off when the pair of them fixed disbelieving glares on him. Why, why, did Drake have to choose then, of all times? Better than when he was stuck on the truck, that was for sure, but Daniel was not prepared to try getting this past both Austin and Alma. 

Both of them knew him far too well, were far too familiar with his bullshit.

“Dan?” Austin sounded concerned, and that was what had Daniel admitting,

“It was Drake.”

“Officer Drake?”

“Why is that motherfucker calling you?” Alma spat. “What, the moment you’re back in town, he thinks he owns you again?”

“He’s not in El Paso,” he quietly told her. “He’s in Los Angeles. He’s a detective now.”

“That’s why you… You came to mine, afterwards. You reeked of cigarettes.” Austin sounded horrified. “That was months ago.”

“No. No. Dan, no.” Alma was shaking her head. “Why? Buck’s an adult, he doesn’t have any DA friends up there. Why? Why are you giving that man any power over you again?”

“He threatened to take Eddie’s kid away.”

“Of course he did.” She let out a sigh, soft and sad. “And Eddie is such a shitty father that-”

“No!” Daniel snapped, surprising even himself. “He’s a great dad. An idiot, but a great dad.”

“Then why would anyone take his kid away?” Alma asked. Daniel opened his mouth, but it was Austin who answered with,

“They wouldn’t.”

“You don’t know that,” Daniel argued.

“They don’t just come in and take a kid without reason!” Austin snapped. “I’ve listened in on Wilson and them often enough to know that. Someone would show up and take a look, and then call it a day. Because you just said that he’s a great dad.”

“You don’t know that,” he said again, the words weak even to his own ears. Austin let out a huff and threw up his hands, turning on his heel to stomp inside. Daniel winced when the door slammed shut.

“Eddie and Chris aren’t you and Buck,” Alma told him. “Stop giving that man power that he doesn’t have.”

And then it was just Daniel in Iggy’s backyard, the phone still clutched in his hand.

Chapter 29

The sound of his phone buzzing with a new text startled Daniel, even as he’d been expecting it. He stared at the screen, at the command beckoning him over like a dog. Then he took a breath, straightened his spine, and tapped out his response. One word, two letters.

They’d been back from Texas for only a day. Honestly, Daniel had expected Drake to demand his presence earlier than this, and had been dreading it the closer to Los Angeles they got. He was just thankful that no one seemed to have picked up on the awkward air between himself and Austin after they left Alma’s. Helped, no doubt, by Austin’s usual stoicism.

In his hand, his phone began to ring, tearing him out of his thoughts. His heart skipped a beat and he leaped to his feet, to grab his bag. Daniel suddenly did not want to be in this apartment for a moment longer, not alone. Buck was out at Eddie’s, catching up with Chris. Albert was out delivering other people’s meals to them or whatever he did. The apartment was empty, just him and the sound of the ringtone he’d chosen for Drake.

It didn’t take long for Daniel to pack his bag, stuffing in everything he’d need for work in the morning along with fresh civvies. Then he was out the door, the ringing of his phone blessedly ending, only to start up again in the parking lot. It would probably be easier to turn his phone off, or put it on silent, but long years of Buck-related paranoia turned him away from the thought before it was even finished. He was just thankful that Drake wasn’t lurking about as he liked doing, but that was only because he’d been at home waiting for Daniel to come to heel like a well-trained dog.

There wasn’t much thought in where to go, in where to run to, muscle memory leading the way. It wasn’t that far of a drive, thankfully, and he was climbing the few flights of stairs he needed to before reaching the right door. Once there, however, he hesitated just flinging it open and flouncing right in, uncertain if he’d be as welcome as he would’ve been before the argument in El Paso.

So, instead, he raised his fist and rapped it against the wood. The door opened after only a couple of moments.

“Why did you knock?” Austin asked, frowning at him as he stepped aside.

Daniel opened his mouth to answer, only for his phone to cut him off as it began to ring once more. He cringed as he entered the apartment and dropped his bag by the couch before toeing off his shoes. His phone was laid face down on the end table.

“You’re not going to answer that?” Austin asked him.

“Nope.” Daniel gave him a smile that didn’t quite feel right, letting the call go to voicemail once more before flopping onto the couch. The smile slipped away when he saw that there was no sweater draped across the back tonight; Austin was still wearing it, not yet having overheated enough to abandon it.

“Please, make yourself at home.” Austin’s sarcasm wasn’t quite as scathing as it could be. “There’s chicken alfredo in the fridge, if you-”

Once again, Daniel’s phone began to ring. He and Austin both stared at it, Austin’s usual blank expression breaking with a scowl.

“They’re insistent,” he commented.

“He’s pissed,” Daniel corrected. 

Austin’s eyes darted to him and then back to the phone, before picking it up. The scowl on his face deepened as he saw the caller ID. Daniel braced himself for whatever the other man was going to say when he opened his mouth, only to be caught off-guard when all he said was,

“You could block his number, you know.”

“I don’t actually know how,” Daniel sheepishly confessed.

Austin scoffed, rolled his eyes, and did something on his phone. Then he was tossing it to Daniel, who managed to catch it easily enough. Then the question that he’d been expecting came, in the form of a simple,

“Why?”

“Because you were right. You and Alma were both right.” Daniel shrugged. “Me having custody of Buck always felt so dubious, like the slightest mistake would have him getting sent right back to Mom and Dad, and I spent so long terrified of him being taken away, being sent back to Hershey. Or- Or worse. I spent so long listening to Drake’s threats, knowing he could follow through with them, that when he showed up here and started making them again, I just… Went right back to it. Didn’t even think about it.”

Austin huffed and shook his head, but didn’t say anything that he may have been thinking. Instead, he disappeared into the other room, leaving Daniel on the couch debating if he wanted to dig out the alfredo that Austin had mentioned. He’d finally decided on it, and was getting up to pilfer the fridge, when fabric was suddenly thrown into his face.

One of Austin’s sweaters, still warm from the drier.

“I found a place to watch Conan the Barbarian,” Austin said as Daniel tugged on the sweater. Once his head popped out of the appropriate hole, Daniel saw Austin had the alfredo out of the fridge, pouring milk in and stirring it up with a fork to reheat. “Want a beer?”

“Please.”

They watched the movie, poking fun at it as they did, and then watched the sequel to do the same. It did wonders to help Daniel relax, the haunting specter of Drake’s anger forgotten for the moment. When the second movie ended, and it was time to bunk down for the night, Daniel waited for his turn in the bathroom. When he came out and started gathering the usual blanket and spare pillows from the closet, Austin just rolled his eyes and took them from him, tossing them onto the bed.

“I mean, it’s a bit sudden, coming from-”

“Dan.” Austin didn’t even sound upset at the joke, and was probably even expecting it, but Daniel still flushed with a sense of guilt.

“Are you sure? I’m fine with the couch.” That was a lie, Austin’s couch wasn’t quite long enough to be comfortable, but he’d made do before and he would make do again.

“Just get in the bed.”

There were some calls that they responded to which had Eddie really missing Buck at his side. Even though at this point, he’d been doing this job without Buck longer than he’d done it with him, it had still been a lot more fun at times when the other man was there. Even when they were barely friends.

The current call was a woman who’d been shot and left to float facedown in her own pool. Which, okay, maybe not the kind of call that one would normally have fun on, but without Buck there, he was left without anyone to share his thoughts and comments with. Like the fact that this lady had more gnomes in her backyard than Iggy did at his place. Lamer ones, too, the kind of plain kitsch that suburban white people just adored. Or the fact that there was a perfect shoe print on the broken back gate.

“Did someone kick that down?” he asked as he walked past it.

“Yeah, me. It was latched from the inside, same for the front door,” Athena answered. “Crime Scene unit’s on the way, we just need to get medical confirmation that she’s dead.”

“On it.” Chimney dropped his medical kit, which was more than a bit superfluous at this moment, and grabbed a pool hook to pull the body closer. The paramedic had been a bit tense ever since everyone returned from Texas, and there wasn’t any clear reason why that might be.

Eddie, left to twiddle his thumbs, looked about the place. If everything was locked from the inside, then how did the murderer get in? How did they get out? It was a locked-room mystery- No, no, a locked- yard mystery. Buck would get an absolute kick out of this.

Was it a home invasion gone bad? Perhaps a murder for hire? Eddie needed to ask if she was married, because in those true crime stories that Buck had gotten into over the pandemic, in between binge fests of Supernatural with Danny, the husband was usually the culprit.

“Calling it,” Hen declared as she looked over the victim’s hand. She and Chimney had the body at the edge of the pool, anchored to keep from floating away. “Definitely some signs of struggle. Looks like a fresh manicure, too.”

“Guess that the broken nail would have bugged her less than the bullet hole,” Chimney added.

“You got an ID for the paperwork?”

“Delia Narwood.” A detective, one that Eddie didn’t remember interacting with before. He was looking over his notepad as he swaggered along, mouth working at a piece of gum beneath his mask. The drawl was distinctly Texan, specifically Eddie’s part of Texas. “Owns the house, the only person who lives-”

He tripped over a gnome that stood by the pool’s edge, Eddie managing to catch him before he hit the deck and getting a noseful of cigarette smoke for his troubles. The detective barely paid him any mind, choosing instead to glare at the gnome as he straightened up.

“She lived alone,” the detective finished.

Lying not far from the gnome that the detective tripped on was a phone in a pink case, its screen broken. There was a shell casing right next to it. On the nearby table was a pile of mail. A quick glance at them revealed that,

“None of this mail’s addressed to Delia Narwood,” Eddie told the others. “It’s not even the right house number.”

Was she stealing people’s mail? Did she see or find something worth killing over?

“She was on the phone with Nine-One-One when she was shot,” the detective mentioned to Athena. “But she wasn’t calling about an intruder. Probably just a coincidence.”

“Ms Narwood treated Nine-One-One like her own personal grievance hotline,” Athena said. “So I’d say that the odds of that happening were above average.”

“How often did she call?” Eddie asked, curious. The sergeant gave him an unimpressed side-eye, but answered all the same.

“Thirteen times. In the last six months.”

Yeesh.

The last time that Buck had seen Danny this angry, was… He couldn’t remember, actually. Sure, Danny had been angry when he caught Buck in the middle of trying to run off to rescue Hen with just TK for back-up, but it hadn’t been to this level. The time Buck confessed to wanting to try out with the SEALs, maybe? Or before that, the last time Buck had actually spoken with his parents?

Speaking of…

“You invited Mom and Dad to visit?” Danny spat, so venomous that Buck half expected the words to chew away at the walls of the apartment. 

“Yes.” Maddie was managing to weather the force of their brother’s anger far better than Buck would ever manage in her stead. He, currently, had the couch between them and himself.

“And you didn’t think to mention this before!?”

“You were both in Texas,” she said with a shrug. “And I wasn’t completely sure they were coming.”

“So you waited to tell us until they crossed the California state lane.” Danny sneered, an expression that Buck had never seen him direct at their sister before. He’d never seen him this angry with Maddie before. “When it was too late to tell you how fucking stupid that was. Why the hell would you invite them here?”

“I just want my little girl to have a normal family,” Maddie retorted, hands falling to her stomach. “With uncles and grandparents that she might actually know.”

“Then maybe you shoulda gotten knocked up by a guy who has one of those,” Buck couldn’t help but say. His sister shot him a dirty look for it.

“That is not funny,” she chastised.

“Better yet,” Danny said. “Maybe you should take her to visit them after she’s born.”

“Maybe I want them here, now,” Maddie snapped. “They’re my parents, too, Dan. They’re my baby’s grandparents. I want them here, so I invited them.”

“Why!?” Danny snapped back. “Why the hell do you want them anywhere near your kid? There was a reason I took Buck and ran, Maddie! There was a reason why I put so much effort into making sure he never had to deal with them again! And yet here you are, fucking inviting them into his life again because of what you want.”

“I told you he would’ve been fine with them! You didn’t have to center your entire life around protecting him from Mom and Dad, like some damn martyr!”

“Someone had to, because you certainly didn’t bother trying!”

Buck was tempted to hide behind the couch or in his room, getting the same uneasy feeling he did those rare times their parents would get into an argument in front of them.

“Um,” he said, the simple sound enough to get both of their attention. A flash of guilt crossed over both their faces. “I’m- I’m sure it’ll be fine.”

Buck actually severely doubted that was going to be the case. He remembered how Mom reacted to him simply playing football, there was no way she’d react any calmer to his chosen career. 

“Yeah,” Maddie agreed with a nod. “And maybe… Maybe this’ll be a good thing, you know? You could both talk to Mom and Dad, tell them how you’ve been feeling. It could be good for your therapy.”

“Or cause us to need more of it,” Danny grumbled. Buck found himself nodding in agreement.

“Listen, I’m willing to try,” she said. “And maybe Mom and Dad are, too.”

“Fine.” He let out a huff. “Fine! But you and me, Maddie? United front. The moment, the moment, they start in on Buck, we both stop it.”

“They won’t.”

“Maddie.”

“Fine, yes, I promise. But it’ll be fine,” she said again. “Chimney’ll be there, too, and so will Albert.”

“Albert’s coming?” Buck asked, feeling bad for the guy. He was about to get a front row seat to the kind of family drama that was best experienced secondhand. “Why?”

“He’s gonna be an uncle, too,” Maddie pointed out. “Why wouldn’t he?”

Buck and Danny shared a glance, but both of them chose to bite their tongues just then.

So it turned out that the reason Chimney had been so tense was because the Buckley parents were coming into town. Eddie, vividly remembering the one and only time he’d met them, found himself perfectly understanding why that would be the case. Hell, he was feeling tense about it, and he didn’t really have to be there. He was going to be there, though, because he was not going to leave Buck to face that mess alone, and he definitely didn’t want to leave Danny as the sole person standing between the Buckley parents and Buck.

That tension followed Eddie, and Chimney, to the next shift at the station. It felt like watching storm clouds rolling in over the desert, knowing that it was going to be bad when it hit. There was nothing to do but batten down the hatches, though.

“How’s Buck handling it?” Bobby asked as they went about setting the table for dinner. Well, Eddie and them were setting the table. The captain was finishing up the cooking.

“When I texted him, he said he was having an emergency session with Dr. Copeland,” Eddie answered as he carried over the stack of plates. “He’s asking her for advice on de-escalation techniques.”

“What, is he afraid his parents’ visit is gonna turn into a hostage situation?”

“More like he’s worried Danny’s gonna explode on them.”

Bobby paused in thought and then nodded, because he, of all people, understood how reasonable that concern was.

“Have you ever met them, Eddie?” Hen asked, carrying the salad to the table. “You had to have met them at least once, right?”

“Once,” Eddie said.

Hen waited for him to expand on that answer, frowning when he didn’t.

“‘Cause I just look at Maddie and Dan,” she said after a moment. “And then I look at Buck, and I’m like, there’s a story there.”

The laugh that Eddie let out was bitter. The snort from Chimney was just amused. But the little “ha!” from Bobby was surprising.

“I’m guessing Maddie told you?” he asked Chimney.

“Yeah, she did,” the other man said. “You said there weren't any deep, dark Buckley family secrets!”

“It’s not a secret! Cap even knows about it. Apparently.” He turned to Bobby. “When did Buck tell you?”

“His probational year,” the captain answered. “I think he was trying to make me feel better about something. But he referred to himself as spare parts.”

Eddie winced, all too familiar with that attitude from his boyfriend. He wondered how much luck Copeland was having with tackling that topic, or if they’d even begun to broach it yet. There’d been a couple sessions, he knew, that focused entirely on the only other time that Buck had tried therapy, but Eddie hadn’t much of the details beyond that.

“What am I missing here?” Hen sounded vaguely annoyed but mostly curious. “Whatever it is, it’s apparently something big. Which, rude, I’ve known Buckaroo just as long as the rest of you. Most of you.”

“When Danny was a kid, he was sick,” Eddie explained as he set the plates down at each seat. Chimney followed along with the silverware. “He had, uh… I’m not actually sure what he had. Cancer, I think?”

“Leukemia,” Bobby supplied.

“Right, well, according to Buck,” Eddie continued, “Danny was sick as a kid. And that’s why their parents had him, to make Danny better. That that’s what he’s supposed to do, and it’s cool, because at least he’s useful.”

Did that come out bitter? That probably came out bitter.

“He’s a savior sibling,” Bobby said. He was looking troubled about something, frowning heavily at the casserole cooling on the island. “I looked it up afterwards. He’s a genetic match with Daniel for transplants.”

“Their mother apparently wasn’t very shy about telling them about it, either. That Buck was literally made for Danny,” Eddie said. He paused as he set down a plate, tilting his head as a thought struck him. “I think that might be why Danny’s the way he is with him. Took it a bit seriously, I guess.”

“Oh, wow.” Hen was wide-eyed as she looked between them. “Okay, this all explains… A lot, actually.”

“Yeah.” The captain’s words were quiet. “It really does.”

Chapter 30

Chapter Notes

CW at the start for Drake and all the nastiness that his presence implies. Specifically, the implied threat of physical violence, and attempted sexual coercion. Also some ableist language.
Also, the Buckley parents are here.

See the end of the chapter for more notes

“They were gossiping about you today.”

Daniel scoffed and leaned against the tool box. It started to roll away, so he locked the wheels with his foot. The truck bay was empty, everyone else relaxing elsewhere in the station as the hour grew later. He could hear the occasional burst of laughter from the direction of the entertainment room, and the sound of traffic carried through the open bay doors. They’d have to be closed, since everyone would be bunking down soon.  Otherwise someone could just wander in without any of them noticing.

“They were gossiping about me?”

“Well, about your family,” Austin said. “Sharing notes or whatever about Buck being a savior sibling. Cap seemed bothered by something afterwards.”

“Probably wishing that it hadn’t worked,” Daniel said, a joke that came nowhere close to the mark. Austin just scoffed at him. “How did that come up, anyway?”

“Hen asked about your parents, pointed out the age difference between the two of you and Buck.”  

“The age difference isn’t that big.”

“Big enough to be noticeable,” Austin responded. “When is this drama happening?”

“Tomorrow afternoon,” Daniel answered. “Mom actually called me when she and Dad got to their hotel.”

“Are you going to see them?”

“I’m gonna see them tomorrow at Maddie’s.”

“Not what I meant,” Austin said with a sigh. There was a moment of silence on the other end of the call, filled with awkwardness and almost palpable uncertainty. Daniel found himself frowning at his phone. “Do you want me to be there?”

“To be there?” Daniel repeated dumbly.

“Yeah. It’s only fair, right? You come with me to my family get-togethers to keep my parents off my back. Do you want me to be there, do the same for you?”

“God, no,” he blurted out. “You don’t even like going to your own family things, and your family’s great! I know you complain about your folks, but they actually love all their kids. Tomorrow, Mom’s gonna call Buck selfish for doing the same job I do, and I’m gonna have to yell at her and Dad’ll get on my shit ‘cause his wife comes before his kids. Then after that I’ll have to deal with Maddie defending them. It’ll be a shitshow and I- You don’t deserve to suffer through that.”

Daniel almost said “and I love you too much to put you through that,” but managed to catch himself just in time. He knew better than to say that aloud, and he didn’t want to put Austin in that awkward position of having to deal with it.

“Are you sure?”

“Positive.”

“I’ll be a call away if you change your mind,” Austin said. “And you’re always welcome here, if you need to hide somewhere afterwards.”

Daniel ducked his head, finding himself smiling down at his shoes.

“Yeah, I know.”

The call wrapped itself up a short time later, and Daniel remembered what he’d been about to do before Austin called him. He’d been about to put the tool box in its spot against the wall, somewhere out of the way. A kick of his foot had the wheels unlocked again and he pushed it across the bay, passing the engine as he did.

Then, the flick of a lighter, and a voice in that damnably familiar drawl.

“Howdy.”

Daniel stumbled to a stop, the tool box continuing its momentum forward. There, leaning against the side of the engine, was Drake. He was dressed in a suit, the kind he favored while working these days, but he was lighting up a cigarette that hung from his mouth, so he was off-duty. Typically, he resorted to gum for his cravings when he was on the clock.

“You’re not supposed to smoke in here,” Daniel said, feeling dumb and numb, his feet frozen to the floor.

“Call the cops, then,” Drake sneered. The detective pushed himself off and stepped forward, taking a curving path that, because he turned to keep the man in view, put the back of the engine behind Daniel. “You’ve been ignoring me.”

Daniel drew in a shaking breath and straightened up. 

“Yeah,” he managed to get out.

“That isn’t how this works, Dan,” the detective spat. “I tell you to come, you come. Like the well-trained dog you are.”

“No.”

Drake’s expression was one of utter bewilderment.

“No?” he repeated. “I’m sorry, did the whore just tell me no?”

“I told you before, I’m not a whore anymore,” Daniel said. The words came out quiet and trembling. “And I told you no.”

“Did you hit your head?” Drake spat, stalking close. Daniel scrambled backwards, until the back of his legs hit the engine’s bumper and he lost his balance, shoulders falling against the bright red metal. Despite being shorter, it still felt like Drake was managing to loom over him. “Did you forget what I can do? You either spread your legs when I tell you to spread ‘em, or the Diaz kid gets a visit from CPS. Is that what you want? We both know what kind of homes that cripple could end up at.”

“Call them then,” Daniel dared, his heart a wardrum in his chest. “Do it.”

Drake stared at him, brow creased and head tilted.

“You’re serious,” he whispered, taking his cigarette out of his mouth and holding it between his fingers. “What, realize you didn’t care about him as much as you thought?”

“Eddie’s a great dad,” was Daniel’s answer.

Drake blinked at him, and then his face twisted with rage. He lunged forward with the cigarette and Daniel cringed back, unable to go anywhere. But, instead of aiming for his face, the cigarette ended up smashed against the metal of the fire engine. It was right beside Daniel’s head, so close that the detective’s hand brushed against his cheek.

“A whore is a whore,” Drake growled. “I guess I’ll just have to remind you again.”

“Fuck off.”

The detective’s lips curled with a snarl, but he stepped back all the same. Daniel watched, hardly daring to move, as he stomped away and out of the station. The moment Drake was outside, Daniel rushed for the button to lower the doors. He didn’t relax even when they were closed.

Daniel was left with the silence and the come down from the adrenaline and the hope that he hadn’t just made a horrible mistake.

Everyone froze like startled deer at the sound of knocking at the door. Buck drew in his breath, fingers clutching at the box of liquor and spirits he held, as Maddie went to go answer it. He relaxed at the sight of his harried boyfriend.

“I’m here, I’m here,” he said, dashing inside. He went directly for Buck’s side, giving him a quick kiss that Buck would’ve liked to have lasted longer if not for the company. “Sorry, traffic was a pain.”

They were gathered at Chimney and Maddie’s for the Buckley parents’ arrival. Eddie had been taking Chris to the Wilsons, a trip that Buck would’ve gladly joined him on but he knew the temptation to just stay at the Wilsons instead of facing his parents would’ve been too great. But any moment now, Mom and Dad would be showing up.

“You got here just in time,” Buck said, throwing his boyfriend a smile. He set the box down on the island. “Okay, I have wine: red, white, and sparkling, in case you wanna do any celebratory toasts-”

“Why?” Danny asked, leaning against the kitchen counters. “The hell will we have to celebrate tonight?”

Maddie scowled at him and then gestured down at her stomach. Buck decided that they needed to quickly move on before a fight broke out between them; Danny had been in a mood all day.

“Um, uh, we also have tequila.” Buck lifted up the bottle. Well, one of them. Albert took out the other. “I’m not sure why we needed two bottles.”

“Those are for me,” Chimney said, lunging forward to snag the bottles out of their hands.

“You’re sharing that,” Danny declared. Chimney didn’t even argue, just brought down another glass to fill alongside his own.

“Go preheat the oven,” Buck told Albert, smacking him lightly on the arm. The younger Han made a face at him, but he went to do it all the same. “Three fifty.”

“We’re baking stuff?” Maddie’s nose wrinkled a little, a hint of exasperation in her voice.

“Baked brie and fig jam,” he said, holding them both up for her to see.

“Since when did you start liking fig?”

“Since Abuela sent me a jar of the stuff to try,” Eddie answered. “He and Chris-”

Once again, rapping at the door had them all freezing, heads turning to the sound. Buck tossed the brie to Albert, who slid it into the oven. Chimney and Danny both threw back their shots of tequila, looking for all the world like they were preparing themselves for war.

“Remember, Maddie.” Danny wasn’t even looking at her, gaze focused on the door still. “The moment they start…”

“It’ll be fine,” she said as she went to open it. She drew in a breath, put on a smile, and pulled it open. “Mom! Dad! Come in.”

It was weird, Buck thought, to see how old his parents had gotten. Wrinkles were etched into both of their faces, and Dad’s hair was almost solidly gray. It was also weird to see how much they hadn’t changed. Both of them even had pretty much the same hairstyle as years ago, both of them were pretty much dressed the same as they were then.

Eddie’s arm wrapped around his waist, and his hand gave him a comforting squeeze.

“You guys did not have to bring presents,” Maddie said. Dad had a rocking horse- Well, a rocking elephant, a fuzzy grey thing. Mom was carrying a giant basket of stuff, wrapped in plastic. Buck could see clothes and stuffed animals, amongst other things.

“We’re grandparents now,” Dad declared. “Spoiling comes with the job.”

“Mr. and Mrs. Buckley, hi! I’m Howard Han.” Chimney hurried forward. “It’s nice to finally meet you both.”

In unison, Danny and Eddie let out quiet snorts. They sounded almost identical, actually.

“Let me take this from you,” Chimney said, lifting the basket from Mom’s arms. 

A pat on his back had Buck looking to his side, to see Danny going past. Buck drew in a breath and followed him. The comforting weight of Eddie’s arm fell away, and he immediately missed it.

“Daniel!” Mom beamed, wrapping her arms around Danny, who awkwardly patted her on the back and said,

“Hi, Mom. Dad.”

“You’re looking good, son,” Dad said, clapping his oldest son on the shoulder. His eyes moved past Danny and spotted Buck, hanging back. “You both are.”

“Thanks,” Buck mumbled, feeling a bit awkward. Mom hadn’t even looked his way. “Uh, Mom, Dad, you remember Eddie. From El Paso.”

His parents frowned at his boyfriend in confusion, surprise evident, but they nodded all the same.

“Ah, yes, your friend Edmundo,” Dad said. “I didn’t expect to see him here.”

“Here” could’ve meant just in Los Angeles, which was understandable with El Paso so far away. But there was a hint of a question to Dad’s tone which had Buck thinking that “here” specifically meant in Chimney’s apartment, at their family visit. Eddie clearly caught it, too, as he stepped up beside Buck and said, sounding what might’ve been convincingly nonchalant to anyone that hadn’t known him for so long,

“Of course I’m here, we’re dating.”

Dad blinked. Mom let out a little “oh.” There was a moment of painful awkwardness, no one saying anything, until Chimney broke the silence.

“And this is my brother, Albert,” he said, with a gesture to his brother.

“And Buck and Danny’s roommate,” Albert said with a smile that only looked partially faked. “It’s a pleasure to meet you both.”

“Buck and Danny.” Mom’s distaste was clear, and Buck winced. “You’re still letting people call you that?”

“They’re just nicknames,” Danny said, a hint of warning to the words. Mom scoffed.

“I’d just thought you’d outgrown that silliness, though I suppose I shouldn’t be surprised about Evan.” Mom clearly did not notice the glare that Danny was giving her. “We gave you both such lovely names, you should use them.”

“But…” Eddie started, but a glance from Danny had him falling silent.

“You guys don’t like nicknames?” Chimney asked, both he and his brother looking horribly awkward. “But, Maddie…”

“Is the name on my birth certificate,” Maddie informed him, rictus smile in place.

“Would anyone like something to drink? We have many options.” Albert yanked out a pair of bottles from the box Buck brought, seemingly at random. Under his breath, presumably with the intent to not be overheard like he was, he added, “I believe I’ll start with tequila.”

He and Chimney started for living room area, but Dad caught Chimney on the way with,

“So, Howard- Do people call you Howard?”

Chimney threw Maddie a slightly panicked glance, smiled, and said,

“Yes. Yes they do. Please, this way.”

He led them away, leaving Eddie and the Buckley siblings behind. Buck let out a sigh and let himself lean into Eddie’s side a bit.

“It’ll be fine,” Maddie insisted, holding out her hands, pinkies extended.

Danny rolled his eyes, even as he wrapped his own pinky around one. Buck did the same on her other side.

“I’m getting some tequila,” Eddie whispered into Buck’s ear, and he had to smother the laugh.

To start with, at least, things didn’t go that badly. They had dinner around Chimney’s coffee table instead of the dining table, for whatever reason, and conversation was awkward and stilted. For the most part, Buck just slid under the radar, content to allow Chimney and Maddie and Danny to shoulder the attention. Occasionally Mom or Dad would say something that would have Eddie looking at Buck in such a way that he had to struggle to keep from laughing, but it was going far better than the last time he’d seen his parents.

Mostly.

For the most part.

“I’m glad you had a nice drive,” Maddie told them, after they’d regaled everyone with the journey across the states. And by regale, Buck meant that the only reason he didn’t pull out his phone to entertain himself was because he knew it would be rude and he didn’t want to break the peace.

“We saw a lot of the country,” Dad said. He took the drink that Chimney handed him, but his attention was focused on his wife as she spoke.

“The first few days, there was nothing but rain,” Mom added. “Then we got here, blue skies and sunshine.”

“That’s Cali, for you,” Danny said, returning with his own drink. It was almost certainly more tequila.

“Where’s mine?” Eddie asked.

“You’ve got all your limbs.”

“We had a lot of rain earlier in the year,” Buck said, clutching his own glass of wine. Mom turned to look at him, and he quailed slightly at the visible disinterest in her eyes. “But… But lately it’s been dry…”

Mom let out a quiet, polite little hum. Buck shrunk in on himself even further.

Albert, sensing the encroaching awkwardness - or perhaps spotting the darkening expression on Danny’s face - burst out with,

“I can’t believe you drove all the way across the country in an RV. That sounds exciting.”

“Statistically speaking,” Dad said, “it seemed the safest way to travel right now.”

“Yeah, we didn’t want to take any chances,” Mom said. “Given Maddie’s condition and it being a high-risk pregnancy.”

“It’s not really high-risk,” Chimney tried.

“Oh, she’s over thirty-five, that-”

“Mom!” Danny snapped.

“What, Daniel? It’s true. She shouldn’t be taking any chances.” Mom laughed a little as she added, “Not when she’s waited this long.”

“Mom!” Danny snapped again, while everyone else looked increasingly uncomfortable. Maddie especially, a hand going up to clutch at the one Chimney had latched to her shoulder.

“She was just waiting for the right time,” Buck said, rising up to defend his sister as he always used to. “The right guy.”

“God knows it wasn’t Doug,” Dad said, and Mom nodded in agreement.

“Okay.” Maddie’s voice was sharp. “Let’s not talk about him.”

“Of course, I’m sorry, I’m just so happy to see you happy,” Dad said, and then leaned forward a little. “Now, boys, your sister said you’ve both been going to therapy?”

“She- She did?” Buck managed to get out. His brother slowly turned his head to face Maddie and while he couldn’t see the expression on his face, he knew by the set of his shoulders and the way his grip tightened on his glass that it could not have been a friendly one.

Eddie pressed closer to him, a comforting heat along his side.

“Should we be worried?” Mom asked, attention focused on Danny.

“No,” was his short answer.

“What about you, Evan?” Dad asked. “Everything okay there?”

“How is that any of your business?” Danny demanded, voice hard, before Buck could think of an answer. Chimney quickly retreated to the kitchen with a comment about getting water with Albert following in his wake.

“He’s my son-”

Danny’s laugh was sharp and unkind. Buck felt Eddie flinch at the sound of it.

“I was raising him long before the two of you signed the paperwork,” he said. “Hell, even his teachers knew that.”

“There’s nothing wrong,” Buck hurried to say, desperate to defuse this situation before things exploded. “It’s- It’s the job, you know? It’s good to try and get ahead of it.”

“Right. The job.” For once that night, Mom looked at him with something other than apathy. And Buck regretted it, because he knew what was coming. So did Danny, already puffing up to start shouting.

“I saw a therapist,” Maddie broke in, derailing the ensuing argument. Buck let out a sigh of relief when Mom’s attention turned to her, and turned kinder. “You know, after…”

“Yes, the business with the husband who shall not be named,” Mom said. “Your father and I went to see a therapist afterwards, too.”

“Why?” Eddie asked, drawing the word out slightly.

“We felt like there were some things we needed to work through.”

Eddie stared at her and then, slowly, turned his head to give Buck an incredulous stare.

“So you…” Maddie paused, like she was trying to wrap her head around what Mom was saying. “You went and talked to a therapist about my problems?”

“It wasn’t as if you wanted to talk to us about them,” Dad argued. “Daniel was the one who called and told us Doug was dead.”

“Figured you wouldn’t want to find out about it on the news,” Danny snarked.

The silence that followed was tense again, the air heavy. Buck’s fingers tightened around his glass of wine, shoulders hunched up around his ears. It was like Mom and Dad had brought the atmosphere of his childhood home with them to Los Angeles.

“It’s probably time to go pick up Chris,” Eddie suddenly announced. “Buck, c’mon.”

“What?” Buck blinked dumbly for a moment, and then hurriedly nodded. “Right! Yeah!”

He sat the wine down on the table and got to his feet, seeing his brother relax as he did. He felt absolutely no remorse as he followed Eddie out into the hallway, the door closing behind them just as Dad was asking,

“Who’s Chris?”

Chapter End Notes

I consciously dialed back the shouting in this chapter, to save it for later.

Chapter 31

Chapter Notes

CW for Det. Drake just being an awful, irredeemable creep.

See the end of the chapter for more notes

Sometimes, Athena could sympathize with people’s views of her chosen profession. Oh, sure, she’d wish they wouldn’t paint everyone with the same brush, but there were those she worked with - far too many, actually - for whom the color they were painted with was a fitting shade. She’d been doing this job for a very long time, a black woman in a white man’s field who started when things were particularly rough, during the height of Operation Hammer and just before the ‘92 riots. She’d had a few years under her belt by the time of the Rampart scandal. She knew how that all looked to those on the outside. She knew how those on the inside looked at her.

Sometimes, the only thing that had her clinging to her shield was the knowledge that some of the people she pulled over were far safer in her hands than they would have been with another officer. Like that rat bastard that pointed a gun at her baby.

Emmett, her late fiance, hadn’t been like that, though. Nor was his partner, Rick. Nor was Lou Ransone, or her captain, Elaine, or Officer Williams. The police weren’t all the bad apples, the bastards, people declared them to be.

But they definitely weren’t all good guys with a gun, either. She had to admit that, she had no choice but to admit it. Especially when she had to (almost literally, in this case) pinch her nose and work with them.

The shooting death of Delia Narwood, left for dead in her own pool, in her locked backyard, was a mystery she had to really sink her teeth into. None of her neighbors liked her; she'd apparently filed lawsuits against almost all of them, along with complaints to the building department, the zoning board, and the Department of Waste Management. The latter because, apparently, a neighbor didn’t bring their trash can up from the curb early enough. There were police reports, too. 

Delia Narwood traumatized a little girl over her lemonade stand, because she didn’t have the proper permits. She poisoned a couple’s dog, almost killing the poor thing. The closest to a kind word that left a neighbor’s mouth about her was calling her miserable and unhappy, but at least she was won over with baked goods.

It was the kind of case, the kind of mystery, she would have enjoyed getting to the bottom of normally. She would’ve been enjoying it, if she’d been working with Rick or Lou. Unfortunately, however, the detective assigned to it was a transfer from Texas. He hadn’t been with their department long, starting just before the pandemic rolled in, and Athena hadn’t truly crossed paths with him before now. She wished that reprieve lasted longer.

Lucas Drake, as if summoned just by thinking about him, interrupted her while she was finishing up reports. He stopped at the open door, thankfully, because the acrid stench of cigarettes seemed to cling to him at all times. Plus, he hadn’t even bothered to put on his mask properly, letting it dangle from an ear.

“Hey, darlin’,” he drawled. Athena twitched at the endearment, managing to keep the snarl contained. For the moment. She’d already asked Elaine to never, ever be assigned to any of his cases again, if it could be helped. “Got a call about the crime scene this morning. Unit drove by and saw that someone broke the seal on the front door.”

“Someone broke into Delia’s house?”

“Yeah, they ransacked-” Drake cut himself off, turning his head and lifting his mask up over his mouth as he started coughing. It was wet, wheezing and crackling. Just a smoker’s cough, hopefully, but Athena was glad she had both vaccination shots and that there was space between her and him.

She tugged her mask up over her face, all the same.

“They ransacked the place,” the detective continued when he was done, pausing to clear his throat. “Found a bunch of white powder everywhere when I went to go check it out. It’s not drugs - that queer couple seemed more the type for that, anyway.” 

Athena twitched again, because he was referring to the black queer couple. Which was undoubtedly the only reason why he thought they “seemed more the type.”

“So what was it then?” she asked, managing to keep her temper in check.

“Flour, pretty sure,” Drake answered.

The neighbor that claimed to win Delia over with baked goods was named Rita. According to her husband, Melvin, she’d picked up baking as a hobby and was constantly covered in flour.

They dragged out the evidence boxes for the case and dumped their contents out on a table, starting from either end. Their belief was that the person who broke into the house was after something the crime scene techs collected, which was just about everything. Athena ended up pawing through the mail. Mail that, as Eddie had noted at the scene, was not addressed to Delia Narwood. One piece of mail in particular stuck out to Athena, an open envelope addressed to one Jeanine R. Crowder, a name she did not remember as belonging to any of the neighbors.

The address, though, was Rita’s. So was the face that came up when Athena searched for Jeanine Crowder in their database, who turned out to be wanted for larceny, fraud, identity theft, and bigamy. When they arrested her, they also found a gun stashed away in her kitchen.

Drake led the interrogation the next morning, while Athena observed from the other side of the glass and read through the forensics report on the gun. She started to regret not being in there with them almost instantly.

“Yes, I was married to three men at once,” Rita - Jeanine - confessed. “And yes, I ransacked Delia’s house. But I didn’t kill her!”

“Right. So it’s just a coincidence that we found the gun that killed her in your pantry,” Dake drawled. He was right behind Rita, one hand on the back of her chair and the other flat on the table, and loomed over her. Rita was shrinking away from him.

Athena rapped her knuckle on the window, just once, loud enough to be noticed. Drake looked up, face flickering with a scowl for a moment, and stepped away, dragging a paper evidence bag to him. He took out the gun that was inside it and laid it on the table.

“This gun is registered to you,” he said, tapping on it. “Under the name of Conchita Terrano. Gotta say, you’re far too pale to be a Conchita.”

“I said I didn’t kill her!”

“And I said your gun did,” Drake retorted. “Was it Conchita that killed her, then? Or Jeanine?”

“I didn’t have the gun when she was shot,” Rita said. “She did.”

“And how did that happen?”

“She was stealing my mail and using it to blackmail me,” Rita explained. Drake, for some reason, looked briefly amused. “So I went over to tell her we were done-”

“A lot of that going around,” Drake muttered, tone dark, just barely loud enough for Athena to hear.

“I was just gonna threaten her with it, make her back off,” Rita continued. “Then I tripped over that stupid gnome and she took the gun from me. Told me to go home and do what I was good at, conning stupid men.”

“That was probably good advice, that.” Drake grinned. It was slimy. “Always good to know your place. But how did the gun end up in your pantry?”

“Melvin and I were on the porch when we heard the shot,” she said. “I told him I was gonna call nine-one-one-”

“Which you didn’t do.”

“I thought Delia shot someone with my gun!” Rita retorted. Athena, sadly, could not fault her for trying to avoid that becoming known. If she was telling the truth. “I needed to find out, so I went over. Delta kept her place locked, but John and Joe-” The couple with the dog Delia nearly killed. “-didn’t, so I went into their backyard and looked over the fence. Do you know what’s worse than Delia killing someone with my gun? Delia getting killed by my gun. I knew how that would look. I mean…”

She gestured around at her current situation, sitting in an interrogation room because she was a murder suspect.

“So what did you do?” Drake asked, leaning over her again. Athena once more rapped her knuckles on the window, and he backed off. “Climb the garden wall?”

“No, there’s a little hole at the bottom. I used one of their dog toys. Y’know, that ball throwing thing? Archie - their corgi - got excited, so I tossed the ball and then used the toy to reach in and drag the gun over.”

“That’s a story,” Drake drawled. “Got any proof?”

“There’s the dog toy.”

“Cute.”

Athena frowned, flipped back through the report on the gun, and then hurried out of the observation room and into the interrogation room. She was opening the door just as Drake was talking about fetching officers to take Rita back to lock up.

“Show me your hands,” she demanded of the woman.

Rita was visibly confused, but held her hands up all the same. Athena turned them palm down and counted ten manicured, unbroken, unpolished fingernails. There’d been a piece of a fingernail, painted red, caught in the gun slide.

Delia Narwood had nine and a half fingernails when they brought her in, painted red. One of them was broken.

It turned out that Delia shot herself. Athena wasn’t certain why she had the gun at the time, presumably taking it upon herself to handle the block party she’d called 9-1-1 about, but her and Rita’s - Jeanine’s - fingerprints were the only ones on the gun. It also turned out that the hole in the garden wall that Rita mentioned was just large enough for Archie the corgi to squeeze through. So Delia, gun in hand, was startled by the dog she’d tried to murder, tripped over the garden gnome everyone kept tripping over, and shot herself in the chest before falling into the pool.

Death by misadventure. Or maybe karma.

Eddie figured he must love Buck very much, to be suffering through another dinner with the Buckley parents. He knew that Buck loved Maddie very much, to be suffering through one for her. Because that was the only reason Buck was here, Eddie knew: for his sister.

It started okay enough, kind of. Actually, it started pretty weird, in an unquantifiable way that Eddie was incapable of putting his finger on. Margaret and Phillip were just acting oddly, compared to the last dinner. They’d look at Danny, open their mouths, seem like they were about to say something. But every time, they’d change course. Even Chimney was picking up on it, shooting Eddie glances that conveyed his growing confusion.

Things almost derailed, though, before they even sat down for dinner. It turned out that the Buckleys brought their children baby boxes, wooden boxes filled with stuff from when they were kids. Well, more accurately, they brought two baby boxes - one with Mddie’s name, one with Danny’s.

“I thought you might wanna pass on some of these things to your little girl someday,” Margaret gushed.

Danny treated his box like it was a bomb, fitting for the day that Eddie and Chimney had, carefully setting it on the floor by his feet without even a glance inside. Maddie opened hers, pawing through the contents with Chimney over her shoulder, but she was soon frowning between it and her parents.

“Where’s Evan’s?” she asked. She’d been calling Buck by his birth name the entire time their parents were around.

The question had Margaret and Phillip shifting in their seats, and it had Buck shrinking where he stood in front of the stove. He was the one making dinner that night and Eddie hadn’t left his side, even when it meant he got in the way of Buck’s cooking. It was Danny, though, who spoke up.

“I have all of his stuff,” he told her, and then twisted around in his seat to face Buck. “I could get you a fancy box if you’d like, squirt. Need something better to keep those ornaments in than an old shoe box, anyway.”

“Can I choose the box?” Buck asked.

“Sure.”

“You have all of it?” Chimney asked. Eddie saw his eyes darting between the Buckleys and their children.

“A lot of stuff,” Danny hedged. He reached over to snag something from Maddie’s open box, one of those birth forms with the infant sized foot- and handprints. “I don’t think I have this for him.”

“Maybe I should make one for Chris,” Eddie said, craning his neck to look as well. “All of his things are just in folders and tubs. Shannon started a baby book, but she didn’t really keep up with it.”

Maddie’s frown, from what Eddie could see, was deep. But she shook her head and plucked out a tiny little shoe.

“I can’t believe you kept all of this,” she said.

“You thought we’d throw it away?” Phillip laughed.

“Not Maddie’s or Danny’s,” Buck commented under his breath. Eddie leaned in to kiss him on the cheek, getting a slightly dimmed smile in return.

“We may not have agreed with all the choices you made,” Margaret said with a smile that Eddie would’ve described as warm, if only he didn’t hate the woman. “But we never gave up hope that you’d come to your senses. And you did.”

“I liked them better when they were dead,” Eddie whispered to Buck, making his boyfriend snicker.

“Seriously?” Danny scoffed. There was no tequila tonight, much to Eddie’s disappointment, so the drink in Danny’s hand was just water. It had not improved his temperament. “You two didn’t even bother showing up to her wedding.”

“She was making a terrible mistake, Daniel,” Margaret said. “We told her that. We all told her that.”

“We did. She was,” Danny agreed, apparently oblivious to Maddie’s grimace. “You didn’t have to just abandon her for it.”

“At the time we thought cutting her off was for the best,” Phillip argued.

“We didn’t know what was going on,” Margaret said, a statement that had Danny slamming his glass down. “Maddie, I swear, we didn’t know-”

“You would have if you actually cared!” Danny snarled at her, making all of them jump. “I was there for a single day and realized what was going on. You lived in the same town as them! If you actually cared about-”

“Food’s done!” Buck called out, cutting through his brother’s rising voice.

“Oh thank God,” Chimney blurted out, almost tripping in his hurry to get out of his chair.

It was a tentative peace that followed, as everyone got their food and took a seat at the dining table. Not a peace that Eddie thought would last very long. He was fairly certain Buck, who hunched in on himself in his chair, and Danny, who was stabbing at his food, both thought the same. Something was bound to break it, and they came close a couple times, especially when Phillip made a joking comment about Buck’s ability to cook being a surprise.

Letting Chimney tell a work story, especially the story of their shift involving Mad Stan the bomber, who threatened to blow up the company that fired him, was probably, almost definitely a mistake. But he was the only one who seemed able to keep the conversation moving without having it fall into awkward, stilted silences, or petty aggressive quips that had Danny’s stabbing of his food increase in viciousness. So Chimney told Phillip and Margaret about Stan, with Eddie adding in some details, and the Buckley parents listened with polite attention.

“Well, I’m just glad everyone’s okay,” Margaret said.

“You all seem to have very dangerous jobs,” Phillip said. Danny’s fork scraped against his plate and Buck’s shoulders inched up.

“Not really,” Maddie argued. She was rubbing her stomach, almost like she was trying to soothe the baby. Or herself. “Most of the time, it’s pretty run of the mill.”

“And Stan wasn’t a bad guy,” Chimney said. “He just needed someone to see him and understand how much pain he was in. He probably wasn’t actually gonna blow the place up.”

Eddie thought about his second shift with Buck, the pair of them in an ambulance extracting an unexploded ordnance from a man’s leg. He nudged Buck with his elbow until he could catch his boyfriend’s eye, wagging his eyebrows. Buck stared at him in confusion for a moment and then seemed to realize exactly what Eddie was remembering, hiding his laugh behind his hand.

“It still seems very risky,” Phillip said. “I mean, from what I hear, Evan has spent quite a lot of time in hospitals.”

“Not that we’d expect anything different,” Margaret said.

“Mom,” Danny warned.

“It’s true,” she said, heedless of her oldest son’s growing anger as she turned to Buck, whose shoulders were up around his ears. “I thought you would have grown up by now. You’ve always been selfish, getting yourself hurt without caring what it meant for others. What would we do if something happened to you? What would Daniel do?”

“Shut up, Mom!”

Maddie closed her eyes and leaned back in her chair, throwing her napkin down on her plate.

“Now, Daniel,” Phillip chided. “Don’t take that tone with your mother.”

“Your brother has a more important job than firefighting,” Margaret said. “He knows that! It’s reckless and irresponsible of him-”

“Shut up!” Danny snapped, getting to his feet.

“-to be doing something so dangerous! So selfish!”

“How is it selfish?” Chimney asked, the question ignored. 

Eddie, unfortunately, already knew the logic there. He was scooting his chair out, with the full intent of dragging his boyfriend out the door once again. Unfortunately, Buck didn’t seem to be of the same mind, as he spoke up to say,

“I like being a firefighter. I like helping people. I’m good at it.”

“Stop thinking about yourself!” Margaret snapped.

“Stop being a bitch!” Danny snapped back.

“Daniel!” Phillip, this time.

“Oh my God,” Chimney whispered.

“He should be focusing on what’s important!” Margaret shouted at Daniel. “He has always been selfish and self-centered! Has he even thought about what would happen if he can’t donate? What that would mean for you?”

Chimney’s jaw was hanging loose as he stared at Margaret. Maddie, though, was focused on Buck, shrinking down in his seat with every word from their mother. In her eyes, Eddie thought he could see something like heartbreak.

“This is why we left Hershey!” Daniel shouted, slamming his hand down onto the table and rattling everything. “If it was up to you, you’d have him in some glass case, locked away until I get sick again. You don’t care if he’s happy, so long as you’ve got spare parts for me! I took him to El Paso to keep him away from you!”
