Help did not seem to be coming, or at least it wasn’t coming fast enough.

Buck fucked up as a brother, somewhere along the line. He refused to fail as a firefighter here.

The sprinkler system finally burst into life, stale water raining down upon him and Saleh. That was something, it was better than before, but it didn’t seem like it was doing much. Too much fire, too many accelerants. It might slow the blaze down, impede its spread, but it wasn’t going to stop the burning now. Not on its own.

Here, too, was something: Buck had the ax still, and he had a rope, and he had physics. Maybe he hadn’t been the best at school, maybe he’d been one of the worst students, but he wasn’t stupid. He knew about simple machines and how they could multiply applied force. It might just be him here, but that could be enough.

One end of the rope was attached to the vat pinning Saleh, the other end was tied around the handle of the ax, the knot made as tightly as he could manage. Then the ax was tossed over a beam above them, forming a makeshift pulley. Buck gripped the ax tight and he began to pull, with all his might.

He pulled.

And he pulled.

And he pulled.

But it wasn’t enough, he was not enough. He screamed, and he pulled, and he screamed, and he pulled. His foot slipped in the pooling water from the sprinklers, and the rope held his weight because the vat was simply too heavy for him to move alone.

Then there was a person rushing past his vision, and then another, and then half a dozen and more. Hands gripped the rope above his own and suddenly it was moving, it was giving. There was a hand on his shoulder, the weight of it intimately familiar, and people at his back and water dripping down his face. When he looked, he saw Danny dragging Saleh out from under the vat, which had been lifted up.

And Buck let himself relax.

The journey outside was a blur, and he found himself perched on the back of an ambulance with an oxygen mask pressed to his face. There was a scolding in his future, according to Jon Mendoza as he told him not to remove the mask just yet. But Jon had wandered off, to help elsewhere or to talk to Mehta, and Bobby was there.

“I got lost.” Buck felt like he was deflating where he sat. He clutched the oxygen mask in his hand and ignored the way Bobby was pointedly eying it. “I went off on my own, and two seconds later, I didn’t know where the hell I was standing.”

“That place is a maze,” Bobby told him. “And I think the only person surprised you stayed in there was Mehta.”

“Danny’s probably pissed at me.” That weighed on Buck more than anything else. He’d already caused his brother enough problems, hadn’t he?

“Probably.” Bobby looked awkward for a moment. “You know that you can return to the One Eighteen whenever you want, right? There’ll always be a spot open for you.”

“I know.”

“You tried to tell me something once, a long time ago,” Bobby said. “I thought I was listening, but I don’t think I was. Not well enough. And I just kept not listening, I guess.”

“Um. What do you mean?” Buck tilted his head to squint up at him. Perhaps it was the headache, or the smoke inhalation, but he wasn’t quite following along with wherever this conversation was going.

“I didn’t want you to get hurt again,” Bobby said. “That was what I was focused on, what I was worried about. I knew you were upset, but that was okay, because you weren’t getting hurt again. Except that you were. I was hurting you. And I didn’t even know how bad I was hurting you, because I didn’t listen well enough to what you told me.”

“O- Oh.”

“You said I couldn’t let them take your job away, too,” the captain continued. “And I didn’t pay attention enough to know what you meant. I kept not paying attention to everything else you were going through, everything else you were afraid of losing, because I was too focused on trying to keep you from being hurt. Because I wasn’t ready to face that, yet. And I’m sorry.”

“That’s, uh.” Buck licked his lips; they were dry from the heat of the fire. “You’re forgiven?”

Bobby snorted with amusement, and then turned serious again.

“You know that you don’t have to be useful, right?” he asked, sounding earnest. “You’re a good firefighter, you’re a good man, you don’t have to… You’re you, okay? And that’s enough.”

Buck blinked up at them and then laughed at the feeling of deja vu.

“Now you sound like Danny.”

“I’ll try to take the compliment,” Bobby said, and his voice was only a little bit strained. His mouth drew into a flat line when the man in question suddenly appeared to push him out of the way.

“You idiot,” Danny hissed. His eyes flicked down to the oxygen mask that Buck was holding instead of wearing, and he grabbed it to shove it back onto Buck’s face.

“Danny-” Buck tried, voice muffled by the mask. He tried to take it off so he could talk, but his brother held it firm.

“No, no, you shut up. You’re more important, okay?” Danny said, glaring at him. Buck quailed a little under it. “If it’s a choice between you and anyone else, it’s you. I don’t care if that means some random idiot dies in a fire, because you’re more important. I don’t know what I would do if…”

He trailed off, shaking his head and leaning down to just press a kiss into Buck’s hair. The action, at least, meant that Buck could pull off the mask again.

“I’m sorry,” he said, and then, “I didn’t mean to…”

“I know.” Danny grabbed the mask from his hand and pressed it onto his face again. “And you’re grounded.”

Buck glared at him, and then at Bobby when he had the audacity to laugh.

Daniel didn’t really know why he was doing this, except perhaps to avoid having his parents appear at the station again. They were still insisting on talking to him, on seeing him, and there was only so long that he could ignore them before they showed up where Buck was again. At least Maddie was refusing to give them the apartment address, and he knew they’d been asking her for it. He wasn’t sure he’d forgive her if she was the reason they showed up where Buck lived.

They were meeting at Grand Park, in downtown Los Angeles. He’d told them “by the fountains,” and was waiting on one of the stone benches as he watched the few people out and about. Part of him was rather hopeful that they didn’t show up, though he knew they probably would. No, they definitely would. They wouldn’t if it was for Buck, and it was a toss-up when it came to Maddie, but for Daniel?

For Daniel, they showed up, craning their necks as they looked for where he waited. He watched for a moment, then bit back a sigh and raised a hand. His mother brightened when she spotted him and the pair hurried over. Daniel got to his feet, already wishing this was over.

“Daniel!” His mother cried and then rushed to hug him. He stood there awkwardly, allowing it to happen. “We were worried when you left so suddenly and started ignoring our calls. And then Evan said you called in.”

“Well, I’m fine.” Daniel peeled his mother off and stepped back. “See?”

“But we’re still worried, Daniel,” Dad said. “If we’d known… You could have come to us, you could have come home. We would have helped you!”

“Letting you take Evan was a mistake,” Mom said. “He was too much of a burden.”

“Shut. Up.” Daniel bit out the words, doing his best not to shout them like he wanted to. “You didn’t let me do anything, I threatened you. Remember? Because you didn’t want to go through the trouble of me suing you for custody.”

“And you were making a mistake! Clearly. Evan was always getting into trouble, it’s no surprise that his selfishness-”

“Jesus Christ, Mom, shut the fuck up!” he snapped. Mom reeled back and Dad opened his mouth, no doubt to scold him for how he spoke to her, but Daniel pressed on before he could get a word in. “Evan was the best thing you ever gave to me. You walked into that hospital room and told me that I was going to have a baby brother, made just for me, and that was a gift. And I looked at him in that crib and I decided I was gonna take care of him, because he was made for me. You- You never saw him as anything but a bunch of spare parts for me, that’s all he is to you. He was never your kid, or even a person to you.”

“That’s not true,” Dad tried to say, but Mom’s silence and pinched expression was far louder.

“I took him with me to keep him away from you,” Daniel said. “Because he was gonna kill himself if I left him there. You were gonna kill him. I didn’t call you, I didn’t go to you for help, because I didn’t want you anywhere near him. So I did what I had to do to take care of my kid, which is more than you ever did for him. And I’m not ashamed of it, either. I’ll never be ashamed of it.”

“Daniel…” Mom looked like she was about to cry.

“I was a prostitute,” he bluntly told them. They flinched. “It put food on the table and gifts beneath the tree. I did what I needed to take care of my kid, and I’d do it again. Evan was happy in El Paso, happier than he was in Hershey with the two of you. He was happy, and he was healthy, and he was safe. That’s all that ever mattered. So I don’t care if you’re disappointed or worried.”

It was awkward, after that, talking to them. They didn’t seem to know what to say, couldn’t seem to be able to get past it. Daniel didn’t stay much longer, leaving for where he’d parked after a hug to his mother and a handshake with his father. He wondered if he’d be hearing from Maddie and wondered if she’d even want to talk to him again, so soon after their last one.

In the parking lot of his building, he found himself hesitating to get out of his car. He had no faith in an EPO to keep Drake at bay. It wasn’t some magic ward, and the man was no vampire. A piece of paper and the threat of another cop wasn’t going to keep him away. Hell, Daniel would bet that whoever went to tell him about the EPO had laughed about it with him.

But staying in the car wouldn’t make Drake go away, if he really was out there lurking. The best way to deal with him had always been to grit his teeth and get it over with. So that’s what Daniel did, shutting off the engine and stepping out and resigning himself to being bothered by the man once more.

“Seems one of us has good timing.” That was Athena, though her voice still had him jumping a little. She was in uniform and had a folder in her hands. “He’s not here, by the way. I checked.”

“Cool.” Daniel tried not to be so obvious with the relief he felt.

“C’mon.”

Athena led the way inside and then to the elevator. Then she followed him out and down the hall to the apartment. Buck was at the dining table when they entered, a box - Daniel’s baby box - open in front of him. He lifted his head at the sound of the door, eyes immediately going to Danny and then lighting up when he saw who came in with him.

“Oh, Athena! Hey!”

“Hey, Buckaroo.” The sergeant cast a curious gaze to the box. “What do you got there?”

“Danny’s baby box, Chimney brought it over.” The way Buck grinned at him was shit-eating, and then he lifted up an old photo of a younger Daniel in the bathtub. “It has baby pictures. Wanna see?”

“Maybe later. Work first.” Athena set the folder down on the table and then turned to Daniel, tapping her finger on the folder as she spoke. “These are all the forms you need for the restraining order against Detective Drake.”

Buck dropped the photo back into the box and frowned dubiously at the folder.

“That’s a lot,” he said, and Daniel silently agreed.

“I know, but I’ll help with ‘em. A couple you’ll only fill out parts and leave the rest to the court, and a couple you’ll leave blank entirely for either Drake or the person serving the order,” Athena explained. She flipped open the folder and pulled out a pen from her shirt pocket. “We’ll start with the DV-100 and go from there.”

“DV?” Daniel scowled at her. “Domestic violence?”

“The two of you had an intimate relationship,” she bluntly reminded him and held out the pen. “The faster you fill this out, the faster I can turn it all in for a court date.”

Daniel stared at the pen for a moment. Then he sat down, took the pen from her, and wrote down his name in the first blank space.

Chapter 36

Inventorying was not exactly the most exciting of chores that needed to be done in the firehouse. It wasn’t the worst of the bunch, no one particularly appreciated being stuck cleaning the toilets, and it wasn’t very labor intensive. The biggest problem with it, or so Eddie found, was that it was boring.

It wasn’t boring whenever he did it with Buck, but then again, few things were boring when Eddie did them with Buck. And it wasn’t that Eddie minded having parts of his workday be utterly, horribly boring, because excitement usually meant someone was hurt. That didn’t mean, though, that he enjoyed going through a checklist and marking things off for the hundredth time. Or getting stuck as the person running back and forth for the items as they were called off.

“Trauma bag.” Austin’s eyes didn’t even lift up from the clipboard he had in his hand.

“Yup.” Eddie grabbed the bag in question and stuck it into the proper compartment.

“AED.”

“Right here.” It went in next to the trauma bag.

Much like how inventory wasn’t the worst chore to be stuck with, Austin wasn’t the worst person to be stuck doing it with. He also wasn’t the best. Eddie knew that the man had a sense of humor, and that he could be more than a bit bitchy, just from watching him interact with Danny. But God if that just went out the window when Danny wasn’t there, because Austin went right back to that forgettable wallflower persona. They did the job, professionally and reliably, but Eddie knew that if he’d been doing it with Chimney or Hen or, preferably,  Buck, they’d be joking and goofing off.

Somedays, Eddie wondered if they’d ever know the difference if Austin was replaced by a pod person. He already knew they probably wouldn’t notice Austin’s absence, because it was so easy to overlook him.

“How’s inventory going?” Hen asked, her and Chimney striding up to them shoulder-to-shoulder. Eddie did a mental cheer at the reprieve from the doldrums of repetition he was suffering from.

“It’s going,” Eddie answered as he closed the compartment door.

“Uh-huh, uh-huh.” Chimney nodded like a bobblehead, glanced at Austin, and then asked, “News on Dan and Buck?”

Austin rolled his eyes behind their backs.

“Buck’s still grounded,” Eddie said as he leaned against the side of the fire engine. The comment had the paramedics both snickering. “I took Chris over to the apartment and they bullied Albert together.”

“Chim said the parents left,” Hen said. “He also mentioned something about therapy?”

“Maddie said that her parents said,” Chimney explained, “that they wanted to try it with Dan.”

Buck hadn’t mentioned it, nor had Danny. Which was not at all surprising, in truth. Hell, he couldn’t even be certain that Buck was even aware of it.

“Would this be a family thing?” Eddie asked, keeping his doubts to himself about whether or not it would even happen. “Are you and Maddie gonna be joining them?”

“The key word there would be family,” Chimney said. “Which I am not. Technically.”

Austin shot Chimney a pointed look from behind, and then shook his head as he marked off more from the list in his hand.

“Dan told them to go pound sand, anyway,” the driver-engineer spoke up. Hen and Chimney both startled slightly, turning a little to face him. “So no family therapy.”

The man paused in the middle of checking off another item on the inventory list, tilted his head for a moment, and then continued what he was doing. Eddie could ask what that was about, but he figured Austin simply wouldn’t answer. Nor did he really care enough to try and pry it out of him.

“Oh!” Hen suddenly spoke up. “Hey!”

Eddie followed her gaze and spotted another firefighter he didn’t recognize. The guy froze where he was, a bundle of books clutched to his chest and staring at them with wide, startled eyes.

“Uh, y- yeah?” The guy cleared his throat. “I mean, yes, ma’am?”

Hen made a face.

“You’re the new probie on B-shift, aren’t you?” Chimney asked.

“Yea- Uh, yes, sir,” the guy said. “Just finished my first shift.”

“How was it?” Eddie asked him.

“Oh, pretty quiet.”

If he’d pulled out a gun and threatened to shoot them all, the reaction of Eddie’s coworkers would probably have been more subdued. As it was, both Hen and Chimney lurched back with startled yelps, hands going up as they were trying to protect themselves from an unseen threat. Eddie just rolled his eyes at them.

“Did he just say-?” was Hen’s startled question, cut off by Chimney’s desperately hissed,

“No!”

“Sorry.” The probie was looking increasingly overwhelmed. “I just said it was-”

“Don’t say it again!” Chimney snapped.

“Hold on,” Hen said. “Maybe if he says it a second time, it undoes the curse.”

“And maybe!” Chimney sniped back. “If he says it a third time, the Candyman will show up and kill us all. Let’s not test that theory.”

The probie’s head swivelled as he watched the pair of them. Then his gaze moved to Eddie, as the sanest person there.

“What did I…?”

“Ignore them,” was Eddie’s advice. “They just got freaked out ‘cause you said qui-”

“Don’t!” Austin snapped from behind him. His glare was severe enough that Eddie worried for the probie’s health. “We don’t say the Q-word.”

“Who used the Q-word?” Bobby asked from above, leaning over the railing of the loft to look down on them.

The station alarm rang, dispatch rattling off information about a vehicle accident. The others marched off for their turnouts while shooting the probie mutinous glares. Eddie shook his head at them, because it wasn’t the probie’s fault. Not unless he somehow caused the wreck, anyway.

Not that the others seemed to agree with him.

“I can’t believe that probie jinxed us,” Chimney complained during the ride there.

“You guys sound like my abuela’s neighbor’s curandera,” Eddie told them, and made no effort to cover up his judgmental tone.

“Would they know how to undo it?” Chimney asked. “This is going to be the shift from hell. Nonstop calls, all day long.”

“Stupid calls,” Hen added.

“Probably tempted fate. Now the EMS gods are gonna make us pay.”

“I can’t believe you guys actually believe all that,” Eddie scoffed.

Hen sent him a pitying look.

“So Buck never told you about the last time he said it?” she asked, laughing a little.

“Thirty-six calls in one shift,” Bobby chimed in with. “A house record.”

“He told me that someone put itching powder in his clothes afterwards,” Eddie said. He could’ve sworn that, for just a moment, Austin’s reflection in the rearview mirror was smirking. “I think you’re all giving the EMS gods a little too much credit.”

“Give it time,” Hen said. “You’ll come around.”

They arrived at the accident scene and hopped out. It was pretty overwhelming for the build up that Eddie just suffered through. A pair of cars with their ends smashed together, pretty run of the mill. Nothing at all deserving of the way that everyone reacted to a mere word.

“See?” Eddie pointed out to Bobby. “A fender bender, nothing crazy.”

Bobby stared at him, a single eyebrow arching up, and then he pointed. Eddie followed the direction and saw a man on the billboard above them. Izzy Chainz, presumably, since it was both written in large font beside him and was what the guy was shouting at everyone below.

“Is he…?”

“Duct taped?” Hen did not sound impressed beneath her cloth mask. “Yeah.”

The three of them turned to him, expectantly. Eddie just shrugged.

“I’ve seen crazier,” he told them.

“Uh-huh.” Bobby didn’t sound convinced. “Eddie, ladder.”

“Got it, Cap.”

The ladder truck was on the other side of the engine. Eddie went to go prep the ladder, which took a moment with the maneuvering and extending. All the while, Izzy Chainz kept shouting down at the world and wiggling where he was taped. He was a musician of some sort, judging from what he was saying, but Eddie hadn't heard of him before.

“No, no, no!” Izzy shook his head when he saw Eddie climbing up to him. “I don’t need help, go back down.”

“For your safety and others,” Eddie told him, “You need to come on down.”

“I rented this billboard the whole day!” the man argued, gesturing as much as he could. Eddie wondered how strong that duct tape was. “I ain’t leaving ‘til I get what I paid for.”

Below them, a small crowd of onlookers was staring up at them. Most of them had their phones out, either taking photos or recording videos. Eddie gestured to them.

“I think you have,” he said. “Come on, let’s go.”

“No, nope.” Izzy shook his head and then shouted down at the people below to, “Buy my album!”

He laughed, sounding a bit manic. More than a bit, maybe.

“Think they can see my QR code?” the guy asked. Eddie glanced at it, large and impossible to miss in the bottom right corner of the billboard.

“Yeah, pretty sure,” He told him. Izzy howled and Eddie grimaced, then asked something that was bugging him. “Sir, are you wearing anything beneath the tape?”

Eddie was really hoping that he was, because there was only one naked man that he wanted to deal with and he wasn’t here. But the tape only came down to about midthigh on Izzy, and while that didn’t rule out shorts, there was also no sign of any shirt. 

“No,” Izzy sighed. “Why?”

“You’ll figure it out.” Eddie grabbed his radio. “Cap, the tape’s all he’s wearing.”

Bobby was too far away for the sigh to be audible, but Eddie could see the captain’s shoulders rise and fall with it as Athena joined him at his side.

Below the billboard, Chimney and the others were inflating the airbag. Which was probably a good thing, because duct tape was not meant to hold up a grown man who was wiggling around as much as this one was. Eddie made a few more attempts to convince Izzy Chainz to come down the easy and safe way to no avail, before going back down himself to consult with Bobby.

“He isn’t coming down,” he told the captain.

“I’m not coming down ‘til my time is up!” Izzy sang at the top of his lungs, giving a perfect example of why Eddie had never heard of him before.

“And when is that!?” Athena shouted up to him.

“ Eight AM! Tomorrow morning!”

Izzy Chainz cackled again and then started shilling for his album. But what caught everyone’s attention was the sound of tape starting to tear loose. Because the duct tape was not meant to hold up a grown man, especially when the man was moving around as much as this idiot was, and it was finally starting to succumb to the demands of gravity.

“Ay, Dios,” Eddie cursed, racing back up the ladder. He only got half way up before the tape gave completely and Izzy fell with a cackle and a final,

“Download my album!”

He landed on the air bag and then rolled off it. He also rolled out of the tape and Eddie grimaced as he caught an eyeful of far too much of Izzy Chainz than he ever wanted to see. 

The shift afterwards was… Okay, it was abnormally busy, Eddie could admit to that. Nothing they should blame a mystical, unknowable force for, certainly, but busy. They sat down for some of Bobby’s mac’n’cheese - which Buck whined and complained about missing, when Eddie told him what they were having - only to have to immediately rush out before it could even be served.

They had to rescue a cat and its owner from a tree. They got someone out of the head of a lion costume, who thanked them with projectile vomit. There was a kitchen fire, an octopus stuck to someone’s face in a bathroom, a guy stuck in a movie theater seat, a child stuck in a laundromat washing machine, a clown trapped under a pile of helium canisters, and then a stalled elevator. A lot of calls, random calls, but nothing cursed.

“That was a boring call,” Eddie said as they trooped back out to the engine. Because he’d grown up as a brother and with Buck and Danny. He couldn’t help it. “Two people stuck in an elevator. They didn’t even need medical attention or anything.”

“Don’t say it, Edmundo,” Hen warned as they stowed away the gear they carried in.

“How can I not? Y’all acting like a bunch of viejas. There is no curse!”

“Oh, he’s so definitive now,” was Chimney’s derisive response.

“Nobody is saying you have to believe in curses,” Bobby said as they all clambered into the engine. “Just maybe don’t tempt fate.”

“How is that not the same thing?” Eddie asked, pulling himself into the cab and one of the jump seats. He slammed the door shut behind him. “It was a normal call, went like clockwork. Wham, bam, thank you, ma’am.”

“You notice how you never hear anyone say, “wham, bam, thank you, sir”?” Hen asked. Eddie snorted in amusement.

“I just think,” he said, “that this proves the whole jinx thing is a little silly. We should all just be done with it.”

There was the sound of wood cracking, somewhere nearby. Like a tree branch breaking. Then, suddenly, the entire engine shook as something heavy fell on it, startling all of them. A curtain of sparks rained down outside the windows.

Eddie stared out at the white smoke billowing around them.

“Hey, Cap?” Chimney asked. When Eddie turned his head, he found the paramedic glaring holes into his face. “Did a live power pole just fall on the engine?”

“I believe it did,” Bobby responded from the front.

“Shut up,” Eddie told all of them when Hen joined Chimney in staring. “There’s no curse.”

He was very much in the minority when it came to that opinion. Stuck with nowhere to go, he got an up-close view of his coworkers’ descent into insanity as Chimney tried to Google how to break nonexistent curses. Worse, he roped Buck in for assistance, for some reason, which led to Buck calling him. Which Eddie would have been happy about, normally. He was always happy for a chance to talk to his boyfriend when they’d spent all day unable to talk.

Almost always, anyway.

“What do you mean, Eddie doesn’t believe in the Q-word?” Buck’s incredulity was almost offensive.

They were Facetiming, and it looked like Buck was in turnouts and in the 133’s engine. The shoulder of one of the others was just visible on screen beside him, shaking with laughter.

“Curses aren’t real!” Eddie repeated for the nth time, just barely refraining from flinging up his arms. He didn’t want to accidentally fry himself.

“Says the baseball player.”

“That!” Eddie pointed at Chimney’s phone. “Is totally different!”

“You elbowed me in the kidney once because I pointed out a team was getting a no-hitter.”

“You don’t talk about it when it’s happening.”

“Well, well, well.” Hen was smirking. “You’re a hypocrite.”

“That’s different,” Eddie insisted. “You can’t curse an entire shift with a single word. Curses aren’t real.”

“Says the man who hopped over the foul line every time he went up to pitch.”

“Buck, I swear to God.” Eddie hunched down in his seat.

“Okay, so, ways to break this thing,” Chimney said. “Buck, go.”

“Jon said you should go outside, spin around nine times-”

“Widdershins!” someone - presumably Jon - shouted.

“Salud.”

The laughter in the background was distinctly Danny’s.

“We can’t even get out right now, anyway,” Chimney pointed out. “Trapped, remember? We need another way to lift the curse.”

“Is it a curse?” Hen asked. “I know we called it that, but technically, I think it’s a jinx.”

“What’s the difference?

“Well, I feel like a curse implies a person put a hex on you and a jinx is more like a general angering of the gods.”

“Wait, so is a hex and a curse the same thing?”

“Asking the real questions at the One Eighteen,” someone from Buck’s end of the call said.

“If you mean that both are totally made up and not real?” Eddie said. “Then yes.”

“We are trapped in a death box, Eddie!” Chimney snapped. “Thousands of volts of electricity coursing through every nook and cranny. Any one of us could literally get fried like that.”

He snapped his fingers.

“Or,” Bobby said, “we just don’t touch any doors or windows until help arrives and nobody gets fried. With or without a curse, or jinx, or whatever.”

“Everything I’m finding is about animal sacrifice,” someone, a woman, said from Buck’s end.

“I don’t think I’m comfortable with that, Cor,” Buck told her.

Hen tilted her head at Chimney’s phone, a curious frown on her face.

“Look,” Eddie said. “We’ve had a crappy day, but it happens. We weren’t cursed or hexed or jinxed because the new guy said his first day was qui-”

“Don’t!” Bobby snapped from the front.

“Wait, wait, wait,” Jon suddenly spoke up. “If he says it there, do we get jinxed, too?”

“I’m gonna go ahead and hang up,” Buck said, frowning at the screen. “Okay, see you guys soon.”

They all stared at Chimney’s phone as the call dropped.

“What did he mean?” Hen asked.

“You don’t think…” Chimney trailed off.

“Ah, help has arrived,” Bobby said, which got overshadowed by Austin's loud intonation of,

“God damn it.”

Eddie twisted around in his seat to look out the front to see the 133’s engine pulling up. Buck had the window rolled down and was waving at them.

“Seriously!?” Chimney spat as he looked, too. “I hate this curse! Jinx, whatever.”

As they all watched, the 133 hopped out to gawk and laugh. Buck and Danny actually posed in front of the 118’s engine, so someone else could take their picture.

“I am going to kill that probie,” Austin declared.

Eddie settled in, resigning himself to the mocking in their future.

Chapter 37

Sometimes, Daniel thought the people he worked with were a little bit ridiculous. The truck bay still smelled of burnt sage; after they’d returned from rescuing the 118 from a downed power pole, Theo Gray, who’d ridden the engine with them and who still complained about things not tasting right months after being sick, had rushed out and came back with a bundle of the stuff. When questioned where he got it on such short notice, he’d simply said that he knew a guy. Like there was some seedy underground network of people selling herbs and spices that he had to keep secret.

Theo had circled around the engine, spouting cliches at the top of his voice and trailing floral smelling smoke, but the others had done their own little acts of ritual to ward it off, too. Jon Mendoza, for example, had started spinning in circles the moment he got out of the engine, spitting onto the bay floor after every rotation. Corine Luna went to the showers and came back smelling of mint and lavender.

Daniel wasn’t going to complain, however. Whatever kept them from catching any of the bad juju. At least the 118 seemed to be getting a break from it, either because the EMS gods took pity on them or Nash took them offline for a bit, because Austin was now blowing up his phone with aspersions upon the character of some nameless probie and with threats to Daniel’s body. The latter because the picture of Austin trapped in his own engine by the downed power line had been sent to his brother, Ethan. And Ethan, being both an electrician and a father, had a shocking amount of dad jokes available to him on the topic that he was now subjecting his older brother to.

Unlike the 118, however, the 133 had been having a pretty easy day. Presumably because the entire populace of Los Angeles was moving into the 118’s response area to have their emergencies. Some of them did better with boring shifts than others, and Buck spent most of it in the station gym as he tried to burn off his seemingly constant energy. Now, though, Daniel found him in the rec room, curled up in a comfy chair with his legs slung over an arm and a book in his hands.

“What the hell are you reading, squirt?” Daniel asked, squinting at the cover. It was mostly purple, though it had an image of a sunset and a silhouetted couple. “The Five Love Languages?”

“You know, words of affirmation, quality time, gifts, acts of service, physical touch. That kind of thing,” Buck said, resting the book on his chest as he looked up. “Copeland mentioned them in therapy the other day.”

“Yeah?” Daniel perched on the arm of the chair catty-corner to Buck’s. “And what would yours be?”

“We don’t use just one, Danny.” Buck rolled his eyes at him and Daniel reached out to flick him in the head in response. His brother scowled and smacked at him. “Though, this guy seems to think we do.”

“Why are you reading it, then?”

“‘Cause I thought it was interesting.” Buck shrugged. “Speaking of therapy. Eddie mentioned something earlier. About Mom and Dad wanting to do therapy with you?”

This time, it was Daniel’s turn to roll his eyes. He could ask how Eddie heard about it, considering Daniel himself hadn’t even mentioned it to anyone, but it didn’t take a conspiracy board to figure it out.

“What about it?” he asked instead.

“Just curious. You never mentioned it.”

“Because I have no intention of doing it,” Daniel told him. “If they need therapy to deal with my previous employment history, that’s on them. They had no problem going to a therapist to talk about Maddie’s marriage without her.”

Mom would probably cry and then they’d spend the hour making her feel better about her son being a prostitute. She and Dad could do that on their own time and their own dime, thanks much. He had better things to do, like putting off telling Dr. White about Drake being in Los Angeles.

“Do you talk about Maddie and Doug at all?” Buck asked, head tilted in that way that always reminded Daniel of curious puppies. “I know I’ve brought it up with Copeland, but not in like a… I dunno, woe is me kind of way.”

“She’s my sister, of course I’ve talked about her,” Daniel said. “You, too. Dr. White thinks I have an “unhealthy attachment” to you.”

He made sure the air quotes were extra scathing. It got Buck to laugh a little.

“Austin thinks the three of us - you, me, Maddie - should do therapy,” Buck said.

“That asshole,” Daniel immediately spat out. His brother’s laughter was louder this time. “I liked it better when you didn’t remember he existed half the time. Why are you even talking to him?”

“He’s your not-boyfriend, your zucchini-”

“My zucchini?”

“Why wouldn’t I be talking to him?” Buck finished.

“I’m sorry, can we go back to you calling him a vegetable?”

“Sorry, is partner better? Or-” Buck lifted his hips a little as he blindly dug into his pants pocket, tongue sticking out in concentration. He pulled out his phone and turned it on, swiping until he found whatever he was looking for. “There’s, uh. There’s squish? Plush? Marshmallow?”

“How about we call Austin by his name, you weirdo.” Daniel shook his head at his brother. “Or maybe asshole. Why the hell are you two talking about us going to therapy?”

“Well, he mentioned you and Maddie got into it-”

“Christ, no. No, no, this is not how this relationship works.” Daniel was five seconds away from calling up Austin and bitching him out. “He gossips to me about all of you people. He does not gossip to you about me. That is not how this works.”

“I wish he gossiped about you more, maybe I wouldn’t be blindsided about things,” his brat of a little brother said, side-eying him. Daniel glowered in reply. “Listen, he just had the thought that maybe, maybe, it’d be easier for you and Maddie to talk about things without hurting each other’s feelings if there was a third party involved.”

Austin was clearly underestimating Daniel’s ability to say the shittiest thing to another person no matter the audience. Which was silly of him, really, because he’d been there to see some of the most spectacular examples of it for himself.

“Okay, and why would you be there?”

“I…” Buck closed his mouth and the book, then sat up properly in the chair. He craned his neck around them. The room wasn’t empty, there were others there playing foosball and watching TV, but the chair Buck had chosen to read in was tucked away in the corner and no one was paying them any attention. He was still softer and quieter when he spoke next, though. “Look, I- I’ve talked about it a bit with Copeland, y’know? And- And I know that for you, it was just another job. I get that. But this, with him…”

“Buck,” Daniel sighed, knowing where this was going.

“I guess I just feel like I’ve been a shitty brother.”

“Hey, no.” Daniel leaned forward and cupped the back of Buck’s head. “You are the best kid brother, squirt. Stop blaming yourself for shit that isn’t your fault.”

“He was using me to threaten you.”

“Still not your fault,” Daniel told him. “So you’ve talked to your therapist about my employment history-”

“Only a little!” Buck protested.

“What else do you talk to her about?” he asked, sitting back. A bit too far back, as he had to catch himself to keep from falling off the arm of the chair that he was perched on. 

“Oh, uh. You know, things.” His brother wasn’t really meeting his eyes and his shoulders were hitching up a little. “The tsunami, the ladder truck. Mom. Eddie and Shannon. That kind of stuff.”

“Uh-huh.” Daniel narrowed his eyes at him, but let it go. “Why the hell does Austin keep telling us to go to therapy? I don’t think he’s gone to a therapy session in his life that wasn’t department mandated.”

“What would he even talk about in therapy?” Buck asked, scrunching up his face. “His family is so normal. It’s creepy.”

“I know!”

It actually wasn’t very often that they got called out to a fire. If Buck were here, he’d probably be able to spout off the actual statistics or he’d go hunt them down. It surprised Eddie a bit his first year, just how little firefighting they did as firefighters, but that was a testament to how well the push for fire safety had worked.

(Take that, War on Drugs.)

The moment the station was put online again after their too-short break, perhaps even the very second, they were being sent out to a small structure fire. When they arrived, they found a small crowd of onlookers watching as the homeowner used a garden hose to try and beat back the flames eating away at his garage. His efficacy left much to be desired, though the attempt was admirable.

“Go start running a hose line,” Bobby instructed. “Chim, Hen, shut down the utilities here and the neighboring houses.”

They rushed off to do as he bid. While they were doing that, Bobby went to the homeowner. Eddie kept an ear on them out of curiosity as he helped drag out their own hoses, which was easy to do because the voices carried.

“Sir, we’ll take over from here,” Bobby was saying. “Hand me the hose.”

“No, I want to keep going till you’re all set up, okay?”

“Idiot,” Eddie muttered under his breath, and heard someone snort.

“Sir, I understand you want to save your things,” Bobby said, his tone all forced calm. “But right now, you need to back up for your own safety.”

‘Fine!” the homeowner said, relinquishing his hold on the paltry garden hose. “Just hurry up!”

He was actually hauling ass, now, which struck Eddie as strange. Sure, he understood wanting to get away from the fire, but most people, once they were outside of the building, would adopt a pace best described as “moseying along.” This guy seemed anxious about something, which Bobby picked up on.

“Is there something we should know about what’s in there?” the captain asked, voice echoing the same suspicion Eddie was feeling.

“No.” The homeowner’s lie was laughably obvious. Chris did a better job when asked if he had any homework to do. “Just some old files, Christmas decorations. Stuff like that.”

And then, the garage exploded.

As rockets shot through the air, trailing sparks and smoke, Eddie froze. It was not the best reaction he could have had. A better one would have been Austin’s, who immediately dove beneath the engine, or Hen and Chimney’s, who were running from the surprise arsenal as they herded the onlookers away. Eddie froze, because it had been too long and he’d felt too safe and he hadn’t been ready for it.

With the grenade, the one stuck in the collector’s leg that he extracted with Buck’s help, he’d known it was there. He’d known that it was live, that it would explode at any moment. He’d had ample time to sink back into that mentality of being under fire, and so when it did finally explode - thankfully without taking them with it - he hadn’t been entirely blindsided. But this had been just a simple structure fire, far away from the deserts of Afghanistan, in a city where ordinance like this was illegal to own or sell, and he hadn’t been expecting it.

So Eddie froze and he stared while the others dove for cover, and he didn’t come back to his surroundings until Bobby’s voice crackled through the radio, an echo of what the man was saying a few feet away.

“Dispatch, this is Captain Nash requesting assistance at Bay Park Drive. Fire has been upgraded to second alarm. Send more units!”

Eddie was still feeling rattled as the fireworks died down and more stations arrived to assist. Rattled enough that, as people got spread thin and he was left to haul out a hose on his own, he missed the mailbox obstructing the path and allowed the hose to get caught on it. Luckily, there was another firefighter, his helmet marking him as someone from Station 147, close by with nothing to do.

“Hey!” Eddie waved his arm to catch the man’s attention, and then gestured at the hose and the mailbox. “Mind helping me out?”

“Oh, yeah.” The guy, whose coat named him Harmon, jogged over and picked up the literal slack.

“Thanks. We’ve headed for the south wall. I’m Eddie.”

“Brian.”

“Good to meet you.”

Together, they got the hose off the mailbox and the little walled garden surrounding it. Eddie gave himself a mental kick, because if he hadn’t been so frazzled by the fireworks, he would’ve done a better job keeping that from happening. In a situation like this, every second counted; the fire had already spread and turned a tree into a bonfire.

“Guy who did this is some piece of work, huh?” Brian commented as they carried the hose across the manicured lawn.

“Today has been a piece of work,” Eddie complained. “We’re twelve hours into a twenty-four hour on and it’s been non-stop. The rest of ‘em think we’re cursed.”

“Curses aren’t real,” Brian scoffed.

“Thank you! But between you and me, I could use a minute.”

“If you weren’t out here doing this, the whole neighborhood could go up,” Brian pointed out. He was rather earnest about it, too. “Being a firefighter, getting to help people out, that’s all I ever wanted. That’s gotta be worth some tough days, right?”

“Yeah, I guess,” Eddie conceded. He couldn’t really argue with the guy, because he had a point. “Hey, thanks for the hand, man.”

“Oh, yeah.” Brian seemed stunned for a moment and at a loss for what to do thanks. “You bet, Eddie. I’ll see you around!”

After a moment’s hesitation, Brian turned and jogged away. Something about that entire interaction struck Eddie as weird, though he couldn’t really put a finger on what, precisely, it was. Maybe the way the guy just meandered, as if he didn’t really have any idea what he should be doing.

Could’ve just been a probie. ‘Twas the season, after all.

“Hey.” Bobby had returned from overseeing another part of the fire and picked up the hose right behind Eddie. “I came back to check on you, but I see that you got some help.”

“Yeah, that guy from the One Forty-seven jumped in.”

“Couldn’t be the One Forty-seven,” the captain denied.

“It was, I’m sure.”

“There’s nobody at the One Forty-seven, Eddie. Their house got hit by the mudslide, everybody got reassigned until it’s operational again.”

“So who the hell was I talking to?” Eddie asked, half-turning in an attempt to spot Brian again.

Bobby simply shrugged, and then jerked his chin at the fire. Eddie got the hit, turned on the hose, and got to work.

The mystery of the 147 firefighter simply got deeper afterwards. Bobby grabbed his department-issued laptop and brought it up to the loft, so he and Eddie could sit around the larger dining table and peer at photos of the 147 in an attempt to identify the Brian Harmon that Eddie had spoken to.

“I don’t see him on here,” Eddie complained, feeling frustrated. They’d gone through a lot of photos of the 147, from group pictures to their official department portraits. “His turnout said Harmon.”

“Well, that’s Aaron Harmon right there.” Bobby tapped the screen, indicating the guy posed with a turnout that read Harmon.

“Definitely not the guy. He said his name was Brian.” For one thing, Brian had been white and this Aaron guy was decidedly not. “There’s gotta be another Harmon there, right? It happens, look at Buck and Danny.”

“Except Buck’s turnout reads E. Buckley, now.” Bobby tapped the screen again, right on Harmon’s coat. “Did Brian’s say B. Harmon?”

“No,” he admitted. “You think he was fake?”

“It happens,” Bobby said as he leaned back in his seat. “Sometimes they’re criminals, using it as a ruse to get inside people’s homes. Firefighters and paramedics have a distinctly different reputation from a cop, after all. Most everyone trusts us at face value.”

“I don’t think that’s what this one is,” Eddie said. “He seemed more focused on actually helping, not taking advantage of anything. I mean, it’s bad, but it’s not…”

He shrugged.

“It’s worse,” Bobby argued. “They’re not trained, and they can wind up causing more harm than they help.”

“He said all he ever wanted to be was a firefighter.”

“Yeah.” The captain nodded, not seeming the least bit surprised. “Sometimes there are those guys. They try out for every class and never make it, but they also never give up.”

“You gotta admire the perseverance.”

“I do, and their dedication. But I also feel sorry for them.” Bobby let out a sigh. “I’ll tell the chiefs, let them know someone’s impersonating a firefighter. They can spread the word from there.”

“That’s probably a good idea.”

“Yeah.” Bobby looked awkward for a moment as he gently shut the laptop. “I haven’t really spoken with Buck since the factory fire. How are he and Daniel doing?”

“They’re doing fine,” Eddie answered. “I took Chris over to visit them, since Buck’s still “grounded.” We had fun, and then Buck walked us back to my truck.”

Which wasn’t in itself unusual. What was unusual was the way that his boyfriend spent the entire journey across the parking lot looking at every shadow and prospective hiding spot with suspicion. As if he was expecting that Drake guy to be lurking about.

“I told him he still had a spot here,” Bobby said. “Whenever he wanted it.”

“I know, he told me.”

The captain nodded. Then he gathered up his laptop, got to his feet, and went to go make that call.

Chapter 38

Despite what all of them would have preferred, the shift did not settle down after the impromptu fireworks show. Not long after Eddie and Bobby determined that Brian was out there running around and pretending to be a firefighter, they were called out to… Well, Eddie wasn’t entirely clear on the details. The location was a diner, Jim’s Burgers, where one of the employees had, according to a caller, “gone crazy.” 

A chair was thrown through a window, people were told to run for their lives. That kind of crazy. Supposedly, or so the guy claimed, because there was a gas leak. But the sensors that Bobby used didn’t detect any gas.

“All clear, no gas leak,” Bobby told both the worker that threw the chair and Athena, who was interview-slash-interrogating him. They, along with everyone else, were outside on the sidewalk. “However, the gas is gonna remain shut down until further investigation.”

“I’m gonna get canned,” the worker moaned. His nametag read Larry. “Years of customer service up in smoke. Or gas!”

“That’s rough, buddy,” was the best that Eddie could give him.

“He claims he was warned about the gas by a fire chief,” Athena told them.

“Someone else pretending to be LAFD?” was Bobby’s surprised response.

“What do you mean, someone else?”

Bobby’s head did an odd motion, like something caught his attention. His gaze was zeroed in on the crowd of people gawking at the tableau.

“Maybe the same someone,” the captain said.

Eddie looked, too, and saw a guy that was vaguely recognizable. Around the eyes, for sure, and the height. It was mostly the way he stiffened under their collective attention, though, that had Eddie tugging down his mask to call out,

“Brian!?”

The guy, and it was Brian, that much was clear, immediately turned on a heel and sprinted away. Eddie, along with Bobby and Athena and a couple officers, followed a bit more sedately. Perhaps too sedately, because as they turned the corner, they spotted Brian climbing into the engine’s cab.

“Nuh-uh!” Athena broke into a run for her cruiser, as did the other officers. “Not on my watch!”

“Dispatch, this is Captain Nash, One Eighteen,” Bobby spoke into his radio. “Our engine just got hijacked.”

As the police cruisers peeled out after their engine, their sirens wailing, Chimney and Hen reappeared. The former had arms loaded down with bags of food from Jim’s Burgers while Hen had a burger of her own. They peered around in bewilderment before Chimney, through a mouthful of food, asked,

“What did we miss?”

“Our engine just got stolen,” Eddie explained.

“Jones!” Bobby called out. The man in question was standing not too far away, standing very, very still as he glared in the direction the engine drove off in. “When did you last refill that gas tank?”

“I topped it off before we were called out.” Austin’s tone was flat, utterly devoid of emotion. Eddie took a step back to put a bit more space between himself and the driver-engineer. “He can go around four hours, non-stop, before he needs to refuel.”

“Yeah, unless he crashes it first.”

Eddie remembered, briefly, Buck telling him that the reason he was intending to take the 126’s engine to go rescue Hen, when they were in Texas for the wildfires, was that he didn’t want to know what Austin would do if he took the 118’s. Something unpleasant, had been Buck’s prediction. Eddie wondered if he should be more worried for Brian, who was being chased down by Athena but would probably be safely out of Austin’s reach, or the poor B-shift probie, who would undoubtedly be suffering through enforced karma after this.

He was just glad to not be either one of them, especially when both his and Austin’s phones began chiming with text notifications at the same time.

They’d just returned from a scene - nothing spectacular, just a minor traffic accident; they barely had to do or haul out anything - and were pulling off their turnouts when it came over their radios. That was normal, their radios chirped to life on the regular with bits of conversation between dispatch and other first responders. Buck still vividly remembered when Athena was attacked, her radio stuck to sending and they were all forced to listen or switch channels.

This time, like then, Buck’s ears perked up when he recognized the voice. Bobby’s voice.

“Dispatch, this is Captain Nash, One Eighteen. Our engine just got hijacked.”

Everyone froze. Everyone at first stared down at their radios and then over to Buck, as the resident transplant from the 118. Danny was shaking in his turnouts, face screwed up and lips pinched as he so obviously tried his best to keep from laughing.

Mehta broke first, bending slightly at the waist and holding his stomach as he laughed, and then the rest of them followed their captain’s lead. And Buck scrambled to get his phone out as Danny did the same.

Without the engine, they were all left twiddling their thumbs as they figured out what to do. This wasn’t something that they went over in the academy, what to do when someone stole one of the trucks to use as a getaway vehicle. All their gear, except for the turnouts they were wearing, were still on the engine. Including their helmets, left behind on their seats because they hadn’t been needed.

“He thinks he’s a goddamn comedian,” Chimney complained, taking a bite out of his burger while scrolling through his phone with the other. “It’s finally stopped, though  Think he’s run out of material?”

“I doubt it,” was Hen’s reply. “They probably just got sent out on a call.”

Buck, after the initial mocking texts to Eddie and Austin, had made a group chat with all of them plus Danny titled GTA: LAFD. Eddie took one look at it, saw the roasting they were receiving from the brothers, and promptly muted the notifications. They weren’t going to hear the end of this for quite some time, that much was obvious.

To make matters worse, dispatch was soon on the radio with,

“All available units, report to Five-Three-Nine North Hill Street, five-alarm fire. I repeat, all available units, report to Five-Three-Nine North Hill Street. Five-alarm fire.”

They all looked to Bobby, all of them thinking the same thing but none of them actually saying it. Bobby went wide-eyed, seemingly at a loss for a moment, and then rallied.

“Everybody in the ambulance,” he said, answering the unasked question.

They all hurried to get in, Chimney dumping his burger in a trash can. Austin, Eddie noticed, went for the driver seat. Which was a good thing, because both Hen and Chimney followed Eddie into the back, along with Bobby. The doors closed, the sirens came to life with a wail, and they all rocked slightly in their seats as the ambulance pulled away from the curb.

“Are we sure this is a good idea?” Eddie asked as he sat back.

“We’re already jinxed,” Hen said. “We might as well embrace it.”

“Okay, Buck’s not here to state the obvious, so I’ll do it for him,” Chimney said. “We’re on the way to a fire without any of our gear.”

“It’s a five-alarm,” Bobby pointed out. “There’ll be other units responding to it. We’ll assist any way we can.”

“We don’t even have our helmets,” Chimney pointed out. “Without your equipment on-scene…”

“Maybe there’s a way to get it there,” Eddie said, an idea coming to him as he grabbed the mic for his radio. At that house fire, it had seemed like all this guy wanted to do was help. Maybe that would still hold true now. “Brian? It’s Eddie Diaz. You there?”

No response.

“Brian, if you’re there,” Eddie said, “key the radio so I know you’re listening.”

That was, of course, assuming Brian knew what that meant. Maybe he didn’t, given the silence that responded to him. Chimney shook his head, but Eddie didn’t want to give up just yet.

“I just wanted to say thank you for helping us out at the garage fire,” Eddie said. “I needed your help, we needed your help, and you were there.”

More silence, and Eddie was starting to wonder if he was even on the right channel. And then it crackled with static, all of them sitting up to take note as Brian’s voice came over the radio.

“That’s it. That’s all I ever wanted to do, was help people.”

“I know that’s what you had planned when you put on that uniform,” Eddie told him, tamping down on his excitement that this was actually working. “But things don’t always turn out that way we planned. It sucks, I know, but you can’t let yourself get stuck. You gotta let go and move on. Which sounds scary, but you can do it.”

“No! I’m- I’m not brave. I want to be, but I’m not a hero like you.”

Eddie didn’t flinch at the word, but it was a near thing.

“You wanna be a hero?” he asked Brian. “There’s a five-alarm fire right now. We need your help, people’s lives depend on you.”

“No one’s ever given me the chance before.”

“I am now. Here’s your chance. I know you want to do the right thing, Brian. You’re so close.”

“I can’t. I can’t do it, I’m not a hero.”

If only he’d thought of that before deciding to impersonate a firefighter.

“We need you, Brian.” Was Eddie laying it on a bit thick? It felt like he was laying it on a bit thick. “We need you.”

Brian didn’t respond, which meant Eddie had no way of knowing if his words were reaching the man. He wasn’t certain what they’d do if this didn’t work, aside from twiddling their thumbs outside the fire as they waited for the engine to run out of gas somewhere.

Luckily, it didn’t seem like they were going to have to figure it out, though.

“Suspect is turning onto Hill,” someone announced over the radio. “He’s turning onto Hill.”

Eddie let out a breath, mentally cheered, and relaxed in his seat.

“Good job on the emotional manipulation, Diaz,” Chimney said, reaching across Hen to give him a pat. “Nicely done.”

The fire was a big one. One of the first things Mehta had done when they arrived on the scene was take one look at it and then call for assistance. Now, Daniel and Buck were running a hose from the engine, having already hooked up the supply line to the hydrant.

“Hey, hey, hey.” Buck came to a stop and started smacking Daniel on the arm. He barely felt it through his turnout coat, but it caught his attention nonetheless. Enough that he stopped, too, and looked at him. “That’s the One Eighteen’s engine.”

The engine in question was pulling into the parking lot of the burning building. It was looking a bit worse for wear, and Daniel winced at how scraped up the passenger side of it was. Austin was not going to be happy about that.

A fleet of cop cars came hounding on its tail, squealing to a stop. The whacko that stole the engine hopped out, took one look at them - specifically, at the very unhappy Athena stepping out of her car - and booked it in the opposite direction. That it meant he was running towards the fire was simply a testament to how stupid this man was, if the fact that he stole a fire engine wasn’t proof enough.

Neither Daniel nor Buck spoke, but they acted in unison nonetheless. They pulled the hose taut and it caught the guy at the ankles, sending him sprawling onto the wet pavement. Athena was on him in an instant, directing the other officers to haul him to his feet and cart him off as an ambulance pulled up and cut its sirens.

When Austin stepped out of it, Daniel waved an arm to catch his attention.

“Hey! We found your engine!” he called out, and then pointed to it. “Don’t worry, uh. I’m sure it’ll buff out!”

As Daniel watched, Austin scowled and rushed over to the engine, the others - with the exception of Bobby, who stopped to talk to Athena - close behind. He knew when the man spotted the damage, because he circled the front of the vehicle and then went still. Daniel glanced to Buck, who nodded, and then jogged over.

“It’s not too bad.” Daniel slung an arm around Austin’s shoulders. The other man barely reacted, attention focused entirely on the long scrapes along the side and the section of dented bumper and what looked like scorch marks. The others from the 118 were hurriedly pulling out their gear. “Just… Some paint, some elbow grease, it’ll be good as new. Is that a traffic barrel caught on the undercarriage?”

There was a bright orange misshapen something jutting out from just behind the front bumper like a piece of lettuce stuck in someone’s tooth. It was impressive that it hadn’t been yanked free, it must’ve been wedged in there good.

From the state of the engine, that guy must have led the cops on quite the destructive chase. They should all be thankful that the water tanks on it were still full, because Daniel had seen the results of an engine with a half-empty tank of water taking a turn too sharply. The ghost of Sir Isaac Newton was a deadly son of a bitch at times.

“Hey, look on the bright side,” Daniel said when the only response he got was frosty silence. “At least this one didn’t explode. How many ladders and ambulances have you guys gone through?”

“I want to murder him.” Austin’s voice was disturbingly calm as he said it. “Him and that probie.”

“Don’t do it in your uniform. I’ll help you hide the bodies,” Daniel told him, jostling him a little before giving him a small shove. “C’mon, grab your shit and get to work.”

Austin grumbled the entire time.

The end of their shift was met with great relief. Eddie dragged himself through the routine of changing out of his uniform and into his civvies, and then dragged himself out of the locker room behind Hen and Chimney. The knowledge of what was awaiting him, though, gave him that extra little boost of energy he needed.

“I hope that’s the end of that jinx,” Hen groaned. “It has to be, right? Next shift is back to normal?”

“I might call in sick just in case,” Chimney admitted.

“It’ll be back to normal because jinxes aren’t real,” Eddie said, and got a pair of stink eyes for it. “They aren’t!”

“Hey.” Bobby was waiting for them, also dressed in his civvies. “I know you guys are eager to get the hell out of here, but I’d like to buy you all breakfast.”

“Sorry, Cap. Can’t.” Eddie adjusted the strap of his bag. “Got a breakfast date.”

“I thought Buck was grounded?” Hen asked.

“Danny’s a soft touch when it comes to him.” That, and the only reason that Buck was ever going along with it was because he’d been reluctant to leave Danny alone. “See y’all later!”

“Tell him we said hi!” Bobby called after him.

“Will do!”

Outside dining was always a thing in Los Angeles, thanks to the near constant sunny weather. After the pandemic, though, just about every diner and restaurant turned to it as a means to keep their doors open while obeying the guidelines about distancing. This one wasn’t very far from the 133, close enough that he wasn’t surprised to find his boyfriend already waiting for him at a table with the menu in hand. He barely waited for the hostess with her plastic face shield to wave him through.

“Not a word,” was how Eddie greeted him, tugging off his mask so he could kiss him before taking a seat. “Everyone says hi, by the way.”

Buck, smiling, gave a broad wave but said nothing. Eddie stared at him and then rolled his eyes.

“You know what I meant,” he told him.

“Someone’s grouchy,” Buck teased. “Didn’t get enough sleep?”

“I slept fine.” For the two hours they were allowed to sleep before the alarm woke them up. “Have you ordered already?”

“Not yet.” Buck set down his menu, lips curling on the ends. “So…”

“Not a word, I said!”

“Eds, I told you what happened when I said the Q-word at work.”

“I didn’t say it. And jinxes and curses and hexes aren’t real,” Eddie said and then, when the other man opened his mouth to no doubt retort with something about baseball, snapped out a, “Shut up.”

Buck threw back his head and laughed.

“So who the hell was that guy, anyway?”

“Some wannabe firefighter,” Eddie answered. “He managed to get some gear from the 147, someone named Harmon’s.”

“There’s an Aaron Harmon from the 147 on our B-shift.” Buck tilted his head. “I know he had to get new turnouts, I wonder if it’s the same guy.”

“Probably, there weren’t any other Harmons on the roster,” he said. “Guy just wanted to help people, I guess. Be a hero.”

“I get that,” Buck said with a nod.

They fell silent for a bit as they scanned through their menus. Well, Eddie scanned. Buck, when he looked up to ask him what he was thinking about getting, seemed almost as if he was about to say something. But then a waitress appeared to get their drink orders - coffee with too much sugar for Buck and just water for Eddie, as he intended on crashing as soon as he got home - and the moment disappeared.

When Austin stepped through the door of his apartment, it seemed for a moment as if he was about to turn around and walk right back out. Which Daniel felt was a little rude, all things considered. He was a delight to have for company, after all.

“Hi.” He smiled and waved from where he stood by the microwave; he got a dirty glare for it. “How was work?”

“Fuck off,” was Austin’s rude response. “They took the engine for detailing, which meant I spent this morning helping move everything over to the temporary replacement.”

“Did you get a chance to eat, at least?”

“No.”

Daniel nodded, expecting this, and opened the microwave to take out the McDonald’s bag inside. Austin yanked it out of his hands and dug into it without even a word of thanks, but Daniel didn’t mind.

“So,” he said, watching his not-boyfriend - or his zucchini, as Buck would apparently call him - stuff his mouth. “Does this one have a steering lock?”

The only thing that kept him from having food flung at his head was that Austin was too hungry to waste it.

Chapter 39

Chapter Notes

I took the opportunity to pick up a thread that I'd left dangling since Spare Parts, so.
Content Warning: mention of the Dr. Wells incident; Buck's unhealthy view of sex (especially in regards to himself); reference to drug use

See the end of the chapter for more notes

There was, apparently, a limit to Danny’s tolerance for Buck’s hovering. It had been the main reason that Buck was willing to go along with his “grounding,” his reluctance to leave his brother on his own. There was nothing really stopping Drake from showing up to harass him, after all, because it wasn’t like the temporary restraining order was magically able to keep him at bay. Buck wanted - needed - to be there to send him packing if he did decide to crawl out of the gutter again.

Danny, however, apparently thought otherwise. When he somehow - Buck couldn’t decide if it was from Eddie himself or Austin sharing gossip - heard about Eddie’s intentions to take him out for a date night, he’d practically shoved Buck out the door. Buck might’ve dug in his heels, might’ve tried to twist it around to Eddie bringing Chris over again, except Albert was staying in tonight so he was mollified that Danny wasn’t entirely on his own.

The place they went to was a restaurant that Buck had mentioned a grand total of once, but which Eddie very obviously remembered. It was another outdoor dining experience, though Buck knew that this one had been doing it before the pandemic, the tables set up along a reflecting pool and each covered in white cloth with vases of flowers in the middle of them. At one end of the dining area was a small bar, and there were strings of lights that stretched from pole to pole.

“Alright, hold on.” Buck sat down his glass of wine - red, of course - and leaned in. “They were bleeding from their eyes?”

“Their eyes, their noses, mouths, just…” Eddie made an encompassing gesture with his hand towards his own face. “From everywhere, basically. And still found time to hit on me.”

“Well yeah, you’re you.”

“Thanks.” Eddie smiled prettily at him. “Anyways, they’d been smoking something from some dispensary, Puff-”

“Puffer’s Paradise.” Buck nodded. “They lace their product with what’s basically rat poison, something about prolonging the high? We’ve had a couple calls.”

“We had to go door-to-door, because the ladies apparently decided that sharing was caring.”

“Sharing your drugs is very neighborly.” They both laughed. “Did I ever tell you the time I walked in on Danny and his girlfriend getting high?”

“I don’t think that’s ever come up, no,” Eddie told him.

“It was back in Hershey. On Valentine’s Day, I think? Valentine’s night. Mom and Dad were out and so was Maddie. I woke up and went looking for him, found him in the backyard with his girlfriend… Vanessa? No, that doesn’t sound right. Her name started with a V, I remember that much. Anyway.” Buck flapped a hand. “I found them in the backyard and I could smell it. He told me it was a skunk.”

“And you believed that? Would skunks up there even be out by then?”

“I was like, nine!” Buck protested as his boyfriend laughed at him. “Why would I have known what pot smells like?”

“But you know what it smells like now,” Eddie teased.

“I don’t know what you mean, I’m completely innocent.”

“Oh, I’m sure,” he said, shaking his head as Buck pretended to draw a halo above himself.

“Hi!” Buck had seen the waitress coming, but Eddie had not. He jumped in his seat, and then glowered at Buck when he did a poor job of hiding his laughter. “How are you all doing? Would you like to order any dessert?”

“Uh, actually, yeah.” Eddie dropped his fork onto his empty plate and picked up the dessert menu. “Where’s- There. The chocolate cheesecake sounded good.”

“Oh, that does sound good,” Buck said, looking at his own dessert menu. “You wanna just share?”

Eddie gave him a flat stare.

“I wouldn’t get hardly any of it, that way.”

“Rude.” Buck sniffed. “Two slices, then. Please.”

“Looks like we’ll have to get some extra cardio in,” Eddie quipped, wagging his eyebrows at Buck while the waitress left to put in their order. Buck meant to laugh, or at least smile, but the expression turned into a grimace instead. All the humor left his boyfriend’s face. “Alright, what’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

“Yeah, no. Something’s been bugging you for a couple days now.”

“Nothing’s wrong,” Buck insisted. His boyfriend was not buying it, though. “Okay, fine. It’s just… Something Copeland brought up.”

“Which was?” Eddie urged, putting his elbows on the table and leaning forward a little.

“I-” God, Buck didn’t even know how to talk about it with Eddie without it sounding pathetic or upsetting him. “I wanted to have sex with you every time we’ve had sex.”

Eddie stared at him, a myriad of expressions crossing his face as he processed that statement.

“Okay,” he finally said, drawing out the word. “Honestly, I was never worried you didn’t. Until now. Now I’m very worried.”

Buck rolled his eyes.

“I just said-”

“Yeah, yeah, yeah,” Eddie interrupted. “But that implies there was a possibility of us having sex when you didn’t want to, and I am very concerned about that. What the hell were you and Copeland talking about that that came up?”

“I’m not really sure?” Buck admitted. “I was talking about relationships I’ve had, mostly about Abby, and then that got into why I turned Abby down at first, and just… I dunno. Copeland got weird when I mentioned Wells, too.”

“Wells?”

“A therapist Bobby recommended after the roller coaster rescue. I had sex with her,” Buck said. Eddie blinked, opened his mouth with the clear intention to say something, and Buck hurriedly told him, “There was- I had- Don’t worry about it.”

He didn’t really want to talk about her with Eddie. Not after the way Copeland had gone quiet when he mentioned the very same, her face going blank, and then she started asking questions in that gentle, careful tone people used when they didn’t want to frighten an animal away. It had all made Buck’s stomach squirm with something uneasy, especially the long moment of silence that followed him admitting that he wasn’t sure he’d wanted to have sex with her. 

They moved on back to Abby shortly after, but Copeland’s questions and remarks had taken on a different shade from before as he talked about why he’d turned Abby down at first. Every time the conversation circled back around to sex, Dr. Copeland’s face took on a more pinched expression. And all the while, the squirming in Buck’s stomach got worse and worse. The questions she asked, the words she used, they made it seem like Copeland thought-

( “So what would you have done if the date hadn’t been interrupted?” Copeland asked him. “If you got to the end of the date and she wanted to have sex, what would you have done?”

“Had sex with her, I guess,” Buck answered with a shrug. He thought that was kinda obvious, really.

“But what if you didn’t want to have sex with her at the time?”

“I don’t know,” he admitted. “What does that matter?”

Copeland took a breath, audible through the tablet’s speakers, and simply said,

“Okay.” )

Buck gave his head a quick shake and refocused on Eddie across the table from him. He didn’t want to ruin their date night by thinking and talking about a conversation with his therapist that he desperately did not want to think or talk about. Which meant the best course of action, before Eddie insisted on talking about it, was to change the subject.

“Has Austin murdered that B-shift probie yet?” he asked.

“No,” Eddie answered, after a brief moment spent silently frowning at him. “I think you’re right that it was him with the itching powder, though. The probie was like a dog with fleas at shift-change.”

“Austin’s revenge is quiet and unpleasant,” Buck intoned with a nod, as dramatically as he could. Eddie rolled his eyes. “And he’s sneaky, too. How often do you forget that he’s there? Even when you’re in the engine and he’s the one driving? The man must’ve been a ninja in a past life.”

“A ninja?” Eddie scoffed. “Maybe it’s just that you don’t pay attention and everyone’s distracted by your noise.”

“So what’s the excuse, now that I’m not there?”

By the time the waitress came back with their slices of chocolate cheesecake, Eddie was still unable to come up with one.

“I had no idea what to say afterwards!” Eddie complained as they slowly stalked down the sidewalk of the quiet neighborhood they’d been called to. “He ended up changing the subject, and then our dessert came and we just pretended like he never said it.”

“Personally,” Austin said, plucking a blackberry from the plastic container he was carrying. The blackberries were meant to be used for bait, but Eddie was’t certain they’d last that long. “I want to know why you’re talking to me about this.”

“Because Danny would overreact and I can’t vent to Buck about Buck.”

“I miss when everyone would forget I existed,” the other man complained, popping the berry into his mouth.

The 118 had been called out to a neighborhood because a wild turkey apparently went on a rampage, attacking various people just going about their day. Eddie didn’t have much experience with turkeys that weren’t plucked and stuffed and ready to be carved, so he couldn’t say if the reported level of violence was typical of them. All he knew was that Chimney and Hen had their hands full with treating the various lacerations that the feathered fiend’s victims were sporting, while Eddie and Austin hunted down the perpetrator.

Eddie took the opportunity to vent with the one person in the entire station that he could confidently say wouldn’t go spreading it around. Because he needed to vent to somebody about the fact his boyfriend felt like he had to reassure him that he’d actually wanted it every time they’d had sex. Because there was no way to interpret that any other way but that there were times Buck had sex that he hadn’t wanted it, and Eddie was still feeling some sort of unpleasant way about that.

“Why are we the ones doing this?” Austin asked. “This is a job for animal control.”

“You heard Cap,” Eddie told him. “They’re delayed getting here.”

“It’s a turkey, it can wait until they do. I’m missing out on good gossip,” Austin said. “Hen’s in a mood about something. I could be eavesdropping on that right now.”

“My problems aren’t good enough gossip?” Eddie asked. “I’m worried now that there were times when Buck and I had sex that he didn’t want it.”

Sure, Buck said that wasn’t true, but he was just as likely to lie his ass off to avoid upsetting Eddie, so the reliability of his statement was questionable.

“Diaz, I am literally the worst person for this. Save it for Dan.”

“No! If he thinks- He’d murder me with his bat.”

“No he wouldn’t.”

Austin sounded very confident about that. Strangely confident. Before Eddie could press him about it, though, the sound of something rustling in the hedges behind them had them both stopping and then turning. He fumbled for the net launcher he’d been issued as Sonny the turkey, once beloved neighborhood pet turned terror, waddled out onto the sidewalk.

The turkey didn’t seem very intimidating, but the wounds he left on his victims more than made up for his meek appearance. The bird stared at them, his wattle of flesh flapping on his neck and the pink snood hanging from his beak - thanks, Buck, for that random bit of knowledge - looking quite obscene. And then, as Eddie swung the launcher around, Sonny began to rush them.

The bird gobbled very unhappily as the net wrapped itself around him, sending him flying in a flurry of feathers.

The visit to Maddie and Chimney’s apartment was unplanned, prompted mainly by Albert and Danny both being out, though for different reasons, and the knowledge that Buck hadn’t really seen his sister since all the drama surrounding their parents’ visit. Eddie, bless him, wasn’t bothered by impromptu plans and just gamely went along with it.

And that mostly explained why the three of them - Chris had come over as well - were now standing around the kitchen island, helping put together little gift baskets.

“No, no, no,” Chimney tutted as he went past on his way to the other room. “Three inches. Those are too short.”

“That’s what she said,” Eddie muttered under his breath, just loudly enough for Buck to hear. Buck snorted a laugh and shoved at him.

“Why are we helping you again?” he asked his sister, setting down the scissors he’d been using to cut pieces of ribbon.

“You’re the ones that showed up unannounced,” Maddie pointed out.

“Hey, don’t look at me,” Eddie said. He pointed at Buck. “It was his idea.”

“Is this three inches?” Chris asked, holding up his ribbon.

“Looks it to me,” Maddie told him with a firm nod. “What are Dan and Albert doing tonight, since you’re here pestering us?”

“Rude. I am a delight to be had,” Buck said, and then smacked Eddie for the way he scoffed. “Danny’s doing something for Athena, and I’m pretty sure Al’s got a date.”

“Let’s hope he doesn’t end up defiling your guys’ couch,” Chimney commented as he came back with a box filled with tiny glass bottles.

Buck caught Eddie’s eye and then had to hurriedly look away, lest they both started laughing.

“What does defile mean?” Chris asked, face screwed up with concentration as he carefully cut up his ribbon into pieces. They weren’t all the same length, some too short and some too long, but none of them were going to point that out.

“Make it dirty,” Eddie explained.

“Oh. Danny could just make him clean it, then.”

“Yeah,” Buck agreed, clearing his throat. Eddie’s face was red with the suppressed laughter. “He could.”

“Okay, we have sleep masks, ear plugs, some time-release melatonin,” Chimney said, listing off the things they were putting into the gift baskets, and then plucked out one of the tiny little bottles from the box. “And if all else fails, booze. Everything you need to get a good night’s rest when you’re next-door to a crying baby.”

“Are you sure this isn’t a little excessive?” Maddie worriedly asked. “I mean, we’re just having a baby. We’re not launching a campaign of shock and awe.”

“I dunno,” Eddie said, smiling down at Chris. “Having experienced both, they’re pretty much the same. This one was a loud little thing.”

“Dad!” the kid whined.

“They say good fences make good neighbors, but a gift basket never hurt anyone,” Chimney said, and then asked Maddie, “You think it’ll work?”

“If nothing else,” she said, “we’ll get to know our neighbors.”

“Careful what you wish for,” Buck warned. “You might get a Tia Alma, but you might also get an Old Man Joe.”

“Was he the one who’d wander around talking to thin air?” Eddie asked.

“No, no, you’re thinking of Crazy Carl. Old Man Joe was the racist guy who always answered his door with a gun out and thought everyone with a tan was part of a cartel. And Crazy Carl was only crazy when he was on- Er, y’know. His stuff.” Buck realized mid sentence that it was probably inappropriate to talk about his old neighbor’s drug use in front of the child. “He was a pretty cool guy the rest of the time, though. Helped me pass chemistry.”

The last bit was said to Maddie and Chimney, who were both looking more and more horrified with every word that left his mouth.

“I’m sure your neighbors aren’t like that,” Eddie told them in a clear attempt at reassurance.

“Oh, yeah, this is a nice place!” Buck hurriedly added. “I bet none of them have guns. Or, they might, actually. A couple of them probably do. And drug use isn’t really limited to… Er, I’ll stop talking now.”

“I think that would be for the best,” Maddie said, voice strained. “Thank you.”

Daniel wondered what, exactly, was going through Athena’s head when she came up with this oh-so-clever plan of hers. Sure, he hadn’t seen a problem with it at first when she called him up and asked him to go visit Michael, saying that she was worried that being stuck at home and isolated was getting to him.
