It had been a while since they’d had their last “support group” get together, so it hadn’t taken much to get him to agree.

Apparently, with a lack of jobs due to the pandemic, Michael usurped leadership of his building’s homeowners association, which he then had approve the installation of an entire wall of windows. That was where Athena’s concerns began, because Michael also got a telescope for people watching. It was apparently how he spent most of his time now, spying on the people in the building across from him.

The problem with Athena’s plan, however, was that Daniel was not the only person she recruited for it. He’d just finished greeting Michael and Harry when someone else knocked at the door and when Michael answered it, in came fucking Nash with bags of food. The fire captain had frozen just inside, he and Daniel simply staring at each other while Michael looked on in absolute delight.

Things were awkward, suffice to say. Even worse, the food was good, too. It made Daniel hate Nash a little bit more.

“Dinner was great,” Harry announced when his plate was picked clean. “You should come visit more often.”

“Uh-huh, and you should do your homework,” Michael told him.

“I can do it tomorrow morning,” the kid said, and then caught his father’s eye. “Or not.”

He got up from the table and they watched him walk away to his room, before Michael turned back to Bobby.

“He’s right, though,” Michael said. “Please thank Athena for forcing you to bring it over.”

“She didn’t force me,” Bobby denied. “But she did think maybe you could use someone to talk to.”

“Oh, is that why you both showed up at my door? I’m fine, really.”

“Athena told me about your new hobby,” Daniel said, leaning his elbow on the table. Nash went to the telescope as Michael hurriedly chased him. “I didn’t peg you as someone who got off on watching.”

The comment earned him a disapproving glower from the fire captain before the man went back to peering through the telescope, but it just had Michael stammering out denials.

“It’s not- It’s really just a way to pass the time, y’know? I have so much of it lately,” the man said, and then laughed. “But, you know, there is something weird going on across the street.”

“You mean the guy? The guy with the women?” Nash asked. “With all the women young enough to be his daughters?”

Daniel rolled his eyes at the man as he got up to go take a look for himself. This was almost certainly not what Athena intended to happen when she sent them over.

“There’s so much foot traffic,” Michael explained while Nash continued to peer through the telescope. “I mean, young women, older women, a few men. They’re in and out all the time every day. I’ve seen some of ‘em with bruises and a couple of them have bandages.”

“She just gave him money.”

“What? Let me see.” Michael practically shoved Nash out of the way.

“So, what do you think?” Nash asked. “Personal injury attorney? Underground boxing instructor?”

“What are you on?” Daniel couldn’t help but blurt out. Nash’s glare was glacial. “He’s a prostitute, obviously. Rent here’s worse than El Paso.”

“And the bruises and bandages?”

“Don’t kink shame them.”

“None of that justifies the trash,” Michael said, interrupting before their comments could start edging towards the truly cutting.

“The trash?” For once, Daniel and Nash were in agreement for something. It was horrible. “What about the trash?"

Chapter End Notes

This became my second longest fic at some point. It was not meant to be this long.

Chapter 40

Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

If Athena was under the impression that Nash and Daniel’s presence would somehow rein Michael in, somehow pull him away from his newest people watching obsession, the sergeant was horrifically mistaken. Almost the exact opposite happened, with Michael digging out a pair of binoculars so he and Nash could both spy on Probably-a-Prostitute across the way. They’d even turned off the lights in the apartment so they weren’t so easily caught.

Daniel was perched on the end of the dining table as he texted Austin all about the ridiculousness he was witnessing, since the other two were hogging the binoculars and telescope, when David, Michael’s surgeon boyfriend, got home. The first thing the man did, while throwing out a confused greeting, was flip on the lights. Nash and Michael immediately swirled around, hissing at him to,

“Turn it off! Turn it off!”

David did so, looking terribly confused, and the two men turned back to their voyeurism. Daniel turned where he sat and exaggerated his eye roll, making sure David could see it. They hadn’t interacted much since Daniel helped rescue him and Michael from the elevator, the pandemic having gotten in the way of socialising.

“Oh, she definitely wasn’t ready to leave,” Michael observed, entirely focused on watching the people across the street once more instead of greeting his boyfriend.

“You see the way he kept trying to move her to the door?” Nash asked him. “He wanted her gone.”

“Mhmm.”

“What is happening right now?” David asked as he joined the two men at the window.

“They’re spying on the prostitute,” Daniel answered, and the surgeon quickly turned to him to yelp out,

“The what!?”

“Prostitution is your theory,” Michael retorted. “A theory that doesn’t even explain all the trash!”

“I told you, condoms and lube,” Daniel said. Nash wasn’t even reacting anymore, which took away half the fun Daniel had been having. “Lots and lots of condoms and lube.”

“Wait, this is about the guy with the trash again?” David shook his head at them, his exasperation made clear by every motion he took. “Michael, we talked about this.”

“It’s just too much trash!” Michael exclaimed, barely looking away from the telescope’s eyepiece.

“Everyone has too much trash,” David pointed out. “We’re all getting our lives delivered. The other day, you got a box the size of a toaster with dental floss in it.”

“Just dental floss?” Daniel asked, curious.”Was it a jumbo thing of it or something?”

“No! It was a regular thing of dental floss in a toaster sized box.”

“It’s not just that,” Michael argued. “This guy lives alone and all manner of folks come in perfectly fine, then leave battered and bruised. So whatever’s going on over there isn’t innocent, and it probably isn’t legal.”

“They’re all consenting adults!” Daniel burst out. Loudly enough, evidently, that David startled where he stood. “Whatever he’s doing to them, it’s because they asked and paid for it. And there are a lot of people who are perfectly happy to walk away covered in bruises and declare it a good night.”

Nash tore himself away from his binoculars to give him a stare filled with reluctant curiosity.

“What did you do in El Paso?” the fire captain asked.

“Bold of you to assume I did any of that in El Paso,” Daniel retorted. Michael and David glanced between them, eyebrows inching skyward. “You don’t know what my social life here is like.”

Nash grimaced. Michael laughed.

“Well,” Nash said, trying to get his metaphorical legs under himself again. “Maybe… Maybe all that trash is him dumping the evidence of whatever he’s doing.”

David shot him a very unimpressed look.

“I wish there was a way to see what was inside of those bags,” Michael lamented, going back to the telescope and the show across the street.

“You could always look in the dumpster,” David suggested, proving he was not actually above it all.

Michael shot up straight and shared a look with Nash, before they both turned to the surgeon.

“Great idea!” Nash told him. “Do you know where they are?”

“Right there, next to the building.” Michael pointed them out as he spoke. “And I don’t think they’re locked.”

“Okay, give me a second,” Nash requested, clearly thinking things through. Daniel texted Austin an update while he waited for Nash to have a complete thought. It took a moment. “Alright. Michael, you stay here and keep an eye on our shady friend. If he decides to go on another trash run, you call me.”

“Got it.”

“David, we’re gonna need some surgical gloves,” Nash said, slapping the man on the shoulder as he headed for the door. “Let’s go!”

“Wait, but.” David blinked in bewilderment. “Why me? Why not Dan?”

Michael was still laughing at the question for some time after Nash and David left the apartment. Daniel picked up the binoculars Nash had discarded and used them to track the duo’s progress across the street, the fire captain giving a salute up to the window. As they got to the dumpster, Daniel swiped through his contacts list.

“What?” was Athena’s distracted greeting.

“Quick question: is it illegal to go through someone’s dumpster?”

“Why?” The sergeant managed to pack a lot of suspicion into that single, hissed out word.

“‘Cause your ex-husband’s boyfriend and your current husband are shoulders deep in someone’s bin right now.”

Michael popped up from the telescope with a glare.

“You called Athena!?”

“It’s a legal gray area.” Athena did not sound pleased. Someone in the background - Daniel was fairly certain it was Hen - asked a question. “I sent idiots to babysit an idiot.”

“I really don’t know what you were expecting,” Daniel told her.

“Not whatever this is, that’s for sure.”

Michael glared at him a moment longer and went back to the telescope. Then immediately let out a worried,

“Oh, no.”

“What?” Daniel asked. “What is it?”

“He’s taking his trash out,” Michael said, pulling out his own phone and fumbling with it for a moment, before pressing it to his own ear. “C’mon, Bobby.”

“Try the other one,” Daniel advised, peering at the duo with his binoculars. As he watched, Nash somehow managed to send his phone flying into the depths of the dumpster.

“What’s going on now?” Athena demanded.

“Uh, nothing,” Daniel answered as Michael tried to call David. The sound of a phone vibrating against wood had the two of them turning to the dining table, where David’s phone lay. “Oh, wow, we really are a bunch of idiots.”

Michael scoffed and then dashed out of the apartment.

“Okay, I want it to be known that none of this was my idea,” Daniel told Athena as he turned back to track Nash and David. Nash had finally found his phone and had it pressed to his ear as he called someone. Then the two of them hurriedly started back, David cradling a large trash bag in his arms. “This is something Buck and Eddie would’ve done, back in the day. Or today, even.”

“How pissed off am I about to be, Dan?”

“That depends. How d’ya feel about having to post bail for us?”

There was a tired huff of a sigh, and then the line dropped. Minutes later, Nash and David were bursting back into the apartment.

“He’s not a prostitute!” Nash declared. “Where’s Michael?”

“Uh, over there.” Daniel pointed across the street, glaring at Nash when the man yanked the binoculars out of his hand to look. David went for the telescope. “Pretty sure Athena is on the way.”

“You called her?”

“Of course I called her,” was Daniel’s incredulous response to that question. “If there’s going to be cops, I want the only one I trust to be here.”

Plus, he wasn’t certain if the temporary restraining order would hold in this case. He wasn’t at any of the places listed on the order and it wasn’t like anyone had a reason to suspect he was even here, which meant they had no reason not to send Drake, if the situation called for a detective. Daniel kinda hoped that Athena would somehow just… Get ahead of that.

“What the hell is he doing?” David demanded.

“Breaking and entering?” was Nash’s answer.

“Wait, is he inside the guy’s apartment?” Daniel asked.

“What’s going on?” Harry had come out of his room, bleary eyed and dressed in his pajamas. Daniel figured that he’d finally been roused by the raucous they were making.

“Um,” David managed to get out, sending a wild-eyed look of panic Nash’s way.

“Well,” Nash said, and then paused.

Daniel rolled his eyes at the two men. It was very clear they needed practice at coming up with bullshit cover stories for when the younguns interrupted things. It was a very useful skill to have when one had a curious kid sticking their nose into everything. On the bright side, Harry wasn’t in any way Daniel’s kid, so he didn’t have to worry about what answer he gave here.

“Just some minor criminal acts,” he told the kid, and got two sets of glares for it. “Don’t worry about it, go back to bed.”

“What?” was Harry’s confused reply.

“Don’t worry about it,” Daniel repeated, tugging out his phone again.

Athena answered after a couple rings, with a snappish,

“What now?”

“Michael broke into the guy’s apartment.”

“I’m gonna kill him!” was exclaimed at the same time Harry shrieked, “Dad did what!?”

“He didn’t…” Nash tried, but quickly gave up with a sigh.

“You’re the only one with any sense there, somehow. God help us all. Go over and pull him out by his ear,” Athena instructed. “I’m on my way.”

“Copy that.”

David ended up going with him, the pair of them leaving Nash behind to keep an eye on Harry. They hurried down the stairs, Daniel having decided that waiting on the elevator took too long, and across the street.

“So what did you find?” Daniel asked as they dashed along like they were in some kind of thriller movie. “Nash sounded really certain about me being wrong.”

“Surgical supplies,” David answered, right on his heels. “Bags of used surgical supplies. Bloody surgical supplies.”

“That’s…” Daniel paused for a moment, before hurrying along again. “Okay, yeah, I was wrong.”

The sound of sirens reached them as they burst through the doors to the building’s lobby, and Daniel saw a police cruiser squeal to a stop through the glass just as they got to the stairs. The sight of them had adrenaline pumping through his veins, and he picked up the pace while ignoring David’s worried comments. They reached the floor that the shady guy lived on, and it was more guesswork than certainty that led to them entering the apartment with the door that was ajar.

The first room was the living room, and no one was immediately visible. A door was open, immediately to their right. David was the first one there, letting out a dismayed cry of

“Michael!”

The inside of the room looked, by accounts, like a surgical suite. There was medical equipment and an exam table and an IV stand with fluids still hung up. Hell, there was even one of those plastic wall trays with a patient file stuck inside it. Michael was sprawled out on his side, unconscious, with a small tank of what might have been oxygen or nitrous oxide discarded by his feet.

There was also the sound of multiple sets of booted feet rushing into the apartment, but Daniel didn’t pay them any mind as he dropped to his knees beside Michael. He felt Michael’s pulse, felt around his head, grimaced at the knot he could feel. Being felt up was enough to have Michael groaning into awareness, thankfully.

“Easy,” David cautioned, helping his boyfriend up and into a nearby stool. Daniel rose with them. “It looks like you took a pretty good hit to the head.”

“That is nothing compared to what I’m gonna do to you four… amateur detectives,” Athena snarled as she stomped into the room with them. Daniel was willing to bet that she was substituting for more colorful words. When did she even get there? Just how close had she been when he called her about Michael?

“Hey, hey. I didn’t do anything,” Daniel pointed out. The sergeant’s glare was fierce, and it would probably have sent Buck running for the corner like a scolded puppy, but he just stared back at her. “Is he…?”

Daniel didn’t finish the question, and Athena didn’t need him to clarify any of the details.

“No, they haven’t sent any detective yet,” she said, tone softening for a moment. Daniel relaxed, tension draining away that he hadn’t even been aware of. “Where’s my husband?”

“Bobby’s at our place with Harry,” David said. Athena’s glare came back to life as she focused on him, sniffing the air a little.

“You smell like trash,” she stated.

David didn’t respond to that observation, the air around him taking on a tinge of embarrassment, and pulled out a penlight from his pocket.

“Do you always have that with you?” Daniel asked.

“Not always,” David answered, clicking it on. He shone it into Michael’s eyes, who immediately cringed away and batted at it.

“Is the woman okay?” he asked, still sounding groggy.

“What woman?” David and Daniel asked at the same time.

“The woman that was on the table.” Michael twisted a little where he sat, to pat the cushioned top of the exam table. “She was right here.”

“There wasn’t any woman when we got here,” David said, looking to Daniel. Daniel shook his head in agreement. “There wasn’t anybody at all. Just you, unconscious.”

“How did you know I was here?”

“Uh, telescope, remember?” Daniel reminded him. “Pointed right at the window there?”

“Right, right,” Michael faintly said, blinking a little. “There was a woman here, and she was not okay. She looked dead, and- and she asked me for my help.”

“They’re checking all the cameras out on the street,” Athena said with a frown. “Do you remember what she looked like?”

“Yeah, um. Brunette, shoulder-length hair. Medium build,” Michael rattled off. “She looked half-dead. She was so pale I thought she was dead, at first.”

“And she was injured?”

“She had two bloody spots on her belly.” He indicated on his stomach where they’d be. Daniel tried to think of what kind of surgery that would be, since the woman probably came here and paid for it. A botched tummy tuck, maybe? “The front of her gown, it was… It was soaked through, ‘Thena.”

“Alright.” Athena sighed, and tugged her mask on. “Give me a minute.”

“You took a pretty good hit,” David said to Michael, after the sergeant left them to go confer with the officers going through the rest of the apartment. “We should get you to the hospital, get some scans done.”

“No, that’s too much hassle these days,” Michael complained. “I gotta get home, Harry’s probably terrified.”

Daniel scoffed.

“Bet ya anything he thinks it’s the coolest thing ever,” he said. “Until the next coolest thing ever comes around.”

Daniel was right, of course, mainly because he remembered how Buck had been at that age. Between him and David, they got Michael back to his own apartment, where they then regaled an enraptured Harry with the tale of what had occurred while David kept a steady supply of ice packs going. Michael, of course, groused about it from his couch the entire time, but Daniel couldn’t really blame him any for the ill-mood.

Concussions were not fun, even unconfirmed ones.

“Nope, gotta stay awake,” David told him, giving Michael a fresh ice pack to press to his head. “We really should have just taken you to the hospital, you lost consciousness.”

“Why did I have to fall in love with a brain surgeon?” Michael groaned. “Anything from Athena?”

“Nothing yet,” Nash said. “They checked all the cameras, but they didn’t find any sign of the woman. Just the fake doctor leaving the building with a bag.”

“You don’t think she was in that bag, do you?” Harry excitedly asked.

“Harry,” Michael tutted. And then, like they were all thinking, followed it with, “You don’t, do you?”

“Athena said it was a pretty small bag,” Nash told him, an answer that had Michael relaxing into the couch cushions.

“Maybe she’s in the dumpster,” Daniel suggested. “The two of you could go diving in it again.”

It was an idea that had Nash glowering at him.

“There was no bag,” Michael suddenly blurted out, sitting up. “The woman, I saw her clothes and her shoes, but there wasn’t any bag.”

“That doesn’t mean anything,” Daniel pointed out. “Maybe she just didn’t have a bag.”

“But there wasn’t a wallet, either,” he said. “Or even a phone. Just a keychain. But no one saw her leave the building.”

There was a beat of silence, and then they all reached the same conclusion. Daniel loudly swore and Nash didn’t even give him the stink eye for it, because he was too busy dialing Athena. The sergeant quickly rallied the troops, leading the officers on a door-to-door search of the other building’s apartments. Daniel and David followed behind, staying out of the way, because as a paramedic and a brain surgeon, respectively, they’d be needed when the injured woman was found.

Which she was. At one apartment, no one answered Athena’s banging. A universal key, in the form of a portable battering ram, provided ingress. Athena went in on the heels of a pair of officers, and then immediately came back out into the hall to call for Daniel and David.

The woman was on her couch and she was in a far worse state than when Michael first found her, pale and limp. She didn’t even move when David pressed his fingers to her neck.

“Pulse is steady,” David reported. “My best guess, she’s down about a liter and a half.”

“How far away is the bus?” Daniel asked Athena, digging out dressings from the medical kit David brought. He shoved them onto the woman’s stomach, over the two lacerations that were soaking through her gown, and pressed down.

“A minute or two,” the sergeant answered.

When on-duty paramedics arrived from the 122, Daniel let David rattle off the information they needed to know. Now that the victim had been located, and the perpetrator was officially in the wind, a detective was bound to be on their way to the scenes of the crime. Athena didn’t seem surprised when, after the woman was loaded up, he announced that he was taking off regardless of whether or not anyone needed to ask him anything.

Austin definitely wasn’t surprised when Daniel let himself into his apartment, looking away from whatever he was watching for long enough to greet him with a,

“How was the playdate?”

“I had to spend it dealing with Nash,” Daniel complained as he toed off his shoes, leaving them by the door.

“How awful.” Austin was lounging on his couch, looking stupidly cozy in one of his sweaters. “This is me, shedding a tear for your suffering.”

“You are such an asshole,” Daniel told him. A moment’s debate had him sprawling across Austin’s lap. “Why do I even like you?”

“I ask myself that very same question about you every day,” was the other man’s bland reply. “There’s a thing about your brother I need to tell you about.”

“Is it gonna piss me off?”

“Probably.”

Daniel let out a groan and then wiggled around to get comfortable.

“Tell me later.”

Chapter End Notes

There's a minor plothole in this episode, that being: there is a giant fucking telescope pointed right into the guy's living room that they were using to spy on him, and you're telling me neither Bobby nor David saw the guy dragging a limp body out of his apartment????

Chapter 41

It took a stupidly short amount of time for Danny to talk Buck into doing this with him. The only thing that made Buck pause and question any of it was the simple logistics, given the current state of the world. But Danny simply told him that,

“It’ll be fine, squirt. Don’t worry about it.”

Realistically, Buck knew and understood that maybe, just maybe, he shouldn’t just take his big brother’s word on everything. Especially when he said things like “it’ll be fine” and “don’t worry about it.” Because Danny’s views on what counted as “fine” and what didn’t need to be worried about were a bit… Broad, so to speak.

Buck chose to trust him anyway. He was his big brother, after all.

Buck’s friend - well, “friend” here was as broad of a term as Danny’s “fine” - agreed with Danny’s assessment. Jane and Buck had met years ago, when they both worked at one of the bars that Buck tended after first moving to the city. Before Danny gently shoved him into firefighting, before he was Buck. They hadn’t really, truly kept in touch after Buck quit, not beyond that vague periphery of Facebook friends that never interacted or even acknowledged the other’s existence outside of yearly birthday wishes. Not even that, anymore, since he hadn’t been on his Facebook in an age. It was enough, however, for Buck to reach out and inquire about doing what Danny was wanting. Jane had accepted with startling quickness.

So here they were, in a tattoo parlor that was empty of anyone except the three of them. A tattoo parlor that he was fairly certain was supposed to be empty of everyone including them, because as far as he was aware, they hadn’t been given the go ahead to reopen yet. But Jane said it was fine, and Danny said it was fine, and now Buck was perched in a chair several feet away from where Danny and Jane were while he waited his turn.

Buck came back from his Neverending Gap Year Road Trip with several tattoos, and then got another while in Los Angeles, so he was no stranger to letting a stranger repeatedly stab him with a needle. This, however, was Danny’s first time. And probably his last, judging from the way he was handling it.

He was sitting in the client chair, shirt balled up in his lap and hands gripping the armrests so tightly that his knuckles were white. He was also looking anywhere but at where Jane had the tattoo gun pressed to the left side of chest, right above his heart. Even though Jane was masked up - all three of them were - and was wearing a shiny face shield, Buck could tell she was finding his brother’s reaction to be very funny.

“So what made you decide on this for your first one?” she asked. The tattoo in question was a five-pointed star within a fiery circle.

“Danny’s a nerd,” Buck crowed. His brother turned his head to glare at him. “Well you are! You and Austin are both nerds, he’s perfect for you.”

“I am not a nerd.”

“Honey.” Jane raised a single, pierced, condescending eyebrow. Her eyebrows were a dark brown that contrasted to the bright green of her hair; it had been platinum blond when Buck first met her, and then a deep blue when he left the bar they both worked at for other pastures. “I’ve done this tattoo on a dozen clients, and each and every one of them was a queer nerd.”

“I am not a nerd,” Danny insisted. His head twitched like he wanted to turn and glare at her, before thinking better of it.

“You spent last Saturday rolling dice and pretending to club imaginary monsters,” Buck teased.

“Austin doesn’t have anyone else to play it with except his nephews, our schedules are too weird.”

“Right, and I’m sure there’s absolutely no other firefighters in the whole of Los Angeles that would be interested in playing.”

Danny opened his mouth, no doubt to shoot off another retort, and then he paused with a scowl. Buck was willing to bet that the thought of Austin finding other first responders, ones with the same unwieldy schedule as them, to play the game with had never occurred to his brother before now. He wondered if the whole thing was Austin’s idea or Danny’s, and how little convincing his brother needed if it was the former. Probably very little, knowing his brother.

“Face it, Danny, you’re a nerd,” Buck taunted with a grin. “Next thing y’know, you’ll be going to conventions while wearing fake ears and a onesie.”

“Shut up, you brat,” his brother half-heartedly snapped.

“There’s nothing wrong with it! I just have something else I can make fun of you for. Y’know, besides how many times that show made you cry like a baby. It was a lot of times, Jane. A. Lot.”

Buck smiled at Danny’s responding glare.

They bickered as Jane finished up the tattoo on Danny’s chest, and then while she covered it up and got things ready for Buck’s turn in the chair. Unlike his brother, he didn’t have any queasiness about the process. He watched, intrigued, as the needle followed the path of the stencil Jane was using - in the same spot Danny got his - and got into talking with her about what she’d been doing during the pandemic.

The answer seemed to be that she’d had to take more than a few trips to Nevada and Arizona for clients. Which, again, Buck probably should’ve found questionable, but she and Danny were both still insisting that everything was fine and he was trusting them on that. Even though they had to park behind the tattoo parlor, sneaking in and out of the place like burglars.

After they’d gotten care instructions for their new ink, which Buck was already more than familiar with, they paid and headed out. He felt bouncier than usual, thanks to the endorphins, and mercilessly annoyed his brother through getting themselves food from a drive-thru and then the drive back to the apartment. Their bickering came to an abrupt end when they let themselves inside and were greeted by a startled shout after they turned on the lights.

Two startled shouts, actually.

“Buck! Danny!” Albert popped up, shirtless and hair mussed. A woman’s head slowly eased into view, as well. Behind them, the TV was showing the selection menu for Netflix. “You’re home. I didn’t think you would be coming back tonight…”

“I can tell.” Danny’s voice was strained. “And you have a guest.”

Buck stuffed a handful of fries into his mouth to keep from laughing.

“This- This-” Albert stammered while the woman looked at them from just over the back of the couch. “This is Veronica.”

“Hi.” Veronica gave them a tiny wave.

“Please tell me you’re both still wearing pants,” Danny almost begged, bending down to pick a shirt off the floor and tossing it to Veronica when she held out her hand for it. “I sit on that couch, Al.”

Neither Albert nor Veronica clarified the state of their pants, but both of them hunkered back down with an air of embarrassment. There was an awkward shuffling as limbs were shoved through holes and zippers done up, and then they both got up without meeting Buck or Danny’s eyes.

“I’ll, um. I’ll walk you out,” Albert told Veronica as the pair of them went scurrying out the door.

“I didn’t miss this,” Danny groused to Buck. He sat his bag of food down on the dining table and went digging through the closet they kept their cleaning supplies in. “Why the hell would he invite his girlfriend here to have sex on my couch? Doesn’t she have her own couch for that!?”

“It’s ironic that you’re a prude,” Buck said, sitting down at the table with his own food.

“I’m not being a prude! I just don’t want to sit in someone else’s wet spot when I go to play a game.”

Buck conceded the point, because that was very fair, but also-

“What was your excuse when you tried forbidding me and Eddie from having sex while he was staying here?”

“Uh, the fact that I didn’t want to hear or see my kid brother having sex?” Danny pulled out of the closet, the cleaner they used on the upholstery in hand, and closed the door. “How ‘bout that for an answer?”

Once again, Buck couldn’t think of an argument against that one.

“How are you feeling about tomorrow?” he asked instead, a question that got a shrug from his brother and nothing else.

Tomorrow was the court date for the restraining order, which they were having over a video call from the comfort of their own home. Buck was feeling hopeful about it, while Danny was decidedly not. He wasn’t going all doom and gloom, but it was very obvious that he wasn’t expecting much to come out of the ordeal. It probably had an influence on the timing of the tattoos, actually.

By the time Albert slunk back upstairs, Buck and Danny had finished off their food. He looked disheartened when he tried creeping in only to find them both staring at him in expectation. The guy literally slumped in place.

“You’re gonna clean the couch,” Danny told him, with not an ounce of sympathy in his voice. He tossed the upholstery cleaner at Albert, who managed to catch it without fumbling. “Scrub it until it smells like new.”

“It smelled like old shoes when we bought it,” Buck reminded his brother, not that his brother paid him any attention.

“Fine.” Albert scuffed the toe of his shoe on the floor. “Sorry, I guess.”

“Oh, but we’re not done,” Danny told him.

He got out of the dining chair he was sitting in and moved to the coffee table, gesturing for Albert to take a seat across from him. Buck started laughing when he realized what was going on, while Albert simply looked confused and even more awkward as he sat down. That changed to mortification when the first thing out of Danny’s mouth was,

“Before you clean, let’s talk about safe sex-”

“Danny!” Albert wailed. He attempted to stand and flee, only for Danny to lunge forward and push him back down.

“And then the importance of proper lube.”

Buck settled in to watch, because it was far funnier when it was someone else suffering.

Eddie had made a lot of very poor, very rash, very stupid decisions in his life. Decisions he still regretted, even as he made up for them or would make them again because he wouldn’t give up some of the consequences for the world. But working as a first responder really helped him to put it all into perspective, really solidified the fact that a lot of people made worse life decisions than him.

Sometimes, the 118 was called to scenes in the expectation of them being needed. That was the case now, a police chase stalling into a negotiation. Some genius was caught breaking into a house and decided to flee across the rooftops like some comic book vigilante. Except he ended up in a cul-de-sac and now he was surrounded with nowhere to go, like he’d been treed by hunting dogs.

He’d already been there for two hours, so far, and Eddie had little hopes that it would wrap up soon. Not with the way that negotiations were going.

“Just shut up!” the guy shouted down at the negotiator, waving his gun in a particularly careless manner. All of Eddie’s military training had him wincing at the lack of trigger discipline. “You’re a liar, you said you’d help me find a way out!”

“I didn’t mean with a helicopter.”

“Shut up! I need to think!”

“He should’ve tried thinking before he ended up on a roof,” Eddie said to the others. They were gathered around the fire engine, simply watching and waiting. “I mean, he cornered himself.”

“That there is a whole series of bad life choices culminating in this one unfortunate moment,” Hen said, perched as she was on the side of the engine. “It’d be tragic if it wasn’t so moronic.”

“Why don’t they just storm the roof?” Chimney asked. He was looking at Bobby, so it was probably directed at him. “It’s not that high, we can give ‘em a ladder.”

“It’s a tactic negotiators use to drag out the process in order to wear down the suspect,” Bobby told him, knowledge gained from either experience on the job or being married to a police sergeant. “Eventually they hit a breaking point.”

“Or we do.”

“Ten buck says he falls right off that roof,” Hen said.

That was wholly unprofessional. Also-

“Twenty says that he makes a leap for the tree,” Eddie said, pulling out the bill. There was a tree just close enough to the house that an idiot might think they could manage it.

Bobby was looking very judgmental.

“C’mon,” Eddie said. “The guy’s got at least one more bad life choice left in him.”

Chimney clearly agreed, pulling out a bill of his own and holding it out to Hen. She yanked both out of their hands and tucked it away, to go to the winner.

“Any word from Buck?” Hen asked, casual as anything. It still had Eddie’s stomach dropping and the other two perking their heads up in interest.

“Not yet,” Eddie answered.

The court hearing regarding Danny’s restraining order against that asshole detective was scheduled for that day. He had no idea how long it would last, or even how long they had to wait to be seen. They could still be waiting, twiddling their thumbs at the apartment - because everything, including this, was done virtually now - or they could be putting forth their arguments to a judge. Eddie didn’t know, and was hesitant to ask in fear of interrupting anything.

“Maddie was supposed to be giving testimony or something. She’s missing work for it,” Chimney said. He tugged out his phone to check it. “But she hasn’t said anything, either.”

“How do you think it’s gonna go?” Hen asked. Eddie wasn’t certain how much she knew of what was going on, wasn’t certain how much Chimney knew. Less than himself and Bobby, probably.

“Buck sounded confident when I talked to him this morning,” Eddie told her. He didn’t mention that, every time the subject came up, Danny had not been nearly as optimistic.

It was hours later that they got an actual answer for their curiosity. Hours of them waiting for the guy to be coaxed off the roof, hours where they found anything they possibly could to entertain themselves. They’d played cards, ordered pizza, lost their minds and chanted encouragement for the guy to jump.

Buck showing up at the scene was unexpected, but very much welcome.

“You’re all working so hard,” he remarked as he waltzed up to them. “They should give y’all a raise.”

“Oh, you’re hilarious.” Eddie rolled his eyes and then poked Buck in the chest, right where he knew it would be sore. The other man yelped a little and recoiled.

“Are you hurt?” Hen asked, peering at Buck from behind her wide-lensed glasses.

Eddie shook his head at her.

“He and Danny got matching tattoos yesterday.”

“Oh, that is adorable.”

“Where is he?” Austin asked, popping up from wherever he’d been hiding. His usual stoic face was lined along the edges with worry.

“Over there.” Buck jerked his thumb over his shoulder, and Eddie spotted Danny talking to Athena. They both seemed agitated.

Austin gave Buck a nod and hurried over to them.

“How did it go?” Bobby asked, with Chimney looking just as interested in the answer.

Buck's face dropped as he shook his head.

“Judge said there wasn’t enough,” he told them, a statement that had them all grimacing in sympathy. “Danny’s been…”

Buck trailed off, half-turning and gesturing helplessly to his brother. The man didn’t seem upset, or at least not as upset as Austin and Athena both looked, but that was not a good indicator of anything. Eddie wasn’t surprised when he caught Chimney stepping away from them, phone already to his ear. 

“What are the two of you going to do now?” Bobby asked.

“I have no idea. Murder, maybe. I’m sure between all of us, we could make it look like an accident.” Buck said it like a joke, but in a way that was clearly not actually a joke.

None of them ended up winning the bet. While Buck was talking to Taylor Kelly, who’d been covering the stand-off all day - and Eddie could not think of a good reason for why Buck would want to talk to the reporter - the guy was suddenly pushed off the roof and onto a car. Apparently, the homeowner reached the end of his patience, grabbed a ladder, and put an end to everything himself.

Danny was bent over and clutching at his sides, he was laughing so hard.

The knocking at the door started late in the evening. Danny was in the shower, Albert was off somewhere with Veronica, and Buck was vegetating on the couch. The knocking, insistent and harsh, had him perking up like a meerkat.

There was a moment’s debate of simply ignoring it, as anyone important that would be showing up at this time all had keys to the apartment, but curiosity won out. So he got to his feet, grabbed his mask, and answered the door.

And then he grabbed Danny’s bat.

“What the fuck are you doing here?” Buck snarled.

“I thought I’d come pay your brother a visit,” Drake answered, clearly smiling behind his mask.

“You’re not seeing him,” Buck said, planting himself firmly in the doorway and blocking the man from even seeing inside. “You’re gonna go, right now. And you’re not coming back.”

“Or what?”

In answer, Buck raised the bat. Drake’s eyes darted to it and he let out a laugh that trailed off into a hacking cough.

“Really?” the detective asked when the fit was done. “Threatening a cop?”

Buck didn’t reply. He simply stood there, the bat in hand, and glared at the other man. He was big, after years of staying fit for firefighting, and he was definitely bigger than Drake. It was a fact that seemed to slowly dawn on Drake, because he was looking more and more uncertain, his eyes darting between the bat and Buck’s face.

It was dawning on Buck that the man was not expecting this. He’d seen how Danny acted when Drake was harassing him in the parking lot, the way he shrunk against his car. Drake was used to Danny not standing up to him, because Danny had spent so long terrified that Drake would do something to Buck and then to Chris.

Fine then. Buck would do it for him.

“You don’t have it in you,” Drake taunted. It lacked the confidence of before.

“Try me,” Buck dared, and adjusted his grip on the bat.

When Drake left, slinking away with a sneer, Buck closed the door and locked it. It was just in time, too, because the shower had shut off. He set the bat back in its spot just as his brother stepped out of the bathroom, still toweling off his hair.

“Who was at the door?” he asked. “I heard ‘em knocking.”

“No one important,” was Buck’s flippant answer. 

He lied better when he wasn’t really lying.

Chapter 42

Chapter Notes

This is a long one, but it's worth it.
CW: canon typical violence, some harsh language, COVID related maladies, and a character taking pleasure in someone's imminent death.

Maddie’s due date came and went, which meant that Eddie got to watch Chimney and Buck both spiral out over it. Separately, of course. The baby was apparently entirely Buckley in her stubbornness, refusing to vacate her comfortable abode until she was good and ready. She was also entirely Buck in her propensity to annoy people, because she’d sent Maddie and Chimney rushing to the hospital at least once, only for it to be a false alarm.

“Hey, anybody got any suggestions for baby names?” Chimney asked the group, while they were finishing up with all the small things that needed to be done on the trucks in-between calls. Or they were, at least - he was on his phone, texting away. Presumably with Maddie. “Not any of your names.”

Hen, instead of answering, stomped away for other parts of the stations. She’d been in a mood all shift, snappish and short with everyone. Eddie was fairly certain he knew why that was, mostly thanks to Buck. He’d taken to avoiding interacting with her whenever he was able.

“Buck said you guys were pulling them out of a hat,” Eddie said, the words not-quite coming out as a question.

“Yeah, we were,” Chimney said. “Maddie didn’t like the idea, she wrote ‘I really don’t want to pick our baby’s name this way’ on every piece of paper.”

“I don’t think that would fit on a driver’s license.”

“That’s what I said!”

“Well, Shannon and I didn’t know what we were gonna name Christopher,” Eddie told him. “Not until I held him in my arms for the first time and was really wishing Buck was there to see him.”

Shannon hadn’t argued against it, but she also never knew it was Buck’s middle name.

“That’s sweet,” the other man said, tone veering dangerously close to patronizing. He was focused on his phone, fingers tapping away at the screen. “But you’re right, we’re way ahead of our skis here.”

Chimney’s phone chimed in his hands. Whatever Maddie sent back, it had him scowling in confusion.

“She didn’t like that?” Eddie guessed.

“I think she called me a psycho.”

Eddie didn’t really know where to go with that, so he simply gave Chimney a pat on the back and a silent wish for good luck before taking his leave. There were some things, after all, that were best stayed out of. Since Hen wasn’t an option at that moment, as she was simply a dark cloud of anger in the locker room, he sought out someone else to bother. 

In the year and change since Buck’s transfer, Eddie had gradually figured out some of the places that Austin disappeared to between calls and meals. Not all of them, certainly, but definitely a couple of the places he used most regularly. Like now, in a little corner tucked away in the space under the loft that conveniently allowed Austin to see the station’s truck bay while staying mostly out of sight.

The driver-engineer was a people watcher, which was not actually as surprising to learn as Eddie thought it maybe should’ve been.

Austin didn’t acknowledge his presence at first, content to keep watching their coworkers. Chimney had gone to one of their buses, apparently to start doing inventory or restocking. Eddie didn’t know why, it had literally just been done. Bobby went over to talk to him, and then Chimney was calling for Hen.

“What’s crawled up her ass?” Austin asked as he and Eddie watched her make her way to Chimney. She brought the storm cloud with her.

“Buck said that they were easing Nia back into her bio mom's custody,” Eddie answered.

Nia was the little girl that the Wilsons started fostering just before the pandemic started. Cute, adorable, prone to calling both Karen and Hen “mama.” With how long they’d been fostering Nia, the Wilsons had hoped that they’d be adopting her. Only, things were not turning out that way, and Hen was not taking it well.

She’d also upset Buck, another reason that Eddie was giving her some space today. Apparently, she made the mistake of voicing her frustrations with how they didn’t know what the bio mom did “wrong” to have Nia taken away, how they couldn’t know if Nia’s bio mom was still unfit or not. Given everything they now knew about Danny and Drake, how terrified Danny had been of losing custody of his brother for literally no other reason than someone else’s cruelty, Buck’s reaction was probably to be expected.

(“What do you mean, what she did wrong!?” Buck snapped, loudly and sharply enough that it startled Eddie on the couch. He met Danny’s eyes over Chris’ head, the older man mirroring his surprise. “You don’t know that she did anything wrong! You’re just-... Assuming makes an ass out of you and me, Hen!”)

“And Chimney and Maddie haven’t picked out a name, yet,” Eddie said.

“That I knew,” Austin told him. “Dan’s campaigning for Danielle.”

“Of course he is.”

They responded to a lot of traffic accidents as firefighters, far and away more than they did actual fires, but rarely were they as bad as this one. Someone decided to get onto the 710 freeway and drive south, which would have been fine if they were in the southbound lanes. As they were in the northbound lanes, however, things were very much not fine.

The 118 were the first on the scene, making Nash the incident commander, but the 132 and the 133 were not far behind them. Daniel and Buck hadn’t wasted much time listening to their marching orders from Captain Mehta, instead quickly falling into step and going car-to-car to identify those who were most in need of assistance and who could be extracted the easiest without causing further harm, while others put out the small fires that had erupted from leaks and sparks.

They also had to make sure the cars were de-energized and the airbags disabled before any extraction occurred, because otherwise things tended to explode in these circumstances.

The car that started the whole mess was smashed into the front of an airport shuttle and was just a mass of twisted metal. There was a woman behind the wheel and her son in the back, and the 118 ended up having to cut the roof off just to get to them. After that, it became very clear, very quickly, what attributed to the crash: Athena found a mostly empty bottle of liquor in the front.

“How many people have to die tonight because she was drunk and stupid?” the sergeant asked no one in particular.

Daniel was busy helping stabilize and prepare the kid, Jacob, so they could get him out, but he got to see Nash’s face fall at his wife’s scathing tone and almost tangible disgust. It gave Daniel the warm fuzzies.

After Jacob was removed from the vehicle, placed on a gurney, and then wheeled away to one of the awaiting ambulances, Daniel moved up to focus on the mother. Hen hadn’t gone with the others and was on the driver’s side, so Daniel crawled through the passenger side to get to the patient. It had always been easy for him to pack away his personal feelings when it came to things like this, aiding and treating whoever was put in front of him without much care about how they ended up there.

For some people, however, it was a bit more difficult to be that callous. Hen, bent down to pull out a c-collar from her medical bag, was making her personal feelings very clear.

“Drunk driving with your only child in the car…”

“You good here, Hen?” Nash asked her, pausing on the way to wherever else he felt he was needed.

Hen didn’t say anything right away. Daniel saw her turn to cast a heavy look at the drunk driver.

“Not one bit, Cap. But I got it,” she finally answered. “It’s our job, right?”

If Nash gave a reply before he left, Daniel didn’t hear it. Hen reached in and stuck the collar around the neck of the barely conscious driver. Her face was a bloody mess from the shards of safety glass, with burns from the airbag, and she was disoriented. It was always a pain trying to assess an inebriated patient for concussions and brain injuries, because the symptoms for both were almost the same.

The woman would probably be walking away from this with a couple new scars and not much else, though. Daniel had seen it before, dozens and dozens of times, and he’d see it again.

“I need a gurney at the north end of this mess,” he radioed.

“Copy that, Danny,” Eddie replied. “Bringing one now.”

“Y’know,” Daniel said, while they waited. “When Buck first started, I told him we weren’t in the business of deciding who deserved anything, that we just help the people who need it.”

“Thanks,” Hen spat. “I know the job.”

“But it would be easier if she was the one with the TBI,” he continued, unperturbed. The woman in question was barely coherent, and who the hell cared if she got offended by him saying something like that? “And the kid was the one walking away with cuts and bruises.”

The other paramedic kept glaring at him for a moment, and then she sighed.

“Yeah, it would be.”

A few cars away, not far from them, there was an explosion. The only reason that Daniel didn’t hit his head on the roof of the car as he jumped to look was because the roof of the car was laying on the road beside them. He saw that one of the cars, one that he distinctly remembered as being not on fire, was now fully involved. Other firefighters were already hitting it with hoses, and Chimney was sprinting in that direction with Buck.

Eddie arrived with the gurney, and the three of them worked to get the drunk driver transferred onto it from the car. They wheeled her to an awaiting ambulance and got her loaded up, handing her over to the awaiting paramedics. Athena caught up to them just before they closed the doors.

“Which hospital is she going to?” the sergeant asked them.

“First Presbyterian on Altamont,” Eddie answered.

“Alright, I’ll follow behind,” she said. “Make sure the hospital knows she’s gonna need her BAC as soon as she lands.”

“Athena…”

“Already got the warrant, Eddie,” Athena said. The paramedic inside the bus, someone from the 132 that Daniel didn’t recognize, gave a hesitant nod and then pulled the doors to. “It’ll meet me at the hospital.”

She turned to leave for her cruiser, only to stop when she came face-to-face with a gloomy looking Nash. Daniel spotted Chimney and Buck not too far behind him.

“Are you okay?” she asked the captain.

“I’m doing fine,” was the flat sounding answer.

“Captain Nash.” Sue’s cheery sounding voice came over the radio. “Can you spare a paramedic for a woman in labor at Dispatch Metro?”

A woman in- Oh. Oh!

“Pretty sure there are some paramedics a lot closer to your location than we are,” Nash responded, because he was slow on the uptake.

“Yes, but none of them are the baby’s father.”

That was enough for the penny to drop for all the rest. They turned to Chimney, standing around and looking a bit stunned.

“Why are you still here?” Daniel blurted out. He’d love to rush off, but baby daddy trumped brother in this instance. Especially these days. “Go, go.”

“But-”

“Go,” Nash interrupted. “We’ve got it from here.”

“I’m following that ambulance,” Athena announced. “You can ride with me.”

That was enough to get Chimney moving, hurrying off to the sergeant’s cruiser. Buck bounced over to where Daniel and Eddie were.

“Danny, Danny, Danny,” Buck chanted, practically vibrating where he stood.

“Yeah, squirt, I know.”

Where was Austin? He needed to let him know.

“We’re ‘bout to be uncles!”

“I mean, I already am,” Daniel pointed out, without looking at Eddie. “C’mon, we’ve got work to do while she’s busy.”

The work, at this point, was clean up. Going car to car, making sure everyone that could be helped was receiving it and that anyone beyond their help was tagged. They also made sure that nothing was going to explode again.

He found Austin, who filled him in on the gossip after he passed on the news about Maddie. Apparently, Renfrow from the 132-

“Fucking Renfrow,” Daniel groused, because he’d worked with him before and did not come away with high opinions of the man.

Renfrow from the 132 failed to disable the airbags of the car before starting to extract the driver. They went off, something sparked, and combustion occurred. Both the driver and Renfrow was shipped off to the burn unit, the latter with half his face given the Dark Knight Harvey Dent treatment, while the former was…

Well, apparently Buck described his skin as like paper, which was never good for a burn victim.

Speaking of Buck, he was grouped up with the others, looking worried. Daniel and Austin joined them just in time to hear May’s voice over the radio, saying,

“Isn’t that Chimney’s brother?”

“What about Al?” Daniel asked, looking between them.

“I thought that call was dropped,” Nash said into his radio, ignoring the question.

“I called the number back, it gave me his voice mail.”

“Wh- What did the message say?” Buck asked.

“He gave his name, and then said not to leave a message because um…”

“‘Cause that’s what texts are for,” Daniel said at the same time as Buck, his stomach curdling.

“Yeah.”

Daniel barely paid attention as Nash told them to start searching vehicles. He was busy radioing Mehta, relaying the relevant details that he knew, with Buck adding his own. It was while he was describing Albert’s car as he paced through the wrecks that he realized the not-so-minor detail.

“I’ve been through all this,” he stated to no one in particular, turning on the spot. “I haven’t seen Al’s car anywhere here. I’d know if I had.”

“Yeah, that’s…” Buck had sprinted back and forth, calling for Albert. “Cap! We’ve been up and down this road twice, he’s not here.”

“Dispatch, this is Captain Nash,” the 118’s captain spoke into his radio. “That very first caller who reported seeing the vehicle, which exit were they calling from?”

“It says exit forty-three.”

As one, Daniel and Buck turned to check the sign for the nearest exit ramp: Exit 46.

They ran for the 118’s engine, parked on the north end of the mess and the closest engine to exit ramp 43. Buck hopped into the cab like it was a reflex, settling into the seat across from Eddie and tangling their legs together. Daniel ended up taking the seat beside him, craning his neck to look out the window while Austin drove them.

Buck spotted the tire tracks when they pulled to a stop and got out, sprinting off to follow them where they disappeared at the edge of the road. Daniel was not too far behind, coming to a stop with him as they spotted Albert’s car below them at the bottom of the easement. It was on its roof, dented and mangled.

“Cap, we need a bus at exit forty-three,” Daniel relayed as they slid to the bottom. “We found our missing caller.

“Mendoza’s on the way,” Mehta replied.

“I see him!” Hen called out.

Buck and Eddie struck at the doors with halligans, forcing first the driver’s side door and then the passenger’s open. Hen and Daniel crawled in from opposite sides. Albert was upside down and blood was dripping from him like rain, soaking the roof below him. The sirens of the oncoming ambulance cut through the air.

They got him out, they got him loaded up. Daniel climbed in first and then Hen, Eddie slamming the doors closed behind them and thumping it with his fist.

“BP’s sixty over thirty,” Daniel rattled off what the Lifepak was telling them. “Hypertensive and tachycardic.”

“He must be bleeding internally,” Hen said. They’d torn open Albert’s shirt, revealing bruises upon bruises along his torso that she palpated with gloved fingers. “We’re probably looking at a ruptured spleen, he’s hemorrhaging right now inside.”

Daniel was about to grab the radio to call ahead to the hospital and tell them to have a transfusion standing by. Before he could do that, though, the Lifepak began to shriek as the valleys and peaks of Albert’s heartbeat flattened out.

“Starting compressions!” Hen announced, hands going to Albert’s chest. “Push epinephrine.”

Daniel did, digging out the syringe and injecting it into the IV they’d set up. Hen’s arms worked as she pressed on Albert’s chest and her pleading overlapped with the Lifepak’s droning. Daniel grabbed the intubation kit, shoving it down Albert’s throat and then working the bag to force air through.

And then, the Lifepak switched to simple, bright sounding beeps, and Albert’s eyes fluttered open for a moment to look up with an unfocused gaze.

Daniel let out the breath he did not know he was holding.

Buck had never been on this side of things before. In his experience, he was usually the subject of this sort of grim news. He hadn’t taken the time to imagine what Danny felt, or how he looked, whenever someone informed him that Buck was hurt. He definitely hadn’t taken the time to imagine how Chimney would look in his place.

The nurse at the desk gave him the room number he was looking for in the maternity ward, after kindly but briskly informing him about the current rules regarding visitors. That being that there were no visitors being allowed at the moment, but they were making an exception for him since he came in uniform with both the baby bag and news that needed to be told in person. The baby bag had been in the back of Albert’s car, miraculously unscathed. They’d found it shortly after he’d been loaded up into the 133’s ambulance.

Maddie’s room was at the very end of the hall. Buck got to see her and Chimney, and a little bundle in her arms that had yet to be named. Chimney looked up, spotted him, and came out to meet him halfway.

“Hey, it’s good to see you.” Chimney kept his words quiet, as if he was terrified of waking the infants in the rooms around them. “The hospital has a strict no visitor policy right now.”

“I - I know,” Buck said, trying to figure out how to tell him. “Chim…”

“The girls are both doing great, Maddie was a warrior in there.” Of course she was. “Oh, hey, where’d you get that?”

That being the baby bag in Buck’s hand. Buck looked down at it and then back up to Chimney.

“Is Albert here?” Chimney asked.

“He’s… He’s downstairs,” Buck told him. “Chim, he… He was at the pile-up.”

“He- What?” The other man blinked, shook his head. “What do you mean, Albert was at the pile-up?”

“He’s in the ICU.”

“How bad?”

“It’s bad, Chim.”

Chimney stared at him, silently and unmoving. Then he slowly reached out and took the bag out of Buck’s grip, before turning to walk back into Maddie’s room. Through the window, Buck gave his sister a limp wave and got a tired one in return.

Then he left, because he didn’t feel like sticking around to watch Chimney try and decide where he needed to be more.

Daniel was not supposed to be working today. One of the B-shift paramedics called in, and he volunteered to cover for them. Normally, after the exhausting shift they had, he’d be as eager as everyone else to go home, but he didn’t quite feel like heading to the apartment and being confronted with Albert’s dirty dishes today.

Buck hung out for a bit, because he’d ridden to work with Daniel and didn’t have his jeep. It mostly meant he spent some time being an irritant to people he didn’t normally interact with all that much and getting on Captain Shore’s nerves. At least until Eddie swung by to pick him up.

Shortly before lunch, they had a medical call come through. Someone collapsed on the sidewalk with difficulty breathing. It was a common call after the last few months, one they’d all responded to countless times by this point. A call none of them wanted to go on.

The paramedics rock-paper-scissors’d it, and Daniel ended up going. He and the other one that lost, Vince Hewitt, bundled up in PPE and got onto the bus, heading for downtown. Their patient was splayed out on the sidewalk with people giving them a wide berth. The two of them got out, unloaded the gurney, and went to load the guy up.

And then Daniel froze, because he recognized the man laying there.

Drake was on his back, chest heaving as he struggled to draw in a breath. A cigarette, still smoking, was on the sidewalk beside him. The lighter, a disposable bic, was not far from it. The man’s eyes bounced between their faces, lingering on Daniel’s.

Daniel stood there, met the man’s eyes, and then forced himself into motion. He and Hewitt got him on O2, loaded him onto the gurney, and then loaded the gurney into the back. And when Daniel volunteered to ride in the back, Hewitt was not shy with expressing his relief, hurriedly closing the doors behind them and then rushing for the relative safety of the front.

“Hi.” Daniel’s smile wasn’t visible behind his mask, and there was no way he was taking it off, but he knew his tone conveyed it well enough. Drake was glaring daggers at him. “This is awkward. They always said smoking would kill you.”

“F- Fuck you… Whore…” Drake rasped, a pitiful attempt at lashing out.

Years ago, Daniel told Buck that they didn’t decide who did or didn’t deserve their help, and Daniel was usually pretty good at following that. He was usually able to pack away whatever his personal feelings and opinions were and do the job. Usually.

Today, he reached over and tugged off the oxygen mask covering Drake’s face. It left the man gasping like a fish left on the beach to cook beneath the unforgiving sun.

“You’re gonna die,” Daniel bluntly told him, looking the man directly in the eye as he spoke. “They’re gonna admit you, and the only people you’ll ever see again will be doctors and nurses covered head to toe. Complete strangers. In a couple days, when your breathing gets worse, they’ll intubate you. They’ll stick a tube down your throat and turn on a machine to breathe for you. It will never, ever come out. And a couple days after that, they’ll roll you out the back with all the other corpses.”

Drake glared at him, a weak and pathetic attempt at intimidation. Daniel just held the oxygen mask hostage and watched the man struggle to breathe until the ambulance was pulling up at the ER.

No one on shift asked him why he came back from the call cheerfully whistling.

Chapter 43

Chapter Notes

CW: discussion of a past suicide attempt, COVID-related deaths

“I haven’t seen him this happy in a while,” Maddie remarked as Danny practically danced with an infant.

“Yeah,” Buck agreed. “He’s been like that lately.”

Buck and Danny were at Maddie and Chimney’s, for their most recent visit to see their sister and their niece, plus Albert. The latter had moved in with them after being released from the hospital, and things were still rough. Definitely an improvement from how he’d been when the 118 found him at the pile-up, but there were times Albert would knock something over when trying to grab it and get upset with himself. Occasionally, he and Buck would have entire conversations that would be forgotten the next time they came over.

Sometimes, Buck wasn’t certain if they visited to see Maddie, to check on Albert, or so that Danny could hog little baby Jee-Yun all to himself. Because that was what happened, each and every time that they came over after Maddie’s doctor gave the all-clear to have visitors. Buck had started timing how long it took before Danny was sitting on the couch with their niece, the longest being about twenty minutes and the shortest was when Danny yanked her out of Chimney’s arms almost the moment they entered the apartment.

He’d been awkward about it the first time, sitting stock still like he was afraid he’d do something wrong and break her. Buck took a picture to send to Austin, just on a whim.

“I only got to see you once when you were this age,” Danny told Buck that first visit, with him holding Jee-Yun in his arms as if she were a fragile doll wrapped up in a blanket burrito. “I begged Mom and Dad to let me see you. Dad stood outside my room at the hospital and held you up to the window.”

But Danny’s good mood had been a thing since shortly after Jee-Yun’s birth and Albert’s accident. Buck would think it was due to the former, except that it only really made its appearance following Danny covering for someone on B-shift. The next time that Buck saw Danny after that, he was literally whistling as he cleaned the apartment, seemingly just moments away from bursting into song like a Disney princess. He’d stayed like that for days and weeks after.

The reason for it became very clear, though, when Buck came back from Eddie’s to find something new stuck to the fridge with magnets. A little newspaper cut-out, right next to the crayon drawing that Chris made for Danny of a dragon sleeping on top of a fire engine. Buck saw it, and suddenly his brother’s good cheer for the past few weeks made absolute sense.

Now, while Albert napped and Chimney ran an errand, Buck and Maddie watched their brother make goofy faces at Jee-Yun while changing her diaper. He looked lighter, somehow. Lighter than Buck had seen him in years.

“Drake’s dead,” Buck said, without any attempt at easing into it.

Unfortunately, Maddie had been in the middle of taking a sip of water when he said it, so she ended up choking and sputtering.

“What?” she managed to get out with a cough. “How?”

“COVID,” Buck explained. “Danny stuck his obit on the fridge.”

“Good riddance,” was all Maddie said.

That about summed up Buck’s feelings, too.

In their line of work, with entire days at a time spent in close quarters with the same people, it was extremely noticeable when a coworker was absent. Chimney being gone for paternity leave wasn’t quite so off-putting to Eddie as Buck being out for his leg and then transferring to the 133, but it still caused an upset to their regular set-up. Suddenly, there were new faces coming in and out to cover for him, or Eddie was shuffled into the ambulance more often.

Not that Eddie hadn’t seen or spoken to Chimney at all during that time. Buck had FaceTimed him and Chris whenever he went over to visit, so he could show off tiny little Jee-Yun to them. Eddie talked to Maddie and Chimney then, too, and Albert, whenever the younger Han brother was up to it. Which was more and more often than when he first got discharged from the hospital.

That didn’t mean, however, that the moment Chimney was back at the station, he didn’t start showing pictures of the baby to Eddie like Eddie had never laid eyes on her before.

“That’s the first time she smiled,” the new father gushed as he swiped to another picture on his phone. It was pretty much the same as every other one that came before it.

Eddie leaned across the kitchen island to get a better look, regardless.

“Are you sure that’s a smile?” he asked. “Looks like the classic gassy Buckley face to me.”

Chimney peered at the picture for a moment.

“It kinda does,” the paramedic agreed, making Eddie laugh. “God, I love her so much. I don’t even feel like the same person anymore. Is that weird?”

“What’s that saying?” Bobby asked, setting down two mugs of coffee in front of them. “Having a kid is like walking around with your heart outside your body.”

“Okay, that’s weirder. And morbid.”

“Just means it’s a whole different kind of love.”

“He’s not wrong,” Eddie commented, softly blowing across his coffee to cool it down some. “How’s Maddie doing? First solo shift with the baby.”

“Babies, plural. She’s pulling double duty with Albert and Jee-Yun,” Chimney said. “Dan keeps offering to take him back to his and Buck’s, but he needs round-the-clock care. He can’t be on his own for whole hours. With the new schedule, one of us is always home.”

“If you and Maddie are working opposite schedules,” Eddie said, “when do you two actually see each other?”

“Haven’t quite figured that out yet.”

Movement at the stairs caught Eddie’s attention, and he spotted Hen cresting the top with a cake box.

“She’s here,” he hissed to Chimney, who hurriedly tucked away his phone and changed the subject to a loud,

“So, uh, yeah! The doctor said Albert’s physical therapy is doing great.”

“Welcome back!” Hen cried out when she reached them, placing the cake box on the island.

“Hey! I was just filling them in on Albert’s recovery.”

“I am disappointed in you guys. Where’s the banner? Where’s the balloons?” Hen flipped open the box, revealing the cake inside. It was round, clearly red velvet with a picture of a stork in a fireman’s helmet carrying a baby and surrounded by the words Welcome Back, Daddy. “This is not how we do when somebody comes back to work.”

“I said it was okay,” Chimney told her. “I don’t need that kind of stuff. Not when, uh…”

“No, no, no. We celebrate every good moment when we can,” she argued. “Now, let me see those baby pictures.”

Chimney didn’t need much more convincing than that, hurriedly pulling his phone back out to show off the baby pictures to a new audience. 

The reason they were all so hesitant to celebrate Chimney’s return from paternity leave, or rather, hesitant to mention Chimney’s new parenthood, was that little Nia went home to her biological mother that morning. The last couple of months, they’d been easing her transition with visits, though neither Hen nor Karen ever met the bio mom. The whole thing had been wearing down on Hen, something that was obvious to all of them even as she denied it.

“I don’t think I could foster,” Buck told him over FaceTime. He called Eddie to check in on Hen, because apparently he didn’t trust the woman’s insistence over texts that she was actually fine. “I’d get too attached.”

“After so long, anyone would get attached,” Eddie pointed out.

Nia was not meant to have spent so long at the Wilsons, Eddie managed to glean that much from Hen and Karen’s comments. Whatever the reason behind Nia going into the system, whatever the cause for why her biological mother lost custody of her, it was never meant to be something long term. But then people started to get sick and the world shut down for a bit, and a temporary arrangement turned into a year and change.

“I got attached to Chris almost from the moment I met him.”

“Chris is a special case,” Eddie said with a smile. “Is that Danny?”

Someone on Buck’s end of the call was singing along with music, competing with the other sounds of a station filled with firefighters going about their day. Buck grinned and suddenly he was taking Eddie for a headache inducing journey through the 133’s truck bay. When he came to a stop, the video was suddenly flipped and the screen taken up by bright red metal until Buck, evidently, leaned out from behind the engine to show Danny.

The older Buckley brother had the engine’s cab lifted so he could get into the guts of it for maintenance. A radio set to a classic rock station was sitting on top of the rolling toolbox, the source of the music, and was currently playing Werewolves of London. As Eddie watched, Danny threw his head back to howl with the chorus. There was even a little shimmy to go along with it.

“So he’s still in a good mood,” Eddie remarked.

The screen was taken up by his boyfriend’s face again.

“I’ve had four people ask me if he’s on new meds,” Buck said with a laugh. Subdued, to keep his brother from hearing it and realizing he was being watched. “I know I’m not supposed to be glad someone’s dead, but…”

“Good riddance to the fucker,” Eddie bluntly stated, making his boyfriend throw back his head with more laughter.

“You have a very lovely singing voice,” was how Alma greeted him when he answered the phone.

“Thank you.” Daniel stuck a plate of left-over pizza into the microwave and set the timer. “What, did Buck send you a video?”

He was home alone, with Buck over at Eddie’s and Albert now staying with Maddie and Chimney. The latter hadn’t been his idea, and no one ever asked him his opinion about it, but he couldn’t exactly argue against the logic of it. Daniel worked twenty-four shifts, sometimes longer, and Albert getting himself to the bathroom on his own was something worth celebrating when he was first discharged, and he lost track of time and he forgot things. Important things, like his medication. There was no way he could be left to his own devices for too long.

The apartment was distressingly empty, now. The TV was on just so there was something filling up the silence, though it got muted when Alma called. Daniel would’ve gone to Austin’s, except his not-boyfriend actually enjoyed solitude and Daniel didn’t want to intrude on it too often. At least he could walk alone through the building’s parking lot now and not keep looking over his shoulder in constant fear that he was about to be accosted by Drake.

It was a fact that had him smiling even now.

“It was Austin, actually,” Alma told him, answering his question. “When are you coming to visit?”

“Who says I’m coming to visit?” Daniel asked her as he leaned against the counter.

“Well. I heard they installed a new gender-neutral bathroom in town. I thought you’d make a trip for it.”

Daniel’s smile grew even wider. The city of Los Angeles had held the usual pomp and circumstance funeral for Drake, as they did for every other dead cop, a funeral that Athena had strongly advised that Daniel not go to. She probably thought that he’d kick over the casket and piss on the corpse then and there, which… Wasn’t a baseless concern, actually, because he had thought of doing it. But despite the funeral taking place in Los Angeles, Drake was shipped off to El Paso for burial.

“Maddie hasn’t been to El Paso, maybe we’ll make it a family trip when she and Jee-Yun are up to it,” Daniel said. “You could see the little princess in person, instead of through all the pictures that Buck’s been sending you.”

“And it has been an awful lot of pictures.”

There was, suddenly, knocking at the door. Daniel pushed off the counter and stared, trying to figure out who would be showing up at the apartment. Buck had a key, so that scratched him and Eddie off the list, Maddie was supposed to be finishing up her first shift back at Metro Dispatch since Jee-Yun was born, and Austin was more likely to call him than come over unannounced. There was the momentary, irrational thought that it was somehow Drake, but he shook it away.

“Hey, someone’s at the door-”

“Go answer it, then,” Alma instructed. “And don’t be a stranger. I will come up there.”

“Yeah, yeah.”

Daniel rolled his eyes and hung up on her, before heading for the door. He reached it just as the microwave dinged to tell him it was done reheating the pizza. When he opened the door to tell whoever was on the other side to go away, he came face to face with an agitated Athena Grant.

“I don’t think I like this,” he blurted out.

“There is nothing about today to like,” Athena said, yanking off her mask as she stepped past him. “May is dodging my calls.”

“Well.” Daniel felt backfooted, trying to figure out what was going on. “She isn’t here?”

“Clearly.”

He shut the door and watched as she aggressively shoved her purse down on the kitchen table. The sergeant’s feathers were all ruffled over something, though Daniel couldn’t figure out what it had to do with him. He hadn’t threatened Nash even once since the New Year.

“I’m not about to be arrested for anything, am I?” he asked.

“Have you done anything to be arrested for?” she asked in return.

“Not today.”

Athena just scoffed and shook her head at him.

“You are literally the only person I think will be fully on my side about this,” the sergeant told him. She pulled out a chair and sat down.

“About what?” Daniel mentally tried to figure out what he had to offer guests, which wasn’t much. “I, uh. I think I have some juice, but I definitely have beer if you want that.”

“Tempting,” she said, even though Daniel was fairly certain she much preferred wine. “Do you remember when we first met?”

“When Abby’s mother went missing.”

“And you used it as an excuse to check out the cop getting friendly with your brother and maybe threaten them a little.” Athena side-eyed his attempt at looking innocent. “I’m not an idiot, Dan, and it was even more obvious in hindsight after I learned about him.”

“I don’t remember actually threatening you, though,” Daniel pointed out. He pressed the button on the microwave to make it stop chirping at them, and then went to the fridge to see if there was any juice left. “What about it?”

“That little bitch is back in my baby girl’s life.”

“Oh.” Nevermind, definitely going for the beer, then. “The girl you used your badge to exact revenge against or whatever.”

“Apparently,” Athena spat, “she reached out to May to “apologize.” May met her for coffee, said she felt like she owed it to her to listen. Said they’ve both changed so she’s giving her a second chance.”

Daniel popped the caps of the bottles and then sat them down on the table, the glass clinking against the wood. Athena stared at hers for a moment, and then she grabbed it to take a long draw. 

“All of Buck’s bullies ran away from him when I was done with ‘em,” he bragged as he took the seat across from her. “Want me to handle it?”

“Tempting,” Athena said again, quieter this time. “I should’ve done worse than finding a reason to arrest her.”

“See, I don’t feel right, encouraging a cop to abuse their authority. But…”

“She tried to kill herself last time.” The confession was a whisper spoken into her drink, haunted by whatever memory she was seeing as she said it. Daniel had just picked up his own drink, but he set it back down. “I found her on the floor of her bedroom…”

Daniel sighed.

“Buck used to get himself hurt a lot,” he said. “Because Mom ignored him pretty much all the rest of the time. But she got annoyed with it after a while, started berating him for it. One day, I got a call telling me he was in the hospital ‘cause he fell down some stairs at school and broke his arm. I left work early and got there in time to hear Mom just tearing into him, and Dad not saying or doing a damn thing to stop her. I got Buck the hell out of Hershey almost as soon as school let out, because I just knew that if he stayed for much longer…”

Anything and everything was worth getting and keeping Buck away from their parents. From their mother, especially.

“I am terrified it’s going to happen again,” Athena said. “She was living under my roof and I didn’t even know something was wrong. She didn’t tell me there was anything wrong. I had no clue until it was almost too late.”

“I know a good lawyer, and some people willing to be my alibi,” Daniel told her. “You know, just in case.”

The sergeant snorted.

“Tempting.”

Buck was just stepping out of the jeep, grocery list in hand, when his phone buzzed in his pocket. He dug it out and answered it with a cheerful,

“Go for Buck.”

“You were right,” Hen said with a sigh.

“I like hearing that,” he told her as he headed for the store’s entrance, adjusting the mask on his face. “Right about what?”

“Karen hired a private investigator to find Nia’s birth mother-”

“Is that allowed?”

“No.” Hen sounded sheepish as she said it. “But it made me feel better, knowing that Nia’ll be okay.”

“Because…” Buck prompted, grinning beneath his mask.

“Because you were right,” she said again, and kindly ignored his cheer. “I made an assumption and made an ass of myself. She didn’t do anything wrong, she just… Got evicted and was living in her car.”
