That could’ve been him and Danny, Buck was well aware. He may not have known just how close they came to it, but he could figure it was far too close for comfort. Or else Danny would have never picked up his side hustle and kept with it.

“You guys gonna foster again, or…?”

“Maybe,” she said. “We’re gonna ask Denny first.”

“Good plan. Hey, so, what was this about a guy sabotaging his trellis to make his kid fall?”

“Oh, right. So the dad kicked his kid out - the kid’s like, in his twenties - so the kid started breaking in at night…”

Chapter 44

Chapter Notes

Ignore the fact that it's been twenty days since the last update. <3

Typically, when they were called out for a hit-and-run, they were sent out to a street. Usually a busy one, where the cars sped through without care about pedestrians. Buck had been to a few since becoming a firefighter, most notably the call with Shannon. But this time, however, the scene of the accident was in a parking lot for a store at 3rd and La Brea.

“Car was parked over by the dumpster,” the caller, a security guard, was telling Captain Mehta while the paramedics - Jon Mendoza and Aiden Huff, this time - rushed to the victim. “He hit the gas, then he hit her. Looked pretty bad.”

“And he just drove away?” Mehta sounded pretty appalled.

“He didn’t even slow down.”

“You’re gonna be okay, sweetie, okay? Help is here.” The man, presumably the victim’s husband, was knelt down beside her. “You’re gonna be fine, okay?”

“Sir, give us some space?” Mehta phrased it as a question, but Danny was already pulling the man up and away.

Jon and Aiden got to work, talking to each other and to Mehta. Danny, though, was staring down at the victim, head tilted slightly and brow furrowed. Buck was about to ask what was bothering him, but then his brother blurted out,

“Sue?”

“Sue?” Buck repeated, and then took a look for himself. “Sue Blevins!?”

“The Sue from Dispatch?” Mehta joined them in looking down at Sue while Jon and Aiden worked.

“Yeah, our sister’s boss,” Danny confirmed, heading to get the oxygen when Jon asked for it.

Buck didn’t know Sue very well, only meeting her a couple of times. She’d visited Maddie at the hospital, after everything that happened with Doug, and Buck spoke to her a bit following Dispatch being held hostage last year. He was not expecting to run into her here.

They got Sue onto a backboard, and then onto a gurney, ready to be loaded up. They paused, though, as she was trying so very hard to tell them something.

“Nine… one… o-” Sue broke into a cough.

“Nine-One-One?” Buck tried to clarify.

“Well, we’re here,” Danny commented.

“Nine one…” she tried again, as they loaded her into the ambulance. The doors closed, cutting off the rest of her sentence. If there was anything else.

“He was inside buying flowers,” the security guard told Buck. She looked upset, but not as distraught as Sue’s husband. “And someone was trying to kill her.”

“It wasn’t an accident?” Buck asked.

“The guy never took his foot off the gas,” she said. “It was like he wanted that lady dead.”

“It doesn’t make any sense,” Maddie said. She looked… Buck wasn’t sure how she looked. It was probably just concern for her boss. “Who would want to hurt Sue?”

They were at Metro Dispatch, in the break room just off the call center floor. Buck and Danny swung by after their shift ended and just as Maddie’s was starting, to pass along the news themselves.

“The security guard only saw the accident, she didn’t know what happened before,” Buck said. He was standing while the others sat. “Maybe it was some kind of parking lot rage thing?”

It was the only thing that he could think of. It didn’t make much sense, because like Maddie said, who would want to hurt Sue Blevins? But it was often the case that the things they encountered on the job made little sense.

“I was talking to her,” Josh stated. He was sitting at the table with Maddie and Danny, the latter of whom set down his phone to stare at him. “Last night, we were on the phone. She was in the car, waiting for Don- Her husband,” he added for Danny and Buck’s benefit. “She just hung up. God, I should call him. He must be beside himself.”

“Do you want to go to the hospital?” Maddie offered. “I’m sure she’s out of surgery.”

“No, she’d want me here,” Josh said. “Like she says, the calls don’t stop and we don’t either.”

“Did she say anything to either of you when you were there?” Maddie asked Buck and Danny.

Buck and Danny looked at each other and then shrugged at her.

“Not really,” Danny said.

“She just kept saying Nine-One-One,” Buck said. Or, he was fairly certain that was what she was saying.

They talked a bit more. Or, well, Maddie and Josh and Danny talked a bit more. Buck was too busy trying to come up with what else he could do. Because it wasn’t sitting right with him that there wasn’t anything, that this guy would probably get away with it. One minor incident in the entirety of Los Angeles, and it probably wouldn’t even make the news cycle aside from a short blurb.

Buck’s thoughts slammed to a stop, reversed, and then ran that last bit through his head again. Maybe there was something he could do.

“Hey, uh, you remember Taylor?” Buck asked later, as he and Danny walked through the parking garage for Metro Dispatch.. 

“The reporter from Channel Eight, the one Eddie was trying to explode with his eyes.” Danny paused as he unlocked his car to side-eye Buck in suspicion. Buck smiled pleasantly at his big brother. “Why are you asking?”

“Wanna meet her for brunch? There’s a food truck downtown that does all-day breakfast.”

“Why?” Danny drew the word out as he crossed his arms on the roof of the car.

“Because you need more friends,” was Buck’s first bullshit explanation, one that was immediately shot down with a simple look from his brother. “Because I need more friends?”

“You do, actually. But I know you’re past the age of needing me to hold your hand for it.”

“Okay, then… Then I’m trying to not-so-secretly set you up?”

“If this was coming from Maddie, I’d probably believe it. But you actually like Austin.” Danny’s statement was almost enough to send Buck off track, wanting to know why Maddie wouldn’t like Austin and why she would actually try to set Danny up with someone else, but thankfully his brother put him to rights himself. “Why do you want to chat up the pretty TV reporter, squirt?”

“I was just thinking that… Okay, it sounds awful, but most people won’t care that Sue’s in the hospital or that the guy who put her there is probably gonna get away with it. Not unless someone tells them to care.”

“And conveniently, the pretty TV reporter can go on TV and tell them to care.” Danny nodded and opened the car door. “Alright. But I’m gonna take a picture of you with her and send it to Eddie.”

“Why!?”

“To torment the both of you, duh.”

“You’re an asshole,” Buck snapped at him, and then asked, “Hey, did Maddie seem weird to you?”

Danny paused in the motion of getting into the driver’s seat. He frowned, and then he shrugged. Entirely unhelpful.

Taylor, at least, was just as easy to talk into getting brunch as Danny. And when Danny took the picture while they waited in line to order, and explained why he was taking it, she’d smirked and pressed herself as close to Buck as humanly possible. She even twined her arm around his. Which meant that Buck was stuck juggling his food and his phone on the way to a table, fending off Eddie’s peeved texts.

“This is your fault,” Buck snapped at Danny, balling up a napkin from the dispenser and throwing it at his head. His brother just grinned and shrugged, already already taking a fork to his chicken and waffles. “Taylor, what do you know about the nine-one-one call center?”

“Next to nothing,” she answered. “Your sister works there, right? I saw the three of you when I was covering the hostage thing last year.”

“Yeah. And uh, her boss, Sue, is really great,” Buck said. “She’s actually been at the call center since it opened.”

“Since the sixties?”

“No, that’s when they created the number. The call center here in LA didn’t open until Nineteen Eighty-four. And dispatchers aren’t even classified as first responders in most parts of the country.”

“Which is weird,” Danny commented. “‘Cause they’re literally the first call in an emergency.”

“Yeah! It only changed here in California last year.”

“Interesting.” But even though she said it was interesting, Taylor didn’t seem very interested. She’d picked up her phone and started messing with it, and she tilted it away when Buck got curious enough to try and peek.

“Sue got hit by a car last night,” Danny stated, not at all attempting to soften the bluntness. He was scowling at Taylor. “Hit and run.”

“Oh.” Taylor looked between them. “That’s awful.”

“Did you know that less than ten percent of hit-and-runs ever get solved?” Buck asked her.

“I did, actually.” She set down her phone. “But it doesn’t feel like this is just you sharing another piece of trivia you’ve learned.”

“The police don’t have any leads, I checked.” A benefit of being a firefighter, and especially of being friendly with a police sergeant. “And I figured that, maybe, the public could help. But the public would need to know about the hit-and-run.”

“Ah.” Taylor was smiling, the kind of smile that one wore when they finally understood a joke. “Like if, say, they saw it on the news?”

“And I just so happen to know a fantastic reporter.” Buck gave her his best smile and got an eye roll in return, but she was still smiling, too. “Could ya do me a favor? Maybe?”

“I could take you out to eat again,” Danny offered.

When Buck stared at him in horror, because he did not intend to trade his brother for a news story, Danny simply shrugged once more. It seemed to be his response to a lot of things today.

“Maybe save that for my assignment editor,” Taylor said, before Buck could actually get anything out of his mouth. “Cause I’m gonna need a better hook than just another hit-and-run.”

“Okay, like what?” Buck asked.

Taylor paused, clearly giving it some thought, and then picked up her phone.

“Tell me more about the call center.”

The first thing that Athena saw as she pulled up in her cruiser was the angry black woman with the baseball bat. She was standing in the driveway, a car - hers, Athena guessed - blocking the end and preventing a second car from getting out. The driver of that one was cowering in the driver seat, his window rolled down just enough to talk.

Not that there was much of a dialogue happening at the moment.

“Come on out, coward!” the woman shouted, brandishing the bat.

“If you hit that vehicle, I will have to arrest you,” Athena warned the woman as she approached them. The driver of the other car was visibly relieved to see her.

“My daughter’s missing! I know he did something to her!”

“I understand you’re upset,” Athena said, trying to get her to calm down. She put herself between the woman and the car. “But getting yourself arrested won’t solve anything.”

Another cop, Athena couldn’t help but think, probably would have arrested her anyway, without any attempt at deescalation. And for some uncomfortable reason that she opted to ignore, the voice in her head that said it sounded far too much like Daniel Buckley.

“Why are you talking to her!?” the driver demanded. “She’s been terrorizing me for the past half and hour. You need to arrest her!”

“Shut your mouth and that window,” Athena snapped at him. He flinched back in his seat and then, under her glare, rolled his window up. She turned back to the woman with the bat. “Tell me about your daughter.”

“Tracie, just turned twenty-one,” the woman said, voice thick with emotion. “She’s been gone for two days. She hasn't been home, hasn’t been to work. Her friends haven’t heard from her. I am losing my mind here.”

It sounded like Athena’s worst nightmare.

“And you think he knows where she is?”

“She broke it off with him a few weeks back.” Ah, ex-boyfriend. Now it made sense why the mother was accosting him in particular. “And he’s not the type who likes to be told ‘no.’”

“Oh, I’ve met the type,” Athena growled out. 

She held out her hand and, after a moment’s hesitation, the other woman gave up her bat. Then Athena turned and marched for the car, the driver sinking lower in his seat the closer she got. She rapped on the window with the butt of the bat and waited impatiently for him to roll it down again.

“Talk,” she ordered. “And don’t even think about lying to me.”

“I don’t know where she is,” he hurriedly answered. “I haven’t seen or talked to her in weeks, I swear!”

“Where have you been the last two days?”

“Moving into my mama’s basement. A million people saw me there.”

“You better start making a list of all those people.”

Athena waited for him to nod, and then she went back to the mother.

“Did you file a police report?” she asked.

“They asked me if I was sure she didn’t just run away. Then they said they’d get back to me,” the mother answered, bitterness coloring the words. “I’m not holding my breath, it didn’t seem like my baby girl was a high priority.”

Every day, it seemed, Athena was handed another reason for Daniel Buckley to be justified in his utter disdain for her profession. Minor reasons, major reasons, it was becoming increasingly impossible not to see it. This time it was the fact that one of their detectives took one look at a case of a missing black girl and basically tossed it aside.

“There is nothing in that case file,” Athena later complained to Detective Ransone, one of her friends in the department. They’d worked together before, notably on that Realtor Rapist case. “Just the barest of details, a photo of Tracie, and the initial statement from her mother.”

Ransone picked the file up off the desk to look through it himself. Not that it took very long, it was only that single page within the manilla folder.

“This is Nelson’s case, right?”

“It would be if he was actually working it.” Athena did her best to keep her temper from lashing out. Ransone wasn’t the person she was angry at. “Instead, he’s gonna wait and see. Maybe she’ll just come back on her own.” She scoffed. “She isn’t the kind of missing girl that makes the evening news.”

If Tracie Webber was blond haired, blue eyed, and, most importantly, white, then Nelson would probably give a damn. But instead, she was languishing God only knew where and the people that were supposed to care, didn’t. Athena herself wouldn’t even know to care if she hadn’t responded to that call, if she hadn’t taken the time to talk to Mrs. Webber.

“Solid job, solid family, no history of drugs or alcohol,” Ransone read off. “Oh, but there is an ex.”

“Already checked him out, he has an alibi,” Athena told him. “She works at a car dealership. I was gonna swing by when it’s open tomorrow, talk to the folks there.”

“You want some company?” Ransone offered. “I’m sure Nelson won’t mind.”

Athena scoffed again, and could not help how harsh it sounded.

“I’m sure Nelson won’t even notice.”

“Oh, look Buck, it’s the woman you abandoned us for.”

Buck rolled his eyes at his boyfriend’s melodramatics. Eddie had been particularly bitchy all day, ever since Buck had brunch with Danny and Taylor. Buck would be more annoyed with it, but it was also kinda cute.

“If you’re gonna be this grumpy every time I hang out with someone I’ve had sex with,” Buck said, “I have terrible news for you.”

“You had sex with her!?” Eddie yelped, sitting up straight on the couch.

“Oh, shit.”

“When did you have sex with Taylor Kelly?” his boyfriend demanded.

“It was- It was after all that, y’know-” Buck floundered for an answer. “It was when you were hooking up with your wife.”

He hadn’t meant to phrase it quite like that, and he wasn’t certain how true it was, because he didn’t actually know what the timeline on that had been. Buck knew that it was after Shannon’s interview to get Chris into his school, but he didn’t know - he didn’t want to know - how soon it was after that, that she and Eddie started knocking boots again. It could’ve been right away, it could’ve been a week or two later. He didn’t know, and he wasn’t interested in finding out.

Eddie’s expression was pinched, looking for all the world like he’d bitten into something sour. That was the other reason that Buck hadn’t meant to phrase it that way, because it came out sounding as if he was wielding it like a cudgel against his boyfriend. He didn’t want to get into a cycle of throwing Shannon back into Eddie’s face each and every time Eddie decided to be a jealous butt.

“It was literally years ago,” Buck said, hurrying on. “And it has nothing to do with now.”

“She’s a shark,” Eddie grumbled, sitting back on the couch again. Then he wagged his head as he mockingly quoted, “Sharks are beautiful, misunderstood creatures.”

“It was for a good cause,” Buck argued, and threw his hand out to gesture to the television. “See?”

Taylor Kelly was reporting from the scene of Sue’s hit-and-run. The chyron had the headline of “Local Hero Struck Down,” which seemed a bit much, but it was what was needed to get Taylor’s assignment editor on-board with it.

“Sue Blevins remains in critical condition at this hour,” Taylor was saying. “Police currently have no leads and fear that this case could end up like most hit-and-runs in our city: unsolved.”

Eddie made a face at the screen as she started rattling off the phone number for the tipline.

“Why don’t you like her?” Buck asked.

“Why do you?” Eddie shot back.

“She’s fun, she’s bitchy,” he said, and then grinned. “Kinda like you!”

He probably deserved the throw pillow to the face.

Chapter 45

The car dealership that Tracie Webber worked at wasn’t the largest in the city, but it also wasn’t small. The showroom floor inside was filled with shiny sports cars that were all pretty much the same model, ranging in color from bland whites and greys to a bright blue and a striking red. There were two floors for the offices of the sales and service people, and a table to the side of the showroom that offered free coffee.

There was also a large television situated just above the coffee machine, showing a rerun of Channel 8’s coverage of Sue Blevin’s hit-and-run.

“You know her, right?” Lou Ransone asked, clutching his own cup of coffee. “The hostage thing at dispatch last year.”

“Oh, we go further back than that,” Athena told him, vividly remembering Taylor Kelly’s coverage of Station 118 and the mess with the drugged brownies that occurred during it.

“According to witnesses,” Taylor was saying, or rather, had already said, “Blevins was hit by a red Vero Galaxy, prompting a nine-one-one call…”

“I checked the log.” That was the manager of the dealership, Tracie’s boss. Athena had asked him to find out the exact time Tracie left on the day she disappeared. “Tracie signed out of the employee lot at six-oh-seven.”

“I thought you were open until nine,” Ransone said as he and Athena pulled their masks back on. They were both vaccinated by this point, but neither one of them was risking it.

“For sales,” the manager clarified. “Service department closes at six, and the girls are usually gone by six-fifteen.”

“The girls?” Athena asked. Maybe one of them would know more.

“Meredith works the desk with Tracie.”

The manager gestured over to a woman that hurriedly looked away from them and proceeded to pretend as if she was suddenly engrossed in anything else. She was definitely someone who knew more about the night Tracie disappeared. An air of resignation fell over her as both Athena and Ransone approached the desk, the latter hanging back a little while Athena took point.

Meredith was hesitant in the way all witnesses were, when they knew something but, for whatever reason, felt it was better to keep a secret than to share information. Often, it wasn’t even something that would actually be worth concealing. Sometimes people simply had skewed ideas of what to keep to themselves, and when do to it.

“It’s like I told Mrs. Webber,” Meredith said. “We finished work. I was ready to leave. She wanted to hit the ladies’ room first, so we said goodnight. That was the last time I saw her.”

“Okay, good.” Athena glanced back at Ransone, who’d been close enough to hear. From the look on his face, or the parts of it that the mask didn’t cover, his bullshit meter was pinging pretty loudly, too. “Now I want you to tell me what you didn’t tell her mother.”

What Meredith failed to share with Mrs. Webber, but which she really, really ought to have, was that Tracie had a hobby. Considering the hobby, Athena could understand why she would be reticent to tell Mrs. Webber about it. Considering the circumstances, Athena thought it was pretty fucking stupid not to say anything earlier, because this information was invaluable and they wasted far too much time getting it. Because now they had an actual location for Tracie’s last whereabouts, and a possible new suspect.

There were several casinos in the city of Los Angeles, state-licensed and regulated by the California Bureau of Gambling Control. Tracie Webber apparently liked to go a couple nights a week and play poker. Win at poker, too, judging from the security tape that she managed to wrangle up.

“Alright, so,” Ransone said, back at the precinct. He hadn’t gone with her to chase down the lead about the casino, choosing instead to let her handle it. “She was hustling guys at cards?”

“Maybe, maybe not, but she is good,” Athena said, watching Tracie celebrate a winning hand. “Whatever the guys assumed about her skills, that’s on them.”

They probably took one look at her and decided she was easy pickings. Admittedly, that was probably half of what Tracie was banking on.

“What about this guy?” Ransone gestured to the man sitting at the table to Tracie’s left. Like everyone else, he was wearing a mask. Unlike the others, however, he also wore a ballcap the entire time. The bill of it conveniently obscured the half of his face that wasn’t covered by the mask. “They’re talking, she’s being friendly, but she’s keeping her distance from him.”

“Customer service friendly.”

“Exactly. I’m guessing they probably didn’t come in together.”

“No,” Athena confirmed. “But they did leave together.”

On the screen, Tracie got up from the table and then stumbled, having to catch herself. The guy she was talking to got up as well, grabbed her purse from where it was hanging off the back of her chair, and then helped her walk off.

“Too much to drink?” Ransone guessed.

“The waitress I talked to said she didn’t serve Tracie anything alcoholic, just two iced teas and a water,” Athena told him, a horrible suspicion growing as she rewound the footage. “Right there, when she leans down to look at her purse.”

The man’s hand was right above Tracie’s glass of iced tea. He was holding his own drink, a bottle of beer, but his fingers twitched like he was dropping something.

“He put something in her drink,” Ransone concluded.

“And then walked her right out the door.” 

Athena felt rage and disgust and horror all bubbling up in her stomach. Another screen was footage from the casino’s parking garage, showing the pair of them walking along to the man’s car. They walk off screen and then, a few moments later, a car drives through.

“Plates obscured, he must have one of those blocker covers,” Ransone complained. “But it looks like a Galaxy.”

A red Galaxy, to be exact. The exact same red Galaxy that was caught on footage hitting Sue Blevins that same night.

“Why are we here?” Chris asked from the backseat of the jeep, all guileless curiosity.

Buck grinned at him through the rearview mirror.

“Well, buddy, we’re meeting a friend of mine,” he told him.

“Which friend?”

“Um. Her name’s Taylor,” Buck said, and then cringed as he hesitantly said, “Maybe don’t tell your dad? We can just say that, uh. I took you out to get ice cream.”

God, he was asking his boyfriend’s son to lie for him. This was a new low.

“Can we really get ice cream? Please?”

“Absolutely, bud.”

Buck pulled the jeep into an empty spot not far from Taylor’s. She was leaning against it, her attention focused on the tablet in her hand. He went to help Chris get down, and then helped him get his bright fire engine red mask properly situated over his face. Because while he knew Taylor was vaccinated, and he trusted her, he was not risking Chris, thanks very much.

(He probably shouldn’t have brought Chris out like this, come to think of it, but Taylor had sounded excited when she called him.)

“Hey!” Buck called out with a wave. “Got here as fast as I could.”

“Hey.” Taylor wasn’t wearing a mask, so it was easy to see the confusion that played across her face when she spotted Chris tapping along behind him with his crutches. “And you… Brought a guest.”

“Eddie’s working a shift today.” It wasn’t often that their schedules didn’t match up, but it happened. “Taylor, this is Chris. He’s the cooler Diaz.”

“Uh, hi.”

“Hi!” Chris chirped back, all sunshine cheer. “Dad called you a bad thing when he saw you on TV. He told me not to repeat it.”

“Chris!” Buck yelped, feeling his face heat up. “Taylor, you- you said you found something?”

“Don’t think we won’t be coming back to that,” Taylor warned. “But I talked to one of the security guards, and she let me see the parking lot surveillance footage. There’s something weird here.”

“Let me see.”

Buck held out his hand for the tablet, only for Taylor to pull back with it. She clutched it to her chest, fingers tapping anxiously on it.

“Maybe I should just tell you,” she hedged.

“Why?”

“Because you know her.”

Oh, that was concern. She was concerned he’d be upset over seeing what happened. He knew she’d changed in the years since they got drugged with the brownies.

“Come on, let me see anyway,” he cajoled.

She hesitated, but then held out the tablet so he could see the screen. The footage was paused, Sue just coming up from the bottom edge with her hand up. When Taylor hit play, Buck got to see Sue rush forward, clearly trying to stop the car, only for the car to hit her and keep going.

“Wow,” Buck said, a bit stunned. “He really did not slow down.”

“Can I see?” Chris asked, attempting to stand on his tippy-toes and craning his neck to get a look.

“No!” Buck and Taylor said together.

The kid scowled up at them and huffed.

“I just can’t figure out why she’s running towards the car,” Taylor said.

“Maybe she saw something,” Buck suggested. “She looked like she was trying to stop him from driving off, so she gets out to confront him and…”

He didn’t want to say the words, not in front of Chris, so he trailed off and simply gestured at the frozen image of Sue rolling up and over the guy’s hood.

“What could she have seen? I mean, look at where the car was parked.” She waved her hand at the tablet’s screen, and then over to the actual spot in the here-and-now. “The only thing over there are the dumpsters.”

Oh. If Buck were an actual dog, his ears and tail would be perked up right now.

“You know,” he started, as he headed in the direction of the dumpsters. Chris followed along, as did Taylor. “A couple months ago there was this case of a plastic surgeon working out of his apartment. Danny helped catch him, but the guy was tossing the evidence into the dumpster.”

“And maybe our mysterious driver did, too.” Taylor was following along with his logic. Perfect.

“Should we call the police?” Buck asked her, and then, remembering his audience, looked down at Chris and said, “We should absolutely call the police.”

“Absolutely,” Taylor agreed. “But I mean, we’re already here.”

That was very true.

“I do happen to have gloves in my car,” Buck told her. That way, they wouldn’t be contaminating anything. Plus, who knew what else was in those dumpsters.

A car pulled to a stop right behind them, honking its horn. The three of them froze, and then Buck slumped when he heard Athena, over the loudspeaker of her cruiser, say,

“Don’t even think about it, Buck.”

He turned, spotting an unfamiliar man in the passenger seat with her. Athena was giving him a stern look, the radio clutched in her hand.

“Hi, Athena.” He gave her a wave. “Don’t tell Danny?”

It was Spring in southern California, but her glare was positively wintry.

“Your dad is going to be so angry,” Buck whined to Chris. “I’m gonna have to flee the state again.”

The pair of them were in one of the interrogation rooms at Athena’s station, Taylor in another. One of the other officers had dug up crayons and a sheaf of printer paper, so Chris was sat at the metal table and happily scribbling away. Buck was not looking forward to explaining this to Eddie, and so simply responded to his boyfriend’s last check-in text with a bland, evrythngs gr8!

He’d even thrown in a few emojis, just for flavoring.

“You promised me ice cream,” Chris cheerfully reminded him.

“I’ll get you some before Eddie murders me.”

The door to the interrogation room opened up, finally, and Buck leaped to his feet to greet Athena as she stepped in, carrying what looked like a bag of evidence. And then he cringed as Danny followed her inside.

“Uncle Danny!” Chris chirped, looking up to smile brightly at him. “I’m drawing the elephants we saw at the zoo.”

“Athena, why?” Buck whined.

“You think there’s a world where my baby brother ends up here and she doesn’t tell me about it?” Danny huffed and went to peer over Chris’ shoulder at what he was drawing. He tapped on the picture. “You should make that one pink.”

“Danny.” Chris rolled his eyes, putting his whole head into the motion. “Elephants are gray.”

“Yeah, Danny,” Buck teased and then turned to Athena. “So, uh. Did you guys find anything in the dumpster?”

“We found a handbag and the ID of the missing girl,” Athena answered, setting the evidence down.

Because the reason that Athena and Detective Ransone had shown up when and where they did was because they were chasing a lead for the case of a missing girl. A case that, somehow, Sue was a part of.

“I still don’t understand what this girl has to do with Sue,” Buck admitted.

“The girl, Tracie Webber, was kidnapped less than a mile away from the supermarket,” Athena explained. “We think she might have been in the car that hit Sue. It would explain why the driver was gunning for her, he didn’t want her to tell anyone what she saw.”

Buck blinked, and then turned to Danny. His brother was staring right back at him, the same expression of realization on his face that Buck felt on his own.

“Sue kept trying to say something at the scene,” Buck said.

“We thought she was saying nine-one-one,” Danny added. “It didn’t make sense at the time, because, y’know. We were already there.”

“But what if she was trying to tell us about the car?”

“A license plate number?” Athena frowned. “Those don’t start with three digits. Not unless it’s a vanity plate.”

“She never said nine-one-one, though, we just assumed,” Buck said. He remembered her trying to say it, and how it seemed like she kept cutting off part way through. “Maybe- Maybe it was more of a wuh sound? Nine, one, wuh.”

“Okay, let’s run it.” Athena approached the mirrored window that all the interrogation rooms had. Buck wondered who was on the other side, watching them. “Red Vero Galaxy. Partial plate, Nine One William.”

There wasn’t any immediate sign that she was heard by whoever was on the other side, but Athena turned away from the window all the same. Danny leaned on his fists against the table top and fixed the sergeant with an expectant stare.

“So?” he prompted. “How much longer do these two have to stay here?”

Athena’s mouth drew into a tight line as her eyes flickered over Buck.

“If I let you go, will you end up at another one of my crime scenes?” she asked, crossing her arms over her chest. “Or are you going to try imitating my fool husband at a different dumpster?”

“He promised me ice cream,” Chris chimed in. “So I wouldn’t tell Dad about it.”

“You were going to bribe my nephew into lying?” Danny let out an exaggerated gasp of horror and pulled Chris back a bit so he was held protectively against his stomach. “For shame, squirt.”

“Oh, bite me,” Buck snapped. “I just don’t want Eddie to get pissy over me seeing Taylor again. Speaking of, what about her? Is she free to go?”

“Yes, but I think Lou’s gonna go talk to her once he’s got the car identified,” Athena said. “I assume she’ll be up to reporting on it.”

“Alright, c’mon then.” Danny grabbed Chris’ crutches from where they were leaning against the table and held it out to him, while Buck gathered up the drawings Chris had been working on. “Let’s get out of here, this place is giving me hives.”

Athena rolled her eyes, but she held the door open for them and she walked with them all the way to the parking lot.

“What is with you Buckleys and going dumpster diving at crime scenes?” Austin asked Daniel the next day.

They were lounging on Daniel’s couch, beers in hand and a mostly empty box of pizza on the coffee table in front of them. Taylor Kelly was on the television once more, detailing the rescue of Tracie Webber the night before and the capture of her kidnapper. Austin had been there, apparently - the 118 had been called to a container depot after someone called in the red Vero Galaxy and the cops found Tracie in one of the shipping containers.

There’d been a harrowing moment, according to Austin, where the 118 were stuck sheltering in place while the kidnapper tried to give everyone the runaround in the labyrinth of boxes.

“I didn’t go dumpster diving,” Daniel said. He sat down his drink and grabbed a handful of Skittles from the bag he’d been working through, offering some to Austin. “I watched Nash and David go dumpster diving from the comfort of Michael’s apartment.”

“My apologies.” Austin smirked at him. “How pissed off were you yesterday? I couldn’t really tell from the texts.”

“Not as pissed as I could have been,” he admitted.

The very first words from Athena, when she called him, had been to say that Buck was not, in any way, under arrest. She’d said it before she even explained why he might’ve been under arrest, which had kept him confused for long enough that Athena was able to explain everything to him without him raging. He still, of course, insisted on rushing over to make damn sure everything was okay for himself.

Athena had not been surprised to see him and, in-fact, she had seemed to be waiting for him.

There was knocking at the door. Sharp, rapping, familiar. Daniel twisted around on the couch to frown at it, and then at Austin, before getting up to answer. Somehow, he was not surprised to find Athena on the other side again, though she was surprised when she walked in and spotted Austin sitting on the couch.

“Oh, I’m sorry,” she said. “I didn’t realize I was interrupting. I should have called, instead, or something.”

“Give it a bit, you’ll forget he’s even there. Everyone does,” Daniel told her. “Second time you’ve come over in a month, when you never have before. What’s up?”

“May’s wanting to move out.”

“I’ve heard. Michael said you’re being shockingly accepting of the idea.”

“How did you do it?”

“How did I…? Oh, shit.” Daniel gawked at Athena for a moment. “Is this parenting advice? Did you come to me for parenting advice?”

Last time, Athena had come over to bitch and commiserate about May letting her former bully back into her life. That was all fine and dandy, perfectly normal. But it was weird for her to come to him for parenting advice. When Eddie did it, it had made sense, even when their relationship was still so fraught. Daniel had shown up for the guy far more often than Ramon, who was constantly fucking off to elsewhere, or even Helena. Hell, he’d taught the kid how to drive.

But Athena wasn’t his baby brother’s idiot boyfriend.

“I’m going to let her, I’m not going to be my mother and try to hold her back,” Athena said, and Daniel nodded along. “But you might be the only person I know who’s done this before. Hen understands, a little, but Nia was… It’s not the same.”

There was a difference, Daniel understood, in letting your foster daughter, however close you’d gotten to them, go back home to their biomom, versus letting your kid leave home on their own. The former, in the end, was simply letting the baby bird switch nests. It was letting the baby bird go back to its nest.

“You let Buck go gallivanting across the country on his own,” Athena said. “And here I am, terrified about my baby girl moving across the city.”

“He wasn’t supposed to be on his own,” Daniel said. “And things weren’t quite the same as they are with May.”

Athena’s eyes met his, understanding passing between them. Sure, there were the obvious differences between Buck and May, but there were also the circumstances, too.

“But you still did it. How did you do it?”

“I made sure he would be as safe as I could, that he knew he could always come home whenever he wanted, and made him promise to let me know he was still alive every day,” he told her. “And then I suffered.”

“Dan doesn’t like being alone,” Austin quipped from the couch.

Daniel flipped him off without turning around.

“I’ve been making a list of neighborhoods,” Athena said. “Things to look for in a building, things to avoid. A list of conditions.”

“But moving into a shitty building is good for character building,” Daniel said. “I’m pretty sure Crazy Carl was the reason Buck managed to pass chemistry.”

“For your kid’s sake, don’t ask,” Austin warned just as Athena opened her mouth.

“I won’t.” She sounded grave. “This hasn’t been as helpful as I was hoping.”

“Sorry.” Except Daniel wasn’t, really. “Baseball bats make good housewarming gifts.”

The sergeant cocked her head to the side, and then she nodded.

“That,” she said. “That was helpful.”

Chapter 46

Daniel knocked on the door, and Mrs. Lee answered. Her face broke into a smile when she saw him, the same as it always did whenever he came and visited.

“Come in! Come in!” she urged, stepping back and opening the door wider. “We just got back from his physical therapy.”

“This was his last one, right?” Daniel asked as he slipped off his shoes.

“Second to last,” Mrs. Lee corrected. “He still has one more.”

When both Maddie and Chimney went back to work, a couple months after Jee-Yun was born and Albert had his accident, things had been hectic for them. It had been okay while they were on leave, since both of them were at their apartment all the time, but juggling the care of an actual baby along with someone with Albert’s injuries while on opposite shifts from each other proved to be a mite too much for them. And it wasn’t like they could get a home aide like Carla, not with the pandemic still raging. Eddie was still having to make do without the actual Carla, after all.

The solution had been to move Albert in with the Lees, Chimney’s… Daniel figured “former foster parents” was the most accurate thing to call them. Both of them were retired, so they had much more free time to dedicate to making sure Albert didn’t fall on his face trying to get his pants on.

(That was a very real danger, Daniel had seen it happen. He only felt a little bad for laughing at him for it.)

Albert was in the Lee’s living room, sitting on the couch with Mr. Lee. There was a baseball game playing on the TV, and Daniel couldn’t help the face he made as he sat down.

“Does it have to be baseball?” he asked. “There’s gotta be a basketball game playing somewhere.”

“We watch baseball in this house, Dan,” Mr. Lee told him. He bent down to pull out a plastic container from the bottom shelf of the end table, and set it out on the coffee table. There was a bunch of brightly colored plastic stones inside. “You know that.”

Daniel reached into the container and plucked out five of the little plastic stones: a blue, a yellow, a red, a green, and a pinkish purple. They were each vaguely glittery, bits of something inside the plastic that reflected the light.

“But it’s so boring. I’m pretty sure there’s a guy taking a nap standing up in the field there.”

“No there’s not,” Albert denied, but he leaned forward and squinted at the screen to check for himself all the same. “‘Sides, Buck said you and he watched Eddie play all the time.”

“Do you see my brother’s idiot boyfriend out there?” Daniel asked with a scoff. “I also went to every one of Buck’s football games, but you don’t catch me watching it in my free time.”

Albert tilted his head and frowned in thought.

“Would you watch it if I was playing?”

“Can you catch the ball without fumbling it?” Daniel asked in return, sidestepping the question. He turned his wrist, dumping out the colorful bits of plastic that he’d selected out onto the table. “C’mon, Al.”

It was called gonggi. Albert compared it to jacks, which Daniel figured wasn’t too far off. The rules were actually fairly simple, for the most part: you tossed one of the stones up in the air, and then you tried to snatch the other stones up before it came down. There were more details to it, obviously - for the first round, you picked up one stone at a time, while for the second it was two and the third was three and so on - but Daniel only half paid attention to it.

The most important bit was that it was simple to play, and Albert had fun doing it. Well, he had fun doing it now. At the beginning? Not so much. It took a surprising amount of hand-eye coordination to do, along with dexterity and timing, and each of those was something that Albert’s injuries left him struggling with after his accident. He’d gotten frustrated easily and quickly at first, when he couldn’t manage to get through the rounds without messing up.

It wasn’t much of a problem anymore.

“Anything fun happen on shift?” Albert asked, eyes focused on the stones. He tossed one up, snatched one off the table, tossed it again, snatched another.

“Buck managed to help solve a hit-and-run and a kidnapping,” Daniel bragged as he watched Albert.

 Not too long ago, the younger Han would mess up, fail to catch the falling stone and beat himself up while Daniel took his own turn. Now Daniel usually found himself sitting and waiting while Albert went through all five rounds, only sometimes messing up with the last bit. It involved catching the stones on the back of his hand, so it was usually when Daniel messed up, too.

Albert dumped the plastic stones onto the table top, tossed one into the air and then grabbed two, before repeating the action.

“How did he manage that?”

“By getting caught trying to go dumpster diving…”

There was a dead man on the television screen, and he was speaking to Buck.

Okay, really, it was a pre-taped video that Hollis Harcourt, a local Los Angeles author, had made. And he was speaking less to Buck and more to everyone and anyone that was watching. He was famous enough that dying in his sleep was newsworthy, with Taylor Kelly standing outside his mansion as she reported on the story. The most important thing about it, however, was that it was going to be this week’s cause for the city’s regular bouts of insanity.

“Behold, my final gift to the citizens of Los Angeles.” Harcourt was sitting at a desk in his office, an actual treasure chest sitting in front of him. He opened it to reveal it was filled with, well, treasure. “Rare and priceless treasure. Though, if I had to put a price on it for tax purposes, I’d call it about five million dollars.”

Danny, standing beside Buck as everyone crowded around the station’s TV, let out a low whistle.

“Coulda used that fifteen years ago.”

“Could use that now,” Jon Mendoza replied.

“I’m gonna bury this chest somewhere in the city of Los Angeles,” Harcourt continued. Mehta let out a groan of dismay somewhere from the other side of Danny. “If you are clever, as I know you are, one of you will find this chest and the treasure will be yours.”

“We spoke with Harcourt’s longtime assistant, Jeremiah Ruiz, moments ago,” Taylor said in a voiceover, before they cut from Harcourt to her interview someone outside the mansion.

“Hollis was… Passionate. He had high standards,” Ruiz said, refusing to speak ill of the dead. Buck figured he could translate it fairly accurately, all the same. “But he was a good soul. He cared about people and their stories. He will be missed.”

The footage cut to Taylor standing in front of the gates again.

“And he won’t be forgotten, at least not any time soon,” she said. “According to his final video, Hollis buried that five million dollar treasure somewhere in the city that was the setting for most of his work. A poem he recited in the video is said to provide all the clues needed to locate it.”

It was a poem that turned out to suck.

Channel 8 news moved on from the dead author and his treasure, but the firefighters of the 133 didn’t. Buck found himself sitting in the station’s den area with Danny and some of the others, all of them reading off the poem from their phones. Buck cringed with every line.

“I walked along the river’s edge, to hide my secret treasure. A heron soared, a gray bridge roared, a bullfrog croaked ‘Good measure,’” Flowers recited, face twisting with disgust as he read it. “I stopped beneath a willow tree in the narrow place. And then I saw the light beam fall upon my treasured place.”

“I think I prefer Jabberwocky,” Danny said. “He shoulda stuck to prose.”

“No, his prose sucked, too,” Nola informed them. “Drowned in Downey was just awful, I couldn’t even finish it. It’s doing a good job keeping my table from wobbling, though.”

“You didn’t like it?” Flowers asked with a frown. “I thought the twist was neat.”

“What twist?” Nola scoffed. “With his books, it’s either obvious from the start or something he pulled out his ass at the last minute. Like that poor Nutcracker from a couple Christmases ago. Remember that?”

“I drank to forget it,” Jon told her.

“I think I’m gonna drink to forget this poem,” Flowers said. “He has a rhyme inside the second line, but none of the others, and then rhymes place with itself! And the meter is the same between the first two lines, then it changes in the middle of the third, and then again in the last one.”

They all stared at him in silence that had the apparatus operator shifting in his chair.

“What?” Flowers demanded, a bit defensive. “So I like poetry. My wife didn’t marry me just for my good looks.”

“Oh, I’ve been saying she married you in spite of your looks for years, now,” Jon quipped.

“Where’s something to throw? Someone find me something to throw at him.”

“I’m less worried about the poem,” Nola said. “And more worried about the idiots.”

“Yeah, Eddie said they had to rescue some guy off Devil’s Point,” Buck told them, wagging his phone like they would magically be able to read his texts with his boyfriend with the screen off. “Guy was there looking for five days. Busted his ankle, ran out of food and water, and still didn’t want to be rescued because he thought that’s where the treasure was and wanted to keep looking.”

Eddie had also said the whole thing was “stupid” and “reckless” and “complete bullshit.”

“Christ, this is going to be so annoying,” Danny grumbled as he pushed himself out of his chair. “We’re gonna be out all day as soon as it picks up.”

Flowers let out a groan as he stood as well, the others following suit.

“We should go make sure everything’s stocked up before the crazy hits,” Jon said. “You comin’, baby Buckley?”

“In a moment.” Buck’s phone had started ringing in his hand.

The others nodded before they went off to the truck bay, Danny going out of his way to ruffle Buck’s hair as he went by. Buck scowled at him, before looking at who was calling him. He already knew it wasn’t Eddie, just based on the ringtone.

“Hey,” he answered. “I just saw you on the TV.”

“And I heard a rumor that the One Eighteen responded to a call about a treasure hunter in Malibu Creek,” Taylor replied.

“You’re asking me about a call I wasn’t even on?”

“I don’t have the number of anyone there, do I?”

“Eddie said the guy didn’t find anything,” Buck told her, and then hastily tacked on, “Not that there’s anything to find, right? It’s probably fake. Right?”

Sure, Buck would like to believe that there was a chest filled with actual treasure buried somewhere in Los Angeles county, because that child in his heart would probably never die. But, realistically, he couldn’t think of anyone that would actually carry through with anything like that. It was more likely that Hollis Harcourt lied about it just to fuck with the entire city and then cackled his way to the grave.

“I’m not so sure,” Taylor said. “Hollis’ assistant confirmed he saw the treasure himself before Hollis died.”

“I didn’t see that part on TV,” Buck said as he leaned forward, elbows resting on his knees.

“He wanted to keep it off the record. He doesn’t want anyone to come looking for him in case this thing gets crazy.”

“Then he probably shouldn’t have given an interview as the guy’s personal assistant,” Buck pointed out. “So this is real? There’s five million dollars out there, just waiting to be found?”

“Looks like it.”

Oh, this was a bad idea. It would almost definitely annoy or piss off several people in his life. But Eddie had made his opinion on this whole thing clear, because he had a terminal lack of whimsy, and Danny… Well, Danny would probably happily join in, come to think of it. Not that Danny’s participation made it a good idea.

But it was also $5,000,000. Even half of that could buy a lot of forgiveness.

“You know,” Buck said, “I bet if we compared notes, we could probably figure out where he buried that treasure.”

The reporter clearly had access to information he didn’t, information that he might need to find the treasure. Who knew what else Harcourt’s assistant might’ve said, after all, or what else Taylor may have learned about Harcourt himself.

“You’re saying you want to team up?” She had no business sounding so incredulous about it, honestly. “Look for the treasure together?”

“We’d be, you know, doing a public service,” Buck said, doing his best to sell the idea. “If we find it first, no one else has the chance to get hurt.”

“And clearly, it’s my duty to keep the city informed.”

“Exactly! You get it. The sooner the treasure is found, the safer this city will be.”

“Yeah, okay,” Taylor said. Buck pumped a fist in celebration. “Let’s find the treasured place. For the city’s sake.”

“For the city’s sake.”

There was something weird going on with Eddie’s boyfriend. Which, to be fair, wasn’t unusual. Buck was a weird guy, always had been. It was part of his charm, really, at least in Eddie’s opinion. But recently, he’d seemed to take on a different flavor of weird.

For several days now, Buck was… Not distant, he was still there, but he wasn’t around as much. Sure, it wasn’t unusual for him to split time between Eddie’s place and the apartment with Danny, but now that time seemed rather lopsided. He’d either leave Eddie’s early, or come over late, or just not come over at all.

Something was very clearly going on, and on an evening that Buck scrambled for an excuse to not come over, Eddie’s patience for it ran out. He texted Danny, asking if Buck was actually at the apartment, and then bundled Chris into the car to drive over. If Danny was there for whatever was going on, then Eddie didn’t have to worry about protecting Chris from it.

And there was definitely something going on.

“Are you kidding me!?” he blurted out when he let himself in.

Buck leaped in surprise from where he’d been bent over a map covered in pins. Taylor fucking Kelly, standing on the other side of the table that the map was on, straightened up a lot more calmly.

“Eddie,” Buck squeaked. “Hi.”

“Hey, Eddie.” Danny pushed himself off the counter to head for the fridge. “Chris, want some juice?”

“Yes, please,” Chris politely answered, already pulling himself into a chair at the table.

“What is this?” Eddie demanded as he stomped over to Buck. “Is this- Are you looking for the treasure? Together? Behind my back?”

“You called it stupid!” Buck yelped out. “And- And reckless! And bull- Um, not real!”

“So you’re doing it with her!?”

“It’s because I’m prettier,” Taylor taunted. She was smirking at him, the harlot.

“No, you’re not,” was Eddie’s kneejerk response, given with a sneer.

“Your dads are being dumb,” Danny told Chris as he set a glass of apple juice in front of him.

“I’m sorry, Eds.” Buck ducked his head, fluttered his eyes, and smiled. “You can look with us? If you want?”

“Damn right,” Eddie grumbled as he took the offered beer from Danny. “I guess this explains why you were suddenly telling me so much about arroyo willows.”

It was hard to tell when one of Buck’s sudden interests were relevant to what was going on with their lives, because so very often he just clicked links until he ended up somewhere reading about the history of the spoon. That was an actual example, Eddie once woke up to ten texts about it and now knew that the word spoon was derived from an Old English word for chips of wood, while the Spanish word for it, cuchara, came from cochlea, the same word for the spiral-shaped bit in the inner ear, because shells - presumably spiral shaped ones - were used as spoons back in the day.

Eddie didn’t necessarily need to know these facts, but he knew them anyway.

“I guess we’re splitting it five ways, then,” Taylor said, already going back to the map. “An even million for each of us.”

“Five?” Eddie screwed up his face. “I know Buck’s bad at math-”

“Hey!”

“But there were only three of you. With me, it’s four.”

“I made a deal with my cameraman,” Taylor explained, and then tapped one of the pins. Danny came over to stand beside her as he looked over the map, too. “We have too many options, we need more data to rule some of these out.”

“You mean more data than just the One Thirty-three and whatever info Austin’s feeding Danny?” This time, it was Eddie’s turn to smirk. “I think I know a guy.”

Hen was not stupid. Sure, her brain might be a bit fried these days from juggling medical school with work, but she was not dumb. It was insulting that certain coworkers, certain friends, apparently thought otherwise.

“Do you feel that, Hen?” Chimney asked her. He was proving himself to be one of the only people here that she could depend on in the face of this betrayal.

“Oh, I feel a definite chill.”

“We’ve been left out in the cold.”

They were watching through the glass walls of the locker room as Eddie schmoozed up to the b-shift probie, the same one that jinxed them months before. There was absolutely no reason for Eddie to be talking to the guy, not when he’d made zero attempts and shown zero interest before today. Except for the obvious reason, of course. And Hen had no doubts whatsoever that if Eddie was leaping feet first into this treasure hunt mess, then Buck was not far behind.

He was probably leading the charge, actually.

“I think it’s time we show them how it’s done,” Hen said, and then shared a smirk with Chimney.

Chapter 47

“They lowered me into a septic tank, Buck.”

Eddie was glowering through the screen of Buck’s phone, reminding Buck of a very pissed off cat. Behind him, the busy truck bay of station 118 was visible. People passed him by, but they all gave him a wide berth.

“I hope you took a shower,” Buck told him as he leaned against the 133’s outside wall, just beside the open bay doors. “Because I am not getting into bed with you again until you do.”

“I’ve taken two,” Eddie grumbled. “Austin and Javier nearly got into a fight about whether or not I was gonna ride the engine or the ladder back to the station.”

Javier Ortiz was the apparatus operator for the 118, the guy who drove the ladder truck. He was probably the only other person at the 118 aside from Eddie, and Buck, before he transferred, that spent much time with Austin. Not that that was really saying much.

“Who won?” Buck asked.

“I ended up taking the ladder, so I guess Austin,” his boyfriend answered. “I took my first shower and came out to find Javier standing right outside with cleaning supplies, and he wouldn’t leave me alone until I scrubbed the inside of the truck. The whole thing smells like lemon zest.”

“So why were you in a septic tank?”

“Treasure hunters.” Eddie rolled his eyes with a huff, which was a bit hypocritical since he was a treasure hunter, now. Sure, they hadn’t actually gone out and hunted for the treasure, yet, but still. “Some woman and her boyfriend were at the River’s Edge Bed and Breakfast, and she was standing above the tank when the roof collapsed. Rusted right through.”

“Gross.” Buck made a face, and then lowered his voice as he asked, “So, uh… Did they find the treasure?”

“No. So we can mark it off the list.”

“Pretty sure it wasn’t even on the list.”

“Oh! And it turns out, the woman’s boyfriend? Already married. She was his side piece,” Eddie said. He was very excited about sharing the gossip, entire face lighting up with it. “Hen and Chim said that wires got crossed and she accepted what she thought was his marriage proposal. He called her his adventure on the side. It was all very awkward.”

Buck nodded in agreement, then said,

“I think you should talk to Austin more, you’d get along.”

“Why did that sound like an insult to me?” Eddie asked, suspicion lacing his words. “Why do you think we’d get along?”

“‘Cause you’re both a pair of chismosos.”

Buck smiled oh-so-prettily at his boyfriend, who scowled in return. Any reply that Eddie might’ve given was cut off before he could start by Danny calling Buck’s name.

“Oh, gotta go. Danny and Flowers are doing maintenance on the trucks,” Buck told Eddie. “Gotta go hold the flashlight.”

“They need you for that?”

“I guess? I dunno.” Buck shrugged. “Love ya.”

“Love you, too.”

Danny and Flowers were both hanging around the engine when Buck re-entered the station. The former was leaning against one of their rolling toolboxes, while the latter had the maintenance checklist for the engine in his hand. Buck spotted the one for the ladder laying on the toolbox, beneath Danny’s elbow.

“Done making kissy noises to each other, squirt?” Danny asked in greeting.

“Fuck you,” Buck retorted without any heat. “The treasure isn’t at the River’s Edge B&B.”

“I know, Austin already told me, even though he thinks the whole thing is dumb and wants nothing to do with it. And Josh said they marked off the 4th and 6th Street bridges.”

“Why would the treasure be there?” was Flower’s incredulous question. “It’s all concrete and pavement, there’s nowhere to bury anything.”

“Didn’t stop someone from trying to kill themselves looking for it there.”

“Josh told you?” Buck interrupted to ask. “Why is Josh telling you anything?”

“Because I’m hot,” Danny answered with a shrug. “And I am not above using that for information.”

“That feels wrong.”

“Hold on.” Flowers squinted at them both, and then used the clipboard in his hand to gesture between them. “Are you two looking for the treasure?”

Buck looked at Danny. Danny looked at Buck.

“No,” they both said together.

“You fuckers.”

“Do not!” Danny snapped at him. “I caught you with Mendoza in the bunkroom this morning, talking about checking some places out. You both went quiet the moment I walked in and then scurried away.”

“...I’m cheating on my wife. We were talking about date ideas.”

“With Mendoza?” Danny’s tone was incredulous.

“I’m discovering new things about myself, Dan,” Flowers said, entirely straight faced. Buck was honestly a bit impressed with his acting skills. “I thought you’d be supportive.”

“Oh, that is such bullshit.”

“So what places were you and Jon talking about?” Buck asked.

“What places have you two been looking at?” Flowers asked in turn.

“That is none of your business.” Danny reached over and yanked the clipboard out of his hand. “C’mon squirt, let’s get this done.”

“I think I’m gonna tell Jon that he’s having an affair with Flowers,” Buck remarked as he took the clipboard that his brother handed him. Flowers was grumbling, but the brothers ignored it. “He should probably know, right?”

“You’re absolutely right,” Danny agreed. “He should know.”

“I hate you both,” Flowers complained.

With how insane the city, and her husband, had been acting in regards to this foolish treasure hunt, Athena could not rightly say she was surprised to be called out to Hollis Harcourt’s obnoxious mansion. Honestly, it was a bit of an inevitability and it was surprising that she or another officer hadn’t already been sent here before now. Or maybe the author’s home was a bit too obvious of a place for the buried treasure.

There were two cars parked in the circular drive of the mansion. One was sitting empty, while the other had a man waiting beside it. Athena vaguely recognized him, but she couldn’t be sure from where.

She parked her cruiser beside him and got out.

“Got a call from the alarm company about a break-in?”

“They called me, too,” the man said, sounding anxious. “Jeremiah, I was Mr. Harcourt’s personal assistant.”

Ah, that was where Athena recognized him from. He’d done an interview with Taylor Kelly at the start of this circus, right here in this driveway. But in fairness to her, she hadn’t exactly paid much attention to that drivel except for how it was making her life more difficult.

“The door was like that when I got here,” Jeremiah explained. The front door of the mansion was ajar. “I haven’t touched a thing. I figured it was probably some treasure hunters looking for clues.”

She wondered if she could have the man give a seminar on how not to interfere with police work. There were three people she knew that would benefit from it. At least three.

Athena told Jeremiah to stay where he was, and then she made he way to the mansion’s front door. She unholstered her gun as she crept up the brick stones, past the stone lions flanking them and the suits of armor flanking them. The door wasn’t open very far, just enough to peek inside, and closed more than enough to hide someone.

“This is LAPD,” she announced. “The door is open, and I am coming in.”

There was no one on the other side, just a small entry way and a long hall running from her left to right beyond that. A flight of stairs started on her left, curving around to follow the wall. When she crept across the entry way and to the hall, she could hear what sounded like someone digging through desk drawers to her right and followed that sound to an office. Hollis Harcourt’s office, where he made the video for that treasure hunt announcement.

Whoever it was that broke into this mansion, they were hiding on the other side of the desk.

“LAPD,” Athena announced, raising her gun. She had, unfortunately, learned this lesson the hard way. “Get up, slowly, with your hands in the air.”

And then a ghost revealed itself to her.

“What are you doing in my house?”

“Hollis Harcourt?” Athena lowered her gun with a huff. “You’re looking mighty good for a dead man.”

“You’re alive!?” Jeremiah’s voice surprised Athena slightly. She turned and found him in the doorway to the office, looking very upset. “I’m gonna kill you!”

Athena stopped him just as he started marching forwards, not wanting to find out just how intent he was on following through with that statement.

“I have not known this man for long,” she told him. “But I’m confident he’s not worth it.”

“You’re such an ass,” Jeremiah spat at the author.

“What happened to, ‘he had such a good soul’?” Hollis asked. He was sitting in the chair behind the desk, now. “And who changed my alarm code?”

“Oh, I don’t know. Maybe the person who’s not supposed to be dead? And who was conveniently left out of the will?”

Jeremiah scoffed and stomped out of the room, Athena and Hollis watching him go. The author seemed entirely unaffected by his (former?) assistant’s anger.

“I’m sorry for wasting your time,” he said. “But as you can see, there’s been no break-in. Just a simple misunderstanding. I think your work here is done.”

He sat forward and started messing about with his computer, the dismissal clear. Athena did not move, however.

“Is it?” She shook her head. “Fraud, filing a false report, forging a death certificate. All of those are crimes, Mr. Harcourt.”

“And they are, but I didn’t do any of that. I just had my lawyer release a press statement,” Hollis said. “Then came the heartfelt tributes and outpourings of emotion.”

“I’m feeling some kind of emotions myself right now.” All of them were negative. “Your ridiculous treasure hunt has the city completely off the rails.”

“Isn’t it great?” Hollis gushed. “Confirms everything I ever thought about this town. Full of selfish, greedy morons.”

“Those morons are dropping like flies. You need to call this whole thing off.”

“I can’t,” he admitted. “I need to find out how it ends.”

“You buried it. Pretty sure you know how it ends.”

“Not the hunt. The book.”

Athena stood there, in disbelief, as Hollis Harcourt explained the problem that led to this harebrain scheme. His next novel, Gutted in Glendale, was unfinished, despite him working on it for two years. There was a huge advance, the movie rights were sold, but Hollis could not figure out the ending. And after blowing through three deadlines, and when the legal and financial ramifications for not finishing the book started to loom large, Hollis concocted the treasure hunt.

“But I am so close,” Hollis finished. “I’m gonna find my ending, I just need a little more time. So maybe you keep the news that I’m not dead between the two of us? I could just sneak back out and-”

“The alarm call went out over the radio,” Athena said. “So I’m probably gonna run into some curious reporters back at the station.”

“And what are you gonna tell them?”

“The truth,” she answered, and enjoyed the way his face fell. “Mr. Harcourt, you might not have committed any crimes with the false announcement of your death, but this treasure hunt? It’s the equivalent of shouting fire in a crowded theater. People are getting hurt because of it, people might be killed because of it, and the blame for that will come back on you.”

Athena left Hollis alone to dwell on that. She had breaking news to announce.

“I can’t believe I fell for it,” Taylor complained. “I feel like an idiot.”

They were in Buck and Danny’s apartment, washing away their woes with shots. The treasure hunt was over, if it was ever even a thing, and they’d - well, those of them at the 118 - had agreed to give up and chalk it up as a loss. Eddie didn’t know about Buck and Danny, but they seemed despondent enough to have done the same.

Eddie slapped his glass down and told her,

“You are.”

Taylor glowered at him, while Buck elbowed him in the ribs - they were practically in each other’s laps - for being rude. Not that Eddie cared about being rude to Taylor Kelly.

“We all got fooled,” was Buck’s attempt at reassurance.

It didn’t really work.

“But I should have known better, I’m a trained journalist,” Taylor said. Eddie made a face at her, not that she was paying attention, because she made it sound like that made her some sort of professional mystery solver or something. “Or at least I was, before I got caught up in this dumb treasure. What was I thinking?”

“You were thinking that there was five million dollars worth of treasure buried in a chest somewhere.” Danny reached past Eddie, and over their map of the county, to grab the whiskey bottle. He didn’t refill his shot glass, but sat the bottle aside. “And you were thinking about what you could do with even a fifth of that.”

“I was,” Taylor whispered as she stared down at the map. “We were so close, I could feel it.”

“We were,” Buck agreed. “And then that selfish, lazy bastard ruined everything.”

“That’s not entirely fair,” she said. “He wasn’t completely lazy. You know, he did like to jog…”

She trailed off as she used her finger to trace a line along the map.

“What?” Eddie leaned forward to get a better look. “What is it?”

“I think…” Taylor tapped at a spot on the Los Angeles river, on the other side of Griffith Park. “I think I know where the treasure is.”

As it turned out, Taylor Kelly had a use after all, as she knew the route that Harcourt jogged. A route that took him past the Glendale Narrows part of the Los Angeles river, which Bobby liked to tell everyone wasn't actually a river, just a concrete channel with water in it. In a fit of excitement, they scrambled out of the apartment to rush over, Taylor splitting off to the news station.

Except they weren’t the first ones there. They found Bobby and Athena waiting for them, along with Hen and Chimney.

“Well,” Bobby said. “So much for giving up.”

“I cannot believe you guys,” Chimney said. “We agreed we’d all stop looking.”

Danny stepped forward slightly, finger raised.

“Uh, no,” he said. “You all did, because you’re quitters.”

“Did you three really bring your gear?” Athena asked as she gestured at Eddie, who was indeed carrying a bag of gear. He kept it in his truck, usually.

“Wasn’t sure what the terrain would be like, I wanted to be ready,” he sheepishly explained, and then pointed accusingly at Hen and Chimney when she scoffed at him. “They brought their med kits!”

“This treasure hunt has been nothing but medical rescues and injuries,” Hen argued. “I was not about to be one of them.”

That was actually fair. Eddie couldn’t find a way to argue against that.

“So what tipped it off for everyone?” Chimney asked.

“Hollis has an unfinished novel, Gutted in Glendale,” Athena explained. “Put it together with the narrow place in the poem, and…”

“It was the river for us,” Buck said. “Taylor knew he’d jogged through here.”

“And like you said,” Danny added. “Narrows, narrow place.”

The five of them turned to Chimney and Hen, and stared at them in silent expectation. Hen broke after a couple moments, explaining that,

“My wife wrote an algorithm that detects changes in satellite images.”

“That explains nothing,” Danny told her.

She just shrugged.

“Okay, what do we do now?” Buck asked everyone. “There’s seven of us, there’s one treasure.”

“Technically,” Athena said, “Bobby and I pulled up first.”

Everyone broke into protests against that.

“That’s only because you kept the name of Hollis’ unpublished novel to yourself,” Hen said.

“I didn’t know it was important,” Athena said. “And I’m pretty sure that is the first time any of us are hearing about an algorithm.”

“Okay, guys, look,” Bobby cut in. Eddie was pretty sure that the way Danny scoffed and scowled the moment the captain started speaking was a reflex at this point. “It’s five million dollars, we can split it five ways.”

“Five?” This time, Danny’s scoff was not a reflex. “Can you not count?”

“It’s eight ways,” Eddie said.

“Can he not count?” Bobby asked.

“We have a preexisting deal with Taylor. And her cameraman.”

“The cameraman with no name gets a cut?” Chimney asked, incredulous.

“No, no, no,” Hen said. “No one who is not physically here should get a cut.”

As if on cue, the news copter flew in to hover over them, shining a spotlight down. Danny looked up and waved.

“She knew where we were going,” Buck pointed out.

“Okay, fine, look, we split it eight ways,” Bobby said, clearly making a desperate attempt to keep blood from being spilled. Eddie had his money split between Danny and Athena, if it came down to it. “I don’t know the exact math, but that’s enough.”

“It’s uh…” Buck had his phone out. Eddie leaned over and saw he had the calculator app up. “Oh. It’s an even six-hundred twenty-five thousand.”

“See? Perfect,” Bobby said. “We found the treasure, so let’s go enjoy it. Together. Come on.”

“And then we’ll hold hands and sing kumbaya,” Danny grumbled beneath his breath as they followed the captain to the nearby bridge.

Buck smacked him for the comment, and then Danny smacked him back, and then they got into a minor slapfight that ended when Athena cleared her throat and glared at them.

They had to go through an ironwrought gate, emblazoned with herons, to reach the bridge. They gathered in the middle and looked over the edge.

“It’s got to be buried on one of those little islands, the sandbars,” Athena said.

“I see willow trees,” Eddie said. “But how will we know which one it is?”

“There’s supposed to be a marker,” Hen said. “H marks the spot.”

Of course.

“Or maybe,” Athena said. “We’ll find someone else already there, beating us to it.

Because there was Ravi the probie from b-shift, the one that everyone claimed had jinxed them, already digging away on one of the sandbars. Worse, when they got down there and joined him, when he pulled out the chest, they found it completely empty. Not one piece of the treasure they’d seen on the video was inside.

They went to Hollis Harcourt’s mansion to demand answers. They found the gate wide open, and the front door. Athena pulled rank, by virtue of gun and badge, to go inside alone and check things out while they stayed outside. When they followed her, because of course they followed her, they found the author lying dead on the ground.

Danny’s suggestion of poking him with a stick, to make sure he was actually dead this time, went ignored as the cops arrived. Which was weird, because none of them called the cops. They got lined up outside while the police scoured the mansion and a detective that Athena sometimes worked with, Romero, grilled them for answers.

“So, you all found an empty treasure chest, drove down here like an angry mob to confront him, and now he’s dead,” Romero said as he paced in front of them. “But these facts are unrelated to each other.”

“Rick, he was dead when we got here,” Athena said. “We didn’t kill him.”

“We just wanted to,” Buck said.

“Buck!” It was weird to hear Danny and Bobby scold him like that at the same time.

“You’re new.” Romero had stopped in front of Ravi, who was at the end of the line beside Danny.

“Yeah,” the probie said, and then threw them all under the bus with, “I’m not really with them, I barely know these people.”

Luckily, an actual murder was prevented when another cop came over with video proving they were all innocent. It showed the pregnant wife of one of the would-be treasure hunters, who was currently in the hospital, showing up in a delivery driver’s uniform. It didn’t show what happened when she went inside.

But it was enough to let them all go.

“This has been nice,” Bobby said.

Buck was standing with him outside, in the Grant-Nash’s backyard. Everyone had gathered here for a debrief - everyone except for Danny and Taylor, anyway - following the events from last night. They sat around the dining table and had breakfast together for the first time in Buck wasn’t sure how long. More than a year, at least.

It turned out that Hollis had a heart attack, stressed by an angry, pregnant wife smashing all of his valuables. She left him there to die, which was very cold blooded, but only after calling 9-1-1 but not telling the dispatcher anything. That was why the cops showed up.

“It has,” Buck agreed. “It would be nicer if we were a few thousand dollars richer, though.”

Hollis Harcourt’s assistant, the person who was the one that buried the chest, had absconded to the Maldives with the treasure. Probably right after he found out that Hollis wasn’t really dead. Buck couldn’t really blame the guy, especially since he’d worked for Hollis for so long and wasn’t even mentioned in his will, fake or real.

“Do you think,” Bobby started to say. He looked awkward and uncomfortable. “Do you think you might come back?”

“I like it at the One Thirty-three,” Buck told him. Bobby’s expression fell a bit before it blanked. “I like working with Danny more than I thought I would. But it’s not the same, and I… I’ve missed this, too. Hanging out with all of us together. So, maybe? One day? But…”

“But you have to trust me first,” Bobby finished for him.

“Yeah.” Buck ducked his head and stared at the gross beneath his feet. “I have to trust that, the next time I make a choice about my life or my career that you don’t like, that you won’t punish me for it.”

“I wasn’t- I didn’t mean-” Bobby cut himself off, shook his head, sighed. “I would like to say I wouldn’t do it again, that I wouldn’t get caught up in myself again and ignore what you wanted. That I wouldn’t hurt you again to avoid seeing you be hurt, and then claim it was for your sake.”

“But you can’t say it.”

“I’m only human, Buck,” Bobby said. “I could say it now, when you’re perfectly fine, but it would just be words until, God forbid, we’re put in that position again. That’s how faith and trust works.”

It wasn’t a very satisfactory answer. But it was an honest one, and Buck didn’t think he would have believed Bobby if he’d given any other.

Daniel let himself into the apartment to find Austin, ever the morning person, already awake. He was making breakfast at the stove and, without even glancing Daniel’s way, reached into the fridge to pull the bacon and eggs back out to add more to what was already on the skillet. Daniel had come over after originally going back to his, only to be reminded how much he didn’t like being there alone.

“I told you it wasn’t worth it,” Austin told him.

“Yeah, yeah.” Daniel slipped off his shoes and flopped onto the couch. There was one of Austin’s sweaters neatly folded on the arm, still smelling faintly floral from Austin’s laundry detergent. It didn’t take long for Daniel to slip it over his head. “But think of all the stupid minis and gamebooks you could’ve bought with it.”

“Because I have so many expenses keeping me from doing that now.”

“Good point.” Daniel drew his knees under him as he twisted around on the couch to face Austin, folding his arms on the back. “You could’ve… Bought a house?”

“I’d hate having to mow.”

“Then you could’ve bought an apartment. Can you buy just an apartment?”

“I think I’d have to buy the apartment building.”

“That would make you a landlord, and I’d be morally obligated to cut you out of my life.”

Daniel did not particularly like landlords. Sure, his current one was okay, in that Daniel had only ever laid eyes on the guy once and dealt with the property manager the entire rest of the time. The landlord for the shitty apartment building in El Paso, however, turned out to have almost no redeemable qualities pretty early on in their living there.

“Maybe I should start buying up property then,” Austin said.

“Oh, wow, just say you don’t want me around.”

Austin didn’t say that, though. Of course he didn’t. 

Daniel watched as he finished up the food, bustling about to pull down plates for the both of them from the cabinets and forks from a drawer. If he could, in an ideal world, Daniel would have this every morning. If he could, in an ideal world, he’d have a place with room enough for the five of them - Him and Austin, Buck and Eddie and Chris - and he wouldn’t step foot in an empty and quiet apartment ever again. That $5,000,000 would have been nice for it.

But even if Daniel could afford a place like that, he still couldn’t have this. Austin would never go for it, he was far too much a fan of being able to close the door behind people once they left. Daniel might’ve been able to push the limits there, he might’ve been able to barge in when everyone else in Austin’s life still knocked, but he knew that there was a point that Austin was relieved for him to go, too, and leave him to his solitude again. That was simply how Austin was.

If Austin didn’t prefer the city so much, he would probably find a cabin in the woods and disappear from the world.

“Why are you looking down all of a sudden?” 

Austin’s voice jarred Daniel out of his thoughts. He was coming over with the plates, and so Daniel twisted back around to sit properly before taking his.

“Nothing,” he answered as he scooped up a forkful of scrambled eggs.
