“Right.” Austin eyed him for a moment before sitting down next to him. “So the chest was completely empty? He just went to all the effort of burying an empty chest, when he could’ve just not buried anything?”

“No, the chest was full when it was buried,” Daniel said. “But his assistant was the one that buried it, and then he went back and dug it up again. Buck said he’s in the Maldives.”

If he could, in an ideal world, Daniel would have this every morning. If it was an ideal world, he could let out the words that kept catching in his throat and not be afraid of shattering everything. But it wasn’t an ideal world, and so he would take what he could get.

And he was content with it.

Chapter 48

Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

Even after more than a year, Daniel still wasn’t sure how he felt about therapy. He needed it, he couldn’t deny that, but he just didn’t know if it was actually helping. Maybe it was the doctor he was seeing, or maybe it was him. There were things about Daniel that Dr. White, that Maddie, that so many people in his life felt needed to be “fixed,” but which he thought were perfectly fine.

So what if so much of his life was built around his brother? Buck was made for him. It only made sense.

So what if he sold his body to strangers for money? A job was a job, and at least he could choose his own hours.

So what if he couldn’t find it in himself to feel sorry for people like Nash? Fuck Nash, that guy was an asshole.

And anyway, those were never the reasons he finally folded to Austin’s badgering a year and a half ago and started seeing a therapist. That would be all the wonderful scars, physical and not, left on him by Drake, and by the cancer, and even by his parents. That would be the increasing number of things that he found he couldn’t talk about elsewhere.

Which was ironic, really, because he’d spent their first few sessions not wanting to talk to Dr. White about anything. He’d been the one who chose to see her, but he’d also dragged his heels the entire time. The most he willingly talked in a session, without her having to pry it out of his mouth like a stubborn dog with a new toy, was when he was trying to avoid talking about something else.

Dr. White had not been very impressed with him, when he confessed to her that Drake had been tormenting his life again for months and he never mentioned it. Not to her, not to Athena, not to Austin or Alma, nor Maddie or Buck. She hadn’t quite been scolding, but Daniel swore he could feel her judgment oozing out of the computer screen.

She had been a bit less judgmental when he told her about how they’d responded to a COVID call only to find Drake laid out on the sidewalk, gasping for air. Sure, the judgment had still been there - “You know, Dan, others probably wouldn’t take pleasure in denying a man oxygen.” - but far less than when she tried to get him to be empathetic for someone and failed horribly in the endeavor. And it was absent entirely when he casually admitted to celebrating the bastard’s death.

But however much of therapy was annoying and, sometimes, a waste of time and money, there were those things that he didn’t feel comfortable talking to anyone else about. Not to Maddie, not to Buck, not to Alma or Attica. There were some topics that he didn’t even talk to Austin about.

“I could probably talk Buck and Eddie into it,” Daniel said, leading back in his chair so the front two legs lifted off the floor. He was sitting at the kitchen table, his laptop open in front of him. “But Austin wouldn’t go for it. He likes having an apartment of his own, with his own space and no yard to worry about and a door he can lock to keep everyone out whenever he feels like it.”

“Get a big enough place and he could still have space carved out for himself,” Dr. White replied. She was sitting in her office, as she always did during their sessions. “Compromise is the cornerstone of every healthy relationship.”

Daniel made a face at her. He wasn’t exactly certain how they got to this point, where his therapist was offering advice for his fake relationship with the guy he was in love with, but here they were.

“We compromise enough, Doc. He kindly lets me invade his space without complaining.” Much. “And I play his nerd games and keep from breaking everything with my feelings.”

“An interesting way to phrase it. And rather pessimistic.”

“Realistic,” Daniel countered.

They’d had this argument before, where he told her that saying the L word would be like lobbing a brick through a window. Everything would be shattered and there would be no coming back from it. She, in turn, argued that he was catastrophizing and immediately assuming the most negative outcome. To which he, every time, pointed out that it wasn’t his fault that the most negative outcome was also the most likely one.

Dr. White knew how it would go if she pressed, so she didn’t.

“Is there anything else you would like to talk about today?” she asked instead.

There was, actually.

“I’m worried about my sister.”

On the screen of the laptop, Daniel saw Dr. White tilt her head a little as she took in the statement.

“What for?”

He sighed and sat forward, all four of the chair legs once again meeting the floor.

“Jee-Yun’s been colicky, and nothing’s really helped,” he said. “The last couple times I’ve talked to her, she kinda seemed… Checked out.”

“She’s probably just tired,” Dr. White said. “If your niece has colic, it’s likely that no one in that apartment is getting much sleep.”

“That’s what everyone else has been saying.”

Except, Chimney didn’t seem nearly as affected by it. Maybe he was simply better at functioning while sleep deprived. Daniel hoped that was the case.

It would be a shame to have to kill the man because he was shoving everything onto Daniel’s sister.

There was madness happening in front of Buck, and he was steering well clear of it.

“What do you think?” Eddie asked as he stepped back to look over his work. “That’s better, right?”

The “that” in question was the couch and the throw pillows he just spent a full ten minutes shifting about and rearranging. Eddie had been like this all evening. All day, even. Buck watched him spin a table lamp in circles, apparently trying to decide which side was its good side.

“Yeah, Eds,” Buck agreed. “That looks… Wonderful.”

“It looks the same,” Chris said.

Buck nudged him with his elbow and shot him a look that hopefully conveyed the message to play along. Except it was too late, because Eddie was now frowning at the pair of them.

“I just want everything to be perfect,” he said, switching around a pair of the pillows.

“The first time I went to your dad’s place,” Buck stage-whispered to Chris, “your Tia Sophia said he spent all day making sure that everything was presentable.”

“Not that you deserved it,” Eddie grumbled.

There was a knock at the door, and Chris started to vibrate in excitement. He hurried over as quickly as he could, which was admittedly not very quick, and opened it with a loud and cheerful,

“Carla!”

“Hey!” Carla laughed as she drew Chris into a hug, and laughed louder when both Buck and Eddie piled on, as well. “What is that delightful smell?”

“I made pozole,” Buck told her.

“I’ve had to smell it all day,” Chris whined. “I’m so hungry.”

“We better get you fed, then,” Carla told him. “Which would be easier if you let me walk through the door!”

They bustled her towards the dining room, making her sit as they served up the food. Buck hadn’t realized how much he’d missed Carla until now, seeing her in person. It had been a year, just about, since the last time she was over. A very long, very miserable year.

So they ate, and they talked, and they caught up. Chris, excited as he could be, regaled Carla the entire time with tales from school, such as it was. Stories of mishaps over zoom, of cats and dogs interrupting things, of parents not realizing they were within view of the camera. Afterwards, they brought out a cake with far too many candles to make up for the birthday that they had missed.

She stuck around even after the candles were blown out, the dishes were rinsed, and Chris was reluctantly tucked into bed. They sat in Eddie’s living room, Buck and Eddie on the couch and Carla in one of the chairs.

“It’s good to have you back,” Eddie said. “We missed you.”

“Seriously, things got pretty dire without you,” Buck added. “Sorry about your dad.”

Carla’s father passed away just the month before. Thankfully not of COVID, as weird as it was to be thankful for any cause of death. But it meant that instead of him being isolated in a hospital with Carla’s only forms of contact being over the phone and through hospital staff, she could be there with him. Small blessings and all that.

“I’m grateful I was able to spend that time with him,” she said. “But I know I left you in the lurch, and I’m sorry for that.”

“Hey, no. No, no, no.” Eddie shook his head. “You were where you were supposed to be. I’m glad you had that time, too.”

“And besides,” Buck added. “You’re here now.”

The emergency that the 118 were responding to was about a woman that had partially fallen through the balcony of her apartment. It was her son that had called. When they got there, Bobby and one of the others climbed the ladder to the balcony below her, and then Eddie took it to the one in question.

The woman, blond and terrified looking, was sticking half-out of her balcony and clutching at the supports of the railing. He’d caught a glimpse of her legs frantically kicking as he climbed.

“Hey.” Eddie gave the woman his best smile as he awkwardly clambered off the ladder and onto the balcony. He was attached to a safety line, to keep him from plummeting if the balcony went, but he wasn’t sure how much it would help if he just got stuck like she did. “How’re you doing?”

“I know I put on a few quarantine pounds,” she said. “But I didn’t think it was this bad.”

“Well, from the looks of you, I don’t think you have anything to worry about.” 

From what he could see of her, she was thin. Not underweight, certainly, but she did not weigh near enough to just break through the balcony floor like this. These balconies were supposed to be able to hold the weight of several people of average size. Someone was getting reported for code violations after this.

“But you are stuck in there pretty good,” Eddie told her, and lifted the rescue strap off his shoulder. “I’m gonna put this around you and secure you to the ladder. That way, if the rest of this balcony goes, neither of us go with it. Sound good?”

“Sounds great,” she said, lifting her arms as he slid the strap around her. “But also a thing I didn’t know to be afraid of until right now.”

“No need to be afraid, I’ve got you.”

He tightened the strap, so she didn’t simply slip through. She twisted around slightly as he did, to look through the door that led into the apartment. There was a boy standing just inside, with dark bags under his eyes, and he was definitely underweight. The kind of underweight that came from being chronically ill.

“It’s okay, sweetie,” she told the boy. “Don’t worry.”

“Your son?” Eddie guessed.

He gave the kid a small wave. The kid waved back, awkward and unsure. Dispatch had said the caller’s name was Charlie, that must’ve been him.

“Yeah. Who would’ve guessed the worst part about being a single mom is having nobody to pull you out of the balcony after you’ve crashed through it?”

“The wood looks completely rotted. Probably water damage, maybe termites,” Eddie told her. “It’s a good thing he wasn’t out here.”

More importantly, it was a good thing there was no one to try and pull her out on their own. That would have been a surefire way to tear her open on some jagged piece of wood, and then they’d be in much worse circumstances.

“It figures.” She sounded exasperated and disgusted. “The place is practically falling down around us. I can’t afford to do any repairs, and my landlord never fixes anything.”

Danny and Buck’s landlord, back in El Paso, had been like that. The elevator for the apartment was broken about half the time, and lights went out in the stairwell that went unreplaced for weeks or months at a time. They joked about it being shitty, but most of their stories undersold it.

“Maybe a visit from the fire department might change his attitude.” Eddie grabbed his radio and thumbed it on. “How are we looking down there?”

“The balcony is shored up as best as we can,” Bobby answered. “We have a platform in case she falls.”

“You’re not gonna fall,” Eddie immediately assured her. “I gonna leave for just a moment, I have to go let our paramedics in the door.”

He waited until she nodded in understanding before going inside, tugging up his face mask as he did. The boy shied away at his approach.

“You must be Charlie the hero.” 

“I didn’t do anything,” the boy denied, glancing at the front door when knocking started.

“You did exactly what you’re supposed to, you called nine-one-one,” Eddie told him as he went to let the paramedics in. “It was quick thinking of you, you really helped out your mom.”

Hen and Chimney didn’t waste time. The moment the door was open, they were bustling past Eddie and heading for the balcony. Bobby came up as well, while they were taking her vitals. And halligans, too, made their way up.

The rescue plan was simple: make the hole bigger. They pried away the rotted wooden slats until it was wide enough to safely pull the woman - Sheila, according to Bobby - out without tearing anything further. It was when they got her onto the gurney and were ready to take her out that they ran into an unexpected issue.

“Looks pretty bad, the wood really tore her leg up,” Chimney said to Bobby. There was a long and deep gash on Sheila’s thigh. “She’s gonna need stitches.”

“I can’t go to the hospital!” Sheila sounded pretty agitated by the idea.

“Ma’am,” Hen said, tone placating. “A doctor needs to clean this and sew it up so it can heal properly. Not to mention a tetanus shot.”

“No, but Charlie-”

“He can ride with you to the hospital,” Bobby assured her. “We’ve got plenty of room.”

“He has an autoimmune disease,” Sheila insisted. 

That did explain why Charlie looked so frail and sickly. Eddie wasn’t familiar enough with autoimmune diseases to even begin to make a guess at what it could be,  but he thought he could scratch lupus off the list. It was never lupus.

“The hospital is the worst place for a sick child,” Sheila said. “All those germs. And I don’t really have anyone to stay with him.”

“I can stay with him,” Eddie immediately offered. Because she was right, a hospital was the worst place for someone with a compromised immune system, especially these days. “I have a kid around Charlie’s age, we’ll get along fine.”

“No, that’s… I can’t ask you to do that.”

“You didn’t ask, I offered.”

Sheila was not exactly placated by it, and protested the entire time she was carted out. But very quickly, it was just Eddie and Charlie in the apartment.

Taking care of Charlie while waiting for his mom to be treated and then discharged wasn’t difficult. Awkward, there was no denying that, but not difficult. Charlie was a bit older than Chris, and generally easygoing. When he complained about being hungry, Eddie managed to scrounge up bread and cheese and served him grilled cheese sandwiches with a side of tomato soup.

It was always a real hit with Buck, and it proved to be the same with Charlie.

“You’re lucky,” the kid told Chris. Eddie had called Carla, who was watching him again, so that they could talk to Charlie white he ate at the tiny dining table. “My mom’s a terrible cook, but your dad’s great.”

“Did he order take-out?” Eddie’s faithless son asked.

“I was thinking the same thing,” Carla tacked on.

“Hey, watch it, I’m right here,” Eddie protested without any heat. “You’re obviously spending too much time with Buck and Danny. Maybe we should cut it back some.”

“No,” Chris whined, dragging out the word. “Uncle Danny’s cool.”

Charlie laughed as he reached for his cup of water, not really looking. He ended up knocking it over and spilling its contents all over the table. 

“No worries, I got it,” Eddie assured him, getting up. He left his phone with Charlie. “Where does your mom keep the paper towels?”

“Upper cabinet.”

Eddie went to the one that Charlie pointed at. Inside were the rolls of paper towels, along with an awful lot of eye drops. Maybe dry eyes were a symptom of whichever autoimmune disease Charlie had? Or a side-effect of whatever medication he was on for it; it was the case for  a lot of medications.

“Charlie,” he heard Carla say as he went back to wipe up the spill. “What school do you go to?”

“I don’t go to school,” Charlie answered. Again, it made sense. Schools weren’t much better than hospitals when it came to germ-infested hordes.  “Because I’m sick. We move around a lot. I’m not supposed to go out, except for doctors’ appointments.”

The kid was practically living in a bubble. Eddie doubted the pandemic affected this place at all.

“What kind of doctors?” Chris asked.

“I don’t know, all kinds.” Charlie shrugged. “We’re always going to see a new one.”

Eddie let out a low whistle as he retook his seat beside the kid.

“That sounds expensive,” he said. “What does your mom do for work?”

“She always says her job is to take care of me.” That sounded like something Danny would say. “We’re lucky because we get donations from a Fund Me page.”

The door to the apartment opened and Eddie got to his feet just as Sheila let herself in, walking on her own two feet.

“Look who’s back,” he said. “And all patched up.”

The white wound dressings were visible through the blood-stain rimmed tear in her pants. She smiled at Charlie, and then her face dropped with surprise when her eyes landed on the remnants of his lunch.

“You cooked for him.” Her voice sounded a bit strained. “He has a very sensitive stomach.”

“Figured you’d be a little wobbly when you got back, just wanted to make it easier for you,” Eddie told her with a shrug. “And I didn’t know when you’d get back, either.”

“Don’t worry, Mom.” Charlie smiled brightly up at his mother. “I don’t feel sick or anything.”

“That’s great, sweetheart,” she said. 

There was something odd to her tone, but Eddie passed it off as just the discomfort of a total stranger feeding her kid.

“Oh! And this is my new friend, Christopher.”

“Hi, Charlie’s mom,” Chris said, waving through the screen. “Bye, Charlie’s mom. Bye Charlie. Bye, Dad.”

“He’s super cool,” Charlie said once the call ended. “Do you think we could hang out sometime?”

Sheila sighed, and Eddie could already guess the answer. The actual answer, not the “we’ll have to see” that Sheila said aloud. Charlie knew it, too. He visibly drooped where he sat.

Poor kid.

Chapter 49

Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

People would probably laugh if they heard anyone describe Daniel as trusting. And sure, he eyed people with a healthy amount of suspicion these days, but he also put his life in other people’s hands on a regular basis. More importantly, he put his brother’s life in those very same hands. If that wasn’t a big enough sign of trust, he wasn’t sure anything would be.

He hadn’t always been as cynical as he was these days, and it would be easy to divide his life and blame his current world views on what happened in El Paso. But he’d had his streak of cynicism long before leaving Hershey, and he kept trusting people long after he moved to El Paso. He’d trusted Alma, after all, and that was never a mistake.

So Daniel would never describe himself as inherently distrustful. But…

“Something about this whole thing sounds off,” he told Austin. He was under the engine, on the wheeled creeper, phone on his chest and a tray of tools within easy reach. “She gets all her money through Fund Me?”

He’d heard about the sick kid, Charlie, and his mother secondhand through Eddie and Buck. Eddie seemed taken with the whole thing already, apparently fully prepared to contribute to the charity case. It very much was not a testament to Ramon or Helena’s parenting, Daniel could confidently say that much.

“You’re just jealous you didn’t have that option,” Austin said over the phone’s speaker.

“I mean… Yeah, okay, a little bit. It would’ve been far less of a pain in the ass, let me tell ya.” Daniel grinned as he listened to the other man laugh. “But it’s not just that. The kid’s too sick to go to school, but they’re constantly moving around? The kid keeps going to different doctors?”

“Maybe she’s looking for someone to cure it.”

“You don’t cure your immune system, Austin,” Daniel said. “You treat it with immunosuppressants. Keep your white blood cells on a leash so they aren’t gnawing on bits they’re not supposed to. But that also means you can’t sic ‘em on trespassers, which is why the kid’s not going to school. Not that anyone’s going to school right now.”

It was more like school came to them, these days. He’d hosted Chris a couple times, now, while he was taught over Zoom. He hadn’t been very impressed with the whole set-up.

“Did you already know this?” Austin asked. “Or did you look it up when you heard about the kid?”

“I spent months in a bubble because they burnt my immune system out entirely,” Daniel reminded him. “The first time I got sick afterwards, you’d have thought I was on my death bed with the way Mom acted.”

She turned into a monster every single time, hovering and fretting and playing the nursemaid. He was force fed chicken noodle soup and medicine, and dragged out for trips to the doctor over the simplest of sniffles. His patience for it did not last very long, especially when Mom started making noises like she wanted to keep him bubbled up again.

Dad, at least, had put his foot down before it got that far.

“But that was after my immune system was strong again,” Daniel continued. “If the kid is as sick as Eddie says he is, they wouldn’t be moving around. Hell, he wouldn’t be at home. He’d be in a clean room in some hospital. Maybe Cedars-Sinai, they have that Kao Autoimmunity Institute now.”

“But the kid is sick.”

“Yeah.” He trusted Eddie’s judgment on that, at least. But… “No one ever said what autoimmune disorder he has.”

“Pretty sure the mom never told us.”

Yeah, Daniel would never describe himself as inherently distrustful, but this whole thing was smelling of a whole ocean’s worth of fish.

Eddie raised the best kid. He knew at least one person would disagree with him there, that they would insist they raised the best kid, but he wasn’t wasting any time with that debate today. Not when his kid, after one conversation with Charlie, decided he wanted to help the sick boy.

Right now, they were in Chris’ room dividing up his belongings. It hadn’t even been Eddie’s idea, it had all been his kid’s. The best kid.

“Does he like video games?” Chris asked. “I have some old ones I don’t play anymore.”

“Of course he likes video games,” Buck said. He kept getting distracted by the toys they were sorting through, right now it was a little figurine with movable limbs, so he wasn’t being the most helpful with their current endeavor. “Who doesn’t like video games?”

“You know what, I’m not sure.” Eddie reached over and snagged the action figure out of Buck’s hand, leaning forward to quickly kiss the pout away. “I didn’t see a television when I was there. Let’s just stick to books and toys, okay?”

“No TV?” Chris made a face, as if the idea of an absence of electronics was heresy to him. So maybe there were areas where Eddie’s parenting could be improved. “He really does need our help.”

“Just remember,” Carla said, leaning forward, “that help doesn’t always come in the form of screen time.”

“Wow, lots of charity happening here.” Danny was looming in the doorway to Chris’ bedroom. Something had him agitated, though Eddie couldn’t figure out what it could be. “You sure you want to give all this away, Chris?”

“Yeah.” Chris nodded, his curls bouncing with the motion. “I don’t play with ‘em anymore anyway.”

“Good kid.” Danny reached out to ruffle Chris’ hair. “Hey, Eddie, can I talk to you?”

Eddie shared a frown with Buck, and then the pair of them stood up.

“Sure,” Eddie said, then told Carla, “Don’t let him give away the whole house while I’m gone.”

They followed the older Buckley on the short trip across the hall and then through the dining room, in the kitchen. Danny’s laptop was sitting out on Eddie’s kitchen table. The more distance they put between themselves and Chris, the more agitated Danny appeared to become.

“So, what’s up?” Buck asked, breaking the silence. He hopped up on the counter, absentmindedly thumping his heels against the bottom cabinets.

“Did they ever tell you what autoimmune disorder Charlie has?” Danny asked, propping himself up with his fists at the table. “There’s like, over a hundred.”

“Sheila didn’t say,” Eddie told him, crossing his arms and leaning against the counter beside Buck. “Didn’t think it was any of my business, anyway.”

“Did you see any medication sitting out?”

“No.” Eddie thought back, but nothing came to mind. “I didn’t go snooping through their cabinets, Danny.”

“Maybe you should’ve,” Danny muttered, and then turned his laptop around so they could see the screen. “I was thinking about what you said, about all their money coming in through Fund Me, so I went looking.”

“You mean that you went snooping,” Buck teased.

“Yeah.” Danny shrugged, unbothered by the accusation. “There’s something wrong with them, Eddie.”

“That’s a leap,” Eddie said. “You haven’t even met her.”

“But I can still call bullshit.”

Danny had Sheila and Charlie’s Fund Me page pulled up. As Eddie watched, he clicked on the next tab and- It was another Fund Me page. Sheila and Charlie again, but the last name was different. Another tab, another Fund Me. Another and another.

“Buck,” Eddie said, not taking his eyes away from the screen. “Go get Carla, please.”

“Y- Yeah.” Buck slid down from his perch. “Okay.”

Carla was initially confused when she came in to sit down, and then concerned when they explained Danny’s suspicion and the evidence. She took a seat on Danny’s other side from where Eddie was now sitting. Buck hadn’t retaken his spot on the counter, opting to instead press himself against the back of Eddie’s chair.

“That’s a lot of Fund Me pages,” Carla noted, echoing Eddie’s own thoughts.

“Sheila and Charlie Burns in El Paso, ironically enough,” Danny said as he went through them. He was still standing. “Sheila and Charlie Young in Phoenix, Sheila and Charlie Watts in Santa Fe…”

“That’s the same kid every time.” Buck’s tone landed somewhere between disgusted and horrified. “Younger in some of them, but… What the hell?”

“Charlie said they moved around a lot,” Eddie said. “That would explain the different accounts and the different cities. But-”

“But not the different names.”

“Yeah.”

“What did his mom say his illness was?” Carla asked.

Danny scoffed.

“Autoimmune,” he answered. His lip was curled in a sneer. “Just… Autoimmune.”

“That’s awfully general.”

“I know, right?”

“You said that Charlie told you they went to a lot of doctors,” Carla said, sounding thoughtful. “Which is what you do when you’re not really sick, you’re just looking for a doctor to say that you are.”

“You think she’s lying?” Eddie asked her.

“Uh, yeah,” Danny said. He sounded like Eddie was stupid for even asking, and maybe Eddie was. “Everyone thinks the bitch is lying. Most of her pages were shut down, but you should see some of the lovely comments people left.”

“This woman is a fraud and a scammer,” Buck read from over Eddie’s shoulder. “Do not trust her.”

“She’s a con artist looking for money and attention,” Eddie read, and then- “Oh, God.”

“I know,” Danny said as he dropped into his unused chair. Anger thrummed through his words.

“What?” Carla asked.

“I think she’s making her kid sick,” Eddie read. “God.”

“It would make sense,” Danny said, and this explained everything about his agitation since appearing at Chris’ door. He thought she was hurting her own kid, and he was pissed. “Because that kid is sick, but if she’s lying about everything else…”

“Munchausen by proxy is a big accusation to make,” Carla cautioned.

“Nonspecific autoimmune disease, revolving door of doctors…”

“He’s frail, he’s weak, he’s always throwing up.” Eddie felt like he might throw up, just thinking about it. “She’s poisoning him.”

“Poisoning him?” Buck’s voice shook. “W- With what?”

Eddie didn’t have the answer at first, but then he remembered. He’d thought that package of eye drops in the cabinet had been weird, but he brushed it off as treating dry eyes as a symptom of the disease or a side-effect of whatever medication he was taking. But now?

And then Eddie remembered how odd Sheila sounded when she saw that he’d cooked for Charlie. The way she said he had a sensitive stomach, the way Charlie told her not to worry and that he didn’t feel sick. As if feeling sick after eating was a regular thing for him.

“She’s putting eye drops in his food,” Eddie said, a bit numbly. “There was a whole thing of them in the same cabinet as the paper towels.”

“The symptoms would fit with tetrahydrozoline,” Danny said, leaning back in his chair. Tetrahydrozoline was a drug used in eye drops. “It doesn’t show up in a standard test, you’ve gotta specifically be looking for it. And it can kill someone if they ingest enough of it.”

“She’s probably putting just enough in his food to keep him sick.”

“But- But why?” Buck sounded horrified. “Why would she do that?”

Danny simply pointed at the screen of his laptop, and the Fund Me page still pulled up.

“That’s why, squirt,” he said. “That one Fund Me raised her over seventy thousand. That’s more than I made in my first year as a firefighter. Hell, that’s almost as much as I made in my first year as a driver-engineer.”

“She’s using sympathy to con people out of their money,” Carla said, shaking her head.

“So- So do we call the police?” Buck asked. “Athena?”

Danny made a face at that idea.

“We’re mandatory reporters,” he said. “We’ll call CPS, tell them our suspicions. They’ll take it from there.”

“I’ll go call them,” Eddie said, pushing himself out of his chair. “There’s a number to call this late, isn’t there?”

“There’s a hotline,” Carla said as she got up as well. “I’ll get it for you.”

“I need a drink,” Danny said. “Eddie?”

“Please.” Eddie dragged a hand down his face. “I need two drinks.”

And to think, he’d been in such a good mood just twenty minutes before.

“So this bitch,” Nola said, disgust dripping from every word, “she’s poisoning her kid to get money?”

“That’s what Danny and Eddie think,” Buck said, nodding to his brother beside him.

They were in that limbo period at the station, their shift filtering in while the previous shift gradually filtered out. One of the first things Buck and Danny did when they came in was to tell their coworkers about their suspicions regarding Sheila and Charlie. The response had been pretty much universal.

“Eddie said she has a whole stash of eye drops,” Danny added. “She’s been lacing his food with it for… I don’t know, maybe years.”

“A couple years ago, a paramedic in North Carolina was accused of using  tetrahydrozoline to kill his wife,” Buck told them. “And in South Carolina, a woman used it to murder her husband.”

“The hell is going on in the Carolinas?” Jon asked.

“They ran out of cyanide on the east coast,” Danny said. “Eddie’s meeting with social services at the One Eighteen this morning to report it.”

“The deficit of cyanide in the Carolinas?”

“I’m pretty sure social services are the wrong people for that,” Buck said, sharing a grin with Jon.

“You’re both idiots,” Nola said, rolling her eyes. And then she groaned as the station’s alarms went off, a dispatcher rattling off information about an overdose.

They were in that limbo during shift change, where they technically weren’t on the clock yet while the shift before them hadn’t clocked out. Still, though, it was close enough that they were the ones who piled onto the engine and into one of the ambulances, sirens blaring as they rushed for an apartment downtown. It wasn’t terribly far away, and they made it there in ample time.

Buck was not expecting to see the captain’s truck from the 118 squealing to a stop with them. He definitely wasn’t expecting his boyfriend to leap out of the driver’s seat, phone pressed to his ear.

“Eddie!” he called out. “What’re you…?”

And then the pieces came together for him as he glanced up, spotting the balcony with the hole. Eddie here for an OD meant-

“Oh, God, is this them!?” Buck asked.

“You called this in, Diaz?” Mehta asked as they rushed for the apartment doors.

“Yeah.” Eddie’s answer was to both their questions as he led them along. “Their apartment is this way.”

The apartment door was locked, but everything was about as flimsy and poorly maintained as the apartment Buck and Danny lived in down in El Paso. Which was to say ingress was achieved with very little force required. Inside was a very tiny looking apartment, the kitchen and dining room first and then the living room. There was a kid standing over an unmoving woman, and Buck recognized them both from the pictures on the Fund Mes.

“I- I don’t think she’s breathing,” Charlie said as they approached.

“We’re here now,” Eddie told him, gripping him by the arms and gently maneuvering him out of the way. “We’ve got her.”

“Do we know what she took?” Mehta asked as Nola and Jon knelt by Sheila.

“Eddie thinks it’s tetrahydrozoline poisoning,” Buck answered. The paramedics looked to him, to the kid, then to him again. He nodded. “Eye drops.”

“She always puts drops in my food,” Charlie said. “She thinks I don’t see her, but I do. I just wanted to see what would happen if I gave them to her. I- I’m sorry.”

“Hey, no, that’s okay.” Eddie kept the kid from rushing to his mother’s side in guilt. “You didn’t mean to hurt her.”

“He’s gonna need treatment, too,” Danny told Mehta, jerking his chin over at Charlie. “The mom’s been putting the same stuff in his food. Smaller doses, over a longer period of time.”

“Alright, I’ll call another bus,” Mehta said, reaching for his radio. “Buckleys, go get the gurney.”

“Got it, Cap.”

It was the 221 that responded to Mehta’s request for an additional RA unit. In the time it took for them to arrive, Sheila was stabilized and awake. They got her on the gurney and taken downstairs to be loaded up into the 221’s ambulance, because Nola and Jon did not trust themselves. Charlie was going on their bus.

“What about my mom?” the kid asked Eddie. “Will I see her at the hospital?”

Buck heard Danny scoff at the question, but it thankfully went unnoticed by Charlie.

“Nah, she’s a little more sick,” Eddie told him. “She’s going to a different hospital. This is your ride.”

“My baby! Where’s my baby?” Sheila was very much not happy to be separated from her kid, and no one was being very sympathetic towards her. “Where’s my-”

The doors of the 221’s ambulance slammed shut, cutting her off. The 133’s followed suit immediately after. Eddie stood between them, shaking his head.

“Should’ve gotten here sooner,” he said.

“That kid is just lucky he met you,” Buck told him. “Hey, are you gonna take the captain’s truck to the hospital, meet him there?”

“Maybe, I think Bobby would-”

There was a crack. Loud, unfamiliar, cutting through the noise of the street they were on.

There was a whistling noise.

Eddie’s shoulder jerk forward.

And then something warm and wet splattered all over Buck’s face.

Chapter 50

Chapter Notes

CW for canon-typical violence and the aftermath thereof.

See the end of the chapter for more notes

It was not the first time Daniel had ever heard a gunshot, far from it. It was impossible to live and work in a city like Los Angeles, with a job like his, and not ever hear a gunshot in real life. And while El Paso was one of the safest cities in Texas, perhaps the nation, the same could never have been said for Juarez.

It was not the first time Daniel had ever heard a gunshot, far from it. He ducked reflexively, craning his neck to figure out where it was, where it came from. That’s how he spotted Buck and Eddie, the pair of them simply standing there and staring at each other. That’s how he saw Eddie, with a bloody hole in his shoulder, sway and then collapse sideways. That’s how he saw Buck, simply standing there as he watched.

It was Mehta that reached him first, as he was closer to them than Daniel. He tackled Buck into the side of the engine just as another gunshot rang out and a bullet sparked off metal with a ting sound. Daniel saw Mehta press Buck into the pavement as he grabbed his radio.

“Shots fired! Shots fired! Firefighter is down!” Mehta’s voice was more audible over Daniel’s radio, the screaming of everyone running for cover making it hard to actually hear him otherwise. “I repeat, firefighter is down! Shots fired!”

Tires squealed as the ambulances peeled out, fleeing the danger zone. Daniel was pressed against the rear end of the engine, ducked down and out of sight. Bullets continued peppering their position, and Mehta was desperately shouting into his radio for assistance. He had a good view of Buck as he raised up on his hands and Daniel knew what his brother was about to do.

“Buck, don’t!” Daniel shouted at him. “Don’t you fu- Evan, no!”

But of course, Buck ignored him. Daniel could only watch as he rolled under the engine and crawled into the line of fire, calling out to Eddie the entire time. With his heart in his throat, Daniel dashed forward to right next to the cab of the engine and where Mehta was crouched down.

“My brother is a fucking idiot,” he snarled, and ducked as another bullet wheezed past. “And why is that on fire!?”

The 118’s captain’s truck had, at some point, somehow started to burn.

He heard Buck grunting and yelling in exertion, followed by Eddie’s pained cries. His brother came crawling out from under the engine, dragging Eddie by the arm. They didn’t waste time to stare, they all simply started moving and yanking open the doors.

“Get him into the cabin!” Mehta instructed. “Get in the trucks!”

Daniel was torn for a moment with indecision before he scrambled across the captain’s chair and into the driver’s seat. He saw Buck get Eddie onto his feet and then throw him over his shoulder, before the others helped pull him into the back. Bullets broke the glass of the windows.

“Go!” Mehta ordered as he got in as well, pulling his door shut. “Go! Go! Go!”

Daniel did not actually need to be told what to do. Even before Mehta was telling him to back up, the windshield spiderwebbing just in front of the captain with another bullet, the engine was already in motion. There was a screech of metal as he scraped against the side of the burning captain’s truck, the still open passenger door getting yanked off entirely.

And then he was hitting the gas as the rocketed forward, tires screeching with the speed of them taking the corner, enroute to the nearest hospital.

In the rearview mirror, Daniel could see Buck, his face splattered with red, as he tore open a package of gauze and then bent down out of sight. And he could hear him, just barely, over the wailing sirens and the wind through the gaping hole and Mehta keeping dispatch informed. He could hear him talking to Eddie, could hear him begging Eddie to keep his eyes open.

“Hang on, Eddie,” Buck was saying. “Hang on, keep your eyes open. I just need you to- Danny, drive faster!”

Buck’s voice broke with the demand, wild with desperation. Daniel didn’t respond and simply put more weight onto the gas pedal.

Byrne Memorial had that stupid fountain in the middle of the ER bay. Daniel drove the engine around it, pulling to a stop with the squeal of brakes, and leaped out as soon as the ignition was turned off. He ran to the other side, where they were unloading an unconscious and unmoving Eddie to be transferred onto the gurney that the nurses and doctors met them with.

“Through and through, upper torso!” Mehta relayed. “Large caliber!”

“We’ve got a transfusion ready,” one of the nurses or doctors said. “Did you say a large caliber?”

“It was a fucking sniper,” Daniel spat, just before someone called out that,

“Pulse is weak!”

They wheeled Eddie away in a rush of motion, talking to and at and over each other. They disappeared behind the emergency room doors, leaving the 133 standing around their ruined engine. Buck was simply standing in place, eyes fixed on those doors. When Daniel pulled him close, Buck tucked his head into Daniel’s shoulder and his whole body began to shake.

There were some logistics that needed solving. The engine, for example, could not stay parked where it was, as it was blocking any ambulances coming in. It was also technically a crime scene, or evidence of a crime, so Daniel didn’t know where he was supposed to park the thing. But there was also Buck, who needed to be cleaned up.

Buck, who was wearing Eddie’s blood on his face and on his uniform and on his hands.

The choice was easy, and Daniel’s priorities had always been clear. He moved the engine off to the side, just out of the way, before returning to where he’d deposited an unnervingly silent Buck in a chair inside. The members of the 133 that had been on the truck were all hovering awkwardly around him, as if they wanted to help but couldn’t come up with a way to do it.

“C’mon, squirt.” Daniel gently urged him to his feet, and his baby brother went without any resistance. “Let’s get your face washed off.”

“We’ll tell you if we hear anything,” Mehta promised, even though there wouldn’t be anything to hear this soon.

Well, they hoped there wouldn’t be. News this early was never good.

They went to the men’s room, and Daniel had Buck sit on the closed seat of one of the toilets. Then he wetted some paper towels to begin wiping away the blood. He started with Buck’s face, his cheek and his chin and under his nose. The blood was smeared all over, as if he’d rubbed at it at some point.

Their phones rang, one after the other, again and again. They both went ignored.

“Reminds me of when you would eat shit on your skateboard,” Daniel said, trying to lighten the mood. “Mom freaked out about the blood more than you.”

“He asked me if I was hurt.” Buck’s voice was a croak. “Danny, is- is Eddie…”

“Hey, no, no. Eddie’s… Eddie’s gonna be just fine, squirt,” Daniel promised, and desperately hoped he wasn’t lying. For all their sakes. “Okay? He’s gonna be just fine.”

Doubt and fear still filled Buck’s eyes. So Daniel raised his hand between them and made a fist, sticking his pinky out. Buck stared at it and then raised a shaking, bloody hand, and hooked his own pinky around Daniel’s. It left a smear of red on Daniel’s skin, but he didn’t pay it much mind.

“Let’s get you out of this,” he said, tapping Buck’s uniform shirt. 

The blood on it was a dark stain against dark fabric, but it was drying in the crevices of the various badges they wore. It was splattered across his name tag and staining the first half of their surname, the Buck half. His undershirt was thankfully blood free, except for some drops around the collar.

By the time Buck was clean, or at least no longer looking like a murder victim, and they left the bathroom, several other firefighters had made camp in the ER waiting room. Daniel sneered reflexively when he spotted Nash, standing and talking to Mehta. Nash was, strangely enough, not in uniform like the others.

Buck made a beeline for Nash, while Mehta, upon spotting them, came over to Daniel.

“I’ll put in an order for him for a new uniform,” the captain said, gesturing at the top hanging from Daniel’s hand. “Badges and patches and everything.”

“Thanks,” he said. “He wants to go check on Eddie’s kid.”

“We’re leaving the engine here,” Mehta told him. “Too wrecked to go back on the road.”

And the poor lady was wrecked, too. It would be out for repairs for a while, if they didn’t just scrap it entirely. Not that it mattered, because forcing Buck to sit where Eddie’s blood was still soaking into the floorboards was out of the question.

“I’ll call a ride.” Daniel took out his phone and shot off the text as he moved past him, to where Buck was, and grabbed his brother’s shoulder. “C’mon, squirt. Let’s go.”

“I’ll stay here,” Nash immediately offered.

“Thanks, Bobby,” Buck said.

“I’ll come back,” Daniel told them both. “Tell us if you hear anything before then.”

“What?” Nash scoffed. “Is Eddie yours, too?”

Daniel didn’t give that statement the courtesy of an answer as he guided Buck out. It was insanity outside. News reporters were swarming the place, kept at bay by police and barricades. The moment they spotted the pair, they started calling out questions.

“Just ignore them,” Daniel advised.

“What am I going to tell Chris?” Buck whispered.

Daniel was saved from having to answer by the appearance of Taylor Kelly, managing to get her way past the barriers and calling out for Buck.

“No- No comment, Taylor,” Buck stammered, ducking his head.

“That’s not why I’m here. Really,” she tacked on at Daniel’s disbelieving stare. “I’m not working this one. I just heard a firefighter was shot, you weren’t answering my calls, and I got worried.”

“Sorry, I- I haven’t been checking my phone.”

Daniel watched as Buck dug his phone out with shaking hands. The action also drew Taylor’s eyes down and to his legs, to where there were patches of fabric that glittered red in the sunlight.

“Is that blood?” she asked, voice pitching upwards.

Buck looked down and his face crumpled a little. 

“It’s not his,” Daniel told her.

“It’s Eddie’s. He- He was standing in front of me…” Buck said, voice going distant. “I- I need to talk to Christopher.”

“Austin’s on his way,” Daniel said. “We’ll go wait over here until- What the fuck?”

An ambulance had come squealing to a stop in front of the ER doors. That wasn’t what caught Daniel’s attention, though. It was the firefighters still in their turnouts that did it. It was the visible pockmarks in the metal of the vehicle.

“She’s been shot!” one of them shouted. “Let’s go!”

“We were ambushed,” another explained to the incoming nurses and doctors. “The shot came out of nowhere.”

“What the hell is going on?” Buck asked, but none of them had an answer.

Time was weird. Buck was drifting. He was a cloud, nudged along at the will of others. He felt like part of himself was still in that street where- And that part of himself was still at the hospital, with Eddie.

Austin picked him and Danny up in his car, not saying a word. The silence in that car was comforting and welcome, because Buck did not feel like talking to anyone. Austin took them to station 133, where the silence was not comforting. It was oppressive, weighty, accompanied by the stares of everyone who hadn’t gone on that call and from Jon and Nola, who’d come back in the meanwhile.

Danny, thankfully, blessedly, intercepted them all before they could begin to badger Buck. He took the opportunity to slip into the lockers, to strip out of the bloodstained pants and toss them as far from himself as possible. There was a trashcan in the station specifically to dispose of any biohazards, including blood covered clothing, but Buck wasn’t thinking about that.

He just wanted them far, far away from him.

The shower he took was long and scalding, and he spent forever scouring himself of any blood that Danny hadn’t wiped away. He’d felt like a child in that bathroom, just like Danny had joked. Ten years old and doing risky stunts for attention, coming home with gashes and bruises. Then, like today, Danny would sit him down and patiently clean away all the blood.

Unlike today, Danny could take away the hurt back then.

When Buck came out, skin red from heat and friction, the stares from everyone had taken on a sympathetic quality that made him itch. It made him want to run and hide, and it made him want to shout at them. He was thankful when Danny bullied him into his car, walking past the jeep sitting in the parking lot, and took him away.

Danny used Buck’s keys to let them into the house, and Carla stood up from where she’d been sitting on the couch. The news was playing on the TV, but the volume was muted. They just stared at each other for a long moment as Danny closed the door behind them.

“Where’s Chris?” Buck asked.

“In his room, playing one of his games,” Carla answered, and he blinked at what she said. Was it already that late in the day that school was over? “The news said…”

“It’s Eddie,” Danny told her.

Buck left him to update her on everything they knew as he drifted out of the room and down the hall. Chris’ door was wide open, and the kid was on his bed. He was entranced with whatever game was playing on his Switch, and Buck stood there like a creep while he tried to figure out what to tell him.

Before, when Eddie was buried in well, Danny had said that Buck didn’t have to tell Chris anything until they knew more, until he had to know. When they got to that point, they hadn’t really needed to tell Chris anything because the hospital released Eddie while the kid was in school the next day, they just told him the barest of details.

But now…

Buck swallowed, took a breath, and took a step into the room. Chris looked up and smiled at him, happy as ever.

“Hi, Buck,” he greeted him.

“H- Hey…”

Buck crossed the room and knelt down in front of Chris, so he was looking up at him instead of down. Chris looked at him, then past him, at the door.

“Where’s Dad?” he asked.

“Chris, your dad, he’s- he’s not coming home tonight,” Buck said. “He got hurt at work today…”

Telling Chris, trying to explain it to him the best he could without also terrifying him, left Buck feeling like he was tearing his own heart out of his chest. When the text from Bobby came through on his phone at the end, carrying with it the news that Eddie was out of surgery and that the doctors said it went well, he felt such relief that it broke him. Chris ended up comforting him.

“I- I don’t know where to be,” Buck told Danny afterwards, still wiping at his eyes. “I want to be there, with him, but Chris…”

“He’d want you to be with Chris, just like I would’ve wanted someone with you,” Danny said. “I’ll go over once visiting hours start tomorrow, sit with him. I don’t have anywhere to be anytime soon, anyways. Our engine’s out of commission for a bit.”

Buck opened his mouth, but all his words got caught in a knot in his throat. He closed it and leaned forward instead, to rest his head against his brother’s shoulder. Danny didn’t say anything, either. Danny just wrapped his arms around him and didn’t let go.

The night of the shooting, Daniel stayed over at Eddie’s to watch over Buck and Chris, and ended up on the couch with spare bedding. Part way through the night, he’d gotten up to check on them both because the lack of snoring from the bedroom told him that sleep was not coming easily for everyone. He found his brother wide awake in an empty bed and quietly climbed into it to sit with him, like it was ten or twenty years ago.

The morning after, Daniel got to witness them going through their morning routines with the awkward dance that came from a vital piece being absent. And it left an odd feeling in Daniel’s chest to see Buck stepping up like he was. Because as much as he was very much aware that Buck had grown from the crying infant that Daniel promised to take care of so very long ago, it was still an entire experience to witness him with a kid of his own.

After breakfast, and after Chris was settled at the dining table for Zoom school, Daniel took off to go to Eddie, just like he promised. He made a stop by his apartment first, to shower and to change, because he’d neglected to bring clothes with him. He also called Alma, who’d been blowing up his phone the day before. Apparently, simply telling her through text that he and Buck were okay, and that Eddie was out of surgery, was not sufficient for her.

At the hospital, Daniel had to show his ID - and he wondered what Nash’s reaction was to learning that he was on the list as Eddie’s next of kin, or if he even knew - before he was allowed anywhere near Eddie's room. There was a uniformed officer stationed just outside the door, and Daniel was thankful the mask he wore hid the way he sneered at him. But then his attention was focused on Eddie, laying still in the bed.

He was intubated, the machine pumping for his lungs. The monitor beeped rhythmically, and Daniel checked the stats on it first thing. They looked good enough that he took a seat in the very uncomfortable chair they’d brought in for visitors. He tugged at the sweater he was wearing, threadbare and worn, one that he’d stolen from Austin at some point.

“You fucker,” he told the unconscious Eddie. “You better not break his heart again.”

Daniel had brought two books with him, tattered and old, pages dog eared and a little torn. They went missing from his bookshelf for years before reappearing without any fanfare, and they had gone farther afield than he ever had. He opened the first one, sat back in the chair, and began to read aloud.

“Alice was beginning to get very tired of sitting by her sister on the bank, and of having nothing to do…”

Chapter End Notes

I have had Buck's "Danny, drive faster!" line stuck in my head for literal weeks now.
(Also, with this chapter, Forgive Us Our Trespasses officially overtakes Hold Steady, Hold Steady as my longest individual fic (by word count))

Chapter 51

Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

Buck was woken up by a small hand shaking his sock-covered foot and someone saying his name. When he blinked open his bleary eyes, he found that Chris had let himself into Eddie’s bedroom and was looking down at him expectantly. He lifted his head and pushed himself up with his elbows.

“Yeah, buddy?”

“Can I talk to my dad now?” Chris asked.

“Um.” Buck reached over for his phone, plugged up and lying on the bedside table, only to cringe at the time and stifle the curses he wanted to let out. He’d overslept, and there was no message from Danny or the hospital about Eddie waking up. “N- Not yet, Superman. He’s still resting. Maybe later, okay?”

“Fine,” the kid huffed, and didn’t quite stomp out of the bedroom.

Buck flopped back and allowed himself one moment, just one moment, where he laid there and didn’t get up. His hand went over to the empty space beside him and his fingers dug into the cold sheets. Before now, before this week, he had never slept in this bed alone. Now he’d slept in it without Eddie for several nights in the row.

But the world at large was uncaring of his trauma and drama, and it did not stop turning for anyone.

“Alright, kiddo, we’re way behind,” Buck said, raising his voice as he stepped out of the bedroom. “Quick breakfast, and then get ready for school. Okay?”

“Okay,” Chris said, standing in the doorway to his room.

Breakfast ended up being bowls of cereal and glasses of orange juice, both because they didn’t have the time for anything more and because Buck simply didn’t feel up to it. Chris didn’t complain, thankfully. He just took his spoon and started shoveling food into his mouth right alongside Buck.

When Carla came in, using her key to the house, she shouted out a cheerful greeting and then came to a stop beside them at the table.

“Oh, are we still in our pajamas?” she asked as she looked between them. “School starts in twenty minutes.”

“Sorry, that’s- that’s my fault,” Buck confessed, ducking his head a little. “Slept through the alarm.”

“No, no, that’s good. That means you’re getting some sleep.”

“At least someone is,” Chris complained. “Buck snores loud.”

Buck stuck his tongue out at him and Carla laughed.

“That’s also good to know,” she said, still chuckling.

“Okay, I uh. I think it’s time that someone got ready for school,” Buck said.

Chris let out a sigh.

“I’ll go,” he said. “But I’m gonna need a nap later. Because of all the snoring.”

That was so very Eddie that it made Buck ache. He watched Chris push himself out of his seat and make his way out of the dining room, across the hall, and into his bedroom. Carla sat down in the now vacated chair.

“He seems to be doing okay,” she remarked, voice a little hushed to keep her words from carrying.

“Do… Do you think he understands what’s going on?” Buck asked her.

“Boy’s already lost his mother. I think he understands more than we’d like him to,” she said. “But what about you? How are you doing?”

“I’m…” Buck trailed off with a shrug, because he wasn’t sure how to answer her question. Saying that he was fine would be a lie, but he also wasn’t the one who’d gotten shot. So what did he have to complain about? “Mehta put me on leave, and Danny. You know, since the One Thirty-three doesn’t have an engine right now.”

Danny had said it was no longer parked in front of the hospital. Buck figured someone had moved it, maybe taken it to the fire department’s repair shop. Or to the LAPD’s impound lot as evidence.

“Good. I’m glad,” Carla said. “It’s a mad house out there right now, I’m glad I don’t have to be worrying about you, too.”

“I know. Chimney and Hen said they’re going out in bulletproof vests and with police escorts.” He’d seen it reported on the news, too, Taylor talking about it over shots of firefighters responding to a medical call with a veritable shield wall of SWAT. “You know that you don’t have to be here, right? I’m not working. If- If you’d rather enjoy a day off…”

“I would still be here, because you’re my friend,” Carla said, a bit stern. “I can take care of Chris while you go off and do whatever you need to. Take a shower, take a nap, go do a grocery run. Let yourself have a little breakdown, if that’s what you need.”

“Been there, done that,” Buck mumbled, dragging a hand down his face.

He wasn’t exactly proud of the way he’d broken down into sobs in front of Chris. He felt nothing but shame for the way that Chris had ended up comforting him, when Chris was the one who had just been told about his father being hurt.

“Have you been to see him?” Carla asked, yanking him out of the memory.

“Danny’s been sitting with him,” Buck told her. “I’ve just been focusing on Chris, y’know? And- And he keeps asking when he can talk to his dad and I don’t want to have been telling him ‘not yet,’ only to go see Eddie for myself.”

“Take this as an opportunity for it,” she urged. “He has school, he’ll be busy. I’ll take care of Chris, you go do that and whatever dozen other things need done. Okay, baby?”

“Yeah,” he agreed, and then a bit stronger, “Yeah, okay.”

After clearing off the dining table, and rinsing off the bowls and glasses that he and Chris used, the first thing Buck did was take a shower. A long one, where he spent more time letting himself fall apart and then putting himself back together again than he did actually washing. By the time he came out, wrinkled like a prune, Chris was ensconced with school on his laptop at the dining table and Carla was tidying up in the living room.

There weren't really a lot of things that needed doing, besides the grocery run, and that was done as quickly as Buck could ever manage it. Which meant, after getting the groceries through the backdoor to keep from disturbing Chris’ class, there wasn’t much else to use as an excuse to put off visiting Eddie. And he was putting it off, he knew.

Seeing Eddie in his current state was not going to be anything but painful.

And it was. When Buck reached his room, with the uniformed officer standing guard right outside of it, he came to a complete and utter stop. He simply stared with his heart in his throat, as Eddie laid there with a breathing tube down his. He simply stared and watched Eddie’s chest rise and fall, and he listened to the monitor beep in time with Eddie’s heartbeat and the respirator hiss rhythmically as it pumped air.

Danny was curled up in the lone chair, a book in his hand. He’d been reading aloud, but he stopped and sat up when he realized Buck was there.

“Hey, squirt.” Buck’s brother sounded as tired as he felt. “Here for a visit?”

“Y- Yeah.” Buck stumbled into the room. “How is…?”

“Vitals are good.”

Danny got to his feet, stretched out his back with a groan, and then made his way to where Buck had come to a stop just at the foot of the hospital bed.

“They’re kinda strict about visitors right now,” he said.

“Yeah. They, uh. They told me. At the desk.”

“I’ll let you have him,” Danny said. He gripped the back of Buck’s head, pulling it down enough to press their foreheads together for a moment. “Tell me when you head out.”

Buck watched his brother leave, stepping out of Eddie’s room and giving the officer a wide berth. When Danny was gone, Buck moved to the now empty chair and dragged it closer to the bed, before settling into it. He leaned forward, folding his arms on the mattress right next to Eddie.

He didn’t know what to say, or what to do. He remembered the awkwardness that accompanied them when they finally got to visit Chimney after his accident. And he remembered the nurse telling them that she liked to treat the patients as if they could hear her.

“Chris is fine,” Buck said. That would’ve been Eddie’s very first question, if he was awake to ask it. “Carla’s there, right now. He’s set up at the dining table doing his Zoom school.”

There wasn’t a response except for the hissing of the respirator and the beeping of the heart monitor.

“I, uh. I didn’t tell him a lot of what happened,” Buck continued. “I just said that you were hurt and that you were resting. He’s been asking to talk to you and I don’t really know what to tell him except ‘not yet’…”

“...so rested he by the Tumtum tree, and stood awhile in thought,” Daniel read aloud. “And as in uffish thought he stood, the Jabberwock, with eyes of flame, came whiffling through the tulgey wood and burbled as it came-”

There was a knock on the glass door of Eddie’s room. The entire thing was made of glass, it seemed like, or at least three out of the four walls were. There was no privacy to be found here, but there was never really any privacy in a hospital room.

Daniel looked up at the knocking and spotted Pepa hovering outside. He got up, stretched the kinks out of his spine - it really was not the most comfortable of chairs - and went to let her in. He wasn’t certain why the last nurse to come in and change Eddie’s IV bag had even bothered to close it.

“Hey, Pepa.”

“Buenos días, Dan” she greeted him. Her eyes flicked past him to Eddie. “How is he?”

“The first question, every time,” he joked. “Still asleep, vitals are still going strong.”

Pepa nodded, looking distracted as she stared at her nephew.

“Mama would be here,” she said. “But…”

“Hey, you don’t gotta make excuses to me.”

This century’s plague hadn’t just disappeared, as much as the world was gradually deciding to act like it had. It was still far too risky for someone of Isabel’s age to be here if she didn’t need to be.

“They think he might wake up soon,” Daniel told her. “But they’re not really sure.”

“Good. That’s good.”

“They’re only letting one person sit with patients at a time,” he said. “So I’m gonna head out, let you be.”

“I don’t know how long I can stay.”

He nodded to her and started to leave, to let her have the room and her time with her nephew, but she snagged his sleeve before he could.

“Thank you for sitting with him,” Pepa said.

“‘Course.” He shrugged. “Didn’t want Buck trying to tear himself in two.”

Speaking of the squirt, Daniel could take this opportunity to go check on him and Chris. He’d spent the night on Eddie’s couch again the night before, after visiting hours ended and he was summarily given the boot until the next morning. His brother’s snoring was practically white noise to him by this point, and a comforting sign that he was getting some actual sleep.

But Daniel was not expecting for his brother to have a guest over nor who the guest was. He sat in his car, staring at the one parked on the curb in front of him like it would magically start making sense, for longer than he felt like admitting. He didn’t know why this was throwing him, only that he had, for some reason, never expected it. When he went inside, using the key that Eddie had given him, it was easy to guess where his brother was. 

He passed Chris at the dining table, giving him a nod and a grin in greeting when the kid waved exuberantly at him, and into the kitchen. There, he found Buck standing at the counter as he chopped up vegetables and Austin sitting at the small table.

“Pepa’s sitting with him,” Daniel said, answering the question before Buck even got the chance to voice it.

“I was getting a start on dinner.” Buck turned back around to the food he was preparing. “Austin was telling me about the shift they had yesterday.”

“I think I saw something about it on the news,” Daniel said.

There was something about a construction worker trapped at the top of a crane, with a huge cable pinning him by the arm.

He walked up to Austin, leaning against his back and laying his arms lightly around his shoulders. Austin glanced up at him and then held up a package of Skittles. Daniel hurriedly grabbed it out of his hand and tore into it, so he could stuff his mouth with candy before he said anything stupid.

“So, the guy on the crane,” Buck urged, turning his head to look at them over his shoulder. “Bleeding out, no air support.”

“Right, guy on the crane.” Austin seemed entirely unperturbed with the way that Daniel was just about laying on him. “Really tall crane, surrounded by really tall buildings.”

Daniel winced and Buck did, too. Any other time, that probably wouldn’t be that big of a cause for concern. But with the sniper out there…

“So who went up?” Daniel asked, once he’d chewed and swallowed the sugary treats, along with his feelings. “‘Cause someone had to, unless you all decided to let him die. And I know it wasn’t gonna be you going up there.”

“They spent a while arguing over it,” Austin answered. “But Cap ended up doing the climb by himself. Didn’t want to put anyone else at risk.”

“Did Nash get shot?” 

Perhaps the question was asked with a bit too much eagerness, because it had Buck twisting around to shoot out a terse,

“Danny!”

“No one got shot, you psycho.” Austin was the only person Daniel knew who could sound so fond while calling him that. “The guy coded, though. He’d lost a lot of blood by the time Cap got a tourniquet on him and the cable was cut. They got him to the hospital, but I don’t know anything beyond that.”

“But Nash didn’t get shot?” Daniel complained, and was then left to wonder when his little brother and his not-boyfriend got close enough that they could synchronize their eye rolls.

When Danny called him that evening, Buck panicked. The full body kind, the kind that had his heart beating out of his chest and made his lungs feel like they were in a vice. Because Danny was at the hospital with Eddie and if he was calling, then-

All that fear turned into bubbly relief when he heard his brother say,

“He’s awake.”

It was a good thing that Carla was already there, because Buck wasn’t sure he could’ve waited until someone came over. As it was, he basically tripped out the door to get to his jeep and then barely obeyed the traffic laws. And then he practically sprinted to Eddie’s room, ignoring the bewildered and outraged looks that it earned him from everyone that he bulldozed past.

But there Eddie was, awake and breathing on his own, a simple oxygen cannula having replaced the breathing tube. Danny stood by the bed and glanced between them.

“I’ll leave the two of you alone,” he said, reaching out to brush his hand over Eddie’s hair before heading for the door. He gave Buck’s shoulder a comforting squeeze as he went by. “I have a whole list of people I need to update.”

There was an errant thought to make sure that Bobby was on that list, because Buck wasn’t sure he trusted Danny with that. But to be truthful, his entire focus was on Eddie - Awake! Eddie was awake! - and he had very little cognitive space for much else beyond that.

“Danny said you were with Chris.” Eddie sounded groggy, like he was still waking up.

“Y- Yeah, Carla’s with him now,” Buck said, tripping over his own feet to reach Eddie’s bedside, tugging out his phone as he went. “He’s been asking to talk to you.”

After a text to Carla, his phone began to ring with an incoming video call. He handed it to Eddie, who answered it with a tired smile.

“Dad!” Chris’s excited voice was loud through the phone’s speakers. “I miss you.”

“I miss you, too, mijo,” Eddie said. His smile was tired, but warm. “But I’m gonna see you real soon. I’ll be home before you know it.”

“Let yourself heal first, please,” Carla said. “You don’t have anything to worry about, Buck and I have it under control.”

“Thanks.”

“Love you, Dad,” Chris said.

“Love you, too.”

There was the sound of the call ending, and then Eddie was dropping his arms into his lap and sinking back into his pillow.

“Buck and I have it under control,” Eddie repeated, holding Buck’s phone out to him. “What about Danny?”

“He’s been here,” Buck answered with a shrug as he took his phone back.

“The entire time?”

“Just about.”

Eddie blinked at him.

“Huh,” he said. “I remember when he would’ve happily shot me himself.”

Buck wasn’t too sure that had ever been true, actually. Danny had been pissed at Eddie, certainly. Pissed enough to cut him out of his life entirely. But now, with Bobby, Buck was well aware of how Danny was like when he was angry and wanted to hurt someone. If he’d truly wanted to, Daniel would’ve gone to Bobby at any point after learning that Eddie was at the 118 and told him everything, get him transferred to another shift or station.

But he hadn’t. He’d kept Eddie’s secret.

“How has Chris been?” Eddie asked, tearing Buck out of his thoughts.

“Better than me,” Buck admitted with a laugh. “I didn’t tell him too much about what happened, just that you got hurt. And- And I kind of lost it when I told him. I should have held it together better.”

“You were there for him when I couldn’t be, that’s what matters.”

“Yeah, I- I guess.” Buck ducked his head a little. “You look awful, by the way.”

“Fuck you, I’m still pretty,” Eddie shot back. “Respect your elders.”

They both laughed at the old joke, and then Eddie held out his hand to Buck. Buck took it and, while there wasn’t much strength to it, allowed himself to be tugged until he was half out of his chair and half on top of Eddie.

Buck didn’t leave until visiting hours were over and a stern looking nurse forced him out.

White hot, incandescent rage filled Daniel’s veins. He slammed his drink down hard enough that, if he weren’t so pissed off, he’d be concerned about breaking the wood of the table or the glass of the bottle. As it was, if that had happened, he’d probably just find a bit of caustic joy in the damage.

“Eddie was shot by a fucking cop?” he snarled, and then immediately followed it with, “Of course it was a fucking cop.”

“And Cap’s wife shot him,” Austin said. He was sitting across from the table from Daniel, utterly unperturbed by the temper. “After he shot Cap. Celebrate that now, before your brother sees you.”

Daniel grinned and raised the bottle to Austin in a toast.

“He’ll be fine, though,” Austin said, and ignored Daniel’s groan of disappointment. “What’s the name of Buck’s doctor?”

“The name of- Why?”

“Just curious.”

“It’s Copeland,” Daniel said, and squinted at his not-boyfriend when he started nodding to himself. “Seriously, why?”

“That was the shooter’s name, too,” Austin said.

“Oh.” Daniel felt his face scrunch up. “That’s… Weird. I hope they’re not related.”

That would make Buck’s therapy appointments very awkward.

Buck wasn’t certain who was more excited when Eddie was finally discharged from the hospital, him or Chris. The kid was practically vibrating when Buck left the house to go pick Eddie up, more than he ever did on a sugar high. Not that Buck could blame him for it any; talking to him over the phone was not the same as seeing Eddie in person, he knew that.

When they got home, Buck opened the door to the small surprise party they’d set up for Eddie. Pepa and Isabel were both present and accounted for, as was Danny and Carla. There were balloons and a homemade banner that Chris helped make, and food that made Buck’s mouth water by scent alone.

Buck stood back for a bit, content to allow Eddie to be monopolized by blood relatives for a bit. Except for the brief visit by Pepa, they hadn’t been able to see him at the hospital like Buck and Danny had. So Buck watched from the sidelines as Chris snuggled into Eddie’s side and he was fretted over by his abuela.

“I think I’m gonna cover at the One Eighteen for a bit,” Buck told Danny. “Until Eddie’s cleared.”

His brother turned his head to give him a single questioning stare.

“Pretty sure you begged me to help you transfer because you couldn’t trust Nash anymore.”

“I didn’t beg,” Buck corrected. “And- And Bobby’s gonna be out for a while, too.”

“He’ll be getting back before Eddie does.”

“Yeah, but…” He shrugged. “How can I know if I can trust Bobby again if I don’t give him a chance? And… I miss hanging out with everyone there.”

His brother stared at him for a bit longer, gaze burning into Buck’s head. And then he let out a sigh.

“Fine,” Danny said, as if Buck had actually needed him to agree. “But you’re breaking the news to everyone, I’m not doing it for you.”

Buck made a face at him.

“You would if you actually love me,” he said, and laughed when Danny shoved at him. Lightly, of course.

Danny’s phone started ringing, and Buck saw his brow furrow when he pulled it out to check. He stepped away for a bit, answering it with a,

“What’s up, Josh?”

Buck couldn’t hear what Josh said, but he did see Danny suddenly straighten up.

“She what?” Danny’s words were sharp. “No, she- she hasn’t said anything to me… Not a word… Okay. Thanks.”

He took his phone from his ear and simply stared at it for a moment, frowning heavily.

“What?” Buck blurted out, when his curiosity finally overflowed. “What did Josh call you about?”

“Um.” Danny lifted his head and Buck saw concern in his eyes. “He said Maddie quit her job.”

 

Fin.
